_comment: The plants, fungi, animals and shellfish of Silverdale and central Kitsap County, Washington. Shape: schemas/locale.toml. This is the file that makes foraging, fishing and ecology teach something TRUE rather than generic, so every entry carries its status HERE: a plant that is a crop in one place is a noxious weed in another, and a fish that is legal to keep in one county is federally endangered in the next.
_how_this_was_made: Researched by six agents against federal and state sources, then every plant and fungus record was put to an adversarial verifier that tried to refute it. Forty-eight of sixty were refuted, almost all on the toxicity and lookalike fields, and the corrections were merged record by record. The animal records went through a combined correct-and-verify pass. What that process is for: the first draft said Douglas squirrel had no known status when WAC 220-200-100 protects it by name, said red rock crab needed no catch card when it does, and left black bear with no mention of Trichinella, which the CDC lists bear first among.
_lookalikes_are_the_safety_feature: An empty lookalike list on something you might eat is the defect that hurts people, and it was the single most common finding. Every edible or toxic record now carries one. A lookalike `id` points at another record here; `null` means the species is named but not yet in this dataset, which is a gap to fill rather than a reason to drop the warning.
licence: Public domain. Compiled from US federal sources (USDA PLANTS, the Forest Service Fire Effects Information System, ITIS, FWS, NOAA Fisheries, CDC) and from Washington State agencies (WDFW, the Department of Health, the Noxious Weed Control Board, the RCW and WAC). State works are not covered by 17 U.S.C. 105, so their facts are restated here in our own words with the agency cited, never copied. Nothing came from GBIF, iNaturalist, Wikipedia or OpenStreetMap.

species.protected: Game animal, so it may be taken only under licence in an open season. WDFW: "Mule deer, black-tailed deer, and white-tailed deer are classified as game animals" and "A hunting license and open season are required to hunt them." Separately, a property owner, immediate family, employee or tenant may kill a deer damaging crops on that property only after obtaining a WDFW permit, and WDFW must be notified immediately after the animal is taken.
species.edible_detail: Legal to eat only if you took it lawfully: a valid Washington hunting licence with a deer tag, inside the open season and the game management unit you are hunting, within the bag limit. Seasons, unit boundaries and any special permit requirements are reset every year in the WDFW Big Game Hunting Seasons and Rules pamphlet, so read the current year's pamphlet rather than relying on last year's dates. Washington confirmed chronic wasting disease in the state in 2024, so also check WDFW's current testing rules for the area you hunt before you eat the meat.
species.toxic: Chronic wasting disease is a prion disease of deer and elk that concentrates in brain, spinal cord and lymph tissue. WDFW confirmed its presence in Washington in 2024. It is not a poison and there is no safe cooking temperature for prions, so the handling rule is to have the animal tested where WDFW requires it and not to eat meat from an animal that tests positive.

lookalikes.name: Columbian white-tailed deer
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Look at the tail. A black-tailed deer has a fairly broad tail that is dark brown or black across the top. A white-tailed deer raises a wide, entirely white tail like a flag when it runs. The Columbian white-tailed deer is a federally listed subspecies and shooting one is a serious offence, but it lives along the lower Columbia River, not on the Kitsap Peninsula, so the confusion matters mainly if you hunt in southwest Washington.

lookalikes.name: Rocky Mountain mule deer
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Mule deer have noticeably larger ears and a narrow white rope-like tail with a black tip. They live east of the Cascade crest, so a deer in Silverdale is a black-tailed deer. Both are game animals, so mixing them up is a tagging and reporting problem rather than a protected-species problem.

lookalikes.name: Roosevelt elk
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: An elk is far larger, with a pale rump patch and a dark neck mane. It needs its own tag and its own season, so a deer tag does not cover it.

species.season: Present and active all year. The rut is in November and December, when bucks move most and vehicle collisions peak. Hunting seasons are set annually and published in the WDFW Big Game Hunting Seasons and Rules pamphlet; the dates and the game management unit covering Kitsap County must be read from the current pamphlet, because they change every year.
species.habitat: WDFW describes the subspecies as occurring "from the crest of the Cascades west to the ocean, preferring brushy, logged lands and coniferous forests." Around Silverdale that means second-growth Douglas fir stands, clearcut edges and the brushy greenbelts along Clear Creek and Chico Creek. Deer also browse suburban gardens throughout central Kitsap, which is where most residents actually see them.
species.uses: Food, when taken lawfully. Hide and sinew are usable materials. Be aware that a state hunting season does not by itself make a given place legal to shoot in: county and city ordinances on discharging firearms apply independently across developed parts of Kitsap County, so check the local ordinance for the specific parcel before hunting. The place you see deer and the place you may lawfully take one are often not the same.

species.protected: Both a game animal and a furbearer under WAC 220-400-020. WDFW: "The raccoon is classified as both a furbearer and a game animal. A hunting or trapping license is required to hunt or trap raccoons during an open season." Body-gripping traps are prohibited in Washington: "It is unlawful to use a steel-jawed leghold trap, neck snare, or other body-gripping trap to capture any mammal."
species.edible_detail: Raccoon is eaten, but only lawfully with a hunting or trapping licence during an open season. Cook it thoroughly all the way through. Wild carnivores and omnivores are a recognised source of Trichinella, and CDC warns that "Freezing wild game meats, unlike freezing pork products, may not effectively kill all worms because some worm species that infect wild game animals are freeze-resistant," so freezing is not a substitute for cooking.
species.toxic: The hazard is the droppings, not the meat. Raccoon droppings carry the eggs of the roundworm Baylisascaris procyonis. WDFW: "Raccoon droppings may carry a parasite that can be fatal to humans. Do not handle or smell raccoon droppings and wash your hands if you touch any." People are infected by swallowing the eggs, usually after getting contaminated soil or waste in the mouth, and the larvae can invade the eyes, organs or brain, causing blindness or coma. CDC notes eggs "take 2 to 4 weeks to become infectious" in the environment, so a fresh latrine is safer than an old one, and that a latrine in a yard should be removed carefully and burned, buried or sent to a landfill. Raccoons also carry canine distemper, which is fatal to unvaccinated dogs but does not infect people.

lookalikes.name: none in this region
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No other animal in Kitsap County has the black facemask and the ringed tail together. A raccoon is not confusable with anything protected here.

species.season: Active all year, mostly at night, though a nursing female will forage in daylight. Least active during the coldest stretches of winter. Hunting and trapping seasons are set annually by WDFW.
species.habitat: WDFW: raccoons "prefer forest areas near a stream or water source, but have adapted to various environments throughout Washington." In central Kitsap they are along the Clear Creek and Chico Creek corridors, on the Dyes Inlet tideflats where they forage at low tide, and throughout Silverdale neighbourhoods in storm drains, crawl spaces, chimneys and under decks.
species.uses: Food and fur, when taken lawfully. Removing attractants, which means securing garbage, feeding pets indoors and not leaving pet food out, is the practical way to keep them out of a homestead.

species.protected: Not a game animal, but not unregulated either. WDFW: "Washington state does not classify coyotes as game animals, but a state license is required to hunt or trap them." There is a narrow property exemption: "The owner, the owner's immediate family, employee, or a tenant of real property may kill or trap a coyote on that property if it is damaging crops or domestic animals," and local ordinances may still restrict this. Trap type is restricted statewide: "It is unlawful to use a steel-jawed leghold trap, neck snare, or other body-gripping trap to capture any mammal."
species.edible_detail: Legally takeable with a state licence, or on your own property under the damage exemption above, but coyote is rarely eaten and is normally taken for fur or for livestock protection. If you do eat it, cook it through. CDC lists "fox" and "wolf" among the meat-eating animals whose meat carries Trichinella, and freezing wild game is not a reliable way to kill it.
species.toxic: No toxin. The meat of wild canids should be treated as a Trichinella risk and cooked thoroughly rather than frozen and eaten rare.

lookalikes.name: Gray wolf
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is the most expensive mistake on this list. The gray wolf is Endangered under Washington state law and is also federally listed as Endangered in the western two-thirds of the state, which includes Kitsap County. A wolf is much bigger, roughly 70 to 120 pounds against a coyote's 20 to 40, with a broad blocky muzzle, short rounded ears, long legs and a straight tail carried level. A coyote has a narrow pointed muzzle, tall pointed ears that look oversized for its head, and a bushy tail carried low. Wolves are not established on the Kitsap Peninsula, their population is in eastern Washington and the North Cascades, but a dispersing animal is possible and the penalty is severe, so identify before you shoot.

lookalikes.name: Domestic dog
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Loose dogs are common and a coyote seen at dusk is often somebody's dog. A coyote runs with its tail down; most dogs carry the tail level or up. Shooting a dog is a criminal and civil matter.

lookalikes.name: Red fox
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A fox is much smaller with black stockings and a white tail tip. Fox is a classified game animal and furbearer in Washington, so it has its own season.

species.season: Active all year, day or night, most vocal and most visible in late winter during the breeding season and again in late summer when the year's pups start moving.
species.habitat: WDFW: coyotes "occupy almost every conceivable habitat type, from open shrubsteppe to densely forested areas to urban areas." In central Kitsap they use greenbelts, powerline corridors, the edges of the Silverdale commercial area and residential neighbourhoods. They are the most likely wild predator a Silverdale resident will actually meet, and small unattended pets are the usual conflict.
species.uses: Fur. Livestock and poultry protection is the usual reason for taking one; secure roofed enclosures and removal of food attractants work better than shooting, because a removed coyote is quickly replaced.

species.protected: Furbearer. WDFW: "The river otter is classified as a furbearer" and "A trapping license and open season are required to trap river otters." Body-gripping traps are unlawful in Washington for any mammal.
species.edible_detail: Legally takeable only with a Washington trapping licence during an open furbearer season. River otter is taken for fur, essentially never for food, and the meat is strongly fishy. Treat the legal condition as the binding one: no trapping licence and open season means no take, full stop.

lookalikes.name: Sea otter
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The sea otter is listed as Threatened in Washington and may not be taken. A sea otter floats on its back, often with food on its chest, is much heavier, and rarely comes ashore. A river otter swims belly down with its back arching out of the water and travels overland between waters. Sea otters in Washington are confined to the outer coast, from south of Destruction Island north to Cape Flattery and east to Pillar Point, so a swimming otter on Dyes Inlet is a river otter, not a sea otter.

lookalikes.name: American mink
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A mink is much smaller, roughly cat-sized at most, darker and slimmer, with a bushy rather than tapered tail. Mink is also a classified furbearer, so both need a trapping licence, and the confusion is a pelt and reporting issue rather than a protected-species issue.

lookalikes.name: Harbor seal
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: At a distance on the water a seal head and an otter head look similar. A harbor seal has no visible tail and no visible ears, and it sinks straight down. A river otter shows a long thick tail when it dives and porpoises along the surface. Harbor seals are federally protected, so the mistake matters.

species.season: Active all year, and they do not hibernate. Most often seen at dawn and dusk. Trapping seasons are set annually by WDFW.
species.habitat: WDFW: "River otters are relatively common throughout Washington in ponds, lakes, rivers, sloughs, estuaries, bays, and in open waters along the coast." In central Kitsap they are regular along the Dyes Inlet shoreline, at the mouths of Clear Creek and Chico Creek, and around docks, floats and marinas, where they haul out and leave latrines.
species.uses: Fur, when taken lawfully. Otherwise a wildlife-viewing species. They will raid a poorly protected fish pond and will den under a dock or outbuilding.

species.protected: Protected, federally and by the state. NOAA: "Harbor seals, like all marine mammals, are protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act." Washington also classifies "mammals of the order Pinnipedia" as protected wildlife under WAC 220-200-100, a rule titled "Wildlife classified as protected shall not be hunted or fished." WDFW additionally identifies the harbor seal as a Priority Habitats and Species priority species. NOAA viewing guidance: "Observe all seals and sea lions from a safe distance of at least 50 yards and limit your time spent observing to 30 minutes or less."
species.edible_detail: It is illegal for the general public to take, kill, harass or harvest a harbor seal under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, and Washington separately classifies pinnipeds as protected wildlife that shall not be hunted. Harassment includes approaching close enough to change the animal's behaviour, so an unlawful act here does not require touching the seal. Certain Alaska Native subsistence rights under the MMPA do not apply in Puget Sound. Separately, CDC lists seal among the animals whose meat carries Trichinella.

lookalikes.name: California sea lion
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A sea lion has small external ear flaps and can rotate its hind flippers forward to walk on all fours. A harbor seal has no ear flaps, only a small hole, and humps along on its belly on land. Both are protected under the same federal law, so the identification matters for reporting and for keeping your distance, not for whether you may take one. You may not.

lookalikes.name: Steller sea lion
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Much larger and paler tan than a harbor seal, with the same ear flaps and walking gait as the California sea lion. Also federally protected.

lookalikes.name: River otter
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: An otter shows a long tapering tail and swims with its back out of the water. A seal shows a round head and no tail and sinks vertically. Mistaking a seal for an otter in the other direction is the dangerous version, because otters are lawfully trappable and seals are not.

species.season: Present on Dyes Inlet and central Puget Sound all year. NOAA says females "usually give birth during the spring and summer" and that "the pupping season varies by location," with Washington inland waters running roughly two months later than coastal populations. A pup resting alone on a beach has usually not been abandoned; its mother is feeding offshore and will return. Do not touch it, do not put it back in the water, keep dogs and people well back, and call the NOAA Marine Mammal Stranding Network. NOAA notes that disturbance of haul-out areas, particularly nursing mothers and pups, stresses the animals and degrades the habitat.
species.habitat: Marine shorelines, bays and estuaries. On Dyes Inlet they are seen swimming and hauled out on beaches, log booms, floats and navigation markers, and they follow salmon runs to creek mouths. The most commonly seen marine mammal in central Kitsap waters.
species.uses: Wildlife viewing at a lawful distance, which is at least 50 yards. No lawful harvest.

species.protected: Game animal. WDFW: "Black bears are classified as game animals and an open season and a hunting license are required to hunt them," and a hunter must "purchase a big-game license that includes bear."
species.edible_detail: Two conditions, and both are binding. Legally: a Washington big game licence that includes bear, an open season, and the bag limit. For safety: bear meat must be cooked all the way through. CDC names bear first among the sources of Trichinella, saying meat contaminated with the larvae "comes from meat-eating animals such as bear, wild boar, or walrus," and warns that "Freezing wild game meats, unlike freezing pork products, may not effectively kill all worms because some worm species that infect wild game animals are freeze-resistant." Never eat bear rare, and do not rely on a freezer to make it safe.
species.toxic: The muscle meat can carry Trichinella larvae, which cause trichinellosis in people who eat it undercooked. The exposure is eating the meat, not touching the animal. Thorough cooking destroys the larvae; freezing wild game does not reliably do so.

lookalikes.name: Grizzly bear
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A grizzly is federally Threatened and Endangered in Washington, so shooting one is a serious federal and state offence, and it is also the more dangerous animal to be wrong about at close range. A grizzly has a pronounced hump of muscle over the shoulders, a dished or scooped face profile, and long pale front claws. A black bear has no shoulder hump, a straight face profile from forehead to nose, and short dark curved claws. Do not use colour to decide: black bears are frequently brown, cinnamon or blond. Grizzlies do not currently occur on the Kitsap Peninsula or anywhere in the Puget Sound lowlands; WDFW places them in the Selkirk Mountains of northeastern Washington and notes they "have not been confirmed in the Washington North Cascades since 1996."

lookalikes.name: none in this region for practical purposes
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: On the Kitsap Peninsula a large bear is a black bear. The grizzly entry above matters if you hunt in northeastern Washington, not here.

species.season: Active from roughly March through November in western Washington. They den through the coldest months rather than truly hibernating, and a mild winter can keep them up. Most conflict happens in late summer and autumn when they are feeding hard before denning. Hunting seasons are set annually by WDFW.
species.habitat: WDFW: "Black bears live in a diverse array of forested habitats in the state, from coastal rainforests to the dry woodlands of the Cascades' eastern slopes," and they are common "throughout Washington except the interior of the arid Columbia Basin." On the Kitsap Peninsula they are present but uncommon and mostly move through larger forest blocks and stream corridors rather than settling near Silverdale itself. Sightings in town are usually a young bear passing through.
species.uses: Food when taken lawfully and cooked through, plus hide and rendered fat. The far more useful everyday knowledge is attractant removal: WDFW advises "Keep garbage cans with tight-fitting lids in a shed, garage, or fenced area," removing bird feeders including hummingbird feeders, and keeping fruit trees picked. A bear that finds food at a homestead comes back.

species.protected: Classified as both a game animal and a furbearer under WAC 220-400-020, and handled as small game by WDFW. Licences and open seasons apply to both hunting and trapping. There is also a mandatory reporting rule: WDFW states that "Effective Sept. 1, 2024, Washington small game hunters and trappers are now required to submit the lower jaw of any bobcat they harvest."
species.edible_detail: Legal only with the appropriate Washington small game hunting or trapping licence in an open season, and since 1 September 2024 you must submit the lower jaw of any bobcat you harvest. Bobcat is taken mainly for fur. If eaten, cook it thoroughly: CDC names "wildcat" among the meat-eating animals whose meat carries Trichinella, and freezing wild game is not a reliable kill.
species.toxic: Meat of wild cats can carry Trichinella larvae, which cause trichinellosis if the meat is eaten undercooked. Cook thoroughly rather than relying on freezing.

lookalikes.name: Canada lynx
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The Canada lynx is federally Threatened and state Endangered, so taking one is a serious offence. A lynx has very long black ear tufts, a short tail that is black all the way around the tip, oversized furry feet and long grey legs. A bobcat has short tufts and a tail that is black on the top of the tip only, with white underneath, and it is more reddish brown with clear spotting. The distinction is mostly academic in Kitsap County: WDFW puts Washington's fewer than about 100 lynx in the North Cascades, the Kettle River range and the Selkirks, largely in western Okanogan County, not in the Puget Sound lowlands.

lookalikes.name: Cougar
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A cougar is far larger and has a very long heavy tail, roughly a third of its body length. A bobcat's tail is a stub. Cougar is separately classified as a game animal with its own licence and season requirements, so a bobcat tag does not cover one.

lookalikes.name: Domestic cat
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A large housecat seen at dusk is the most common false bobcat report. A bobcat is roughly twice the size, with long legs, a stubby tail, tufted ears and black bars on the inside of the forelegs.

species.season: Active all year, mostly at dawn, dusk and night. Hunting and trapping seasons are set annually; check the current WDFW small game and furbearer rules.
species.habitat: WDFW: "Found throughout all of Washington, bobcats are probably more common than most people realize," and western Washington animals "tend to be" darker than the buff-coloured eastern ones. For shelter and denning WDFW says "Rock cliffs, outcroppings, and ledges are important to bobcats for shelter, raising young, and resting sites. Large brush or log piles and hollow trees or logs are used in wooded areas." Central Kitsap has little rock, so local bobcats use brush piles, hollow logs, blowdown and dense second-growth thickets along the creek corridors. Present but seldom seen.
species.uses: Fur, when taken lawfully. Otherwise a natural control on rabbits, rodents and, occasionally, unsecured poultry.

species.protected: Furbearer. WDFW: "The beaver is classified as a furbearer (WAC 220-400-020)" and "A trapping license and open season are required to trap and harvest a beaver." Body-gripping traps are unlawful in Washington for any mammal. Beaver dams also sit inside water and fish-habitat rules, so removing a dam is usually not something a landowner may simply do; check with WDFW first.
species.edible_detail: Legal only with a Washington trapping licence during an open season. Beaver is genuinely good eating and the tail is rendered for fat, but the licence and season are the gate. Cook thoroughly, as with any wild meat.

lookalikes.name: Nutria
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Look at the tail, which is the only reliable character in the water. A beaver has a wide flat paddle-shaped tail. A nutria has a round rat-like tail. Nutria is an introduced species in Washington and is also visibly smaller with a white muzzle and prominent orange front teeth.

lookalikes.name: Muskrat
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A muskrat is much smaller, roughly the size of a small cat, and its tail is thin and flattened side to side rather than top to bottom. Muskrat is also a classified furbearer with its own season, so mixing them up is a licensing problem.

lookalikes.name: River otter
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: An otter is slim and fast with a long tapering tail and a low profile. A beaver is bulky and slow and slaps its flat tail on the water when alarmed. Both are furbearers requiring a trapping licence.

species.season: Active all year and does not hibernate, though it stays close to the lodge in the coldest weather. Mostly nocturnal and crepuscular. Trapping seasons are set annually by WDFW.
species.habitat: WDFW: beavers are "found where their preferred foods are in good supply, along rivers, and in small streams, lakes, marshes, and even roadside ditches containing adequate year-round water flow." In central Kitsap that means the Clear Creek and Chico Creek systems draining into Dyes Inlet, plus wetland ponds and ditches. Beaver ponds on these creeks are significant rearing habitat for juvenile salmon, which is part of why dam removal is regulated.
species.uses: Food and fur when taken lawfully, and castoreum has a long history of use. Ecologically the animal is a water-management tool: its ponds store water, recharge summer flow and rear young salmon. WDFW was historically concerned with their reestablishment after they were "eliminated from much of their range in the late 1800s because of unregulated trapping."

species.protected: PROTECTED. The Douglas squirrel is named explicitly in the protected wildlife list of WAC 220-200-100, a rule whose title is "Wildlife classified as protected shall not be hunted or fished." It does not appear anywhere in the game animal or furbearer lists of WAC 220-400-020, so there is no season and no licence that authorises taking one. The earlier draft of this record said only that it was not a game animal and left its status unverified; that understated the protection. It may not be hunted or trapped.
species.edible_detail: Not because of any biological hazard but because it is protected wildlife in Washington and may not be hunted or fished. There is no open season and no licence that permits taking one. The same rule covers the red squirrel, the northern flying squirrel, Humboldt's flying squirrel and several ground squirrels.

lookalikes.name: Eastern gray squirrel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This pair matters because one is protected and the other is not. The Douglas squirrel is small, about 10 to 14 inches including the tail, reddish or brownish grey on top with an orange to yellowish belly, and it is noisy and territorial in conifers. The eastern gray squirrel is much larger, up to about 20 inches, grey overall with a broad plume of a tail, and it lives in yards and parks. If you take a Douglas squirrel believing it was an eastern gray, you have taken protected wildlife.

lookalikes.name: Red squirrel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A red squirrel is brighter rust-red with a white belly, where the Douglas squirrel has an orange belly. Both are protected wildlife under the same rule, so there is no legal consequence to confusing them. Red squirrels occur in northeastern Washington, not on the Kitsap Peninsula.

lookalikes.name: Northern flying squirrel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Flying squirrels are nocturnal, have a loose fold of skin between wrist and ankle and a flattened tail, and have very large dark eyes. Also protected wildlife.

species.season: Active all year, in daylight, and does not hibernate. Most conspicuous in late summer and autumn when it is cutting and caching Douglas fir cones, which it does noisily and drops from height.
species.habitat: WDFW: "The Douglas squirrel is found in stands of fir, pine, cedar, and other conifers in the Cascade Mountains and western parts of Washington." In central Kitsap it is in essentially every mature conifer stand, including Douglas fir and western redcedar in Silverdale greenbelts, parks and wooded yards. It is the small loud reddish squirrel scolding you from a fir.
species.uses: None lawful, since it is protected. It is a significant disperser of conifer seed and a reliable indicator of a functioning conifer stand. Its discarded cone scale middens are worth recognising as a field sign.

species.protected: Not protected and not classified. The eastern gray squirrel is absent from the protected wildlife list in WAC 220-200-100 and absent from the game animal and furbearer lists in WAC 220-400-020, which name no squirrels at all. That leaves it unclassified wildlife. WDFW's published statement of what unclassified means, given for the opossum, is that the animal "is unclassified and may be trapped or killed year-round; no permit is necessary," although a special trapping permit is required for any trap other than a live trap, and releasing a trapped animal elsewhere in the state is unlawful without a permit. Confirm the current rule with WDFW before taking one, and check the county or city ordinance on discharging firearms for the specific place, because those apply independently of state wildlife law.
species.edible_detail: Squirrel is ordinary food in much of North America and there is no biological reason not to eat this one. The condition is legal and identification-based rather than toxicological. It is an unclassified non-native, so state law does not set a season for it, but you must be certain of the identification first, because the two squirrels it can be confused with are both protected in Washington and one is state Endangered. Cook it through. Confirm current WDFW rules and local firearm ordinances before taking one.

lookalikes.name: Western gray squirrel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The native western gray squirrel was "uplisted to state endangered in 2023" after being listed as threatened since 1993, so taking one is a serious offence. It is larger and cleaner looking, steel grey above with a pure white belly and a very long bushy tail edged in white. The eastern gray usually shows brownish or tawny wash on the flanks and face and a greyish buff belly. The two are hard enough to separate that the safe rule is to know where you are: WDFW places the remaining western grays in three isolated populations, in Klickitat and southern Yakima counties, in Okanogan and Chelan counties, and on Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Pierce and Thurston counties. None of these is on the Kitsap Peninsula, so a grey squirrel in Silverdale is an eastern gray, but do not carry that assumption to south Puget Sound.

lookalikes.name: Douglas squirrel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The Douglas squirrel is protected wildlife under WAC 220-200-100 and may not be taken. It is much smaller, roughly 10 to 14 inches including the tail, reddish brown with an orange or yellowish belly, and it lives in conifers rather than yards. The eastern gray is up to about 20 inches and grey.

lookalikes.name: Fox squirrel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also introduced. Larger than the eastern gray and distinctly rusty orange underneath. Uncommon in western Washington.

species.season: Active all year, in daylight, and does not hibernate. Most visible in autumn when caching nuts and acorns.
species.habitat: Urban and suburban parks, campuses, gardens and residential neighbourhoods, and the deciduous edges between them. WDFW notes it "was introduced in Washington in the early 1900s" and that "Since then they have been repeatedly released in parks, campuses, estates, and residential areas." In Silverdale it is the squirrel you see on lawns, fences and power lines, and it is now the common tree squirrel of the developed parts of central Kitsap.
species.uses: Food, subject to the conditions above. Otherwise a nuisance: it raids bird feeders, strips bark, and gets into attics and soffits. It also competes with the native western gray squirrel, which is part of why that species is in trouble.

species.protected: Unclassified, and the least protected animal in this set. WDFW: "The opossum is unclassified and may be trapped or killed year-round; no permit is necessary." Two limits still apply. A special trapping permit is required for any trap other than a live trap, and WDFW states "It is unlawful to release an opossum anywhere within the state, other than on the property where it was legally trapped, without a permit." Local ordinances on discharging firearms still apply in developed parts of Kitsap County.
species.edible_detail: Opossum is traditional food in parts of the United States and there is no season or permit barrier in Washington, since the animal is unclassified and may be taken year round. The conditions are practical rather than legal: handle the carcass with gloves and cook the meat thoroughly all the way through. WDFW advises that "Anyone handling a dead or live opossum should wear rubber gloves, and wash his or her hands well when finished."
species.toxic: No toxin in the animal. The handling hazards are parasites and bacteria on the carcass, which is why WDFW calls for rubber gloves and thorough handwashing. Opossums carry the parasite that causes Equine Protozoal Myeloencephalitis: WDFW states "There is convincing evidence that the parasite that causes Equine Protozoal Myeloencephalitis (EPM), a disease in horses, is carried by the opossum." That is a danger to horses, not to people, and it matters if you keep horses, because opossum droppings in a feed room or hay store can infect them. Rabies is not a concern here: WDFW says "The rabies virus does not exist in Washington opossum populations, and for some unknown reason opossums rarely get rabies elsewhere."

lookalikes.name: none in this region
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The Virginia opossum is the only marsupial in Washington and nothing else here resembles it. Look for the naked scaly prehensile tail, the pointed white face and the fifty teeth. It cannot be confused with a protected species.

species.season: Active all year, almost entirely at night. Does not hibernate, and exposed ears and tail often show frostbite damage after a hard winter.
species.habitat: WDFW says opossums "first arrived in Washington in the early 1900s as pets and novelties" and now occupy "most human-occupied habitats in western Washington." In central Kitsap that means Silverdale neighbourhoods, stream corridors, wetland edges, outbuildings, woodpiles and crawl spaces. Very common and very rarely seen, because it is strictly nocturnal.
species.uses: Food, with the handling precautions above. It eats large numbers of insects, slugs, rodents and carrion, which makes it a useful neighbour on a homestead as long as it is kept out of the poultry run and away from horse feed.

species.protected: PROTECTED. Washington state status is Candidate. Federally protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act as a marine mammal. Washington separately classifies "mammals of the order Cetacea" as protected wildlife under WAC 220-200-100, the rule titled "Wildlife classified as protected shall not be hunted or fished." Not ESA listed.
species.edible_detail: It is illegal to take, kill or harass a harbor porpoise. The Marine Mammal Protection Act applies to all marine mammals, and Washington independently classifies cetaceans as protected wildlife that shall not be hunted or fished. There is no licence or season that changes this.

lookalikes.name: Dall's porpoise
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A Dall's porpoise is boldly marked black and white like a small orca, with a white-frosted dorsal fin, and it throws a distinctive rooster tail of spray when it surfaces at speed. A harbor porpoise is small, plain dark grey, has a low triangular fin, and surfaces slowly and quietly with almost no splash. Both are protected under the same federal law.

lookalikes.name: Pacific white-sided dolphin
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Larger, with a tall strongly hooked dorsal fin and pale flank stripes, and it bow-rides boats. Harbor porpoises avoid boats. Also federally protected.

lookalikes.name: Harbor seal
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A seal shows a round head with a face and no dorsal fin. A porpoise shows a rolling back and a small triangular fin and never lifts its head to look at you. Both are federally protected, so the distinction is for reporting, not for legality.

species.season: Present in Washington inland marine waters all year. WDFW records that harbor porpoises "were a common year-round resident in the Puget Sound in the 1940s," disappeared from the Sound by the 1970s, and made "a comeback to Puget Sound" in the early 2000s, which is why older residents will tell you they never used to be here.
species.habitat: WDFW: they inhabit "coastal waters, including bays and estuaries," and occur in the Strait of Juan de Fuca, Puget Sound, the San Juan Islands and the eastern Strait of Georgia. In central Kitsap they are most likely in the deeper moving water of Port Orchard Narrows, Agate Pass and Rich Passage rather than inside the shallow enclosed basin of Dyes Inlet, though they do enter it. Look for a small dark back rolling once and vanishing.
species.uses: Wildlife viewing only, at a distance that does not change the animal's behaviour. No lawful harvest.

species.form: large toothed whale, the largest member of the dolphin family
species.protected: PROTECTED, and more strictly than anything else in this dataset. The Southern Resident population was "listed as endangered under the ESA" in 2005 and WDFW gives its Washington state status as Endangered. All killer whales are also protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, and Washington classifies "mammals of the order Cetacea" as protected wildlife under WAC 220-200-100. Two separate approach limits apply and you must obey the stricter one: NOAA states that federal regulations prohibit approaching within 200 yards of a Southern Resident killer whale or positioning a vessel in its path within 400 yards, and that "Washington State prohibits the approach of Southern Resident killer whales within 1,000 yards." WDFW confirms that "As of Jan. 1, 2025, boaters are required to stay 1,000 yards away from Southern Resident killer whales in Washington waters." The state rule applies to all vessel operators including kayaks and paddleboards.
species.edible_detail: Taking, killing or harassing a killer whale is prohibited under the federal Endangered Species Act for the Southern Resident population, under the Marine Mammal Protection Act for all killer whales, and under Washington's protected wildlife rule. Harassment includes approaching closer than the distances above, so a violation does not require touching the animal or intending harm.

lookalikes.name: Bigg's (transient) killer whale
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is the important one, and the honest answer is that you cannot reliably tell them apart from a boat. Bigg's killer whales are the same species but a different, mammal-eating population that is not ESA listed, and they are now the killer whales most often seen in central Puget Sound. Separating them takes photo identification of saddle patches and dorsal fin notches against a catalogue, which is not something you do in the moment. Treat every killer whale you encounter in Washington waters as a Southern Resident and give it 1,000 yards. Getting this wrong in the permissive direction is a federal and state offence.

lookalikes.name: Dall's porpoise
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: At a distance the black and white pattern of a Dall's porpoise reads as a tiny orca and is regularly reported as a baby killer whale. A Dall's porpoise is about 6 feet long with a small frosted fin. Even the smallest killer whale calf swims beside an adult, so a lone small black and white animal is a porpoise.

species.season: Present in Washington inland waters mainly in spring, summer and autumn. NOAA: "During the spring, summer, and fall, the range of Southern Resident killer whales includes the inland waterways of Washington State and the transboundary waters between the United States and Canada."
species.habitat: Salish Sea inland waters and the outer coast. Killer whales are rare but documented visitors to Dyes Inlet and are not a routine sight there; the regular viewing water is the main basin of Puget Sound, Admiralty Inlet and the San Juans. Their local ecology is tied directly to salmon: WDFW says the Southern Resident population "feeds primarily on Chinook salmon, chum salmon to a lesser extent, and occasionally other fish," and NOAA notes that "some populations of their preferred prey, Chinook salmon, are also threatened or endangered," which makes prey availability a limit on recovery.
species.uses: Wildlife viewing from shore, which is unrestricted and is the only way most people will ever see them lawfully at close range. No lawful take of any kind.

species.protected: PROTECTED. Federally protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, which prohibits the "take (including killing, capturing, selling, trading, and transport) of protected migratory bird species without prior authorization" from the US Fish and Wildlife Service. Protected in Washington under WAC 220-200-100, whose protected wildlife list includes "All birds not classified as game birds, predatory birds or endangered species, or designated as threatened species or sensitive species"; the heron is none of those, since Washington's predatory birds are only the black-billed magpie, American crow, European starling, house sparrow, rock dove and Eurasian collared dove. WDFW additionally identifies it under its Priority Habitats and Species programme "either as a priority species throughout its Washington range or within specific habitat areas of highly concentrated use or ecological significance."
species.edible_detail: Taking a great blue heron is a federal offence under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act and a state offence under Washington's protected wildlife rule. There is no season, no licence and no bag limit, because there is no lawful take. This is the general position for native birds in Washington: almost every one of them is protected, and the small handful of exceptions are game birds and the six named predatory birds.

lookalikes.name: Sandhill crane
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Watch the neck in flight. A heron folds its neck back into a tight S against its shoulders. A crane flies with its neck stretched straight out in front. Cranes are also protected, and Washington's population is of particular conservation concern, so the confusion has no safe direction.

lookalikes.name: Great egret
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: An egret is entirely white with a yellow bill; the heron is blue grey with a mostly yellow bill and a black head plume. Both are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.

lookalikes.name: Bald eagle
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Only confusable as a large dark shape perched in a shoreline tree. A heron has a long dagger bill and long trailing legs; an eagle has a hooked bill, a heavy body and no trailing legs. The eagle carries three federal laws behind it, so the mistake is expensive.

species.season: Year-round resident on Dyes Inlet and the central Kitsap shoreline. Birds gather at nesting colonies in late winter, roughly February onward, and colonies are in use through the spring and early summer. Disturbing an active colony can cause a whole colony to abandon, so keep well back from one.
species.habitat: Marshes, tideflats, estuaries and shallow water, where it stands motionless and stalks fish. On Dyes Inlet it works the low-tide flats and the mouths of Clear Creek and Chico Creek, and it also hunts voles in wet fields well away from water. It nests colonially in large trees, often well inland of the water it feeds on.
species.uses: Wildlife viewing. No lawful take. It is a useful indicator that a shoreline still supports forage fish.

species.protected: PROTECTED under three separate federal laws. WDFW states bald eagles are "protected under 3 federal laws: the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act, the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, and the Lacey Act." Washington removed the bald eagle from its state endangered species list in 2016, but WDFW is explicit that this "did not remove protections intended to sustain the population," and the species is now classified as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need under the State Wildlife Action Plan. It also remains protected wildlife under WAC 220-200-100 as a bird that is not a game bird or one of the six predatory birds. Possession of eagle feathers or parts is itself regulated under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act, which is a point people get wrong: picking up a moulted feather is not lawful for most people.
species.edible_detail: There is no lawful take of bald eagles outside narrow federally issued permits, principally for Native American religious use. The Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act prohibits taking, possessing, selling or transporting eagles, their parts, nests or eggs, and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act and Lacey Act apply on top of it. Do not collect feathers or remains.

lookalikes.name: Golden eagle
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Immature bald eagles are mottled brown and white for their first four or five years and are constantly reported as golden eagles. A golden eagle has a golden wash on the back of the head and neck and feathered legs all the way to the toes; a bald eagle has bare yellow lower legs and a much heavier bill. Both are covered by the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act, so there is no safe direction to be wrong in. Golden eagles are uncommon west of the Cascades.

lookalikes.name: Osprey
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: An osprey is white underneath with a dark stripe through the eye and flies with a sharp kink in the wing that makes an M shape. An adult bald eagle is dark bodied with a clean white head and tail and flies on flat, plank-straight wings. Both are protected, the eagle more heavily.

lookalikes.name: Turkey vulture
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A vulture holds its wings in a shallow V and teeters constantly; an eagle soars flat and steady. The vulture has a small bare red head. Also protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.

species.season: Year-round resident in central Kitsap. Numbers rise in autumn and winter when birds concentrate on salmon runs and on the carcasses afterward. Nesting starts early, with birds at the nest from roughly January or February, and young fledging in mid summer.
species.habitat: WDFW: bald eagles use "areas close to coastal areas, bays, rivers, lakes, reservoirs, or other bodies of water" and nest "in large trees, usually near marine shorelines, large lakes, or rivers," reusing the same nest year after year. The majority of Washington's population is west of the Cascades. On Dyes Inlet they perch in shoreline conifers, and nests are in large Douglas firs and cottonwoods near the water. Common and easily seen in Silverdale.
species.uses: Wildlife viewing. No lawful take or possession, feathers included.

species.protected: PROTECTED. Federally protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, which prohibits take of protected migratory birds without prior authorisation from the US Fish and Wildlife Service. Protected in Washington under WAC 220-200-100, whose list includes "All birds not classified as game birds, predatory birds or endangered species, or designated as threatened species or sensitive species." The osprey is not a game bird and is not one of the six birds Washington classifies as predatory, so it falls squarely inside that protection. Note that the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act does not cover ospreys, despite the name "sea hawk"; the Migratory Bird Treaty Act is the operative law.
species.edible_detail: No lawful take. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act prohibits killing, capturing, selling, trading or transporting the bird without federal authorisation, and Washington protects it as non-game native wildlife. Nests are also protected while in use, which matters because ospreys nest on human structures and removing an active nest requires authorisation.

lookalikes.name: Bald eagle
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: An osprey is clean white on the belly and underwing coverts with a dark mask through the eye, and it flies with a distinct crook at the wrist so the wings make a shallow M. A bald eagle is dark bodied on flat straight wings, with a white head and tail once adult. Immature eagles are mottled and are the ones people confuse with ospreys. The eagle carries three federal laws, so this mistake is the costly one.

lookalikes.name: Red-tailed hawk
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A red-tailed hawk has a broad rusty tail and a dark belly band, soars in circles over fields, and does not dive feet-first into water. An osprey hovers over water and plunges. Red-tailed hawks are also protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.

lookalikes.name: Gull
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Only at a distance, since both are pale below over water. A gull has a slim straight bill and never hovers and plunges feet-first. Gulls are also protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.

species.season: A summer breeder here, not a year-round resident. Ospreys arrive in Puget Sound in spring, nest through the summer and leave for Central and South America in late summer and early autumn, so an osprey seen over Dyes Inlet in January is a misidentification. Nests are occupied roughly April through August.
species.habitat: Open water holding fish, with a tall exposed structure nearby to nest on. Around Dyes Inlet and central Kitsap they nest on pilings, snags, channel markers, light poles and purpose-built platforms, and hunt by hovering and plunging feet-first. They are almost exclusively fish eaters, which is why they are tied to the water and why they tolerate nesting close to people.
species.uses: Wildlife viewing. No lawful take. Their willingness to use artificial nest platforms makes them one of the easiest raptors to actively provide for on a waterfront property.

species.form: small diving seabird in the auk family
species.protected: PROTECTED, and the most heavily listed bird in this set. WDFW gives its federal ESA status as Threatened and its Washington state status as Endangered. It is also protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. Because it is listed under the Endangered Species Act, harm extends beyond shooting the bird: destroying or degrading occupied nesting habitat can itself be a take, which is why this species drives forest practice rules on old-growth and mature conifer stands in western Washington.
species.edible_detail: No lawful take under any circumstances. It is federally Threatened under the Endangered Species Act, state Endangered in Washington, and protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. The practical rule at sea is broader: do not shoot small diving seabirds at all, because the murrelet is hard to separate from several other alcids on the water and every one of them is protected anyway.

lookalikes.name: Common murre
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A common murre is much larger with a long pointed bill and, in winter, a dark line running back across the white cheek. A winter marbled murrelet is small and stubby with a short bill and shows a white shoulder stripe, the scapular stripe, that a murre does not have. Both are protected; the murrelet is ESA listed, so the mistake is far worse in that direction.

lookalikes.name: Ancient murrelet
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: An ancient murrelet has a clean black cap sharply cut off against a grey back and a pale bill. A winter marbled murrelet is messier, black and white, with the white scapular stripe. Also protected.

lookalikes.name: Pigeon guillemot
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: In summer a pigeon guillemot is entirely black with a big white wing patch and bright red feet, quite unlike the mottled brown summer murrelet. In winter it is much paler and larger. Also protected, and the common alcid of central Kitsap shorelines.

lookalikes.name: Rhinoceros auklet
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Larger and uniformly dark grey brown with a heavy pale orange bill, carrying a small horn at the bill base in breeding season. Also protected.

species.season: Present in Washington marine waters through the year. It is unusual among seabirds in nesting inland in forest rather than on a cliff or island, and adults commute between the nest tree and the sea at dawn and dusk during the breeding season. Because nesting is cryptic and occurs in mature forest, assume any mature or old-growth conifer stand within flight range of salt water is potential nesting habitat during the breeding season.
species.habitat: Two habitats, far apart, which is what makes this bird unusual. WDFW says it nests in "mature and old-growth conifer forests, and sometimes in comparatively younger forests with residual old-growth trees," placing the egg in moss or lichen on a large branch rather than building a nest. It feeds at sea, where "Marine foraging areas are usually within 1.2 to 3 miles of shore, typically in waters less than 100 feet deep," taking small schooling fish such as Pacific herring, anchovy, candlefish and sand lance. In central Kitsap you are far more likely to see one on the deeper open water of Hood Canal or the main Puget Sound basin than inside Dyes Inlet, which is shallow, enclosed and poor foraging water. Kitsap County also has very little of the mature and old-growth forest the species needs for nesting, so treat it as a bird of the surrounding marine waters rather than a Silverdale resident.
species.uses: Wildlife viewing only, and it is a difficult bird to see well. No lawful take. Its listing status is the single largest legal constraint on logging mature conifer forest in western Washington, which makes it worth understanding for anyone managing forested land.

species.protected: Protected. Washington classifies it as protected wildlife under WAC 220-200-100, titled "Wildlife classified as protected shall not be hunted or fished," whose catch-all category is "All birds not classified as game birds, predatory birds or endangered species, or designated as threatened species or sensitive species." It is also protected federally by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, which the US Fish and Wildlife Service says "applies only to migratory bird species that are native to the United States or U.S. territories." It is not on Washington's 2024 state endangered, threatened, sensitive or candidate lists, which is a separate question from whether it may be killed: it may not.
species.edible_detail: There is no legal way to take this bird. It is not a game bird, so no season, licence or bag limit exists for it, and killing, capturing or possessing one breaks both the state protected-wildlife rule and the federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act. Watch it and leave it alone.

lookalikes.name: American robin
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Same size and shape with an orange breast, so people mix them up at a distance. The varied thrush has a solid dark band across its orange breast and two orange bars on each wing; the robin has neither. Both are protected birds and neither may be taken, so mistaking them costs you nothing but a note in your log.

species.season: In the Silverdale lowlands mainly October through April. It breeds upslope in wetter, denser forest and moves down into town in winter, becoming most obvious during cold snaps and snow when it feeds on the ground under shrubs.
species.habitat: Dense, wet conifer forest of Douglas fir, western hemlock and western red cedar with a thick understory. Audubon describes it as "most common in dense, wet forest near the coast, in areas of fir, hemlock, and spruce with dense understory," and in winter in "undergrowth of other woods, especially near streams." Around Silverdale that means the forested ravines above Chico and Clear Creek in the breeding season, and lowland second growth, greenbelts, park edges and suburban yards in winter. WDFW's own page for this species is a photo profile with no habitat text.

species.protected: Protected. It falls in the catch-all protected category of WAC 220-200-100, "All birds not classified as game birds, predatory birds or endangered species, or designated as threatened species or sensitive species," and it is covered by the federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act as a native species. Jays have no hunting season in Washington. Not on the 2024 state listed or candidate lists.
species.edible_detail: No season, no licence and no bag limit exist for jays in Washington, which means there is no lawful way to take one. Being a loud nuisance at a feeder or a campsite is not a legal exception. If a jay is raiding stored food, the answer is a better container.

lookalikes.name: California scrub-jay
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The scrub-jay has been spreading through the Puget lowlands and is blue and pale grey with no crest and a white eyebrow. Steller's jay has a tall dark crest and a sooty black head and chest. Both are protected.

lookalikes.name: Blue jay
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A rare stray this far west. Blue jay has a white face and a white chest with a black necklace; Steller's jay is black from the crest down through the chest. Both are protected.

species.season: Year round resident, present every month.
species.habitat: Conifer and mixed forest and its edges, and any wooded neighbourhood. Audubon describes it as "most numerous as a breeder in the mountains and along the northern coast in forests of pine, spruce, and fir," ranging outside the breeding season "into other woodland types, orchards, and well-wooded suburbs." That last phrase is most of residential Silverdale. It is the bird that finds your unattended food first. WDFW's own page for this species is a photo profile with no habitat text.

species.protected: Protected. Covered by the catch-all protected category of WAC 220-200-100 and by the federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act as a native species. No season exists. Not on the 2024 state listed or candidate lists.
species.edible_detail: No season, licence or bag limit exists, so there is no lawful way to take one. Anglers sometimes resent it for eating fish; that is not a legal exception and killing one is a federal offence.

lookalikes.name: none in this region
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Nothing else on Dyes Inlet looks or sounds like it. A stocky blue-grey bird with a shaggy crest and an oversized dagger bill, hovering over water and giving a long dry rattle as it flies. Females have a rust band across the belly in addition to the blue one, which is unusual: the female is the brighter bird.

species.season: Year round wherever the water stays open, which on Dyes Inlet is all year. Audubon notes they are "mostly partial migrants in the United States where open water and food is available during winter months."
species.habitat: Needs two things together: fishable water with a perch over it, and a bare earth bank to nest in. Audubon gives the habitat as "streams, rivers, lakes, ponds, bays, or coasts in areas with perches and visible prey." Around Silverdale that is the Dyes Inlet shoreline, the Port Washington Narrows, and the lower reaches and mouths of Chico and Clear Creek. It does not use tree cavities: it digs "a long horizontal tunnel with nest chamber at end," generally 2.5 to 6 feet long and sloping upward from the entrance, in an exposed bank. Eroding creek banks and cut slopes that a tidy landowner would armour are the nest sites. WDFW's own page for this species is a photo profile with no habitat text.

species.protected: Protected. Covered by the catch-all protected category of WAC 220-200-100 and by the federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act. No season exists. It is NOT a state listed or candidate species: it does not appear on WDFW's 2024 state listed and candidate species list, and WDFW's own page notes "Pileated woodpecker was removed from Priority Habitat Species List in 2021." Losing a habitat-planning designation does not make a bird legal to kill; the MBTA still does.
species.edible_detail: No season, licence or bag limit exists, so there is no lawful way to take one. Birds that drill into siding are a real nuisance, but the lawful responses are exclusion and repair, not removal.

lookalikes.name: Northern flicker
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The other large woodpecker here, but brown and finely barred with a black chest crescent, and often feeding on the ground on ants. The pileated is crow sized, black and white with a flaming red crest. Both protected.

species.season: Year round resident. WDFW gives the breeding season as late March through early July, with 1 to 6 eggs per clutch.
species.habitat: WDFW: "Pileated woodpeckers inhabit mature and old-growth forests, and second-growth forests with snags and fallen trees," and in developed areas they use "remnant patches of forest, parks, and green-belts." They "excavate large nest cavities in snags or large decaying live trees." Around Silverdale that means the older forest patches in the creek ravines, the wooded edges of the Clear Creek Trail, and any neighbourhood that kept its big dead trees. Diet, per WDFW, is "carpenter and thatching ants, beetle larvae, termites, and other insects." Its tall rectangular excavations in a snag are the easiest sign to read, and the cavities it abandons become nest sites for owls, ducks and squirrels, which is the practical argument for leaving a safe snag standing.

species.protected: Migratory game bird. WDFW: "Canada geese are protected under federal and state law and a hunting license and open season are required to hunt them." Outside the hunting season, lethal control requires a permit from the US Fish and Wildlife Service. Not a state listed or candidate species.
species.edible_detail: Good eating, and the condition is legal rather than biological. You may take Canada geese ONLY during the open migratory bird season, with a Washington hunting licence, a state Migratory Bird Authorization and Harvest Record Card, and a federal duck stamp, and only within the daily bag limit, and only where discharging a firearm is lawful. Washington's 2026 to 2027 pamphlet lists the Goose Management Area 1 regular season as Oct. 17 to Nov. 29 and Dec. 12 to Jan. 31 with a daily limit of 3 Canada geese. Seasons, limits and area boundaries are reset every year, and this dataset could not confirm from the pamphlet which goose management area contains Kitsap County, so look Kitsap up on the current WDFW goose management area map before you hunt: the areas differ in season AND in which goose subspecies may be taken. The tame geese loafing on a Silverdale park lawn in July are the same protected birds as the ones in the sky in November; the date and the place are what make the difference.

lookalikes.name: Brant
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A small dark sea goose of saltwater, which is exactly where a Silverdale hunter would be. It has a small white necklace on the side of the neck instead of the Canada goose's white chinstrap running under the face, and it shows a very white rear end in flight. Brant have their own separate and much more restricted season and are NOT covered by the Canada goose bag limit.

lookalikes.name: Dusky Canada goose
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A dark chocolate-breasted subspecies whose season is closed in parts of western Washington, with a hunter identification requirement in those areas. Breast colour is much darker than the pale grey-brown of common local birds, and the bill is short. Check whether the area you are hunting has a dusky closure before you shoot at any dark-breasted goose.

lookalikes.name: Cackling goose
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Looks like a Canada goose shrunk to mallard size, with a stubby triangular bill and a squeakier call. Washington's pamphlet treats "all subspecies of Canada and Cackling geese" within the Canada goose limit, so this confusion is usually not a violation, but confirm in the current pamphlet.

lookalikes.name: Snow goose
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: White with black wingtips, unmistakable in good light. Counted under a separate white goose limit, not the Canada goose limit.

species.season: Resident birds are present every month of the year; migrants swell the numbers from autumn into early spring. The lawful hunting window is a narrow subset of that, roughly mid October to the end of January in recent seasons.
species.habitat: WDFW: "Canada geese nest in areas that are surrounded by or close to water," and they are "particularly attracted to mowed lawns around homes, golf courses, parks, and similar areas next to open water." In Silverdale that is the waterfront lawns and playfields along Dyes Inlet, the Clear Creek Trail corridor and any large mown area beside the water. WDFW distinguishes "migrating geese" from "nonmigrating (often called resident) geese," and notes the resident birds have increased sharply, especially in urban areas, because towns offer year-round food and few predators. A flock produces "1 to 3 pounds of droppings per day per bird," which is why goose numbers become a water quality question on a small inlet.
species.uses: Food when taken legally in season. Down and flight feathers are usable. The birds are also a working example of a native species that a mown, watered, predator-free landscape can push into overabundance.

species.protected: Migratory game bird with a declining population. WDFW: "Sea ducks are game species, managed under state and federal migratory waterfowl regulations cooperatively through the Pacific Flyway Council," and WDFW "has implemented progressively restrictive hunting regulations for scoters since 1998 in response to population declines." It is a Species of Greatest Conservation Need under the State Wildlife Action Plan, which is a PLANNING designation that guides funding and habitat work; it is not itself a prohibition, and the surf scoter is not on Washington's 2024 state listed or candidate lists. The rule that actually binds a hunter is the waterfowl season and the scoter sub-limit.
species.edible_detail: The condition is legal first and palatability second. Legally: scoters may be taken only in the open waterfowl season with a hunting licence, a state Migratory Bird Authorization and Harvest Record Card and a federal duck stamp. Washington's 2026 to 2027 pamphlet gives a sea duck season of Oct. 17 to 25 and Oct. 28 to Jan. 31, with no more than 3 scoters inside the 7 duck daily limit and no more than 9 inside the 21 duck possession limit, and harvest must be reported to WDFW by February 15. Seasons and limits are reset annually. On palatability: WDFW notes wintering surf scoters "feed mostly on mussels and clams," and a shellfish diet makes for strong, dark, fishy meat. That is a flavour problem, not a safety one, and it is usually handled by skinning and breasting the bird and treating it like liver rather than like a mallard.

lookalikes.name: Marbled murrelet
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The protected bird you must never shoot at on this water. It is listed as ENDANGERED in Washington, and the US Fish and Wildlife Service says "the federally-listed portion of the marbled murrelets range extends from the Canadian border south to central California," which includes Puget Sound. It is not a duck at all: about robin sized, far smaller than a scoter, with a short thin bill, and it flies fast and low over the water on whirring wings rather than in duck-shaped flocks. If a small dark diving seabird is too far off to size confidently, do not shoot.

lookalikes.name: White-winged scoter
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Shows a white wing patch in flight, and the male has a white comma around the eye. Counts inside the same scoter sub-limit, so the confusion is usually not a violation.

lookalikes.name: Black scoter
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Male is all black with a bulbous orange-yellow knob at the base of the bill and no white head patches. The surf scoter male has white on the forehead and the nape and a swollen orange, white and black bill. Same scoter sub-limit.

lookalikes.name: Harlequin duck
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Another sea duck on the same water but under a much tighter separate limit. Small, slate blue, with bold white crescents and stripes on the head and a rusty flank. Know your limit for harlequin before hunting sea ducks.

species.season: A winter bird here. Present from autumn through spring, most numerous roughly October through April, and gone to northern breeding grounds in summer.
species.habitat: Open saltwater. WDFW: "Although surf scoters are found in many marine coastal areas, they are most numerous on Puget Sound," and "Wintering surf scoters feed mostly on mussels and clams at up to 66 feet in depth, before switching to herring eggs or other seasonally abundant prey during spring migration." Around Silverdale, look for rafts on Dyes Inlet and in the Port Washington Narrows, sitting over shellfish beds. WDFW puts wintering scoter numbers on Puget Sound at about 50,000, about 80 percent of them surf scoters, and reports the three year scoter index has fallen more than 50 percent since 1994 to 1996. A duck that eats mussels and then eats herring eggs is a direct link between the shellfish bed, the herring beach and the bird, which is why shoreline work shows up in scoter numbers.
species.uses: Food when taken legally in season, best treated as dark strong meat. Its diet also makes it a useful indicator: scoter numbers track the health of the shellfish beds and herring spawn it feeds on.

species.protected: Migratory game bird with one of the shortest and tightest seasons in the state, plus conservation designations. WDFW lists it as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need under the State Wildlife Action Plan and says it "is identified under WDFW's Priority Habitats and Species (PHS) Program either as a priority species throughout its Washington range or within specific habitat areas of highly concentrated use or ecological significance." WDFW records that the Washington season was closed entirely from 1991 to 2001. It is not on the 2024 state listed or candidate lists. The binding rule is the permit-only season.
species.edible_detail: The condition is a nine day window and a permit. Washington's 2026 to 2027 pamphlet gives a band-tailed pigeon season of Sept. 15 to 23, a daily limit of 2 and a possession limit of 6, requiring a hunting licence plus a band-tailed pigeon authorization, with mandatory harvest reporting by Sept. 30. Outside that window there is no lawful way to take one, and the season is reset annually and has been closed outright in the past. Because the bird is a forest pigeon that will sit on a wire or a feeder like a feral pigeon, the commonest way people break this law is by not checking what they are shooting at.

lookalikes.name: Rock pigeon (feral pigeon)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is THE consequential confusion here. The feral pigeon is non-native and unprotected, and people shoot them around barns year round; a band-tailed pigeon shot outside its nine day season is a state and federal violation. The band-tail is a forest bird with a YELLOW bill tipped black, YELLOW legs, a broad pale grey band across the end of the tail, and a thin white crescent across the back of the neck above an iridescent patch. The feral pigeon has a dark bill with a white fleshy cere at the base, PINK legs, no pale tail band, and wildly variable plumage including pied, rusty and pure white birds. If the bill and legs are yellow, stop.

lookalikes.name: Mourning dove
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Much smaller and slimmer with a long pointed tail edged white, versus the band-tail's square tail with a pale grey band. The dove has its own separate season and limit, so treat them as different birds legally.

lookalikes.name: Eurasian collared-dove
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Pale sandy bird with a thin black half-collar on the back of the neck and a squared tail. Non-native and treated differently in the rules from native game birds; check the current pamphlet rather than assuming.

species.season: Present in the area spring through early autumn. The hunting window is a few days in mid September, and the birds are largely gone south by late autumn.
species.habitat: WDFW: it nests "primarily in conifers, occasionally in hardwoods and shrubs, within closed canopy conifer, or mixed hardwood and conifer forests," and uses "upland forests and limited mineral sources in western Washington." Mineral springs and seeps matter more than their size suggests: WDFW says these sites "provide needed sodium (and possibly calcium) during the nesting season." Around Silverdale, expect them in the closed-canopy second growth above the creek ravines, and in any yard with a heavy fruiting shrub or a big madrone.
species.uses: Food when taken legally in the short season. Its diet is also a ready-made native hedgerow planting list: WDFW names cascara, elderberry, wild cherry, huckleberry and madrone, all of which grow in central Kitsap and all of which feed a great deal more than pigeons.

species.edible_detail: Edible and legally unprotected, but there are three real conditions. FIRST, federal status: USDA APHIS states "As an invasive species, European starlings are not protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) and do not receive any Federal protection," consistent with the US Fish and Wildlife Service position that the MBTA "applies only to migratory bird species that are native to the United States or U.S. territories" following the Migratory Bird Treaty Reform Act of 2004. SECOND, local law: Kitsap County and the incorporated areas near Silverdale restrict discharging firearms and air guns, and trespass and animal cruelty law still applies, so confirm what is lawful where you actually are before doing anything. THIRD, identification: see the lookalikes, because the native blackbirds that flock WITH starlings are fully protected, and a shot into a mixed flock is a federal offence. If you do eat them, breast meat only, cooked through, as with any wild bird.
species.toxic: The bird itself is not poisonous, but its ROOSTS are a documented respiratory hazard. USDA APHIS: "Large flocks of roosting blackbirds and starlings commonly create accumulations of droppings raising health concerns about the fungal respiratory disease, Histoplasmosis," and "The fungus that causes the disease (Histoplasma capsulatum) occurs in the soil in bird roosts where excessive droppings have accumulated." CDC describes histoplasmosis as "caused by breathing in fungal spores from Histoplasma, a fungus that lives in soil," which "also spreads in bird and bat droppings that mix in soil." The exposure is airborne dust, so the risk moment is CLEANING UP a barn, attic or roost site with a dry broom or a pressure washer, not handling one bird. Wet the material down first, use respiratory protection, and do not dry-sweep accumulated droppings. APHIS notes the chronic form is rare but "can be a concern for people with weakened immune systems."

lookalikes.name: Brewer's blackbird, red-winged blackbird and brown-headed cowbird
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: All three are NATIVE and fully protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, and all three flock together with starlings. APHIS itself notes starlings "share similar characteristics and behaviors with blackbirds and are often found in flocks with them." The starling has a short square-ended tail, a triangular pointed silhouette in flight, a long straight bill that is yellow in the breeding season and dark in winter, and heavy pale speckling in winter plumage. The blackbirds have longer, rounder tails and a glossier unspotted look, and the male red-winged shows red shoulder patches. Do not shoot into a mixed flock: you cannot sort them in the air, and killing the native birds is a federal offence.

lookalikes.name: Rock pigeon (feral pigeon)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also non-native and unprotected, and much larger with a small head and a broad body. No legal jeopardy in confusing the two, but see the band-tailed pigeon entry for the native pigeon that IS protected.

species.season: Year round resident, in large mixed flocks in autumn and winter and in pairs at cavity nests from early spring.
species.habitat: Urban, suburban, agricultural and disturbed ground: lawns, playfields, parking lots, livestock yards and building cavities. It competes directly with native cavity nesters, taking over holes that woodpeckers excavated, which is the link back to the pileated woodpecker entry. APHIS puts combined winter populations of starlings, blackbirds and crows at between 750 million and 1 billion birds, and estimates blackbird and starling damage to grain, fruit and berry crops at more than 150 million dollars a year in direct costs. Around a Silverdale homestead the practical damage is to fruit, to poultry feed, and to any nest box you did not size against them.
species.uses: Food, if you want it and local law allows. More usefully, it is the species that teaches why a nest box hole diameter matters: sizing entrances to exclude starlings is the cheapest way to keep boxes working for native birds.

species.protected: ESA THREATENED. NOAA Fisheries lists the Puget Sound Chinook salmon ESU as threatened, listed March 24, 1999 and updated June 28, 2005 and April 14, 2014. The ESU covers naturally spawned Chinook "originating from rivers flowing into Puget Sound from the Elwha River (inclusive) eastward, including rivers in Hood Canal, South Sound, North Sound and the Strait of Georgia," which includes every stream around Dyes Inlet. Fishing happens only where and when WDFW opens it, and in Marine Area 10 every open period in the 2026 to 2027 rules requires releasing WILD Chinook.
species.edible_detail: Two separate conditions, and both bind. LEGAL: a Washington fishing licence and a catch record card are required. WDFW: "Catch record cards are required when fishing for salmon, steelhead, sturgeon, halibut, and Puget Sound Dungeness crab," and the catch must be recorded before you resume fishing. Marine Area 10, which is the water off Silverdale, opened in 2026 to 2027 as: Jun. 1 to Jul. 22 release Chinook; Jul. 23 to 25 one Chinook of 22 inch minimum, release wild Chinook; Jul. 26 to Sep. 30 release Chinook; Oct. 1 to Nov. 15 release Chinook; CLOSED Nov. 16 to Mar. 30; Mar. 31 to Apr. 30 open Wednesday to Saturday with one Chinook, release wild Chinook. So a keepable Chinook here is a HATCHERY fish, defined in the rules as "a Chinook or coho with a clipped adipose fin and having a healed scar at the location of the fin," taken in one of two narrow windows. Freshwater is closed: "All freshwater areas are closed to fishing for salmon" statewide unless a specific water is listed, and the Dyes Inlet creeks are not.
