Seasons change often by emergency rule, so check before every trip. HEALTH: see the toxic field. Puget Sound Chinook is the one salmon here that the state tells you to ration.
species.toxic: Not poisonous, but Puget Sound Chinook carry enough PCBs and mercury that Washington DOH sets meal limits on them specifically, while leaving other local salmon unrestricted. DOH's Puget Sound fish consumption advice for Marine Areas 6 through 13 gives Chinook "No more than 1 serving per week" and resident blackmouth Chinook "No more than 2 servings per month," explaining that "Resident Chinook (blackmouth) have higher levels of contaminants" because "Most blackmouth remain in Puget Sound rather than migrate to the ocean, so they accumulate more contaminants." A serving is 8 ounces of uncooked fish for a 160 pound adult, plus or minus an ounce for each 20 pounds of body weight. The contaminants sit in the fat, skin and organs: DOH says removing "the skin, fat, and internal organs before cooking" and grilling, baking or broiling so the fat drips off can cut PCBs by up to 50 percent. Mercury is different and cannot be cleaned or cooked out, because it "is stored in the muscle of fish." The advice matters most for people who are or may become pregnant, nursing mothers and young children.

lookalikes.name: Coho salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The legally important one, because in Marine Area 10 there are long stretches when coho may be kept and Chinook must be released. Washington's rules give Chinook a BLACK GUM LINE with "large black spots on back, dorsal fin, and both the upper and lower lobes of the tail," and coho a WHITE GUM LINE with "black spots on back with spots only on the upper portion of the tail." Open the mouth and look at the gum line at the base of the teeth. Then check the adipose fin for a clip before you keep anything.

lookalikes.name: Pink salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Pink also has a black gum line, so the gum check alone will not separate them. Pink has "very small scales" and "heavy oval shaped black blotches on the upper and lower lobes of the tail," and it runs only in odd-numbered years here. Chinook are much bigger.

lookalikes.name: Chum salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Chum has a white gum line and "no prominent spots on back or tail." Chum must also be released in Marine Area 10, so both fish often go back anyway.

lookalikes.name: Steelhead
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A threatened sea-run trout, not a Pacific salmon. It has a white mouth and gums and small dark spots radiating across a squarish tail, and wild ones must always be released. Count the adipose fin first.

species.season: Marine Area 10 has summer, early autumn and spring windows and is shut from mid November to the end of March; see edible_detail for the 2026 to 2027 dates. Sinclair Inlet and Port Orchard carry an extra Jul. 16 to Sep. 30 opening with a daily limit of 3. Spring, summer and fall run stocks all exist in Puget Sound. Seasons are reset annually and amended mid-season by emergency rule.
species.habitat: WDFW: "Most chinook spawn in large rivers such as the Columbia and Snake, although they will also use smaller streams with sufficient water flow." That is the key point for Silverdale: the small creeks draining into Dyes Inlet are chum and coho water, not Chinook rivers, so you meet Chinook here in the SALTWATER of Dyes Inlet, the Port Washington Narrows and the wider Marine Area 10, not in Chico or Clear Creek. Resident blackmouth are immature Chinook that never left the Sound, which is exactly why they carry more contaminant.
species.uses: Food, under both the season rules and the DOH meal limits above. The largest Pacific salmon: WDFW gives a typical 10 to 15 pounds and a maximum of 135.

species.protected: NOT ESA listed here. NOAA Fisheries lists four coho ESUs under the ESA, all of them outside Puget Sound: Central California Coast (endangered), and Lower Columbia River, Oregon Coast, and Southern Oregon and Northern California Coasts (threatened). The Puget Sound and Strait of Georgia population is not among them. Protection here is by WDFW season rules, licence and catch record card rather than by the ESA.
species.edible_detail: The condition is season and licence. A Washington fishing licence is required from age 16, and WDFW requires a catch record card for salmon, filled in before you resume fishing. In Marine Area 10 the open salmon periods in 2026 to 2027 carried a daily limit of 2 salmon, and coho are the species you are most often allowed to keep there while Chinook and chum must be released. Freshwater is a different answer: "All freshwater areas are closed to fishing for salmon" statewide unless a water is specifically opened, and the Chico Creek and Clear Creek listings open those creeks for trout and other game fish only, not for salmon. So do not plan on taking a coho out of a Silverdale creek. On health, coho are the easy case: DOH rates Puget Sound coho "Unrestricted," which it defines as 2 to 3 servings per week, and its Healthy Fish Guide puts coho in the healthy choice tier.

lookalikes.name: Chinook salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The confusion that costs you a citation, because Chinook must usually be released where coho may be kept. Coho has a WHITE GUM LINE and "black spots on back with spots only on the upper portion of the tail." Chinook has a BLACK GUM LINE and "large black spots on back, dorsal fin, and both the upper and lower lobes of the tail." Check the gum line at the base of the teeth, then check the adipose fin.

lookalikes.name: Chum salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Chum shares the white gum line but has "no prominent spots on back or tail," where coho is spotted on the back and upper tail lobe. Spawning chum also show purple and green vertical bars. Chum must be released in Marine Area 10.

lookalikes.name: Sockeye salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: White gum line and "no prominent spots on back or tail," with average size scales and noticeably large eyes. Sockeye seasons are separate and usually closed here.

lookalikes.name: Steelhead
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A threatened sea-run trout. White mouth and gums, and small dark spots scattered across a squared tail rather than concentrated on the upper lobe. Wild steelhead must always be released.

species.season: Coho return to spawn in autumn and early winter. Around Dyes Inlet they arrive later than the chum and push further up the creeks, waiting at the stream mouths for the first heavy rain to raise the water. Juveniles then stay in fresh water about a year and a half before going to sea, which is why a coho creek has to hold water all summer.
species.habitat: WDFW: "This species uses coastal streams and tributaries, and is often present in small neighborhood streams. Coho can even be found in urban settings if their needs of cold, clean, year-round water are met." They spawn in "areas of mid-velocity water with small to medium sized gravels," and juveniles hold in the pools. That is a precise description of Chico Creek, Clear Creek and the smaller Dyes Inlet tributaries. Because the young spend a summer and a winter in the creek, coho are the species most sensitive to a stream that goes warm, low or blocked in August, which makes them the best single indicator of whether a Silverdale creek is actually working.
species.uses: Food, unrestricted at 2 to 3 servings per week by DOH advice, taken under season rules. WDFW gives adults as typically 6 to 12 pounds.

species.protected: The local fall chum are NOT ESA listed. NOAA Fisheries lists two chum ESUs as threatened, the Columbia River ESU and the Hood Canal summer-run ESU, both listed in 1999. The Hood Canal summer-run fish are a different population in a different basin, not the fish in the Dyes Inlet creeks, and this distinction is worth keeping straight. Season rules, a licence and a catch record card govern chum where any fishery is open.
species.edible_detail: Edible, but around Silverdale the practical answer is that you watch these fish rather than take them. In Marine Area 10 the 2026 to 2027 rules say "Release Chinook and chum" in the open periods, so chum are not a saltwater harvest here. In fresh water, "All freshwater areas are closed to fishing for salmon" statewide unless a specific water is listed, and Chico Creek and Clear Creek are opened only for trout and other game fish, not salmon. Where a chum fishery IS open elsewhere in the state you need a licence and a catch record card. On health chum are the easy case: DOH rates Puget Sound chum "Unrestricted," meaning 2 to 3 servings per week, noting chum, pink and sockeye "tend to have low PCB levels." Chum flesh is paler and lower in oil than coho or Chinook, which is why it smokes and dries well and why it was the traditional winter keeping salmon.

lookalikes.name: Coho salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both have a white gum line. Chum has "no prominent spots on back or tail"; coho is spotted on the back and on the upper lobe of the tail. In spawning colours chum show bold purple and green vertical bars along the side and males grow hooked jaws with large canine-like teeth, which is where "dog salmon" comes from.

lookalikes.name: Pink salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Pink has a black gum line and "heavy oval shaped black blotches" on both tail lobes, plus very small scales and, in spawning males, a tall back hump. Chum has a white gum line and an unspotted tail, and runs every year rather than only odd years.

lookalikes.name: Sockeye salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also white gum line and unspotted, but smaller, with larger eyes, and in spawning colours brilliant red-bodied with a green head rather than barred.

species.season: Late autumn. WDFW's salmon viewing guidance gives "Peak viewing months are between July and November" statewide; around Dyes Inlet November is the month to go and look. Chum spawn closer to saltwater than coho, so the fish are visible in the lowest, most accessible reaches of the creeks.
species.habitat: WDFW: "Chum use small coastal streams and the lower reaches of larger rivers," spawning closer to saltwater than coho because they are bigger, need deeper water and are poorer jumpers, and "Shortly after they emerge, chum fry move downstream to the estuary and rear there for several months before heading out to the open ocean." That last sentence is why Dyes Inlet itself matters as much as the creeks: the estuary IS the nursery, so shoreline armouring and fill around the inlet hit chum directly. Chico Creek, Clear Creek and the smaller Dyes Inlet tributaries carry the local runs.
species.uses: Food where a season is open, and excellent for smoking and drying. Locally its main use is as the best free wildlife spectacle in Silverdale: WDFW lists seven Kitsap County salmon viewing sites, Chico Salmon Park, Clear Creek Trail Ridgetop Pavilion, Cowling Creek, Grovers Creek Salmon Hatchery, Keta Legacy Foundation Rhododendron Preserve, Poulsbo's Fish Park, and Salmon Haven at Dickerson Creek. Spawned-out carcasses also carry ocean nitrogen into the streamside forest, which is a real nutrient subsidy and not a metaphor.

species.protected: Not ESA listed in Puget Sound. Governed by WDFW season rules; a licence and a catch record card are required for salmon.
species.edible_detail: The condition is season, licence and, unusually, the calendar year. A licence and catch record card are required, and Marine Area 10's open salmon periods in 2026 to 2027 carried a daily limit of 2 salmon. Fresh water is closed to salmon statewide unless a water is specifically listed, and the Dyes Inlet creeks are not. And there is no point planning a pink trip in an even year: WDFW states "In Washington, pink salmon runs only occur in odd-numbered years." On health, DOH rates pink "Unrestricted" at 2 to 3 servings per week and notes pink, chum and sockeye "tend to have low PCB levels." Pinks are soft-fleshed and low in oil, best eaten fresh or canned rather than held.

lookalikes.name: Chinook salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both have a BLACK gum line, so the usual gum check does NOT separate these two, and Chinook must generally be released in Marine Area 10. Use the scales and the tail: pink has "very small scales" and "heavy oval shaped black blotches on the upper and lower lobes of the tail," where Chinook has ordinary scales and smaller distinct black spots. Chinook are also far larger. When unsure, release.

lookalikes.name: Coho salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Coho has a white gum line and spots only on the upper tail lobe; pink has a black gum line and heavy oval blotches on both lobes, plus much smaller scales.

lookalikes.name: Chum salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Chum has a white gum line and no prominent spots. Spawning male pinks grow a dramatic humped back, which chum do not.

species.season: Odd-numbered years ONLY in Washington, returning roughly August through October. WDFW explains the reason plainly: pinks live a strict two year cycle, so "there are no one-year-old or three-year-old fish to establish runs in the other years." The last Puget Sound run was 2025 and the next is 2027, so a simulation set in an even year should show none at all.
species.habitat: WDFW: pinks "use the mainstems of large rivers and some tributaries, often very close to saltwater," and the fry go straight downstream to the estuary without rearing in fresh water. The small Dyes Inlet creeks are not pink salmon streams; around Silverdale you meet pinks in odd years in the SALTWATER of Marine Area 10, not in Chico or Clear Creek. WDFW gives typical adults as 3 to 5 pounds, up to 12.
species.uses: Food in odd years, unrestricted by DOH advice. Best fresh, canned or smoked promptly because of the soft, low oil flesh.

species.protected: ESA THREATENED, and a Washington state Candidate species. NOAA Fisheries lists Puget Sound steelhead as "Threatened on May 11, 2007 (72 FR 26722)," covering naturally spawned anadromous steelhead "originating below natural and manmade impassable barriers from rivers flowing into Puget Sound from the Elwha River (inclusive) eastward," including Hood Canal, South Sound, North Sound and the Strait of Georgia. WDFW's 2024 state list carries "Steelhead - Puget Sound" as state status Candidate, federal status Threatened. Getting this one wrong in either direction is the worst error available in this dataset: it is a protected fish, and the fish in the Silverdale creeks are the listed population.
species.edible_detail: Conditional in the rules, and in practice NO around Silverdale. Statewide the rule is "Release all wild steelhead. Min. size 20\". Daily limit 2," so the only steelhead anyone may ever keep is a HATCHERY fish, meaning one with a clipped adipose fin and a healed scar at the fin site, and only where a season is actually open. No such season exists in the Dyes Inlet creeks: Chico Creek and Clear Creek are opened for trout and other game fish only, under selective gear rules, and BOTH listings say to release cutthroat trout and wild rainbow trout, which is exactly what a resident or juvenile steelhead is. A licence and a catch record card are required for steelhead. Treat steelhead here as a look-only fish and handle any you hook in the water.

lookalikes.name: Coastal cutthroat trout
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The two sea-run trout share the same creeks and both must be released there. The cutthroat has a red or orange slash under each side of the lower jaw, the character it is named for, and usually heavier, more scattered spotting including below the lateral line. Steelhead lack the slash and are brighter silver when fresh from salt.

lookalikes.name: Chinook and coho salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Steelhead is a trout, not a Pacific salmon, and its rules are different. It has a WHITE mouth and gums like coho, but its spots radiate in small dark flecks across a squared-off tail rather than sitting on the upper lobe only, and it has fewer anal fin rays than a salmon. Unlike Pacific salmon it does not necessarily die after spawning: NOAA notes steelhead "are iteroparous, meaning they do not necessarily die after spawning."

lookalikes.name: Bull trout
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A char, not a trout: pale cream to pink spots on an olive-green back and white-edged lower fins, versus the steelhead's dark spots on a lighter body. Closed statewide unless a specific water is listed. Not expected on the Kitsap Peninsula, but the rule is identical if you ever meet one: leave it in the water.

species.season: Winter-run fish enter Puget Sound streams from late autumn into spring. WDFW: "Winter runs spawn closer to the ocean, and require less travel time," preferring "fast water in small-to-large mainstem rivers, and medium-to-large tributaries," while "Most summer runs are east of the Cascades." So the Silverdale fish are winter-run.
species.habitat: Cold, clear streams with clean gravel and good year-round flow. The Dyes Inlet creeks hold Oncorhynchus mykiss: the Chico Creek and Clear Creek rules both require releasing WILD RAINBOW TROUT, which is the same species as steelhead, so the fish are present even though no steelhead fishery is open. Numbers in creeks this small are modest, and the fish depend on the same cool summer flows and unblocked culverts as coho.
species.uses: None available locally. Washington's state fish, and the clearest local example of a species where the right action is habitat work and passage repair rather than harvest.

species.protected: Not ESA listed and not on Washington's state listed or candidate lists, but locally the fishing rule is release. Both Silverdale creeks specify releasing cutthroat: Chico Creek and Clear Creek are open under selective gear rules for trout and other game fish and both say "release cutthroat trout and wild rainbow trout." WDFW also warns that "Many streams in the Puget Sound region are closed to fishing unless stated otherwise in the regulations pamphlet."
species.edible_detail: Conditional statewide, but in the Silverdale creeks the answer is NO: release them. Chico Creek is open for trout from the Saturday before Memorial Day through Aug. 31 and Clear Creek through Oct. 31, both under selective gear rules, and both require releasing cutthroat trout and wild rainbow trout. Selective gear rules mean "artificial flies with barbless single-point hooks or lures with barbless single-point hooks and bait is prohibited," up to 3 hooks, and "Only knotless nets may be used to land fish," all of which exist to let released fish survive. A freshwater or combination licence is required from age 16. Sea-run cutthroat taken in the saltwater of Marine Area 10 fall under the marine rules instead, so check the current pamphlet for the specific water rather than assuming. Where a water does allow retention, cutthroat are fine eating.

lookalikes.name: Steelhead or rainbow trout
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Look under the lower jaw: the cutthroat has a red or orange slash along each side of the jaw, and the rainbow does not. This matters because wild rainbow trout in these creeks are juvenile or resident steelhead from a THREATENED population. Both must be released in Chico and Clear Creek, so if you cannot see the slash clearly, the answer is the same either way: put it back.

lookalikes.name: Bull trout
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Char versus trout, told by spot pattern. Bull trout has PALE cream to pink spots on a darker olive-green back and white-edged lower fins; cutthroat and rainbow have DARK spots on a lighter body. Bull trout are closed statewide unless a specific water is listed and are not expected in Kitsap County, but the check takes one second and the penalty for getting it wrong is real.

lookalikes.name: Coho salmon juvenile
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Young coho share these pools and show tall oval parr marks along the side with a white leading edge on the anal fin. Salmon are closed in fresh water here regardless, so release either.

species.season: Present year round. Sea-run fish move between Dyes Inlet and the creeks through the year rather than making a single concentrated run, so unlike the salmon there is no one month to watch for.
species.habitat: WDFW: "widely distributed throughout western Washington (west of the Cascades)," in "lakes, along with tributaries to the Strait of Juan de Fuca, Hood Canal, Puget Sound, coastal streams," holding in "deep pools or locations along lake shorelines, especially where there is an abundant amount of submerged debris." WDFW calls it "one of three subspecies of cutthroat trout that occur in Washington and one of the two that are native," with both a resident form and an anadromous sea-run form. Around Silverdale that means Chico Creek, Clear Creek and Anderson Creek, wherever there is shade, wood in the water and a pool that stays cool in August. It is the trout that is always there when the salmon are not.
species.uses: Food only where a water allows retention, which is not the case in the Silverdale creeks. The most reliable year-round sport fish in central Kitsap, on a catch-and-release basis.

species.protected: PROTECTED and closed. WDFW gives its federal ESA status as Threatened. Washington's sport fishing rules close it outright: the statewide species rules say "Dolly Varden/Bull Trout: Closed unless otherwise listed in Special Rules," and the statewide freshwater rules say "All freshwater areas are closed to fishing for salmon, Dolly Varden/bull trout, lamprey, and grass carp." WDFW's species page also lists a state status of Candidate, although bull trout does not appear on WDFW's 2024 state listed and candidate species list; the two WDFW sources disagree on the state label, and it makes no practical difference, because the fishing rule is closed either way.
species.edible_detail: There is no open water for bull trout anywhere near Silverdale, so there is no lawful way to take one. WDFW is explicit about what to do if you hook one by accident: "If an angler catches a bull trout in a water closed for bull trout fishing, they must not be taken out of the water. They must be de-hooked and immediately released." Not lifted for a photograph, not weighed, not netted onto the bank. De-hooked in the water and let go.

lookalikes.name: Coastal cutthroat trout
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Char versus trout, and the spot pattern is the whole test. Bull trout is a char: WDFW describes "olive-green backs and pale spots" and "white-edged ventral fins," so LIGHT spots on a DARK body and clean white leading edges on the lower fins, and no black marks on the dorsal fin. Cutthroat and rainbow are trout: DARK spots on a LIGHTER body, and the cutthroat carries the red-orange slash under the jaw. If the spots are paler than the fish, stop and put it back.

lookalikes.name: Dolly Varden
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A very close relative, so alike that Washington's rules do not try to separate them and simply write the closure as "Dolly Varden/Bull Trout." You do not need to tell them apart: both are closed unless a specific water is listed.

lookalikes.name: Brook trout
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also a char with pale spots, but it adds distinct RED spots ringed in blue and strong worm-like pale marbling across a dark back, plus black-and-white edged lower fins. Brook trout are usually open where bull trout are closed, which makes this the confusion that leads people to keep the protected fish. Look for the red-and-blue spots and the marbled back.

species.season: None. Closed year round in every water around Silverdale.
species.habitat: NOT EXPECTED ON THE KITSAP PENINSULA, and this is the single biggest correction in this record. Bull trout need very cold, well-oxygenated water, and the waters WDFW names for them in Washington are in the Cascades, the Olympic fringe and the northeast: Chelan, Clark, Cowlitz, Douglas, Kittitas, Mason, Pend Oreille, Skagit, Skamania, Whatcom and Yakima counties. WDFW names no Kitsap County water at all. The Kitsap Peninsula has no high, cold headwaters, and you should not expect bull trout in Chico Creek, Clear Creek or any other Silverdale stream. A pale-spotted fish caught here is far more likely to be something else; the nearest water WDFW lists is Lake Kokanee in Mason County. Bull trout do range through Puget Sound marine waters from the rivers that hold them, so an encounter is not impossible on the salt, just not something to plan around. Treat this species as background context for why cold clean water matters, not as a fish a Silverdale player will meet.

species.scientific_name: Clupea pallasii Valenciennes in Cuvier and Valenciennes, 1847
species.protected: Not state listed and not closed to harvest. WDFW identifies it as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need under the State Wildlife Action Plan and as a species "identified under WDFW's Priority Habitats and Species (PHS) Program." Both are PLANNING and habitat-mapping designations that steer shoreline permitting and funding; neither is a ban on taking fish. It does not appear on Washington's 2024 state listed or candidate lists. The binding rule is the ordinary forage fish limit.
species.edible_detail: Open and legal, with an ordinary limit. In Marine Area 10, the water off Silverdale, smelt, herring, baitfish and other forage fish are open YEAR ROUND with a "Daily limit 10 lbs., all species combined." Jig gear may be used 7 days a week, and dip nets may be used from 6:00 a.m. until 10:00 p.m. Fridays through Tuesdays. Everyone aged 16 and older needs a fishing licence. No catch record card is required for herring; those are only for "salmon, steelhead, sturgeon, halibut, and Puget Sound Dungeness crab." On health, herring are one of the better choices: DOH's Healthy Fish Guide puts herring in its healthy tier at 2 to 3 servings per week, being small, short-lived and low on the food chain, which is exactly why they carry less contaminant than a resident Chinook. Eat them fresh, pickled or smoked. PARASITE CAVEAT, WHICH THIS RECORD PREVIOUSLY LACKED: CDC names herring among the most common carriers of the roundworm that causes anisakiasis, and FDA states that brining and pickling may reduce the parasite hazard in a fish but do not eliminate it, with larvae surviving 28 days in brine at 21 percent by weight. So pickled and cold smoked herring are precisely the preparations that do not control it. Freezing to FDA's published schedule does control parasites; it does not control bacteria, histamine or biotoxins, which are different problems with different answers.

lookalikes.name: Surf smelt
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both count inside the same 10 pound combined forage fish limit, so confusing them is not a violation. If you want to know: the smelt has a small fleshy ADIPOSE FIN on its back between the dorsal fin and the tail, and the herring has none. Herring is also deeper-bodied with large, loose, easily shed scales.

lookalikes.name: Juvenile salmon or trout
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The confusion that actually matters, because a young salmon or trout is NOT a forage fish and is not covered by the 10 pound limit, and salmon in fresh water are closed statewide. Young salmon and trout also have an adipose fin, like smelt, but they have a thicker trout-shaped body, a larger mouth, and usually oval parr marks along the side rather than a plain silver flank. If a dip net comes up with parr-marked fish, put them back.

lookalikes.name: Northern anchovy
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also inside the combined forage fish limit. The anchovy has a huge mouth with the jaw hinge set well behind the eye and a snout that overhangs it; the herring's mouth is small and upturned.

species.season: Open year round in Marine Area 10 and present in the inlet through the year, schooling in Dyes Inlet and the Port Washington Narrows. Herring spawn on nearshore vegetation, and the spawn is a distinct event that draws birds and predatory fish.
species.habitat: Nearshore and estuarine water. WDFW's page refers to "vegetative species used by herring as spawning substrate" and to "nearshore and estuarine spawning habitat," and notes that in Washington "herring populations have already shown northward movement for spawning and smaller juvenile cohorts." Herring spawning grounds are mapped under the Priority Habitats and Species program, which is a large part of why shoreline armouring, dock building and beach fill are regulated on Dyes Inlet: a bulkhead can remove the vegetation the eggs are laid on.
species.uses: Food for people, at 2 to 3 servings per week. Bait. And ecologically the base the rest of this list stands on: herring feed salmon, seabirds and marine mammals, and surf scoters switch onto herring eggs during spring migration, so herring habitat sits upstream of nearly every other animal in this dataset.

species.protected: Not state listed and not closed to harvest. WDFW identifies it as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need under the State Wildlife Action Plan and as a priority species under the Priority Habitats and Species Program. Both are planning and habitat-mapping designations that drive shoreline permitting, not a prohibition on fishing. It is not on Washington's 2024 state listed or candidate lists. The binding rule is the ordinary forage fish limit, and the earlier claim that recreational rules were unknown was simply a gap: they are published in the Marine Area 10 rules.
species.edible_detail: Open and legal, with an ordinary limit, plus one thing to do carefully. In Marine Area 10 smelt, herring, baitfish and other forage fish are open YEAR ROUND with a "Daily limit 10 lbs., all species combined." "Jig gear may be used 7 days a week. Dipnets may be used from 6:00 a.m. until 10:00 p.m. Fridays through Tuesdays." A fishing licence is required from age 16; no catch record card is needed, since those cover only salmon, steelhead, sturgeon, halibut and Puget Sound Dungeness crab. The care point is WHERE you work: surf smelt spawn in the upper intertidal sand and fine gravel, so raking or dragging a net through spawning beach gravel destroys eggs even when the fish you keep are within the limit. Take fish from the water, not the beach. Smelt are small enough to eat whole, cleaned and fried, which is the traditional handling.

lookalikes.name: Pacific herring
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both sit inside the same 10 pound combined forage fish limit, so the confusion carries no legal risk. The smelt has a small fleshy ADIPOSE FIN between the dorsal fin and the tail; the herring has none and is deeper-bodied with large loose scales.

lookalikes.name: Juvenile salmon or trout
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The one that matters. Young salmon and trout also carry an adipose fin, which is exactly why smelt and young salmonids get mixed up, and some of those young fish are threatened Puget Sound Chinook or steelhead. The young salmonid has a stouter body, a bigger mouth reaching back toward the eye, and usually a row of oval parr marks along the flank; the smelt is slender, small-mouthed, translucent silver and plain-sided. Sort a dip net catch before you bag it and return anything parr-marked.

lookalikes.name: Pacific sand lance
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also inside the combined forage fish limit. Very long and eel-like with a pointed jutting lower jaw and a single long low dorsal fin, and it burrows into sand. No adipose fin.

species.season: Open year round in Marine Area 10. Surf smelt spawn on intertidal beaches, with different beaches and stocks used at different times of year, so spawning fish can turn up in the upper intertidal in more than one season.
species.habitat: WDFW: "surf smelt utilize intertidal beaches for spawning," laying eggs in the upper-intertidal sand and fine gravel, and the agency flags a "coastal squeeze" because "the backshores of these beaches tend to be armored with bulkheads." Around Silverdale that means the sand and pea-gravel beaches of Dyes Inlet, which are also the beaches most likely to be built on, filled or walled. Spawning beaches are mapped under the Priority Habitats and Species program, which is why a shoreline permit near one gets scrutiny: a bulkhead placed at the top of the beach removes the exact band of sand the eggs need and the overhanging vegetation that shades them.
species.uses: Food, eaten whole and fried, under the 10 pound combined limit. Bait. And a forage base alongside herring, feeding salmon and seabirds, so the beach a smelt spawns on is worth more than its square footage suggests.

species.form: small slender silvery schooling forage fish, usually under 8 inches
species.protected: No federal Endangered Species Act listing, and WDFW does not list it as state threatened, endangered or candidate. It does carry two working designations: WDFW identifies it as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need under the State Wildlife Action Plan, and under the Priority Habitats and Species Program it is a priority species throughout its Washington range. Those designations protect its spawning beaches more than they protect the fish itself. There is no directed recreational sand lance fishery in Puget Sound.
species.edible_detail: The condition is legal, not biological. Sand lance are eaten in other countries and are not poisonous. In Washington there is no directed recreational fishery for them, and they are a Species of Greatest Conservation Need. Do not take them unless the current Washington Sport Fishing Rules specifically permit it for your marine area, and in no case dig up or disturb the intertidal sand they spawn in. In practice, treat this as a fish you learn to recognise, not a fish you harvest.

lookalikes.name: Juvenile Chinook salmon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is the confusion that matters. Puget Sound Chinook are listed as THREATENED under the federal Endangered Species Act, and young ones use the same shallow sandy nearshore. A sand lance is long and almost eel shaped with no adipose fin, a pointed lower jaw that sticks out past the upper, and a single long low dorsal fin running most of the back. A juvenile salmon is deeper bodied, has a small fleshy adipose fin between the dorsal fin and the tail, and usually shows dark vertical parr marks on the side. If a small silvery fish in the shallows has an adipose fin, assume salmon and leave it alone.

lookalikes.name: Surf smelt
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Surf smelt are deeper bodied and have an adipose fin; sand lance do not. Surf smelt also spawn in the upper intertidal gravel rather than burrowing into sand. Both are WDFW forage fish, so the practical answer for either is the same: do not take them without checking the current rules.

lookalikes.name: Pacific herring
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Herring are deeper and more laterally flattened with a sharp keeled belly and a short dorsal fin set near the middle of the back. Sand lance are round in cross section with a dorsal fin that runs nearly the whole length. Herring are also a WDFW forage fish.

species.season: Present in central Puget Sound year round. WDFW notes they burrow in sediment and tend to return to the same burrowing sediment habitat from one year to the next, so a given beach holds them season after season rather than only at one time of year.
species.habitat: Clean sand and fine gravel intertidal beaches along Dyes Inlet, the Port Washington Narrows and the wider central Kitsap shoreline. WDFW describes intertidal spawning habitat and a preference for burrowing into sediment. They vanish into the sand within seconds of being disturbed, so a beach can look empty and still be full of them. Expect them on soft sandy stretches, not on cobble or rock.
species.uses: Ecological rather than direct. Sand lance are among the main prey fish for salmon, seabirds and marine mammals in this part of Puget Sound. For a resident, the practical use is as an indicator: where sand lance beaches are intact, the salmon and the diving birds follow.

species.form: large predatory bottom fish with a long body and a very large mouth
species.protected: Not listed under the federal Endangered Species Act and not a state listed species. WDFW identifies lingcod under its Priority Habitats and Species Program as a priority species, which the agency attributes to recreational, commercial and tribal importance rather than to any conservation listing. Harvest is legal but tightly bounded: season dates, daily limits and size limits for Marine Area 10 are set annually in the Washington Sport Fishing Rules and were not fixed at the time this record was written, so read the current rules for Marine Area 10 before fishing.
species.edible_detail: Edible and well regarded, and the condition is legal. You must hold a current Washington fishing licence, fish inside the open season for Marine Area 10, and stay inside that year's daily limit and size limits. Lingcod seasons in Puget Sound are short and area specific, so an open season in one marine area tells you nothing about Marine Area 10. Some lingcod have blue or green flesh, which cooks white and is not a sign of spoilage or poison.

lookalikes.name: Rockfish, including bocaccio and yelloweye rockfish
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is the confusion that can put you in federal trouble, and it is about what comes up on your line beside the lingcod rather than about telling two fish apart on a plate. NOAA lists the Puget Sound and Georgia Basin population of bocaccio as ENDANGERED and the same population of yelloweye rockfish as THREATENED under the Endangered Species Act. NOAA states plainly that recreationally, targeting or retaining any species of rockfish in Puget Sound waters east of the Port Angeles area is not allowed, and Dyes Inlet and all of Marine Area 10 are east of Port Angeles. A rockfish has heavy spines in the dorsal fin, large eyes and a deep stocky body; a lingcod is long, has a huge mouth full of irregular teeth and no heavy spination. If you bring up a rockfish, release it, and use a descending device to return it to depth, because a rockfish brought up from depth cannot swim back down on its own.

lookalikes.name: Cabezon
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Cabezon are also large mottled bottom fish taken on the same gear. A cabezon has no scales at all, a broad blunt head and a fleshy flap on the snout; a lingcod has small scales and a longer, more tapered head. The confusion is harmless to your health but the two have different rules, so identify before you keep.

species.season: Set annually by WDFW and short. Puget Sound lingcod seasons are measured in weeks, not months, and differ between marine areas. Check the current WDFW rules for Marine Area 10, Seattle and Bremerton, before going out. Do not carry over last year's dates.
species.habitat: WDFW describes lingcod as found on the bottom, with most individuals occupying rocky areas at depths of 10 to 100 metres, which is 32 to 328 feet, and records have come from as deep as 427 metres or 1,400 feet. Near Silverdale that means the deeper rocky and high relief ground of the Port Washington Narrows and the open water of Marine Area 10 rather than the shallow soft bottom of Dyes Inlet itself. WDFW notes lingcod are commonly caught by recreational harvesters within Puget Sound.
species.uses: Food. A firm white flesh fish that is one of the better eating bottom fish in Puget Sound.

species.common_name: Manila clam, also called Japanese littleneck
species.scientific_name: Ruditapes philippinarum (A. Adams and Reeve, 1850). ITIS carries this clam under the older combination Venerupis philippinarum, TSN 81477; WDFW uses Ruditapes.
species.form: bivalve clam, oval, hard shelled, strongly ribbed, to about 2.5 inches
species.protected: No conservation protection. Harvest is regulated by WDFW. Minimum size is 1 1/2 inches measured across the longest distance of the shell. Daily combined limit of all clam species, excluding horse clams and geoducks, is no more than 40 clams and not to exceed 10 pounds in the shell. WDFW: anyone digging for clams in Washington must have a valid license that includes shellfish harvest. Most Washington tideland is privately owned, so harvest only on a beach WDFW lists as a public shellfish beach.
species.edible_detail: Excellent eating, and the most commonly dug clam on Puget Sound public beaches, but there are three separate conditions and all three must be met on the day you dig. One, you hold a licence that includes shellfish harvest. Two, the WDFW season for that specific beach is open and you stay within 1 1/2 inch minimum size and the 40 clam, 10 pound combined daily limit. Three, and this is the one that hospitalises people, the Washington Department of Health biotoxin status for that beach is open. Check the DOH Shellfish Safety Map or call the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 on the day you harvest, every time, not once a season.
species.toxic: PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON. The toxin is in the meat of the whole clam, not in any one part you can cut away. Washington DOH states that paralytic shellfish poison is not destroyed by cooking or freezing, and that the toxins are part of the shellfish meat. Early symptoms are tingling of the lips and tongue, which DOH says may begin within minutes of eating toxic shellfish or may take an hour or two to develop, progressing to tingling in the arms and legs, loss of control of the limbs, and difficulty breathing. DOH: if a person consumes enough toxin, the muscles of the chest and abdomen become paralyzed, including muscles used for breathing, and the victim can suffocate, and death has occurred in less than 30 minutes. There is no way to tell a toxic clam by looking, smelling or tasting it. The only defence is checking the DOH status before every single harvest.

lookalikes.name: Pacific littleneck clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The native littleneck is rounder in outline with ribs that run both around and across the shell in a crosshatch, and it sits deeper, 4 to 6 inches down in the mid intertidal. Manila clams are more oval, have a purple stain inside the shell near the siphon end, and sit shallower, 2 to 6 inches down and higher up the beach. Mixing them up costs you nothing legally: both carry the same 1 1/2 inch minimum and both count against the same 40 clam limit.

lookalikes.name: Varnish clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The varnish clam is flat and thin with a shiny brown outer layer like furniture varnish and purple inside. The Manila clam is thicker, ribbed and dull. Both are edible with the same biotoxin caution, but the varnish clam has no minimum size while the Manila clam must be 1 1/2 inches.

lookalikes.name: Butter clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The one worth getting right. Butter clams are larger, heavier and buried far deeper, up to 18 inches, with ribs running only around the shell and not across it. WDFW warns that butter clams retain marine biotoxins longer than other clams, so a butter clam in your bucket can still be toxic after a beach has reopened. If you cannot tell, do not keep it.

species.season: Beach specific and set by WDFW, not a fixed statewide window. WDFW: to safely and legally harvest shellfish for human consumption, both the DOH health status and the WDFW season for a public beach must be OPEN. Look up the specific beach on WDFW's public shellfish beach finder and cross check it against the DOH Shellfish Safety Map on the day you go.
species.habitat: WDFW: buried 2 to 6 inches deep in sand, gravel or mud substrate in the upper intertidal zone, which is shallower and higher up the beach than the native littleneck. Around Silverdale that means the mixed sand and gravel flats of Dyes Inlet and the Port Washington Narrows. Be aware that most Dyes Inlet tideland is private property and that DOH classifies beaches separately from WDFW; only harvest where the beach is both public and open.
species.uses: Food. The standard steamer clam of Puget Sound.

species.common_name: Pacific littleneck clam, also called native littleneck
species.scientific_name: Leukoma staminea (Conrad, 1837). ITIS still treats the older combination Protothaca staminea (Conrad, 1837), TSN 81464, as the valid name and has no entry for Leukoma; WDFW and current marine catalogues use Leukoma.
species.form: bivalve clam, round to oval, thick shelled, crosshatched ribbing, to about 2.5 inches
species.protected: No conservation protection. Harvest is regulated by WDFW. Minimum size 1 1/2 inches measured across the longest distance of the shell. Daily combined limit of all clam species, excluding horse clams and geoducks, no more than 40 clams, not to exceed 10 pounds in the shell. A valid licence that includes shellfish harvest is required. Harvest only on a beach WDFW lists as a public shellfish beach; most Washington tideland is privately owned.
species.edible_detail: Very good eating, and the condition is the same three part test as any Puget Sound clam. One, a licence that includes shellfish harvest. Two, the WDFW season for that specific beach open, and you stay inside 1 1/2 inches and the 40 clam, 10 pound combined limit. Three, the DOH biotoxin status for that beach open, checked on the Shellfish Safety Map or on 1-800-562-5632 on the day you dig. All three, every time.
species.toxic: PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON. The toxin is distributed through the meat, so there is nothing to cut away. WDFW's own page for this species tells harvesters to always check the local biotoxin status before harvesting via the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 or the Department of Health shellfish safety site. DOH states the toxin is not destroyed by cooking or freezing and that the toxins are part of the shellfish meat. First symptoms are tingling of the lips and tongue within minutes to a couple of hours, progressing to loss of limb control and paralysis of the breathing muscles; DOH records deaths in under 30 minutes. A toxic clam looks, smells and tastes normal.

lookalikes.name: Manila clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Manila clams are more oval, sit shallower and higher on the beach at 2 to 6 inches, and usually show a purple stain inside the shell at the siphon end. Native littlenecks are rounder, buried 4 to 6 inches in the mid intertidal, and have ribs crossing in both directions. Confusing them has no legal or health consequence: same minimum size, same combined limit.

lookalikes.name: Butter clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Butter clams grow much larger and heavier, bury up to 18 inches deep, and their ribs run only concentrically around the shell with no crosshatch. WDFW warns butter clams retain marine biotoxins longer than other clams, which makes the mistake a real health risk rather than a bookkeeping one. When in doubt, leave it.

lookalikes.name: Basket cockle
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Cockles are almost heart shaped seen end on, with heavy ribs radiating out from the hinge like the spokes of a wheel, and they sit barely 1 to 2 inches down or even on the surface. The legal difference matters: a cockle needs 2 1/2 inches, a littleneck only 1 1/2.

species.season: Beach specific. Both the WDFW season and the DOH health status for that beach must be open. WDFW: to safely and legally harvest shellfish for human consumption, both the DOH health status and the WDFW season for a public beach must be OPEN.
species.habitat: WDFW: buried 4 to 6 inches deep in cobble, gravel, sand or mud substrate, and they normally occur in the mid intertidal zone. WDFW gives the range as the Aleutian Islands in Alaska south to Baja California Sur. Around Silverdale, look on the mixed gravel and cobble flats of Dyes Inlet and the Port Washington Narrows, lower down the beach than where Manila clams sit. Check that the tideland is public before digging.
species.uses: Food. Firmer and chewier than a Manila clam, and good in chowder.

species.form: large heavy bivalve clam, oval, thick white shell with concentric ridges, to about 5 inches
species.protected: No conservation protection. Harvest is regulated by WDFW. Minimum size 1 1/2 inches measured across the longest distance of the shell. Combined daily limit of 40 clams across all clam species, excluding horse clams and geoducks, not exceeding 10 pounds in the shell. A valid Washington licence that includes shellfish harvest is required. WDFW gives the range as central California to the southeastern Bering Sea in Alaska.
species.edible_detail: Edible and good, but of all the common Puget Sound clams this is the one to be most careful with, and the condition is stricter than for the others. Beyond the licence, the open WDFW season and the open DOH biotoxin status, you need to understand that a butter clam holds paralytic shellfish poison in its tissue long after other clams on the same beach have cleared it. WDFW states outright that butter clams retain marine biotoxins longer than other clams. That means a beach reopening for Manila clams does not make butter clams on that beach safe. If there has been any biotoxin closure in the area in recent months, the conservative choice is to leave the butter clams and dig something else.
species.toxic: PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON, and this species is the worst retainer among the common clams. WDFW warning, quoted: butter clams retain marine biotoxins longer than other clams. The toxin sits in the meat and DOH confirms it is not destroyed by cooking or freezing, because the toxins are part of the shellfish meat. DOH describes early symptoms as tingling of the lips and tongue, which may begin within minutes of eating toxic shellfish or may take an hour or two to develop, then tingling in the arms and legs, loss of limb control, and difficulty breathing; with enough toxin the chest and abdominal muscles including the breathing muscles become paralyzed and the victim can suffocate, and DOH records death in less than 30 minutes. Check the DOH Shellfish Safety Map or the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 on the day you dig. There is no visible, smellable or tastable sign.

lookalikes.name: Pacific littleneck clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A littleneck is smaller and lighter with ribs crossing in both directions, and it sits only 4 to 6 inches down. A butter clam is bigger, heavier, has smooth concentric ridges only, and is buried as deep as 18 inches. The risk runs the other way here: mistaking a butter clam for a littleneck is what gets you into biotoxin trouble, not the reverse.

lookalikes.name: Manila clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Manila clams are small, oval, ribbed and shallow, at 2 to 6 inches down in the upper intertidal. If you are digging 18 inches for it, it is not a Manila clam.

lookalikes.name: Fat gaper, the horse clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A horse clam is much larger with a shell that gapes permanently at one end and cannot close over the siphon, and it has a leathery covering on the siphon. A butter clam closes completely. The legal difference is large: horse clams have their own limit of the first 7 clams dug, and do not count against the 40 clam limit.

species.season: Beach specific. Both the WDFW season and the DOH health status for that beach must be open. Because of the long biotoxin retention, also look at whether the beach has been closed at any point in the preceding months, not just today.
species.habitat: WDFW: buried up to 18 inches deep in sand, gravel or cobble, occurring from the mid intertidal to the subtidal zone. Around Silverdale that is the deeper gravel and cobble of Dyes Inlet and the Port Washington Narrows, dug at a low tide with a long handled shovel. Confirm the tideland is public before digging.
species.uses: Food, traditionally chopped for chowder and fritters because the meat is firm.

species.common_name: Basket cockle, also called Nuttall's cockle or heart cockle
species.form: bivalve clam, nearly round and heart shaped seen end on, with heavy ribs radiating from the hinge
species.protected: No conservation listing, but WDFW has tightened the rules because of declines. Minimum size was raised to 2 1/2 inches measured across the longest distance of the shell in 2026, larger than the 1 1/2 inch minimum for other clams, and WDFW explains the increase as a sustainability measure against heat sensitivity, harmful algal blooms and a newly identified bivalve disease. Daily combined limit of all clam species, excluding horse clams and geoducks, no more than 40 clams, not to exceed 10 pounds in the shell. WDFW: anyone digging for clams in Washington must have a valid license that includes shellfish harvest. WDFW gives the range as the Bering Sea in Alaska south to San Diego, California.
species.edible_detail: Edible, with a stronger flavour and chewier texture than a littleneck. The conditions: a licence that includes shellfish harvest; the WDFW season for that beach open; the 2 1/2 inch minimum, which is larger than for other clams and easy to get wrong if you are used to littlenecks; the 40 clam and 10 pound combined limit; and the DOH biotoxin status for that beach open, checked on the day you harvest. Because cockles sit at or just under the surface, they are easy to gather in quantity, which makes it easy to overshoot the limit without noticing.
species.toxic: PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON. WDFW instructs harvesters to always check the local biotoxin status before harvesting via the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 or the Department of Health shellfish safety site. DOH confirms the toxin is not destroyed by cooking or freezing because it is part of the shellfish meat, so there is no part to discard and no cooking method that helps. Early symptoms are tingling of the lips and tongue starting within minutes to a couple of hours, progressing to loss of limb control and paralysis of the breathing muscles; DOH records death in less than 30 minutes at sufficient dose.

lookalikes.name: Pacific littleneck clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The danger here is legal, not medical. A cockle has heavy ribs radiating out from the hinge like wheel spokes and looks heart shaped from the end; a littleneck has finer crosshatched ribbing and a flatter oval outline. Getting it wrong matters because the cockle needs 2 1/2 inches and the littleneck only 1 1/2, so a cockle that looks like a legal littleneck can still be an illegal cockle.

lookalikes.name: Butter clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A butter clam has smooth concentric ridges, no radiating ribs, and is buried up to 18 inches down rather than 1 to 2 inches. The reason to care is that WDFW warns butter clams retain marine biotoxins longer than other clams, so a butter clam mistaken for a cockle carries more risk than the cockle did.

species.season: Beach specific. Both the WDFW season and the DOH health status for that beach must be open.
species.habitat: WDFW: buried 1 to 2 inches deep in sandy, sheltered beaches, and also found in gravel and cobble substrate, and they occasionally appear on the beach surface. Sheltered sandy flats inside Dyes Inlet fit that description exactly, which is why cockles turn up around Silverdale without any real digging. Confirm the tideland is public and the beach is open before collecting.
species.uses: Food. Strong flavoured, usually chopped for chowder rather than steamed whole.

species.common_name: Fat gaper, usually called horse clam
species.form: very large bivalve clam with a shell that gapes permanently at the siphon end and a thick leathery siphon
species.protected: No conservation protection. Harvest is regulated by WDFW under a limit separate from other clams. WDFW, quoted: first 7 clams dug, regardless of size or condition. Broken clams count towards daily limit. There is no minimum size. Because horse clams are excluded from the 40 clam combined limit, they are counted on their own. A valid licence that includes shellfish harvest is required. WDFW gives the range as Cook Inlet in Alaska south to Oceano, California.
species.edible_detail: Edible, though the siphon needs its leathery skin peeled and the meat is usually pounded or ground rather than steamed whole. The legal condition has a trap in it: the limit is the first 7 clams dug, regardless of size or condition, and broken clams count towards the daily limit. Horse clams are deep and fragile and are very often broken by the shovel, so you can reach your limit with seven damaged clams and must then stop digging. You cannot throw back the broken ones and keep going. Beyond that, the usual conditions apply: licence including shellfish harvest, WDFW season for that beach open, and DOH biotoxin status for that beach open, checked the day you dig.
species.toxic: PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON. WDFW instructs harvesters to always check the local biotoxin status before harvesting via the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 or the Department of Health shellfish safety site. DOH confirms the toxin is not destroyed by cooking or freezing because it is part of the shellfish meat. Symptoms begin as tingling of the lips and tongue within minutes to a couple of hours and can progress to paralysis of the breathing muscles, with DOH recording death in less than 30 minutes at sufficient dose.

lookalikes.name: Pacific gaper, the other horse clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Tresus nuttallii is the other horse clam on this coast, longer and more elongated in outline than the rounder, fatter Tresus capax. It does not matter much in practice because both are horse clams and both fall under the same first 7 clams dug limit.

lookalikes.name: Geoduck
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The confusion is legal and it is expensive. A geoduck is much larger, buried two to three feet down, and its enormous siphon cannot be withdrawn into the shell at all. A horse clam is buried one to two feet down and has a shorter siphon with a distinctly leathery, often barnacled tip. The limits differ completely: geoduck is the first 1 clam dug, horse clam is the first 7. There is also a rule specific to geoduck making it illegal to maim, injure or attempt to capture one by thrusting any instrument through its siphon, or to possess only the siphon or neck portion.

lookalikes.name: Butter clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A butter clam closes completely and has no permanent gape; a horse clam cannot close over its siphon. Butter clams count against the 40 clam limit, horse clams do not.

species.season: Beach specific. Both the WDFW season and the DOH health status for that beach must be open. A good low tide is needed because the clam sits one to two feet down.
species.habitat: WDFW: buried 1 to 2 feet deep in the mid to low intertidal zone in sandy or gravel and cobble substrate, and it extends into the subtidal. Around Silverdale, the lower beach at a minus tide in Dyes Inlet and the Port Washington Narrows. A squirt of water from a large hole low on the beach is the usual sign. Confirm the tideland is public before digging.
species.uses: Food. The siphon is sliced and pounded for steaks or chopped for chowder; the body meat is softer and used in fritters.

species.form: very large burrowing bivalve with a siphon far too big to withdraw into the shell
species.protected: No conservation listing, but the tightest personal limit of any Washington clam. WDFW: personal daily limit is first 1 clam dug, reduced from three per person per day. WDFW: anyone digging for geoducks in Washington must have a valid license that includes shellfish harvest. There is also a conduct rule specific to this species, quoted from WDFW: it is illegal to maim, injure or attempt to capture a geoduck by thrusting any instrument through its siphon or to possess only the siphon or neck portion of a geoduck. Geoducks are excluded from the 40 clam combined limit and counted on their own.
species.edible_detail: Prized eating, and the conditions are narrow. One geoduck per person per day, the first one you dig, whether or not you like the look of it. You need a licence that includes shellfish harvest, an open WDFW season for that specific beach, and an open DOH biotoxin status for that beach checked on the day. You also need the tide: WDFW says tides must be at least minus 2.0 feet or lower to reach intertidal populations, which is only a handful of days a year. You must bring the whole clam out, not just the neck, and you must not spear or pierce the siphon to get a grip on it.
species.toxic: PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON. WDFW's geoduck page carries season and licence information but no biotoxin warning, so the source for this is the Washington Department of Health, which names the species directly: bivalve molluscan shellfish such as clams, mussels, oysters, geoduck, and scallops can accumulate Paralytic Shellfish Poison. DOH: paralytic shellfish poison is not destroyed by cooking or freezing, and the toxins are part of the shellfish meat. Early symptoms are tingling of the lips and tongue within minutes to a couple of hours, progressing to loss of limb control and paralysis of the breathing muscles, with death recorded in less than 30 minutes at sufficient dose. Check the DOH Shellfish Safety Map or call 1-800-562-5632 on the day you dig. A single geoduck is a lot of meat for one person, which makes the dose question worse rather than better.

lookalikes.name: Fat gaper, the horse clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The horse clam is the one people most often take for a geoduck, and the limits differ by a factor of seven. A horse clam is buried one to two feet down with a shorter siphon that has a leathery, often barnacled tip. A geoduck is two to three feet down and enormous, and its siphon is smooth and cannot be drawn in. If you can pull it up from a foot down, it is a horse clam.

lookalikes.name: Butter clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A butter clam closes completely, is a fraction of the size, and lies at most 18 inches down. No real risk of confusion once the clam is out of the hole, but a butter clam show on the surface can look like a geoduck show before you dig.

species.season: Beach specific and tide limited. WDFW: clam seasons are beach specific and may change annually, and current seasons can be located at the WDFW shellfish beaches page or on the state Department of Health Shellfish Safety Map. Practically the season is set by the tide book as much as the rule book, since you need a minus 2.0 foot tide or lower.
species.habitat: WDFW: geoduck clams are found buried two to three feet deep in mud, sand or gravel. WDFW notes the range runs Alaska to Baja California but that they are rarely found along the outer Pacific coast, with populations scarce west of Clallam Bay in the Strait of Juan de Fuca, which makes the protected inland waters around Kitsap the heart of the range. Around Silverdale, the low intertidal of Dyes Inlet and the Port Washington Narrows at a deep minus tide. Confirm the tideland is public first.
species.uses: Food. The siphon is sliced thin for sashimi or blanched and peeled; the body is used in chowder.

species.common_name: Eastern softshell clam, also called steamer clam
species.form: bivalve clam with a thin brittle chalky shell that gapes at both ends, elongated oval, to about 4 inches
species.protected: No conservation protection. Harvest is regulated by WDFW. WDFW states no minimum size for this clam, which is unusual and worth noting if you are used to the 1 1/2 inch littleneck rule. Daily combined limit of all clam species, excluding horse clams and geoducks, no more than 40 clams, not to exceed 10 pounds in the shell. A valid licence that includes shellfish harvest is required. WDFW gives the present range as Icy Cape in Alaska south to Elkhorn Slough, California.
species.edible_detail: Edible and the classic steamer of the Atlantic coast. Conditions: a licence that includes shellfish harvest, the WDFW season for that beach open, the 40 clam and 10 pound combined limit observed, and the DOH biotoxin status for that beach open on the day you dig. Two practical notes. There is no minimum size for this species, so the limit is the only thing stopping you, and the shell is thin enough that most of what you dig will be cracked; cracked clams still count. The clams also hold a lot of mud and need purging in clean seawater before cooking.
species.toxic: PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON. WDFW instructs harvesters to always check the local biotoxin status before harvesting via the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 or the Department of Health shellfish safety site. DOH: paralytic shellfish poison is not destroyed by cooking or freezing, and the toxins are part of the shellfish meat, so purging and steaming do nothing to it. Early symptoms are tingling of the lips and tongue within minutes to a couple of hours, then loss of limb control and paralysis of the breathing muscles; DOH records death in less than 30 minutes at sufficient dose.

lookalikes.name: Varnish clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both are thin shelled and neither has a minimum size, so a mix up costs nothing. The varnish clam is flat, oval and covered in a shiny brown layer like varnish with purple inside; the softshell is chalky white or grey, more elongated, gapes at both ends, and has a distinctive spoon shaped shelf inside the hinge of the left valve.

lookalikes.name: Butter clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A butter clam is thick, heavy and closes completely, and is dug from up to 18 inches in gravel rather than 8 to 14 inches in mud. It matters because WDFW warns butter clams retain marine biotoxins longer than other clams, so a butter clam in a bucket of steamers is the riskiest thing in that bucket.

species.season: Beach specific. Both the WDFW season and the DOH health status for that beach must be open.
species.habitat: WDFW: eastern softshell clams are buried 8 to 14 inches deep in sand and mud substrate, often in estuaries. That is exactly the soft muddy ground at the head of Dyes Inlet and around the Clear Creek estuary at Silverdale. Note that WDFW's page does not state whether the species is native or introduced on the Pacific coast; the common name WDFW itself uses is Eastern softshell clam, and the species was described by Linnaeus from Europe, so it is treated here as introduced to this coast. Confirm the tideland is public and the beach is open before digging.
species.uses: Food. Steamed and dipped, or fried; the thin shell makes them quick to open.

species.common_name: Varnish clam, also called purple varnish clam or savory clam
species.scientific_name: Nuttallia obscurata (Reeve, 1857). ITIS gives the common name as purple mahogany-clam. Note the spelling: two l characters in Nuttallia, though the WDFW page URL misspells it with one.
species.form: bivalve clam, thin, flat and oval, with a glossy brown outer layer and purple inside, to about 3 1/2 inches
species.protected: No conservation protection; the opposite. WDFW lists it among aquatic invasive species, quoted: varnish clams were accidentally introduced from their native range in the Northwest Pacific and are now naturalized throughout Washington and elsewhere in the Northwest. It is managed as an established invasive rather than a prohibited one, so it may be harvested normally. WDFW: no minimum size, and a daily combined limit of all clam species, excluding horse clams and geoducks, of no more than 40 clams, not to exceed 10 pounds in the shell. A licence that includes shellfish harvest is required. WDFW gives the established range as the Strait of Georgia, British Columbia, to Alsea Bay, Oregon.
species.edible_detail: Edible, and because it is an established invasive with no minimum size there is no conservation reason to hold back, but the safety condition is identical to every other bivalve here. You need a licence that includes shellfish harvest, the WDFW season for that beach open, the 40 clam and 10 pound combined limit observed, and the DOH biotoxin status for that beach open on the day you harvest. The meat is slightly bitter and benefits from purging in clean seawater before cooking.
species.toxic: PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON. WDFW's page for this species tells harvesters to always check the DOH biotoxin status before harvesting. DOH: paralytic shellfish poison is not destroyed by cooking or freezing, and the toxins are part of the shellfish meat. Early symptoms are tingling of the lips and tongue beginning within minutes to a couple of hours, progressing to loss of limb control and paralysis of the breathing muscles, with death recorded in less than 30 minutes at sufficient dose. Check the DOH Shellfish Safety Map or call the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 on the day you harvest, every time. Being an invasive species does not make it safer; it accumulates the same toxin as a native clam.

lookalikes.name: Manila clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A Manila clam is thicker, dull and clearly ribbed. The varnish clam is thin, flat and smooth with a glossy brown coating, described by WDFW as a thick, shiny periostracum, and typically shows purple coloration on the interior of the shell. Health risk is the same for both; the legal difference is that the Manila clam has a 1 1/2 inch minimum and the varnish clam has none.

lookalikes.name: Eastern softshell clam
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both are thin shelled with no minimum size. The softshell is chalky and elongated and gapes at both ends; the varnish clam is glossy, flat and oval and closes cleanly.

species.season: Beach specific. Both the WDFW season and the DOH health status for that beach must be open.
species.habitat: WDFW: varnish clams are buried up to 14 inches deep in sand or gravel substrate. They are widespread on central Kitsap beaches including Dyes Inlet, and tend to occur in dense patches once established. Note that a claim sometimes made for this species, that it sits very high on the beach near freshwater seeps, is not stated on the WDFW page and is not asserted here. Confirm the tideland is public and the beach is open before digging.
species.uses: Food. Eaten as a steamer once purged, and taking them does no conservation harm since the species is a naturalized invasive.

species.scientific_name: Magallana gigas (Thunberg, 1793). ITIS treats this as the valid name, with Crassostrea gigas listed as a synonym; WDFW's page uses both.
species.form: bivalve oyster, heavy fluted and irregular shell cemented to hard surfaces
species.protected: No conservation protection. Harvest is regulated by WDFW. Minimum size 2 1/2 inches measured across the longest distance of the shell. Daily limit 18 oysters, and WDFW notes oysters consumed on the beach count toward a limit. There is a rule here that has no equivalent for clams and that people break without realising, quoted from WDFW: oysters must be shucked on the beach. Leave shells on the same tideland and at the same tide height as where they were taken. The shell is the hard surface the next generation of oysters settles on, so removing it removes the reef. A valid licence that includes shellfish harvest is required.
species.edible_detail: Very good eating, and this is the oyster on nearly every public beach in Puget Sound. The conditions are: a licence that includes shellfish harvest; the WDFW season for that specific beach open; minimum 2 1/2 inches; no more than 18 per day including any you eat on the beach; shucked on the beach with the shells left at the same tide height; and the Washington Department of Health status for that beach open on the day you harvest. There are two separate health hazards here, biotoxin and vibrio, and they are not the same closure. Read the toxin field before eating any of these raw.
species.toxic: TWO SEPARATE HAZARDS. First, PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON. DOH names oysters directly: bivalve molluscan shellfish such as clams, mussels, oysters, geoduck, and scallops can accumulate Paralytic Shellfish Poison. DOH: it is not destroyed by cooking or freezing, and the toxins are part of the shellfish meat. Early symptoms are tingling of the lips and tongue within minutes to a couple of hours, then loss of limb control and paralysis of the breathing muscles, with death recorded in less than 30 minutes at sufficient dose. Check the DOH Shellfish Safety Map or the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 on the day you harvest. Second, and quite separately, VIBRIO. DOH states that Vibrio parahaemolyticus is the most common in the northwest, that the bacteria multiply rapidly in warm conditions so shellfish are more likely to be exposed to higher numbers in the summer, and that most cases of vibriosis occur from eating raw or undercooked fish or shellfish. Symptoms are diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache, fever and chills, appearing about 12 to 24 hours after consumption but sometimes taking as long as 4 days. Unlike the biotoxin, this one cooking does fix: DOH says Vibrio bacteria are destroyed by cooking shellfish to an internal temperature of 145 degrees F for 15 seconds. Keep harvested oysters cold, do not leave them in stagnant warm water, and think hard before eating summer oysters raw.

lookalikes.name: Olympia oyster
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The confusion that matters legally. The Olympia oyster is Washington's only native oyster and WDFW states wild stocks in Puget Sound are not currently open for commercial or recreational harvest. An Olympia oyster is small, round and flat, typically only 2 to 2.75 inches at full size and often much less, with a smooth greyish shell. A Pacific oyster is large, elongated, deeply cupped and heavily fluted. The 2 1/2 inch minimum size rule does most of the protecting for you, because very few Olympia oysters ever reach it. If an oyster is under 2 1/2 inches, leave it, whichever species you think it is.

lookalikes.name: Bay mussel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Mussels grow in dense beds on the same rocks and pilings but are smooth, blue black and wedge shaped, attached by fine threads rather than cemented. They carry the same biotoxin risk and DOH notes mussels accumulate toxins more quickly than other shellfish.

species.season: Beach specific. WDFW: to safely and legally harvest shellfish for human consumption, both the DOH health status and the WDFW season for a public beach must be OPEN. Separately, weigh the vibrio risk in warm months if you intend to eat them raw.
species.habitat: Marine shorelines, cemented to rock, cobble, pilings and old shell in the intertidal zone. Around Silverdale that means the hard edges of Dyes Inlet, Ostrich Bay, Oyster Bay and the Port Washington Narrows. WDFW does not state on its Pacific oyster page whether the species is native; the reason it is listed as introduced here is that WDFW's Olympia oyster page states the Olympia oyster is Washington's only native oyster species. Most Kitsap tideland is private, so use WDFW's public shellfish beach list.
species.uses: Food, raw or cooked. The shells, left in place, are also the substrate for the next generation, which is why the leave the shell rule exists.

species.common_name: Olympia oyster, often called the Oly or the native oyster
species.form: small flat roundish native oyster, rarely over 2.75 inches
species.protected: YES. DO NOT HARVEST WILD STOCK. WDFW states the Olympia oyster is Washington's only native oyster species, listed it as a State Candidate species in 1997, identifies it as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need under the State Wildlife Action Plan, and includes it on the Priority Habitats and Species List. On harvest, WDFW states plainly that wild stocks in Puget Sound are not currently open for commercial or recreational harvest. A second rule protects it indirectly: the 2 1/2 inch minimum size for recreational oyster harvest, which very few Olympia oysters ever reach. It is not federally listed under the Endangered Species Act.
species.edible_detail: Do not harvest. The reason is legal and conservation based rather than toxicological: the oyster is perfectly edible and was historically the mainstay of Puget Sound, but WDFW states wild stocks in Puget Sound are not currently open for commercial or recreational harvest, and by 2012 only about 5 percent of the historical oyster bed habitat remained. Farmed Olympia oysters are sold commercially; that is the lawful way to eat one. If you want to help this species, leave every oyster under 2 1/2 inches where it is.
species.toxic: PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON, in principle. As a bivalve it accumulates the toxin exactly as any other does, and DOH names oysters among the bivalve molluscan shellfish that can accumulate Paralytic Shellfish Poison. DOH: it is not destroyed by cooking or freezing, and the toxins are part of the shellfish meat; early symptoms are tingling of the lips and tongue within minutes to a couple of hours, progressing to paralysis of the breathing muscles, with death recorded in less than 30 minutes at sufficient dose. In practice the question does not arise for wild stock, because harvest is closed. If you are on a beach at all and thinking about any shellfish, check the DOH Shellfish Safety Map or call the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 that same day. If you are eating farmed Olympia oysters, the grower is responsible for the biotoxin testing that makes them safe; that testing is the thing you are paying for.

lookalikes.name: Juvenile Pacific oyster
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is the mistake that gets people into trouble in the right direction if they follow one simple rule: if an oyster is under 2 1/2 inches, leave it, whichever species it is. For the record, an Olympia is flat, round and smooth with a greyish or olive shell and a faintly iridescent interior; a young Pacific oyster is already elongated, deeply cupped and sharply fluted at the same size. WDFW notes an Olympia reaches only about 1.5 inches after three to four years and 2 to 2.75 inches at full size.

lookalikes.name: Jingle shell and other small encrusting bivalves
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Several small flat bivalves cement to the same rocks. None of them matter, because the operating rule on this shoreline is the same either way: do not take small flat oysters or oyster shaped shells off the rocks.

species.season: Closed. There is no open season for wild Olympia oysters in Puget Sound.
species.habitat: WDFW describes estuaries and shallow areas, the intertidal and upper subtidal zones, with firm substrates, forming low relief oyster beds, in water between 6 and 20 degrees Celsius. Historically the range ran from Sitka, Alaska, to Baja California. Around Silverdale, the sheltered firm bottomed edges of Dyes Inlet and Ostrich Bay are the right kind of ground, and restoration work in Puget Sound targets exactly this habitat. Treat any bed you find as something to record and leave alone.
species.uses: Historically the foundation of the Puget Sound oyster industry, and still farmed commercially. Its present use to a resident is ecological: the beds it forms are habitat for other species, which is why restoration effort goes into it.

species.common_name: Bay mussel, also called Pacific blue mussel
species.scientific_name: Mytilus spp. The Puget Sound bay mussel is chiefly Mytilus trossulus Gould, 1850, ITIS TSN 567928, but introduced Mytilus species occur on the same shorelines and hybridise with it, so a mussel on a Dyes Inlet piling cannot be named to species by eye.
species.form: bivalve mussel, smooth blue black wedge shaped shell, growing in dense beds attached by fine threads
