species.protected: No conservation protection. Harvest is regulated by WDFW under the same beach by beach season system as clams and oysters, and requires a licence that includes shellfish harvest. The exact daily limit and any minimum size for mussels could not be confirmed from a citable WDFW page while this record was written; WDFW's shellfishing regulations page directs harvesters to the current Washington Sport Fishing Rules for limits. Look the mussel limit up in the current rules before harvesting, and do not assume it matches the 40 clam limit.
species.edible_detail: Edible and easy to gather, which is precisely why they are dangerous. The conditions: a licence that includes shellfish harvest; the WDFW season for that specific beach open; the daily limit from the current Washington Sport Fishing Rules observed, because this record cannot tell you what it is; and the Washington Department of Health status for that beach open on the day you harvest. Mussels are the fastest of the common shellfish to take up biotoxin, which is one reason DOH uses them as a sentinel for monitoring. If a beach has only just reopened, mussels are the last thing to take chances with, not the first.
species.toxic: PARALYTIC SHELLFISH POISON, and this is the highest risk group among the common shellfish for speed of uptake. DOH states directly that mussels accumulate toxins more quickly, and names them among the bivalve molluscan shellfish that can accumulate Paralytic Shellfish Poison. DOH: the toxin is not destroyed by cooking or freezing, and the toxins are part of the shellfish meat, so steaming them open does nothing. Early symptoms are tingling of the lips and tongue which may begin within minutes of eating toxic shellfish or may take an hour or two to develop, progressing to tingling in the arms and legs, loss of control of the limbs, and difficulty breathing; with enough toxin the chest and abdominal muscles including those used for breathing become paralyzed and the victim can suffocate, and DOH records death in less than 30 minutes. WDFW has noted that the Department of Health issues large scale beach closures for harvest of all clam, mussel, oyster and scallop and other mollusk species in many areas due to biotoxins. Check the DOH Shellfish Safety Map or call 1-800-562-5632 on the day you harvest. Mussels also carry the same summer vibrio risk as oysters if eaten raw or undercooked.

lookalikes.name: Pacific oyster
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Oysters are cemented hard to the rock and have a heavy irregular fluted shell; mussels are smooth, blue black, wedge shaped and held on by a beard of fine threads you can pull free. Both carry the biotoxin risk but they have different limits and the oyster has a shuck on the beach rule the mussel does not.

lookalikes.name: California mussel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The larger outer coast mussel, Mytilus californianus, has a thicker shell with radiating ribs and grows on exposed surf swept rock. Bay mussels are smaller and smooth. You are very unlikely to meet the California mussel in sheltered Dyes Inlet; it belongs on the open ocean coast. Either way the biotoxin caution is identical.

lookalikes.name: Dark clumps of small bivalves on floats and riprap generally
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The practical warning is not about telling two shellfish apart but about where you gather. Mussels on marina floats, boat hulls and riprap near stormwater outfalls sit in water that DOH may have closed for pollution or vibrio rather than biotoxin, and those are separate closures. Harvest only from a beach WDFW lists as public and DOH lists as open, not from whatever piling is convenient.

species.season: Beach specific. WDFW: to safely and legally harvest shellfish for human consumption, both the DOH health status and the WDFW season for a public beach must be OPEN. Biotoxin closures that cover mussels are common in Puget Sound and can appear quickly, so a beach that was open last week tells you nothing.
species.habitat: Attached in dense beds to rock, pilings, floats, riprap and old shell in the intertidal zone. Around Silverdale they are on essentially every hard vertical surface in Dyes Inlet, the Port Washington Narrows and the Silverdale waterfront. Their availability is not the constraint; the health status of the water is.
species.uses: Food. Steamed, and the standard shellfish that DOH samples to monitor biotoxin levels for everyone else's benefit.

species.scientific_name: Cancer magister Dana, 1852. This is the name ITIS treats as valid and the name WDFW uses; the combination Metacarcinus magister is also in wide use in current marine literature.
species.form: large crab, broad oval shell wider than long, purple brown above with white tipped claws
species.protected: No conservation listing, but the most heavily regulated recreational shellfish in Puget Sound. Silverdale and Dyes Inlet lie in Marine Area 10, Seattle and Bremerton. Marine Area 10 rules as posted by WDFW: minimum size 6.25 inches carapace width, daily limit five males, and you must release all soft-shell, females and undersized crab. Every Puget Sound crabber needs two things beyond a fishing licence, quoted from WDFW: all recreational crabbers regardless of age who fish for crab in the Puget Sound crab management area must purchase a Puget Sound crab endorsement on their license and obtain a Puget Sound Dungeness crab catch record card. The card must be reported even if you caught nothing, from the day after Labor Day through October 1 for the summer card and from January 1 through February 1 for the winter card, and failing to report brings a 10 dollar penalty with the following year's licence. Gear rules: pots, hand or dipnet only; a half red, half white buoy carrying the owner's first and last name and permanent address; and a biodegradable rot or escape cord affixed to every pot. All crab fishing gear must be removed from the water by one hour after sunset on the last day of any fishing period.
species.edible_detail: Excellent eating, and the conditions here are the strictest in this dataset. You need a Washington fishing licence, a Puget Sound crab endorsement, and a Dungeness crab catch record card that you fill in as you go and report afterwards. You may keep only males, only hard shelled ones, only at 6.25 inches carapace width or more, only five in a day, and only on the days Marine Area 10 is actually open. Marine Area 10 was open July 5 through September 7, Sundays and Mondays only, and was showing as CLOSED when this record was checked, so read the current WDFW crab seasons page for Marine Area 10 every time rather than relying on last year's dates. Then clean the crab properly, which for biotoxin reasons means discarding the guts and butter: see the toxin field.
species.toxic: BIOTOXIN, CONCENTRATED IN THE VISCERA. Crab meat itself is generally not the problem; the crab's digestive organs are. Washington DOH states that crabs can become toxic, that toxins accumulate especially in the gut and butter, and gives this instruction, quoted: even if the crab meat is safe, toxins tend to accumulate in crab gut and butter, the white yellow fat inside the back of the shell. Clean crab thoroughly and avoid eating the crab butter and guts. So do not make a sauce or a bisque from the butter, and do not cook a crab whole and eat everything inside the back. The underlying toxin is paralytic shellfish poison, which DOH says is not destroyed by cooking or freezing because it is part of the meat; early symptoms are tingling of the lips and tongue within minutes to a couple of hours, progressing to loss of limb control and paralysis of the breathing muscles, with death recorded in less than 30 minutes at sufficient dose. Check the DOH Shellfish Safety Map or the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 before you harvest.

lookalikes.name: Red rock crab
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The everyday confusion, and it is a legal one rather than a health one. A Dungeness is purplish brown with a shell notably wider than long, has white tipped claws and a row of small spines along the front edge of the shell ending in a wider, more pointed shape at the sides. A red rock crab is brick red with much heavier black tipped claws and a shell with a smoother fan shaped front edge. Getting it wrong matters because the rules differ completely: Dungeness is five males at 6.25 inches and must be recorded on a catch card; red rock is six crab of either sex at 5 inches and is not recorded on the card.

lookalikes.name: European green crab
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This one you must not keep and must not kill. WDFW classifies the European green crab as a Prohibited Level 1 Invasive Species in Washington, meaning live crabs cannot be possessed without authorization, and it has been detected in the Salish Sea including the Port Gamble area of Kitsap County in spring 2025. The identifying feature is five spines or teeth on each side of the shell, in front of and beside the eyes, on a shell that is broader than it is long and seldom exceeds four inches across. Colour is unreliable, since they are often mottled brown rather than green. WDFW's instruction is to take photos and report it as soon as possible rather than killing it, using the WDFW green crab identification and reporting page. A dead crab or a shell may be retained if you are certain of the identification.

lookalikes.name: Graceful crab
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A smaller relative often taken for an undersized Dungeness. It has a narrower shell and slimmer legs and never reaches Dungeness size. The practical answer is the same as for any small crab: measure the carapace width, and if it is under 6.25 inches it goes back regardless of what you think it is.

species.season: Short, set annually by WDFW, and often restricted to certain days of the week. The Marine Area 10 season most recently posted was open July 5 through September 7, Sundays and Mondays only, and was CLOSED when this record was written. Always read the current WDFW crab seasons page for Marine Area 10 before setting a pot, and remember all gear must be out of the water by one hour after sunset on the last day of any fishing period.
species.habitat: WDFW: the Dungeness crab is frequently found in eelgrass beds and prefers sandy or muddy substrates. That describes the floor of Dyes Inlet and the Port Washington Narrows well. WDFW also notes that in Puget Sound this crab is most abundant north of Seattle, in Hood Canal and near the Pacific coast, so the inner reaches of Dyes Inlet are at the thinner end of its local abundance rather than a hotspot.
species.uses: Food. The signature crab of this coast, and the one most local crab pots are set for.

species.form: medium crab, brick red, fan shaped shell, very heavy black tipped claws
species.protected: No conservation listing. Harvest is regulated by WDFW with looser limits than Dungeness: daily limit 6 crabs of either sex, minimum size 5 inches carapace width in Marine Area 10. Recreational crabbers aged 15 and over must hold a current Washington fishing licence. An important correction to a common misunderstanding: it is true that crabbers are not required to record their catch of red rock crab on a catch card, but WDFW states that all recreational crabbers regardless of age who fish for crab in the Puget Sound crab management area must purchase a Puget Sound crab endorsement on their license and obtain a Puget Sound Dungeness crab catch record card. So in Puget Sound you still need the endorsement and the card to crab at all, even if you only intend to keep red rock crab; you simply do not write red rock crab on it. WDFW gives the range as native to North American west coast estuaries from Alaska to northern Baja California, and common throughout Puget Sound.
species.edible_detail: Good eating, with a smaller body yield than Dungeness but much heavier claws, which is where most of the meat is. Conditions: a current Washington fishing licence if you are 15 or over, a Puget Sound crab endorsement and Dungeness catch record card because you are crabbing in Puget Sound at all, the Marine Area 10 crab season open, a maximum of 6 crabs of either sex, and a 5 inch minimum carapace width. Unlike Dungeness you may keep females. Then clean it properly and discard the guts and butter: see the toxin field.
species.toxic: BIOTOXIN, CONCENTRATED IN THE VISCERA, exactly as for Dungeness. WDFW's species page for the red rock crab carries no biotoxin warning, so the source here is the Washington Department of Health, which states that crabs can become toxic and that toxins accumulate especially in the gut and butter, with the instruction: even if the crab meat is safe, toxins tend to accumulate in crab gut and butter, the white yellow fat inside the back of the shell. Clean crab thoroughly and avoid eating the crab butter and guts. The toxin is paralytic shellfish poison, which DOH says is not destroyed by cooking or freezing because it is part of the shellfish meat. Check the DOH Shellfish Safety Map or the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 before harvesting.

lookalikes.name: Dungeness crab
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Legal rather than medical. A red rock crab is brick red with black tipped claws and a smooth fan shaped front shell edge. A Dungeness is purplish brown, wider than long, with white tipped claws and small spines along the front edge. The limits are completely different: red rock is 6 of either sex at 5 inches; Dungeness is five males only at 6.25 inches, hard shelled only, and recorded on a catch card. A female Dungeness kept in the belief it was a red rock crab is a violation.

lookalikes.name: European green crab
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Do not keep it and do not kill it. WDFW classifies the European green crab as a Prohibited Level 1 Invasive Species in Washington, live crabs cannot be possessed without authorization, and it has been detected in the Salish Sea including the Port Gamble area of Kitsap County in spring 2025. Look for five spines or teeth on each side of the shell, on a shell broader than it is long that seldom exceeds four inches across. Colour is not a reliable clue. WDFW's instruction is to photograph it and report it as soon as possible; a dead crab may be retained only if you are certain of the identification.

lookalikes.name: Juvenile red rock crab and other small crabs
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Measure rather than judge. Anything under 5 inches across the carapace goes back, whatever species you believe it is.

species.season: Set by WDFW alongside the Marine Area 10 crab season rather than separately, so the same open days apply. The most recently posted Marine Area 10 season ran July 5 through September 7, Sundays and Mondays only, and was CLOSED when this record was written. Check the current WDFW crab seasons page for Marine Area 10, and remember all crab gear must be out of the water by one hour after sunset on the last day of any fishing period.
species.habitat: WDFW: rocky substrates, but they can also be found in eelgrass, soft bottom habitat and shellfish beds, from the mid intertidal to depths of about 260 feet. Because they come up into the mid intertidal, red rock crab are the crab you are most likely to meet under a rock at low tide around Dyes Inlet and the Port Washington Narrows without setting a pot at all.
species.uses: Food, mainly the claws, which are heavy enough to be worth cracking on their own.

species.common_name: Spot shrimp, also called spot prawn
species.form: large shrimp, reddish brown with white bars on the carapace and white spots on the abdomen
species.protected: No conservation listing. Harvest is regulated by WDFW with a tight limit. WDFW for Puget Sound and Hood Canal: daily limit of 10 pounds, heads and tails, of all shrimp species combined, with a maximum of 80 spot shrimp if open for spot shrimp. WDFW: shrimpers age 15 and older must have an annual shellfish and seaweed, combination, or Fish Washington license. Seasons are set by marine area and change; WDFW directs harvesters to the regulations by marine area page and to the Shellfish Rule Change free hotline on 866-880-5431 for current closures.
species.edible_detail: Among the best eating shellfish on this coast, and the condition is almost entirely about the calendar. You need a shellfish and seaweed, combination or Fish Washington licence if you are 15 or older, the season for your marine area open, and the 10 pound combined and 80 spot shrimp limits observed. The Puget Sound spot shrimp season is famously short and does not run on the same dates in every marine area, so check the current WDFW regulations by marine area page and the rule change hotline on 866-880-5431 before you go. The heads should be removed soon after catching, because the meat softens quickly otherwise.
species.toxic: Shrimp are not bivalves and are not the main route by which paralytic shellfish poison reaches people, and WDFW's spot shrimp page carries no biotoxin warning. That is not the same as a clean bill of health. Washington DOH biotoxin closures can cover shellfish harvest generally, and crustaceans in the same water concentrate toxin in their digestive organs rather than the muscle, as DOH describes for crab. Where the toxin is present it is not destroyed by cooking or freezing, because DOH says it is part of the shellfish meat. The sensible practice is the same: check the DOH Shellfish Safety Map or the biotoxin hotline on 1-800-562-5632 on the day you go, remove and discard the head and gut rather than eating them, and eat the tail meat.

lookalikes.name: Other Puget Sound shrimp, including coonstripe, pink and humpback shrimp
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The confusion is legal, not medical; all are edible. A spot shrimp is the largest, reddish brown, with a pair of white bars on the carapace and distinct white spots on the first and fifth abdominal segments. The others are smaller and lack that pattern. It matters because the 10 pound daily limit covers all shrimp species combined while the 80 shrimp cap applies specifically to spot shrimp, and because a marine area can be open for other shrimp and closed for spot shrimp.

lookalikes.name: none in this region for health purposes
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: There is no poisonous shrimp in Puget Sound that a person could confuse with a spot shrimp. The hazards here are the season, the limit and the water quality, not the animal.

species.season: Very short and set by marine area, not statewide. WDFW gives no fixed dates on the species page and directs harvesters to the regulations by marine area page, with the Shellfish Rule Change free hotline on 866-880-5431 for current closures. Do not plan around a remembered date.
species.habitat: Not a beach species and not something you will meet wading. WDFW states spot shrimp are most common in Hood Canal, the San Juan Islands, and northern and central Puget Sound, and the fishery is a pot fishery worked from a boat in deep water rather than an intertidal one. WDFW's species page gives no depth or substrate figures, so none are claimed here. For a Silverdale resident this means a boat trip out of Dyes Inlet into deeper water of Marine Area 10 or over to Hood Canal, not a walk down the beach.
species.uses: Food. Sweet enough to be eaten raw as sashimi when very fresh, and the heads make good stock even though you should not eat them whole.

species.common_name: Ochre sea star, also called the purple sea star or purple star
species.scientific_name: Pisaster ochraceus (Brandt, 1835). ITIS treats this as a valid species, TSN 157253, and gives the English common name as ochre stars. Its ITIS hierarchy is phylum Echinodermata, class Asteroidea, order Forcipulatida, family Asteriidae, which is the reason this record is not filed under shellfish: a sea star is an echinoderm, a different phylum entirely from the molluscs and crustaceans that fill the shellfish records in this file, and Washington law agrees, as the protected field explains.
species.form: Five armed sea star with short, thick, blunt arms on a broad disc. King County's identification key for common intertidal sea stars of Puget Sound puts the arm length to disc radius ratio at 2.7 to 4.1, which is the practical measurement for telling it from its neighbours, and describes the arrangement of spines on the topside as forming a netlike pattern. Colour is the classic trap. King County: although its common name implies that it is most often purple, it is as likely to be some shade of orange or brown, but never pink. The National Park Service describes the same animal in Olympic tidepools as showing distinct oranges, purples and brick reds. So colour tells you nothing and the spine net and the stubby arms tell you everything.
species.protected: No conservation listing at either level, and a hard closure anyway. A Federal Register search on 2026-09-15 for Pisaster returned three documents, none of them a listing action for this species. The WDFW printable list of state listed and candidate species, filed under a 2024-03 path, contains no sea star of any kind; neither WAC 220-610-010 (endangered) nor WAC 220-200-100 (protected wildlife) names one. TAKING IS CLOSED, STATEWIDE, AND THAT IS THE ONLY RULE THAT MATTERS HERE. The chain is short and worth following, because it is not obvious. WAC 220-320-010, the Shellfish Classification rule as last amended by WSR 25-20-117 (filed 10/1/25, effective 11/1/25), lists every species Washington classifies as shellfish: mussels, scallops, clams, oysters, squid, octopus, goose barnacles, shrimp, crab, crawfish, California sea cucumber and the three sea urchins. Two echinoderms are on that list and no sea star is. Sea stars are also absent from WAC 220-200-100 (protected wildlife) and WAC 220-610-010 (endangered species), and from the WDFW printable list of Washington state listed and candidate species, the PDF linked from the WDFW threatened and endangered species page and filed under a 2024-03 path, in which the word star does not appear once. That leaves them squarely inside the definition in WAC 220-311-040(1): unclassified marine invertebrates are species existing in Washington state marine waters in a wild state that have not been classified as food fish, shellfish, game fish, protected wildlife, or endangered species. And WAC 220-311-040(2) says: all Marine Areas are closed to the taking of unclassified marine invertebrates and unclassified marine fish. Violation is punishable under RCW 77.15.380. Note how wide the word take is: RCW 77.08.010(64) defines to take and its derivatives as to kill, injure, harvest, or capture. Injuring one counts. This reading is the plain text of two rules read together rather than a WDFW page that names sea stars, so confirm it with WDFW if you are ever near the line; the corroboration is that NOAA Fisheries states the same conclusion in its 2023 status review, that in Washington and Oregon harvest and collection of sunflower sea stars are not allowed while Alaska, British Columbia, California and Mexico permit recreational harvest. DO NOT PRY IT OFF, MOVE IT, OR TRY TO RESCUE IT. The National Park Service page for tidepooling on the Olympic coast passes on tips from its partners at the Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary, with whom it shares management of the intertidal zone, and two of those lines are about exactly this: rough or excessive handling hurts animals, never force an animal off its spot, you may tear off its feet, or squeeze its organs; and apply the touch test, an animal that resists being removed will cling more tightly, respect what the animal tells you with its body language. The same page says to put a rock back the way it was if you lift it, because leaving a rock belly-up is an almost sure way to kill the animals on both of its faces. A wasting star is not helped by being moved to deeper water, and no agency page opened for this record suggests doing so. NOAA Fisheries was still developing draft handling recommendations for bycaught sunflower sea stars at the time of its 2023 proposed rule, for use in scientific surveys, so there was no published public handling guidance then. What you can usefully do instead is record it: the National Park Service directs observations of healthy or diseased sea stars to www.seastarwasting.org.
species.edible_detail: Not a food, and not legally available to try. Taking is closed in all Washington marine areas, so the question is settled before it is asked. Beyond that, be careful what you conclude from the silence: no page opened for this record documents a human food use of the ochre sea star, and none documents a poisoning from one either. The nearest sourced statement is NOAA Fisheries writing about the related sunflower sea star that market drivers for the species are minimal and human consumption is not known to occur. Absence of a documented food use is not the same as a documented hazard, and this record does not claim one in either direction.

lookalikes.name: Mottled star
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The everyday confusion in Puget Sound, and King County's key says so outright: the mottled star might be confused with the purple sea star but has a greater arm to disc ratio. Measure it. R is the distance from the centre of the animal to an arm tip, r is the distance from the centre to the notch between two arms, and R divided by r is what separates them. King County's species accounts give about 5 to 7.5 for the mottled star and 2.7 to 4 for the ochre star; its dichotomous key states the same split slightly differently, as 5 to 8 against 3 to 4.5. Either way the rule of thumb holds: roughly five or more and it is the mottled star, roughly four or less and it is the ochre star. The backup character is the topside, a netlike arrangement of spines on the ochre star against distinctive mottling with white spines on the other. Getting it wrong carries no legal cost, because both are closed to taking.

lookalikes.name: Short-spined sea star, Pisaster brevispinus
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The one you are most likely to meet on a soft bottom rather than on rock, which describes most of the Silverdale shoreline. King County: it prefers relatively shallow water and a sand or mud bottom where it feeds on clams, can grow to be more than 2 feet across with arms more than 3 inches thick, has somewhat longer arms than the ochre star at a ratio of 2.8 to 5.0, and, the clean character, the purple sea star is never pink. Pink and huge on sand is P. brevispinus.

lookalikes.name: Six-arm sea star, Leptasterias hexactis
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The confusion that catches people looking at small stars. King County: usually between 2 and 3 inches in diameter, one of the smallest sea stars in central and south Puget Sound, and while it resembles a juvenile mottled or purple sea star, the bands on the arms help identify it. Before measuring anything, count arms: six rather than five settles it immediately.

species.season: Present all year. What changes is whether you can see it, which is a tide question rather than a season question: it lives in the intertidal zone and is exposed on low tides. The National Park Service advises that the best tidepooling is on tides below 0, and to arrive at least 30 minutes before the lowest tide. Size is the other thing that varies. In the Washington survey by Eisenlord and colleagues, ochre stars under 75 mm arm radius were treated as juveniles because individuals below that size are not reproductive, and the mean radius in their sites fell from 119 mm to 86 mm after the 2014 wasting outbreak, so a beach of small stars is a young population rather than a different species.
species.habitat: Rocky shore. King County describes it as a medium sized animal found on rocky shores where it feeds primarily on barnacles, and notes that in some years numbers bloom to the extent that large boulders show large white patches where they have eaten the barnacles off, leaving just the cement that held the shells to the rock. It eats mussels as well. NPS photographs it in Olympic tidepools among acorn barnacles and green anemones. Be careful about assuming it on your own beach: no source opened for this record documents ochre stars in Dyes Inlet or on the Silverdale waterfront specifically. King County's key covers central and south Puget Sound, and the nearest documented survey sites in the Eisenlord study were in South Puget Sound, at Titlow Beach, Point Defiance and Ruston Way around Tacoma, plus the San Juan Islands and the outer coast. Look for it where there is hard substrate carrying barnacles and mussels, which in central Kitsap means rock, riprap and pilings rather than the soft inlet floor.
species.uses: Nothing is taken from it. Its use to a person here is that it is the animal the keystone species idea was built on, in this state, and that its collapse and partial recovery are legible on a shoreline you can walk to. Between 31 December 2013 and 17 July 2015, Eisenlord and colleagues surveyed 6,568 ochre stars in fixed plots at 16 sites in the San Juan Islands, South Puget Sound and the Washington outer coast. Peak disease prevalence at individual sites reached 100 percent, the overall mean was 61 percent, populations fell 67 percent on average, driven by 80 percent reductions in adults, and adults in the San Juan Islands dropped to a quarter of pre-outbreak abundance. Adults hit zero at Colin's Cove in the San Juans and at Titlow Beach in South Puget Sound. Not everywhere: the outer coast site gained 38 percent over the same period. Warmer water tracked with disease, with each 1 degree Celsius increase raising the probability of a star being diseased by a factor of 1.30 in their model. WHAT CAUSED IT IS NOT A SETTLED QUESTION, AND THE FEDERAL PAGES DISAGREE WITH EACH OTHER RIGHT NOW. Read in date order, opened 2026-09-15: the USGS Sea Star Wasting Disease topic page still says scientists have found a densovirus that may be responsible, Sea Star Associated Densovirus, which is the 2014 hypothesis. The NPS article Where Are All The Sea Stars (last updated May 7, 2020) already qualifies that: SSaDV was also found in sea star tissues collected as far back as 1942, so it is probably not the whole cause. The NPS Redwood page (last updated December 7, 2020) says the cause is still not clearly understood, though evidence points to a bacterial or viral pathogen. The NPS Southwest Alaska Network page (last updated July 19, 2023) gives a different mechanism again: evidence pointing to bacterial infection resulting from an imbalance in the microbiome, a proliferation of bacteria on the surface reducing oxygen so the star essentially suffocates, with the suffocation not transmissible star to star but the bacteria being so. NOAA Fisheries, in the March 2023 proposed rule, says flatly that despite considerable research the causative agent remains elusive, as does the environmental trigger. Then on August 4, 2025 the USGS Western Fisheries Research Center announced that work led by the Hakai Institute and the University of British Columbia, carried out at the USGS Marrowstone Marine Field Station on Puget Sound, had pinpointed a strain of the bacterium Vibrio pectenicida, published in Nature Ecology and Evolution: they found it in a high proportion of infected stars compared with healthy ones and then reproduced the disease in the lab. Two limits on that result are worth stating rather than rounding off. The paper is titled a causative agent, not the causative agent (Prentice et al. 2025, Nat Ecol Evol 9:1739-1751, strain FHCF-3). And the experiments were done in the sunflower sea star; the 2026 Microbe Profile of V. pectenicida lists how the bacterium is transmitted and how it infects sea stars among its open questions, and cites only temperature association, not demonstrated infection, for Pisaster ochraceus. So: strong new evidence in one species, older federal pages not yet updated, and the mechanism in the other species still open.

species.common_name: Sunflower sea star, also called the sunflower star
species.scientific_name: Pycnopodia helianthoides (Brandt, 1835). ITIS treats this as a valid species, TSN 157274, common name Sunflower Star. NOAA Fisheries states in its status review that the species has no known synonyms and that the validity of the species has not been questioned in the taxonomic literature, which is unusual enough to be worth saying. Phylum Echinodermata, class Asteroidea, order Forcipulatida, family Asteriidae. NOAA's status review, following Stimpson (1861), describes it as the type species of the genus Pycnopodia and as the only known species of the family Pycnopodiidae.
species.form: The biggest and the fastest sea star on this coast, and unmistakable at full size. NOAA Fisheries: among the largest sea stars in the world, reaching over 1 metre in total diameter from ray tip to ray tip, uniquely having 16 to 20 rays. King County, writing about Puget Sound specifically, puts it at up to 80 cm in diameter, the largest found in this region, soft bodied, and able to move across the bottom at 160 cm per minute, more than 5 feet, which makes it the fastest as well. The softness is structural: NOAA describes a greatly reduced dorsal skeleton with no actinal plates. Arm count is not fixed for life. NOAA: very young sunflower sea stars generally have fewer than a dozen arms, and additional arms are added by budding in symmetrical pairs as the individual grows.
species.protected: THIS IS THE ONE WITH A FEDERAL LISTING PROCESS ATTACHED, AND THE EXACT WORDING MATTERS. As of 2026-09-15, reading the NOAA Fisheries species directory page for the sunflower sea star, which NOAA itself last updated on 09/11/2025, the protected status field reads: ESA Proposed - Threatened, Throughout Its Range. Proposed. Not final, and not endangered. The history: NOAA was petitioned in 2021 to list the species; the 90-day finding published at 86 FR 73230 on December 27, 2021; NOAA completed a status review and published a proposed rule to list the species as threatened throughout its range at 88 FR 16212 on March 16, 2023; public hearings were noticed at 88 FR 21600 on April 11, 2023; comments on the proposed rule closed May 15, 2023. A Federal Register search run on 2026-09-15 for Pycnopodia and for sunflower sea star returned no final listing rule, so the proposal has been pending for over three years. NOAA's finding, in its own words, is that the sunflower sea star is likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future throughout its range, while it is not currently in danger of extinction throughout its range. Two consequences people get wrong: NOAA did not propose to designate critical habitat, because it is not currently determinable; and the take prohibitions of ESA section 9 attach automatically to endangered species, not to threatened ones, so NOAA stated that should the proposed listing be finalized, any protective regulations under section 4(d) would be proposed in a separate Federal Register notice. Since the listing is still only proposed, the species is not listed at all yet, so no ESA prohibition attaches to it today. At state level there are none either: the WDFW printable list of state listed and candidate species, filed under a 2024-03 path, names no sea star, and neither does WAC 220-610-010 or WAC 220-200-100. What does protect it in Washington is the fishing rule, not the conservation law. TAKING IS CLOSED, STATEWIDE, AND THAT IS THE ONLY RULE THAT MATTERS HERE. The chain is short and worth following, because it is not obvious. WAC 220-320-010, the Shellfish Classification rule as last amended by WSR 25-20-117 (filed 10/1/25, effective 11/1/25), lists every species Washington classifies as shellfish: mussels, scallops, clams, oysters, squid, octopus, goose barnacles, shrimp, crab, crawfish, California sea cucumber and the three sea urchins. Two echinoderms are on that list and no sea star is. Sea stars are also absent from WAC 220-200-100 (protected wildlife) and WAC 220-610-010 (endangered species), and from the WDFW printable list of Washington state listed and candidate species, the PDF linked from the WDFW threatened and endangered species page and filed under a 2024-03 path, in which the word star does not appear once. That leaves them squarely inside the definition in WAC 220-311-040(1): unclassified marine invertebrates are species existing in Washington state marine waters in a wild state that have not been classified as food fish, shellfish, game fish, protected wildlife, or endangered species. And WAC 220-311-040(2) says: all Marine Areas are closed to the taking of unclassified marine invertebrates and unclassified marine fish. Violation is punishable under RCW 77.15.380. Note how wide the word take is: RCW 77.08.010(64) defines to take and its derivatives as to kill, injure, harvest, or capture. Injuring one counts. This reading is the plain text of two rules read together rather than a WDFW page that names sea stars, so confirm it with WDFW if you are ever near the line; the corroboration is that NOAA Fisheries states the same conclusion in its 2023 status review, that in Washington and Oregon harvest and collection of sunflower sea stars are not allowed while Alaska, British Columbia, California and Mexico permit recreational harvest. DO NOT PRY IT OFF, MOVE IT, OR TRY TO RESCUE IT. The National Park Service page for tidepooling on the Olympic coast passes on tips from its partners at the Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary, with whom it shares management of the intertidal zone, and two of those lines are about exactly this: rough or excessive handling hurts animals, never force an animal off its spot, you may tear off its feet, or squeeze its organs; and apply the touch test, an animal that resists being removed will cling more tightly, respect what the animal tells you with its body language. The same page says to put a rock back the way it was if you lift it, because leaving a rock belly-up is an almost sure way to kill the animals on both of its faces. A wasting star is not helped by being moved to deeper water, and no agency page opened for this record suggests doing so. NOAA Fisheries was still developing draft handling recommendations for bycaught sunflower sea stars at the time of its 2023 proposed rule, for use in scientific surveys, so there was no published public handling guidance then. What you can usefully do instead is record it: the National Park Service directs observations of healthy or diseased sea stars to www.seastarwasting.org.
species.edible_detail: Not a food. NOAA Fisheries, assessing whether harvest is a threat to the species, writes that there are no substantial current or historical fisheries directed at the sunflower sea star, that market drivers for this species are minimal, and that human consumption is not known to occur. Harvest and collection are not allowed in Washington. NOAA does record a curio trade in small dried sunflower stars, predominantly stars under 15.25 cm across, sold without listing species or collection site. No page opened for this record documents a human poisoning from a sea star, and this record makes no toxicity claim in either direction.

lookalikes.name: Sun stars, genera Solaster, Crossaster and Rathbunaster
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The genuine many-armed confusion, and the test is to count. NOAA: other sea stars in the northern Pacific with many arms include several sun stars of the genera Solaster, Crossaster and Rathbunaster, but these generally have 8 to 17 arms as opposed to the 16 to 20 commonly found in the sunflower sea star, and all of the sun stars are considerably smaller and less massive. King County's Puget Sound key splits them the same way by feel as well as count: 9 or 10 arms with smooth skin is Solaster stimpsoni, the striped sun star, which also carries a purple or blue stripe down each arm; more than 10 arms with spiny skin is the sunflower star.

lookalikes.name: A juvenile sunflower sea star taken for a different species
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The trap in the arm-counting rule, and it runs the other way. NOAA: very young sunflower sea stars generally have fewer than a dozen arms, and arms are added by budding in symmetrical pairs as the animal grows. A small star with nine or ten arms is therefore not automatically a sun star. Fall back on the body: the sunflower star is soft and floppy with a greatly reduced skeleton, and the sun stars are firm. Given how rare young sunflower stars now are south of the border with British Columbia, a suspected juvenile is worth reporting rather than resolving on the spot.

lookalikes.name: Ochre sea star and mottled star, the five-armed stars
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Only a problem at a distance or in a bad photograph, and arm count settles it: five against 16 to 20. King County's key makes arm count the very first question for exactly this reason. In the water the difference is also in the way they move; the sunflower star crosses the bottom at up to 160 cm per minute while the ochre star stays put on rock.

species.season: Present year round, but the spawning season is genuinely unsettled in the literature and this record will not pick a winner. NOAA's status review lays out the disagreement, and this record drops the author name where NOAA itself spells one two different ways: a 1921 study reported breeding May through June at Nanaimo, British Columbia; Greer collected broodstock at San Juan Island and reported spawning in March and April; Feder obtained fertilizable eggs from December through June in California; Strathmann gave late March through July, peaking May through June, with some large males spawning into December and January; and Hodin and colleagues suggested the female season in Washington begins November through January and ends April and May, though NOAA notes their animals were lab held under an altered photoperiod. NOAA also flags that no one has followed oocyte development in free-ranging sunflower sea stars. There is one local note with a long history: Kjerskog-Agersborg studied sunflower sea stars in Puget Sound at Bremerton in 1918 and suggested that individuals migrated to shallower water during the spawning season and formed large aggregations then. NOAA presents that as a suggestion supported by the behaviour of other sea stars, not as an established fact for this species.
species.habitat: A habitat generalist, which is why it could be almost anywhere here and why the absence is so stark. NOAA: found along both outer coasts and inside waters, which consist of glacial fjords, sounds and embayments; preferring temperate waters, inhabiting kelp forests and rocky intertidal shoals but regularly found in eelgrass meadows as well; occupying mud, sand, shell, gravel and rocky bottoms while roaming for prey; in the low intertidal and subtidal to a depth of 435 m but most common shallower than 25 m and rare below 120 m. Diet is opportunistic and includes sea urchins, snails, crab, sea cucumbers and other sea stars, and NOAA cites a study finding up to 72 percent of the diet coming from clams at subtidal sites within Puget Sound, so almost every shellfish record in this file is on its menu. The honest local picture, however, is that you are unlikely to see one. NOAA cites a 94.3 percent decline across the range after the 2013 to 2017 wasting outbreak, with the six northern regions of that analysis down 40 to 96 percent and the six regions from Cape Flattery, Washington south to Baja down 99.6 to 100 percent, where the species is now exceptionally rare. For the status review NOAA used three coarser portions: Alaska; coastal British Columbia and the Salish Sea; and everything south of Cape Flattery to Baja. Puget Sound sits in the middle one, which held roughly 17.5 percent of the shallow-water population before the pandemic and was the only portion NOAA found to be a biologically significant portion of the range, with extinction risk assessed as moderate. Recent settlement events have been recorded in the Salish Sea. The current global estimate is nearly 600 million animals, which NOAA notes is less than 10 percent of the estimated abundance before 2013.
species.uses: Nothing is taken from it. Its value here is ecological and diagnostic. USGS describes it as consuming lots of sea urchins, preventing urchins from over-consuming kelp and upsetting entire kelp forest ecosystems, which is the mechanism behind the kelp collapse that followed its disappearance further south. NOAA identifies disease, specifically sea star wasting syndrome, as the single greatest threat affecting the persistence of the species both now and into the foreseeable future, and notes that the most intense loss occurred over just a few years from 2013 through 2017, generally commencing later in more northern parts of the range. Sick stars show abnormally twisted arms, white lesions, loss of body tissue, arm loss, disintegration and death, usually within days. WHAT CAUSED IT IS NOT A SETTLED QUESTION, AND THE FEDERAL PAGES DISAGREE WITH EACH OTHER RIGHT NOW. Read in date order, opened 2026-09-15: the USGS Sea Star Wasting Disease topic page still says scientists have found a densovirus that may be responsible, Sea Star Associated Densovirus, which is the 2014 hypothesis. The NPS article Where Are All The Sea Stars (last updated May 7, 2020) already qualifies that: SSaDV was also found in sea star tissues collected as far back as 1942, so it is probably not the whole cause. The NPS Redwood page (last updated December 7, 2020) says the cause is still not clearly understood, though evidence points to a bacterial or viral pathogen. The NPS Southwest Alaska Network page (last updated July 19, 2023) gives a different mechanism again: evidence pointing to bacterial infection resulting from an imbalance in the microbiome, a proliferation of bacteria on the surface reducing oxygen so the star essentially suffocates, with the suffocation not transmissible star to star but the bacteria being so. NOAA Fisheries, in the March 2023 proposed rule, says flatly that despite considerable research the causative agent remains elusive, as does the environmental trigger. Then on August 4, 2025 the USGS Western Fisheries Research Center announced that work led by the Hakai Institute and the University of British Columbia, carried out at the USGS Marrowstone Marine Field Station on Puget Sound, had pinpointed a strain of the bacterium Vibrio pectenicida, published in Nature Ecology and Evolution: they found it in a high proportion of infected stars compared with healthy ones and then reproduced the disease in the lab. Two limits on that result are worth stating rather than rounding off. The paper is titled a causative agent, not the causative agent (Prentice et al. 2025, Nat Ecol Evol 9:1739-1751, strain FHCF-3). And the experiments were done in the sunflower sea star; the 2026 Microbe Profile of V. pectenicida lists how the bacterium is transmitted and how it infects sea stars among its open questions, and cites only temperature association, not demonstrated infection, for Pisaster ochraceus. So: strong new evidence in one species, older federal pages not yet updated, and the mechanism in the other species still open. If you find one, alive or wasting, that is a genuinely useful observation; the National Park Service directs sightings of healthy or diseased sea stars to www.seastarwasting.org.

species.common_name: Mottled star, also called the mottled sea star
species.scientific_name: Evasterias troscheli (Stimpson, 1862), and the spelling is a real trap. ITIS treats the widely used combination Evasterias troschelii, TSN 157224, as INVALID, flagging it as unavailable, a literature misspelling, and gives Evasterias troscheli, TSN 990379, as the valid name. Nearly every source a reader will meet uses the double-i spelling, including the King County identification key, the National Park Service and the Eisenlord Washington survey, so expect to see troschelii in print and troscheli in a taxonomic database and know they are the same animal. Phylum Echinodermata, class Asteroidea, order Forcipulatida, family Asteriidae, the same family as the ochre and sunflower stars.
species.form: Five arms, but long ones on a small disc, which is the whole identification. King County: the mottling on this sea star is fairly distinctive, it might be confused with the purple sea star but the mottled has a greater arm to disc ratio, about 5 to 7.5 against 2.7 to 4 for the ochre star; usually mottled green, red, brown or orange with white spines. One more detail from the same source that no other star here has: it usually has a commensal scale worm, a small segmented animal riding along in the groove on the underside of an arm.
species.protected: No conservation listing at either level. A Federal Register search on 2026-09-15 for Evasterias returned zero documents, so there is no federal listing action for this species at all. The WDFW printable list of state listed and candidate species, filed under a 2024-03 path, contains no sea star, and neither WAC 220-610-010 nor WAC 220-200-100 names one. TAKING IS CLOSED, STATEWIDE, AND THAT IS THE ONLY RULE THAT MATTERS HERE. The chain is short and worth following, because it is not obvious. WAC 220-320-010, the Shellfish Classification rule as last amended by WSR 25-20-117 (filed 10/1/25, effective 11/1/25), lists every species Washington classifies as shellfish: mussels, scallops, clams, oysters, squid, octopus, goose barnacles, shrimp, crab, crawfish, California sea cucumber and the three sea urchins. Two echinoderms are on that list and no sea star is. Sea stars are also absent from WAC 220-200-100 (protected wildlife) and WAC 220-610-010 (endangered species), and from the WDFW printable list of Washington state listed and candidate species, the PDF linked from the WDFW threatened and endangered species page and filed under a 2024-03 path, in which the word star does not appear once. That leaves them squarely inside the definition in WAC 220-311-040(1): unclassified marine invertebrates are species existing in Washington state marine waters in a wild state that have not been classified as food fish, shellfish, game fish, protected wildlife, or endangered species. And WAC 220-311-040(2) says: all Marine Areas are closed to the taking of unclassified marine invertebrates and unclassified marine fish. Violation is punishable under RCW 77.15.380. Note how wide the word take is: RCW 77.08.010(64) defines to take and its derivatives as to kill, injure, harvest, or capture. Injuring one counts. This reading is the plain text of two rules read together rather than a WDFW page that names sea stars, so confirm it with WDFW if you are ever near the line; the corroboration is that NOAA Fisheries states the same conclusion in its 2023 status review, that in Washington and Oregon harvest and collection of sunflower sea stars are not allowed while Alaska, British Columbia, California and Mexico permit recreational harvest. DO NOT PRY IT OFF, MOVE IT, OR TRY TO RESCUE IT. The National Park Service page for tidepooling on the Olympic coast passes on tips from its partners at the Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary, with whom it shares management of the intertidal zone, and two of those lines are about exactly this: rough or excessive handling hurts animals, never force an animal off its spot, you may tear off its feet, or squeeze its organs; and apply the touch test, an animal that resists being removed will cling more tightly, respect what the animal tells you with its body language. The same page says to put a rock back the way it was if you lift it, because leaving a rock belly-up is an almost sure way to kill the animals on both of its faces. A wasting star is not helped by being moved to deeper water, and no agency page opened for this record suggests doing so. NOAA Fisheries was still developing draft handling recommendations for bycaught sunflower sea stars at the time of its 2023 proposed rule, for use in scientific surveys, so there was no published public handling guidance then. What you can usefully do instead is record it: the National Park Service directs observations of healthy or diseased sea stars to www.seastarwasting.org.
species.edible_detail: Not a food, and taking is closed in all Washington marine areas regardless. No page opened for this record documents a food use of the mottled star, and none documents a poisoning from one. This record makes no toxicity claim in either direction rather than guessing from the silence.

lookalikes.name: Ochre sea star
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The confusion this record exists to fix, named as such in King County's key: the mottled star might be confused with the purple sea star but has a greater arm to disc ratio. Measure R, centre of the animal to an arm tip, and r, centre to the notch between two arms, then divide. King County's species accounts give about 5 to 7.5 for the mottled star and 2.7 to 4 for the ochre star; its own dichotomous key gives the split as 5 to 8 against 3 to 4.5, so the two halves of that document do not agree exactly and this record reports both rather than tidying them. The usable version: around five or more and it is the mottled star, around four or less and it is the ochre star. Colour will not do it, since both come in orange and brown; look instead for mottling with white spines against a netlike arrangement of spines. Neither may be taken, so an error costs nothing legally.

lookalikes.name: Short-spined sea star, Pisaster brevispinus
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The other long-armed five-pointed star on soft bottoms. King County gives it an arm to disc ratio of 2.8 to 5.0, overlapping the low end of the mottled star, so the ratio alone can fail here. Use colour, which for once is diagnostic: P. brevispinus is pink, grows to more than 2 feet across with arms more than 3 inches thick, prefers a sand or mud bottom and feeds on clams. The mottled star is mottled green, red, brown or orange, not pink.

lookalikes.name: Six-arm sea star, Leptasterias hexactis
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: King County notes it resembles a juvenile mottled or purple sea star, which is the case that catches people. Count arms first: six, not five. It is also tiny, usually 2 to 3 inches across, one of the smallest sea stars of central and south Puget Sound, and the bands on its arms are the confirming mark.

species.season: Present all year in the intertidal, seen on the low tides like the others; the National Park Service advises tides below 0 and arriving at least 30 minutes before the low. No source opened for this record gives a spawning or breeding season for this species in Washington, so none is stated here.
species.habitat: King County: usually on rocks and cobble but also found on sand, feeding on clams, jingle shells, barnacles, chitons, sea squirts and snails. That diet and that substrate tolerance put it closer to the mixed shorelines of the inner inlets than the ochre star, which wants barnacle-covered rock, but no source opened for this record documents mottled stars in Dyes Inlet or on the Silverdale waterfront specifically, and this record does not assert them there. It was one of the species hit by the wasting outbreak: Eisenlord and colleagues list the mottled star among the dominant stars affected in Washington State in that outbreak, and the National Park Service reports that in the Gulf of Alaska the once dominant stars killed by the disease, the mottled star among them, continue to be rare or absent, while blood stars and leather stars, apparently unaffected, remain.
species.uses: Nothing is taken from it. It earns its place in this file for two reasons: it is the animal most often mistaken for the ochre star, so a keystone story told without it is a story a reader cannot check on their own beach; and it is a second, independent line on the wasting outbreak. The National Park Service describes the outcome plainly for the Gulf of Alaska: areas devoid of sea stars for multiple years have enabled prey species, such as mussels, to flourish, and the precipitous loss of some species reduced the diversity that once existed, making formerly distinct sea star communities more similar to one another. That is the keystone experiment running by itself, at regional scale, without a crowbar.

species.edible_detail: Needles only, and only boiled into a tea. The USDA plant guide records that Douglas-fir needles were made into a tea and drunk by Isleta Puebloans in New Mexico to treat rheumatism. That is a boiled medicinal preparation, not a food. No part of this tree is documented as a raw food: not the needles, not the inner bark, not the seeds, not the cones. Identify the tree before you brew anything from it. Pacific yew is poisonous, grows in the shade directly underneath Douglas-fir, and carries flat needles of similar size and color. A mature Douglas-fir holds its foliage high in the canopy, so flat conifer foliage you can reach from the ground in this forest is more likely to be yew than Douglas-fir. An infusion is the worst way to get that wrong, because it pulls the poison out of a large mass of leaves into one cup.

lookalikes.name: Pacific yew
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Look for a cone, then check the needle tip. Douglas-fir hangs woody cones 2 to 4 inches long and its needles are blunt, yellowish green, about 1 inch long, and set spirally all round the twig. Pacific yew never makes a woody cone at all; it carries a single hard seed sitting in a soft red cup about a third of an inch long, its leaves are half an inch to an inch long and end in a sharp horny point, and the underside is plain dark green instead of chalky white. Yew is a small crooked shade tree, usually 20 to 40 feet, with very thin scaly purplish bark over reddish inner bark. Eating about 50 to 100 grams of yew leaves can kill an adult, and no effective treatment is reported.

lookalikes.name: Grand fir
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Harmless mix-up. Grand fir needles lie flat in two rows and have two bright silvery white bands on the underside, and its cones stand upright on the top branches instead of hanging down.

lookalikes.name: Western hemlock
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Harmless mix-up. Western hemlock has a limp drooping shoot at the very top of the tree, needles of uneven length lying flat in two rows with two white bands underneath, and small cones under an inch long.

species.season: Evergreen, so the foliage is present in every month. New soft growth flushes in spring.
species.habitat: The dominant tree of Silverdale and central Kitsap County. It fills the second growth forest on nearly every upland slope, ridge and greenbelt, from the bluffs above Dyes Inlet through the interior of the peninsula, and it is the standard large tree left standing in yards and on road margins. It prefers deep, well aerated soil and grows mixed with western hemlock, western redcedar and red alder.
species.uses: Material and fuel: the main construction timber of this region, used for framing lumber, plywood, pilings and railroad ties, burned as firewood, and grown as a Christmas tree. Medicine: a boiled needle tea is recorded as a traditional remedy for rheumatism.

species.edible_detail: Three separate documented uses, each with its own part and preparation. Needles and shoot tips can be steeped as a herbal tea. Leaves and young shoots have been chewed as an emergency food to keep a lost person alive in the woods, which is a survival measure and not a meal. Inner bark was made into a coarse bread by Alaska Native peoples, so it is a processed food and not something to eat off the tree. Pitch from cracks in the bark has been chewed as a gum. Before gathering any flat conifer needle, turn it over: western hemlock needles are blunt with two chalky white bands underneath, while Pacific yew needles are plain green underneath and end in a sharp point, and yew is poisonous. No source gives a safe quantity for hemlock needle tea, and none gives a season or a method for the inner bark beyond the word bread, so treat the bark use as undocumented in practice.
species.toxic: The wood and its dust, not the plant as food. The USDA Forest Products Laboratory lists western hemlock as 'May cause dermatitis', a skin reaction from handling the wood and breathing the sawdust. No source found reports that eating any part of this tree poisons people. Note that the sources which describe it are forest ecology and forest products reviews, so a clean toxicity record here means not reported rather than tested and cleared.

lookalikes.name: Pacific yew
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Turn a needle over. The National Park Service tree key for this region splits the two on exactly this character: needles green underneath means Pacific yew, needles white underneath leads on to hemlock. Western hemlock also has a limp drooping shoot at the very top of the tree and small woody cones. Pacific yew has no woody cone at all, only a single hard seed in a soft red cup, its needle tips are sharp and horny rather than blunt, and its bark is very thin and scaly, purplish outside over reddish inner bark. Yew is poisonous, roughly 50 to 100 grams of leaves can kill an adult, and it is one of only two trees here that tolerate deeper shade than hemlock, so the two grow in the same stands by definition.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Not a tree, and not related. Poison hemlock is a weedy plant in the carrot family growing up to about 12 feet, with hollow hairless stems blotched purple, fern like divided leaves and flat white flower heads, found on roadsides, ditches and waste ground. Washington lists it as a Class B noxious weed and states the entire plant is toxic to animals and humans. The edible hemlock is a conifer tree. If something called hemlock is not a tree, it is not this plant.

lookalikes.name: Western water hemlock
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also not a tree. Water hemlock is a carrot family plant of wet ground, ditch banks and stream edges, and USDA calls it the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America, with the poison concentrated in the tubers. Only a small amount produces poisoning in people. Any hemlock growing out of mud rather than standing as a forest tree is the dangerous one.

lookalikes.name: Grand fir
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Harmless mix-up. Grand fir needles are longer, 2 to 6 cm, mostly even in length, with two bright silvery white bands underneath, and its cones stand upright on the top branches.

species.season: Evergreen, present all year. Shoot tips are soft and new only during the spring growth flush.
species.habitat: Abundant across central Kitsap County and the climax tree of these forests. It takes over shaded, humid second growth stands under and after Douglas-fir, seeds readily onto rotting logs and stumps, and is common in ravines, damp slopes and older greenbelts around Silverdale.
species.uses: Food and medicine as described above. Material: one of the best pulpwoods for paper and paperboard, the principal source of the alpha cellulose fibre used in rayon and cellophane, plus lumber, railway ties, mine timbers and marine piling. The tannin rich bark was used as a tanning agent, a pigment and a red dye.

species.scientific_name: Thuja plicata Donn ex D. Don
species.edible_detail: No part of this tree is documented as human food by any source checked. Do not brew the foliage as tea. Cedar tea is a common folk practice in this region and nothing in the federal record supports it: the leaf oil is bioactive enough to be manufactured into insecticides, which is a reason to keep it out of your mouth rather than a neutral industrial fact.
species.toxic: The wood dust and the leaf oil, not an acute swallowing poison. The USDA Forest Service lists this species as 'May cause bronchial asthma and/or contact dermatitis'. The wood contains plicatic acid, which permanently sensitizes some people and causes western red cedar asthma, the best studied of all wood dust allergies. NIOSH set an eight hour exposure limit of 2.5 mg per cubic meter for this dust, the only wood species given its own federal limit, and estimated that about 5 percent of workers handling it become allergic. Dust at 2 mg per cubic meter measurably reduced lung function, and above 3 mg per cubic meter caused eye irritation. Washington Labor and Industries states there is no way to predict who will become sensitized to plicatic acid. Use dust collection and respiratory protection when sawing, sanding, routing or splitting cedar, and change clothes afterwards so you do not carry the dust home. The leaf oil is manufactured into insecticides and must not be swallowed.

lookalikes.name: Pacific yew
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No source documents a true visual double for western redcedar; it is distinctive. This entry is here because both are evergreens someone might strip foliage from. Western redcedar carries flat sprays of tiny overlapping scale leaves that look like green braid, with stringy fibrous reddish bark that peels in long vertical strips. Pacific yew carries separate flat needles half an inch to an inch long with a sharp tip, thin scaly purplish bark, and a single hard seed in a soft red cup. Yew foliage is poisonous. Neither of these should be brewed as a tea.

species.season: Evergreen, present all year.
species.habitat: Common throughout central Kitsap County wherever the ground stays wet. Look for it in ravines, along stream bottoms including the Clear Creek corridor, in damp hollows and seepage areas, mixed with western hemlock and Douglas-fir, and planted widely in Silverdale yards, parks and hedgerows.
species.uses: Material: the classic rot resistant wood of this region, used for shakes and shingles (hand split shakes last about a century on a roof), exterior siding, fence posts, utility poles and boats. Northwest Coast Indigenous peoples built houses, clothing, dugout canoes and fishing nets from it, and shredded the inner bark fine enough for diapers and cradle padding. The leaf oil goes into perfumes, insecticides, veterinary soaps, shoe polishes and deodorants. Not a food.

species.edible_detail: Emergency food only, and only two parts. The Forest Service states that the inner bark and young shoots may be eaten as emergency food and that a tea can be made from the young shoots, and it calls the food value limited. Nothing else on this tree is food: not the mature needles, not the cones, not the seeds, not the roots, and not the pitch, which is recorded for caulking, chewing and medicine rather than eating. The two parts named here, inner bark and young shoots, are exactly the two parts that are poisonous on Pacific yew, which grows in the same moist forest. Identify the whole tree from its cones before you cut anything off it.

lookalikes.name: Pacific yew
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Identify by the cone, not by the bark, because bark stripping happens at the trunk while the identifying parts are overhead. Sitka spruce is a large canopy tree that hangs papery woody cones and has stiff needles set all round the twig. Pacific yew is a small crooked understory tree, usually 20 to 40 feet, that makes no woody cone at all, only a single hard seed sitting in a soft red cup about a third of an inch long, with flat leaves half an inch to an inch long, sharp tipped, dark green on the underside. The bark test matters most here: yew bark is very thin, about a quarter inch, scaly and purplish outside over reddish or purplish inner bark. If you cut in and the inner bark is red or purple on a small contorted tree, stop. Roughly 50 to 100 grams of yew leaves can kill an adult and no effective treatment is reported. Never cut bark from a conifer you cannot name with certainty.

lookalikes.name: Western hemlock
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Harmless mix-up, and a common one, since both grow here. Western hemlock has a limp drooping shoot at the top of the tree, soft blunt needles of uneven length in flat rows with white bands underneath, and small cones under an inch.

lookalikes.name: Grand fir
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Harmless mix-up. Grand fir needles are flat, 2 to 6 cm, silvery white underneath, and its cones sit upright on the top branches rather than hanging.

species.season: Evergreen, present all year. Young shoots exist only during the spring growth flush. No source gives a season for stripping the inner bark, so that harvest window is unknown.
species.habitat: Uncommon in central Kitsap County compared with the outer coast, and tied to salt influenced and consistently wet ground. Look for it near the shoreline of Dyes Inlet and Hood Canal, on the lower ends of stream corridors, and in damp bottomland with deep moist soil. It tolerates salty ocean spray, so the shore side of a bluff is the place to expect it.
species.uses: Food as described above, and only as an emergency. Material: aircraft structure in both World Wars, and now wind turbine blades, sailboat masts, ladders, oars, musical instrument soundboards, timber, pulp and plywood. Indigenous peoples wove the roots into baskets and used the pitch to waterproof canoes.

species.scientific_name: Abies grandis (Douglas ex D. Don) Lindl.
species.edible_detail: Not a food. One ingested preparation is documented: the needles were boiled to make a medicinal tea for colds, and a Salish decoction was made from the branches and cones for respiratory ailments. Both are boiled medicinal infusions. No part of this tree is documented as a raw food, and no source gives a safe quantity. Because needle tea is the one use here, the Pacific yew warning below is the load bearing part of this entry: yew grows in the same wet lowland forest, USDA even names a grand fir and Pacific yew habitat type, and yew foliage will kill you.

lookalikes.name: Pacific yew
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Turn the needle over first. Grand fir needles are 2 to 6 cm, flat, blunt, and strongly waxy and silvery white on the underside, with 5 to 7 rows of breathing pores on each side of the midrib below and none on the top surface, so the underside reads as two bright silver bands. Pacific yew leaves are half an inch to an inch, sharp tipped, and dark green underneath with no silver bands. Grand fir bears upright cones 6 to 12 cm on the top branches only, and its bark is smooth and gray, turning brown and furrowed with age. Yew bears no cone at all, only a single hard seed in a soft red cup, and its bark is very thin, scaly and purplish over reddish inner bark. Rule to carry: if there are no two silver white bands on the needle underside, do not put it in your mouth. Be aware that the ornamental Japanese yew in local hedges does have two pale yellowish bands underneath, so use the cone test as well: no cone means no tea.

lookalikes.name: Pacific silver fir
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Harmless mix-up and a genuinely close one. USDA separates them by bud scales slightly hairy or smooth on grand fir against densely hairy on Pacific silver fir, the upper surface of the twig easily visible on grand fir against hidden by the needles on silver fir, and variably colored mature cones on grand fir against purple on silver fir. Pacific silver fir is mostly a mountain tree and is not expected at Silverdale elevations.

lookalikes.name: Douglas-fir
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Harmless mix-up. Douglas-fir needles stand out all round the twig rather than lying in two flat rows, and its cones hang down instead of standing upright.

species.season: Evergreen, present all year. New soft growth flushes in spring.
species.habitat: Scattered through central Kitsap County on moist valley bottoms and damp lower slopes rather than on dry ridges. Look for it in the wetter parts of second growth forest alongside western hemlock and western redcedar, and along the flatter ground near stream corridors. It is also planted as a Christmas tree and a yard tree in Silverdale.
species.uses: Medicine: a boiled needle tea for colds, and a branch and cone decoction for respiratory ailments. Material: the wood takes glue well and has low shrinkage, so it is used for pulp and light duty lumber, and the species is grown commercially for Christmas trees. Indigenous peoples used pitch from the bark blisters to finish wooden items, burned the boughs as incense, and used dried crushed needles as a baby powder.

species.scientific_name: Pinus contorta Douglas ex Loudon var. contorta
species.edible_detail: Inner bark only, and boiled. The Forest Service records that Native Americans boiled the inner bark of shore pine for food. No source describes the preparation in any more detail than that, and no source gives a harvest season, so do not treat this as a worked out recipe. The serious risk is not the pine, it is what else you might cut into: yew bark is lethal, and bark stripping is done at the trunk where the needles and cones that identify the tree are out of sight overhead. Confirm the tree from its foliage and cones before a knife touches it.

lookalikes.name: Pacific yew
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Check all three of these on the standing tree before cutting any bark. Needles: shore pine carries its needles in bound pairs, two to a bundle; yew needles are single and flat, in two flat rows, sharp tipped, dark green underneath. Cones: shore pine has woody cones; yew has none at all, only a soft red cup holding one hard seed. Bark: mature shore pine bark is thick and furrowed, while yew bark is very thin, about a quarter inch, scaly and purplish outside over reddish or purplish inner bark. The bark test is the unreliable one on young thin barked stems, which is exactly the size a bark harvester prefers, so never identify by bark alone. Yew poisoning causes collapse and death by cardiac failure, warning signs may last only minutes, and roughly 50 to 100 grams of leaves is fatal to an adult. If yew ingestion is suspected, call the poison center at 1-800-222-1222 immediately.

lookalikes.name: Ornamental yew hedges (English, Japanese and Anglo-Japanese yew)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Shore pine is a common planted landscape tree in Puget Sound yards, and clipped yew is one of the most common hedge and foundation shrubs in the same yards. USDA states that all species of yew are highly toxic and that all parts of the plant, including dried leaves, wood and berries, are toxic. Same tests as above: paired needles and woody cones mean pine, single flat needles and a red seed cup mean yew. Never harvest bark or foliage from a landscape shrub.

lookalikes.name: Douglas-fir
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Harmless mix-up. Douglas-fir needles are single rather than bundled in pairs, and its cones hang down from the upper crown.

species.season: Evergreen, present all year. No source gives a harvest season for the inner bark, so that window is unknown.
species.habitat: In central Kitsap County look for it on the two extremes of wet and exposed: peat bogs and boggy flats, and thin soiled saltwater bluffs and headlands above Dyes Inlet and Hood Canal where the wind keeps other conifers down. It is also widely planted as a tough, low, twisted ornamental in Silverdale yards and parking strips.
species.uses: Food as described above. Fuel: the lightweight wood is used mainly as firewood. Material and land use: watershed protection and dune stabilisation. Medicine: pitch was used to treat wounds and buds to soothe sore throats.

species.form: tree (conifer), small understory tree or sprawling shrub
species.edible_detail: Treat this tree as not food. The only part ever reported as eaten is the soft scarlet cup around the seed, and the support for that is weak and hedged: the Forest Service says that although the seeds are poisonous, the fleshy portions surrounding them were sometimes eaten, and in the same section it also says the fruit is sweet but reportedly poisonous to some species. So the source does not clear the red cup either. The USDA plant guide for the ornamental yews states flatly that all parts of the plant, including dried leaves, wood and berries, are toxic. The poisonous seed sits inside the only part anyone claims is edible, no preparation step removes it, and a single crushed or chewed seed can kill. There is no version of eating this plant that is safe to teach, so this entry gives none.
species.toxic: All of it except possibly the soft red cup, and treat that as poisonous too. The toxic compounds are taxine alkaloids (the NIH also lists taxol). Seeds are the worst: the poison is in most parts of the yew plant but the highest amount is in the seeds. Foliage and bark must be treated as poisonous as well. USDA states that all species of yew are highly toxic, that very little material is needed to cause severe illness or death, and that in adult humans 50 to 100 grams of yew leaves are enough to be fatal. Dried leaves and wood stay toxic, and the plant is poisonous in all seasons. The poison stops the heart: death is from cardiac failure, and warning signs may appear only minutes before sudden death, so there is often no time to treat. Symptoms include stomach pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, dizziness, dilated pupils, muscle weakness, tremor, difficulty breathing, blue lips, confusion, convulsions, a slow, fast or irregular heartbeat, rapid collapse and coma. Note one trap in the older forestry sources: they say Pacific yew is reportedly toxic to livestock but that conclusive evidence is lacking, and that livestock in some areas browse it freely. That is a statement about cattle, not about you, and the same sources state plainly that the closely related English yew is poisonous to cattle, horses, sheep, rabbits and man. If you suspect anyone has eaten any part of a yew, call the poison center at 1-800-222-1222 immediately.

lookalikes.name: English yew, Japanese yew and Anglo-Japanese yew (the ornamental hedge yews)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Near identical evergreen shrubs and small trees carrying the same red fleshy seed cup, planted as hedges and foundation shrubs all over Puget Sound, including Silverdale yards, schools and car parks. The plants were long treated as one species, and older names list English yew as a synonym of Pacific yew. All of them are lethal, and USDA calls yew one of the most toxic of all poisonous plants. You do not need to tell them apart: any yew-like shrub in a yard, hedge or landscaped bed should be assumed to be a yew and left alone. The livestock hedge in the forestry sources does not apply to these at all.

lookalikes.name: Western hemlock
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The confusion that matters, because hemlock needles and shoot tips are gathered for tea and yew grows in hemlock's own understory at arm height. Hemlock needles are blunt with two chalky white bands underneath; yew needles are sharp tipped and plain dark green underneath. Hemlock has a drooping shoot at the top of the tree and small woody cones; yew has no cone at all.

lookalikes.name: Grand fir
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both are flat needled shade tolerant conifers of wet lowland forest, and USDA names a grand fir and Pacific yew habitat type, so they grow together. Grand fir needles are 2 to 6 cm with two bright silvery white bands underneath and upright cones on the top branches; yew needles are shorter, sharp tipped, dark green underneath, with no cone.

lookalikes.name: Douglas-fir
