lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Yew grows directly beneath Douglas-fir; in one western Oregon survey Douglas-fir was present on 89 percent of the plots where yew was tallied. Douglas-fir needles are blunt, about an inch, and spiral all round the twig, and it hangs woody cones 2 to 4 inches long. A mature Douglas-fir keeps its foliage high overhead, so flat conifer foliage you can reach in a Douglas-fir stand is more likely to be yew.

lookalikes.name: Sitka spruce
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both occupy moist coastal forest, and spruce inner bark and shoots are gathered as emergency food, which is the dangerous overlap. Sitka spruce is a large canopy tree with woody cones and thick bark; yew is a small crooked understory tree, 20 to 40 feet, with no cone and very thin purplish scaly bark over red inner bark.

species.season: Evergreen, so the foliage is dangerous in every month of the year, and USDA notes yew poisoning of animals is most common in winter when the evergreen foliage is one of the few green things left. The red seed cups appear later in the growing season and ripen within a single season.
species.habitat: Cool, moist, shaded forest in central Kitsap County: the understory beneath western hemlock, Douglas-fir, western redcedar and grand fir, especially on moist flats near streams and in shaded ravines. It is one of the most shade tolerant trees here, so it survives deep in closed canopy stands where little else does. Confirmed for western Washington and the Olympic Peninsula; a Kitsap County specific occurrence record has not been pulled, so treat its presence as likely rather than documented. Ornamental yews in yards and hedges are certain to be present and are just as poisonous.
species.uses: Medicine, in an industrial sense only, not something to attempt yourself: the bark contains taxol, a cancer drug, and the extraction took roughly 20,000 pounds of bark to yield 2.2 pounds of taxol, which is why leaf based extraction was developed instead. The wood is hard, fine grained and was carved for bows and tools. Not food, and not a home remedy.

species.edible_detail: Inner bark only, and only processed. The documented use is drying the inner bark, grinding it to a powder, and using it as a thickener in soups or mixing it with cereals when making bread. Treat it as a famine extender, not a raw food and not a bulk staple. No food use is documented for the leaves, catkins, cones or sap. Two conditions ride with this. First, the drying and grinding is load bearing rather than stylistic: infusions of the same bark were taken as a laxative, so the same part is purgative at infusion strength. Second, the bark is a salicylate, chemically close to aspirin, so anyone who must avoid aspirin must avoid this. No source gives a harvest season, so that window is unknown.
species.toxic: The bark, as a salicylate dose rather than as a poison. Red alder contains salicin, which is chemically closely related to acetylsalicylic acid, better known as aspirin. Treat any alder bark preparation as taking aspirin. Do not give it to children or teenagers during or after influenza, chickenpox or any viral illness, because of the risk of Reye syndrome, which the CDC and the Surgeon General advised against salicylates for. Avoid it with a known aspirin or salicylate sensitivity, and avoid it alongside blood thinning or antiplatelet medication or other salicylate products. Bark infusions are documented as a laxative. No quantitative salicin figure for this species was found, so no dose guidance can be given.

lookalikes.name: White alder
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Out of range here and not toxic, but it is the one tree USDA says is hard to tell from red alder. White alder lacks the red inner bark and the rolled leaf margins. It grows inland, reaching north only to about Chelan County, so it should not turn up in Kitsap County at all. Red alder field marks at Silverdale: thin smooth ashy gray outer bark, usually patched with white lichen; reddish brown inner bark; leaves 6 to 15 cm, dark green, broadly oval with a pointed tip, edges serrated or softly lobed and rolled slightly under, rusty and softly hairy underneath.

lookalikes.name: Cascara
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Listed as a caution, not as a documented confusion. Cascara is a native small tree of the same moist lowland woods with oval, strongly pinnate veined leaves, and its bark is a powerful laxative that the FDA removed from over the counter sale. Both trees are harvested for bark, so tell them apart before cutting: red alder has woody cone like catkins hanging on it year round, which cascara never has, plus the ashy white lichened bark and the rolled leaf edges above. No source documents anyone actually mixing these two up, so treat this as a reason to identify carefully rather than as a known trap.

lookalikes.name: Bigleaf maple
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Harmless mix-up in the same wet woods. Maple leaves are opposite each other on the twig and deeply lobed like a hand; alder leaves are alternate, oval and merely toothed.

species.season: Leaves from spring to autumn; the tree is bare in winter but the woody catkin cones stay on it year round, which makes it identifiable in any month. No documented season for harvesting the inner bark.
species.habitat: Everywhere disturbed and damp in central Kitsap County, and one of the easiest trees to find around Silverdale. It colonises roadsides, clearcuts, old fill, landslide scars and the edges of parking areas, and lines stream banks including the Clear Creek corridor and the wet ground at the head of Dyes Inlet. It grows in pure stands or mixed into Douglas-fir and western hemlock forest.
species.uses: Food and medicine as described above, both conditional. Material: furniture, cabinetry and paper, and a red dye extracted from the inner bark that was used to color fishing nets so fish could not see them. Fuel: red alder coals are the standard wood for smoking salmon in this region. Land use: it fixes nitrogen, roughly 40 to 300 pounds per acre per year, which is why it enriches soil for the conifers that follow it.

species.edible_detail: Sap, boiled down into syrup. The Forest Service states the sap can be rendered into maple syrup although the yield is less than that of sugar maple, and WSU Extension supports a real commercial bigleaf maple syrup industry in Washington, so this is a genuine local food. Two conditions. First, timing: the sap only runs in response to freeze and thaw cycles, so there is a winter window and no sap to collect outside it; tapping in summer gets you nothing. Second, quantity: the sap carries less sugar than eastern sugar maple, so it takes more sap for the same syrup. The boiling here concentrates the sap, it does not detoxify anything, and raw bigleaf maple sap is not poisonous. WSU also records that the flowers, which emerge in early spring, are edible and were used as an early season food.

lookalikes.name: Other native maples (vine maple and Douglas maple)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: All three Washington native maples are safely tappable, so mixing them up costs you yield, not safety. Bigleaf maple leaves are very large with 5 deep lobes and it grows into a full sized tree; vine maple leaves are nearly circular with 7 to 9 lobes and only 3 to 6 cm long, on a sprawling shrub or small tree; Douglas maple has 3 to 5 lobes.

lookalikes.name: Sycamore maple
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is a warning about the part, not about the tree. Sycamore maple is a non-native maple naturalised in the Pacific Northwest whose seeds and seedlings carry hypoglycin A, the same toxin that makes unripe ackee fruit fatal. The safe rule needs no identification at all: do not eat the seeds or the seedlings of any maple. Tapping sap and picking flowers from a correctly identified bigleaf maple is unaffected, since no maple sap has ever been shown to carry that toxin.

species.season: Sap runs only in winter, during freeze and thaw cycles; there is nothing to collect outside that window. Flowers in early spring. Leaves from spring until they drop in autumn.
species.habitat: Common through central Kitsap County in moist woods, ravines and along stream corridors, including the Clear Creek bottomland and the damp lower slopes above Dyes Inlet. It is also a very common large yard and street tree in Silverdale, usually the one dropping leaves the size of a dinner plate.
species.uses: Food: sap boiled into syrup, and edible early spring flowers. Material: lumber, furniture, flooring and veneer, and it is planted as an ornamental. Indigenous peoples used branches and bark for rope, the wood for canoe paddles and utensils, and the shoots for basketry. Ecology: the early flowers are an important first food for pollinators.

species.edible_detail: No human food use is documented for this species by any source checked. Do not transfer bigleaf maple's food uses onto it: the recorded Pacific Northwest maple foods, fresh sap and edible early spring flowers, belong to bigleaf maple, Acer macrophyllum, and no source extends them to vine maple. It is not known to be poisonous either, it is simply not documented as a food.

lookalikes.name: Bigleaf maple
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Identification only, no hazard either way. Vine maple leaves are round to heart shaped, palmately 7 to 9 lobed, toothed, and only 3 to 6 cm long, on a sprawling multi stemmed shrub or small tree. Bigleaf maple leaves are far larger with 5 deep lobes, on a full sized forest tree.

lookalikes.name: Douglas maple
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Identification only. Douglas maple leaves have 3 to 5 lobes against vine maple's 7 to 9.

lookalikes.name: Devil's club
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Not a poisoning risk, an injury risk, and worth knowing because it carries big maple shaped leaves in the same wet shady understory. The Forest Service says its spines coat every exposed surface of the plant except the roots and berries, and that even the leaves are covered with numerous spines, so densely crowded on the stem that they compete for space. They are brittle and break off in the skin. Vine maple stems are smooth and its leaves grow in opposing pairs; devil's club leaves alternate along the stem and the whole plant is obviously spiny. Do not grab an unidentified maple leaved stem in a wet Pacific Northwest understory.

species.season: Leafs out in spring, colors and drops in autumn, bare stems through winter.
species.habitat: Very common in the shaded understory of central Kitsap County forest, under Douglas-fir, western hemlock and western redcedar, and along stream banks and forest openings including the Clear Creek corridor. In the open it forms a dense shrub or small tree up to about 30 feet; in deep conifer shade the stems sprawl along the ground and root where they touch soil, which is where the name comes from.
species.uses: Material: Indigenous peoples called it the basket tree and wove baskets from its long straight stems, and carved the wood into spoons and bowls. It is now widely planted as an ornamental and has no commercial timber value. Not a food. It is important browse for black-tailed deer and elk, and for cattle and sheep, which is itself good evidence that it is not generally poisonous.

species.scientific_name: Populus trichocarpa Torr. & A. Gray ex Hook. (USDA PLANTS and Forest Service FEIS render this as Populus balsamifera L. ssp. trichocarpa (Torr. & A. Gray ex Hook.) Brayshaw)
species.edible_detail: No part of this tree is documented as human food by any source checked. Note one specific trap: the inner bark of black cottonwood was used, but the documented use is making soap, not food. Do not let a note about Indigenous inner bark use get read as an edibility claim. The bud resin has documented medicinal use for sore throats, coughs, lung pain and rheumatism, which is a preparation rather than a food.

lookalikes.name: none in this region
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No toxic double is documented for black cottonwood. The trees you might confuse it with here are quaking aspen, willows, red alder and bigleaf maple, none of which are poisonous. The real danger of this species is physical, not chemical, and the edible and toxic fields do not capture it: this is the classic widowmaker tree of Puget Sound bottomland. The Forest Service documents at least 70 fungal species causing decay in cottonwood, and notes that ice storms and heavy snowfall cause considerable breakage and permanent bending, with wind damage common where cottonwoods stand taller than the vegetation around them. Heart rot is common in mature stands, so a sound looking trunk can be hollow. Do not pitch a camp, tarp or shelter under a mature black cottonwood, and treat felling or limbing one as high risk work.

species.season: Leafs out in spring, sheds its cottony seed fluff in early summer, drops leaves in autumn, bare in winter.
species.habitat: Wet bottomland in central Kitsap County: floodplains, river and creek bars, the lower ends of stream corridors and the wet flats near the head of Dyes Inlet. It is an early coloniser of disturbed wet ground and one of the first big trees to appear on new gravel. Look for the tallest, fastest growing broadleaf tree in a wet spot.
species.uses: Material and fuel: high grade paper, biomass for energy, pallets, boxes and crates, and it is planted in restoration work for its fast growth and ability to resprout. Medicine: resin from the buds was used for sore throats, coughs, lung pain and rheumatism. The inner bark was made into soap. Not a food.

species.edible_detail: Ripe berries only, and in small quantities if eaten raw. The Forest Service says the fruit can be eaten raw, boiled or steamed, and that berries keep a long time if boiled and dried. The fuller record adds the condition the shorter one leaves out: the USDA plant guide says fresh berries were eaten in small quantities, probably because the high tannin content makes them astringent, and that the Miwok chewed fresh or dried berries for flavor but did not swallow them. Most often the berries were processed rather than eaten raw, pounded and leached with hot water into an unfermented cider, or cooked and dried for later. So the honest version is: not sweet, astringent, a few at a time raw, better cooked or made into cider. Each berry holds about 20 hard seeds in a mealy pulp; the traditional cider method strains them out and no source says whether swallowing them is safe. Identify by the tree, never by the berry alone.

lookalikes.name: English holly
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The most likely dangerous mix-up here, because English holly is one of the most common invasive plants in western Washington forest understories and it is red berried and evergreen like madrone. Washington's Noxious Weed Control Board lists it as toxic to humans and as a Class C noxious weed. Tell them apart at the plant, not at the berry: holly is a shrub to about 30 feet with stiff deep green waxy leaves carrying sharp spines that alternate direction along the leaf edge, dark furrowed or green woody stems, and smooth glossy red berries in tight clusters that hang on through winter. Madrone is a tree with smooth bark that peels in thin sheets off a polished orange-red trunk, large leathery untoothed evergreen leaves, and bumpy scarlet berries 8 to 12 mm in loose drooping clusters.

lookalikes.name: Pacific yew
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also red fruited, also evergreen, and lethal. Yew is a conifer with narrow flat needles half an inch to an inch long and thin scaly purplish bark; its red part is a soft open ended cup with one hard seed visible inside it, not a solid berry. Madrone is broadleaved with large flat leathery leaves and peeling orange-red bark. They look nothing alike at the tree and only vaguely alike at the fruit, which is exactly why you check the tree.

lookalikes.name: none in this region (for madrone itself)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No authority documents a true look-alike for the madrone tree; it is genuinely distinctive. Confirm by three things together: bark peeling in thin sheets off a smooth tan-orange trunk, large leathery evergreen leaves, and bumpy scarlet-orange berries 8 to 12 mm in loose drooping clusters with mealy pulp and about 20 hard seeds. The entries above exist because other red fleshy fruits grow in the same county, not because they resemble this tree.

species.season: Berries ripen from early autumn until December or January; seed collectors gather the fruit from October to December. The tree is evergreen, so the leaves are there all year. Those dates are range-wide from USDA, not a Silverdale specific record.
species.habitat: Dry, sunny, thin soiled ground, which around Silverdale means the saltwater bluffs and south and west facing slopes above Dyes Inlet and Hood Canal. It is characteristic of exposed shoreline bluffs and rocky gravelly banks rather than the damp shaded interior forest, and it is also planted as an ornamental in Silverdale yards.
species.uses: Food: berries as described above, historically eaten by West Coast tribes fresh, cooked and dried, or leached into an unfermented cider. Material: the bark was used for tanning leather, the bulbous roots were carved into eating utensils, and berries were strung into necklaces and used as fishing bait. The peeling red bark is the easiest field mark in the region.

species.edible_detail: Acorns only, and only after the tannins are leached out. Shell the acorns, then soak or repeatedly rinse the meats in water until they no longer taste bitter, then dry and grind them into meal for bread or soup. Salish groups of the Puget Sound ate Oregon white oak acorns after the bitter tannins were removed by soaking; elsewhere acorns were dried, ground into meal and made into bread or soup. Unleached acorns are bitter and astringent and must not be eaten. No other part of the tree is food.
species.toxic: Tannin in the acorns and leaves is a toxin, not just a bitter taste. USDA Agricultural Research Service identifies the oak toxin as most likely a gallotannin or a combination of gallic acid and tannic acid, lists acorns, young browse, sprouts, mature foliage on felled trees and fallen leaves among the parts that poison, and describes the result as severe enterogastritis and nephrosis, meaning violent gut inflammation plus kidney damage. That syndrome is documented in cattle, sheep and occasionally horses, animals that ferment the tannins in the gut. It is NOT documented as the human syndrome, and whether unleached acorns damage human kidneys has not been established either way, so nothing here should be read as a measured human dose. The Forest Service review records one livestock incident directly: 30 of 117 steers became ill grazing Oregon white oak woodland in southern Oregon, with green acorns the likely cause. Leach acorns before eating them.

lookalikes.name: English holly
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Oregon white oak is DECIDUOUS: oblong to egg shaped leaves 8 to 15 cm long with 5 to 7 ROUNDED lobes, no spines anywhere, and acorns sitting in scaly cups. English holly is the opposite in every respect: evergreen, thick glossy leaves with spines along the edge, bright red berries in winter, and never an acorn. The Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board lists English holly as a Class C noxious weed, listed in 2025, and flags it as toxic to humans without giving further detail. Its berries are not food. Do not go looking for a spiny leaved evergreen when you are looking for this oak; there is no native spiny leaved evergreen oak in the Puget Sound.

lookalikes.name: other Pacific Northwest oaks
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Not worth telling apart for safety. Every oak acorn in this region is edible once the tannins are leached, so an oak to oak mix up is not a hazard, and the capped acorn itself has no poisonous twin here. The positive check is simple: a deeply lobed deciduous leaf with rounded lobes, plus a nut sitting in a scaly cup, is an oak.

species.season: Leaves out in spring and drops its leaves in autumn. Acorns ripen and fall in autumn, roughly September into October.
species.habitat: Dry prairies, wooded slopes and rocky bluffs on well drained ground, favouring sites with under 20 inches of rain a year and tolerating gravel and heavy clay. Local and patchy on the Kitsap Peninsula rather than widespread: look on the driest, most open, south facing slopes and old prairie edges, not in the wet conifer forest.
species.uses: Food (leached acorn meal). Hard, heavy wood used for fuel and tool handles. Acorns and cover support deer, squirrels and birds.

species.scientific_name: Frangula purshiana (DC.) A. Gray (= Rhamnus purshiana DC.)
species.form: small tree or tall shrub (deciduous broadleaf)
species.protected: No species protection, but there is a harvest rule. Washington State law counts more than five pounds of cascara bark as a specialized forest product, and a specialized forest products permit is required before harvesting or transporting that much (RCW 76.48.021, RCW 76.48.031).
species.edible_detail: NOT A FOOD. Do not eat any part of it. Cascara is a medicinal purgative, a drug that forces the bowels to empty, and it is not a wild edible in any sense. The medicinal form is processed material, never the living plant: the drug is made from bark that has been dried and AGED. NIH LiverTox describes cascara as an extract from the dried, aged bark, and the Forest Service review carries the same requirement, that bark should be stored as long as possible before being used. Historical bark use is on record, for example the Kootenai and Flathead tribes of western Montana drank a tea brewed from the bark as a laxative, but that is a record of past practice, not a preparation instruction. The ripe fruit is a small purplish black drupe and it is not food either. If you cannot positively identify a dark berry in these woods, do not eat it.
species.toxic: Powerfully cathartic, which is not the same as harmless, and the hazard is worst in FRESH, unaged bark. The Forest Service review records a traditional belief that bark stripped downward acts as a purgative while bark stripped upward acts as an emetic, meaning it makes a person vomit. Combined with the universal requirement to age the bark before use, treat fresh bark as a violent purgative and emetic, not a mild laxative. Even the properly aged drug has documented harm. NIH LiverTox lists abdominal cramps and electrolyte imbalance as side effects; records that long term use or abuse leads to cathartic colon, with diarrhea, cramps, weight loss and darkened pigmentation of the colon lining; and states that cascara can cause clinically apparent liver injury when used in high doses for longer than recommended periods, with severe cases of acute liver failure, fluid in the abdomen and portal hypertension described. The FDA does not accept it as an over the counter laxative: 21 CFR 310.545(a)(12)(iv)(C) lists cascara sagrada ingredients (casanthranol, cascara fluidextract aromatic, cascara sagrada bark, cascara sagrada extract, cascara sagrada fluidextract) among active ingredients for which there are inadequate data to establish general recognition of safety and effectiveness, with a compliance date of November 5, 2002; such products are treated as unapproved new drugs and are misbranded. The bark contains anthraquinone derivatives, tannin, resins, starch, glucose and other compounds, and chewed bark tastes extremely bitter and may temporarily numb the taste buds. Two further effects are REPORTED rather than established, and the source hedges both: the Forest Service review says the flesh of some animals that have eaten the drupes is said to retain some of the purgative properties, and that apparently the laxative effect can be transferred through the skin if the plant is handled for a long time.

lookalikes.name: salal
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The realistic local mistake: both carry dark berries in the same woods, and salal is a common wild food. Salal is a low evergreen shrub with thick, leathery, alternate, finely toothed leaves and hairy dark blue black fruit strung along an arching one sided stalk. Cascara is a tall deciduous shrub or small tree whose thin leaves are 3 to 5 inches long with 10 to 12 pairs of prominent parallel veins running straight out from the midrib, and its fruit is a purplish black drupe about 7.5 mm across containing several seeds. If the veins run in bold parallel pairs and the plant is leafless in winter, it is cascara. Eating it brings on violent purging.

lookalikes.name: bitter cherry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The two grow on the same moist bottomlands. Bitter cherry fruit is RED, 6 to 14 mm, and holds ONE stone; cascara fruit is purplish black, about 7.5 mm, and holds several seeds. Bitter cherry bark is dark brown with horizontal light grey bands and rows of orange lenticels; cascara leaves carry the 10 to 12 pairs of parallel veins that bitter cherry lacks.

lookalikes.name: common buckthorn
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Rhamnus cathartica, introduced in the lower 48 and more strongly cathartic than cascara. Whether it occurs in Kitsap County is not established. In practice it does not matter which buckthorn you are holding: nothing on any of them is food, so treat every buckthorn as a purgative rather than a berry bush.

lookalikes.name: glossy buckthorn
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Frangula alnus, introduced in the lower 48 and, like common buckthorn, more strongly cathartic than cascara. Its presence in Kitsap County is not established. Same rule: no buckthorn is food.

species.season: Leafs out in spring and drops its leaves in autumn. Drupes turn from green through red to purplish black in late summer. Bark was historically collected from mid April to the end of August, which is a note on the old commercial bark trade, not an invitation to harvest.
species.habitat: Lower slopes and moist canyons west of the Cascades, and in this region a moist site indicator commonly found with red alder on moist bottomlands but rarely abundant. Around Silverdale expect it along stream bottoms, damp forest edges and alder dominated second growth.
species.uses: Medicine only, and industrial medicine at that: dried, aged bark was the raw material for commercial laxatives, with five million pounds of Pacific Northwest bark processed in a single year. Not a food and not a material. Birds eat the drupes.

species.scientific_name: Prunus emarginata (Douglas ex Hook.) D. Dietr. (authority varies by database; ITIS gives Prunus emarginata (Douglas) Eaton)
species.edible_detail: FRUIT FLESH ONLY, and it is intensely bitter. The USDA NRCS plant guide records the fruits as edible and best used in jams. The cherry is only 6 to 14 mm across and holds one large stone, so it is mostly stone under a thin layer of flesh; yield is very low and this is a flavouring or famine food, not a calorie source. The conditions that matter: cook the fruit down and strain the stones out WHOLE. Never crush, chew, mill or swallow the stones. Never eat the leaves or twigs, and never brew tea or any infusion from the leaves or twigs. Sourcing note worth knowing: the Forest Service fire review often cited for this species never uses the word edible and records only that birds, rodents and small mammals eat the fruit; the human food record comes from the NRCS plant guide. Positive marks for bitter cherry that none of its dangerous lookalikes share: bark generally smooth and dark brown, marked by interrupted horizontal light grey bands and rows of oblong orange lenticels; deciduous alternate oblong to oval finely toothed leaves rounded at the tip; fragrant flowers in clusters of 5 to 12 in April and May.
species.toxic: SEEDS AND LEAVES ARE CYANOGENIC, meaning they release hydrogen cyanide. The USDA NRCS plant guide for this exact species states that it belongs to a genus that produces the poison hydrogen cyanide, that the toxin is found mainly in the seeds and leaves, that it has a bitter taste, and that it is known to cause respiratory failure and death in some instances. This is documented, not an open question. Measured at genus level in the closely related chokecherry, the cyanogenic compound prunasin reaches 5 percent in new stems and newly initiated leaves and stays above 2.5 percent in leaves right through the summer, while the previous season's growth runs lower at 1.2 to 2.2 percent; half a gram of prunasin can release about 46 mg of hydrogen cyanide, and daily doses of 50 mg of hydrogen cyanide per kilogram of body weight are considered dangerous. The cyanide is set free either inside the plant after frost damage or inside the animal during digestion, so wilted and frost damaged foliage is the classic high risk state. Do not eat, crush or chew the pits; do not eat the foliage; do not make tea or infusion from leaves or twigs. One warning about the source itself: the NRCS paragraph goes on to claim hydrogen cyanide is beneficial in the treatment of cancer. That is a discredited laetrile era claim and is deliberately not repeated here.

lookalikes.name: Pacific yew
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The dangerous one, and it is native and common. Pacific yew grows in the deep shade of the western hemlock, Douglas fir and Pacific silver fir forest that covers Kitsap. Its fruit is a red, fleshy, egg shaped, berry like aril about 1 cm long wrapped around ONE large naked seed: the same colour, shape, size and one seeded structure as a bitter cherry. The Forest Service review notes that although the seeds are poisonous the fleshy part around them was sometimes eaten, and that the closely related English yew is poisonous to cattle, horses, sheep, rabbits and people. The SEED is the lethal part. Tell them apart by the plant, not the fruit: yew is an evergreen with flat needles, and its red cup is open at the end so the hard seed shows through; bitter cherry is deciduous with broad, flat, finely toothed leaves and a closed cherry with the stone buried inside.

lookalikes.name: cascara
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Shares the same moist bottomland habitat exactly. Cascara fruit is a purplish black drupe about 7.5 mm across containing several seeds, not a red one seeded cherry, and cascara leaves are 3 to 5 inches long with 10 to 12 pairs of prominent parallel veins running straight out from the midrib, which bitter cherry leaves do not have. Eating cascara brings on violent purging, and dehydration matters if you are out in the field.

lookalikes.name: spurge laurel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Introduced, a Washington Class B noxious weed, and common in forest understory. The Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board states that all parts of the plant are highly toxic to people and livestock, and that the fruits are little black berries with one seed and are poisonous; a few berries can be fatal to a child. Spurge laurel is EVERGREEN, with thick leathery untoothed leaves bunched toward the branch tips and black fruit. Bitter cherry is deciduous with thin, finely toothed leaves and red fruit.

species.season: Fragrant flowers April to May. Fruit ripens July through September.
species.habitat: Cool, moist foothill, montane and canyon sites; best on well drained loam or sandy loam, but it also holds on dry, exposed hillsides. Around Silverdale look along stream banks, moist second growth edges, old clearings and roadsides.
species.uses: Food (fruit only, cooked and strained, as jam or flavouring). The peeling bark was used as a decorative and binding material. Fruit feeds birds, rodents and small mammals.

species.common_name: California hazelnut (also called California hazel, beaked hazelnut, western beaked hazel)
species.scientific_name: Corylus cornuta Marshall var. californica (A. DC.) Sharp
species.edible_detail: Nuts, raw or roasted. No preparation is needed to make the nut safe. Pick them late summer to early autumn and store them until fully ripe before eating. Pacific Northwest and California tribes ate them raw or roasted, pounded them into cakes with berries, meat or fat, and boiled them to extract oil for flavouring; some used low severity summer or autumn surface fires to roast the fallen nuts and burn the husks off before collecting them. The one real restriction on this plant is allergy, not toxicity. Read the toxic field before eating.
species.toxic: Not toxic. No toxicity is reported for the nuts by any source consulted. It is, however, a MAJOR FOOD ALLERGEN. Hazelnut is one of the nine major food allergens recognised by the FDA, listed as Filbert/Hazelnut, Corylus spp., in the birch family, and this plant is a Corylus. An allergic reaction may progress to anaphylaxis, which constricts the airways in the lungs, drops blood pressure severely into shock, and can suffocate a person by swelling the throat and larynx. Symptoms may appear within a few minutes or take a few hours. A mild reaction on one occasion does not mean the allergy is mild. Anyone with a known tree nut allergy must not eat these.

lookalikes.name: none in this region
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No toxic lookalike is documented for this species. The nut sits in a stiff, hairy husk drawn out into a long beak, and nothing else here does that. The leaves are round to oval with doubly toothed edges and do resemble alder, birch and elm, but none of those is toxic and none of them bears a nut. The rule is simply: no beaked husk, no hazelnut, do not eat it. Related caution recorded honestly rather than asserted: whether the stiff hairs on the green husk irritate skin during handling is not established by any public authority consulted.

species.season: Catkins hang on bare branches in late winter. Nuts fill through summer and are harvested late summer into early autumn.
species.habitat: Moist to dry roadsides, waste ground, fencerows, pastures, thickets, wood edges and the understory of open woodland and forest, on well drained to dry soils in sun or light shade. The plant here is var. californica, which runs continuously from southwestern British Columbia south to south central California; true beaked hazelnut, subsp. cornuta, reaches Washington only as scattered populations in the eastern part of the state. Common along Kitsap forest edges and old roadsides.
species.uses: Food (nuts, and oil pressed or boiled from them). Long straight stems were used for basketry and tool material. Nuts feed squirrels, jays and grouse.

species.protected: No species protection, but there is a harvest rule that matters locally. Washington State law counts more than twenty pounds of cut or picked evergreen foliage as a specialized forest product, and the statute names salal explicitly in that category; a specialized forest products permit is required before harvesting or transporting that much (RCW 76.48.021, RCW 76.48.031). Picking a handful of berries to eat is not affected. Commercial brush picking, which is a real industry on this peninsula, is.
species.edible_detail: FRUIT ONLY. Eaten fresh, dried, or mashed into cakes, and used alone or mixed with other wild berries for jelly and preserves. Sweet, mild and pleasant, sometimes described as bland. No cooking is required; raw consumption is documented. The thing everyone calls a berry is botanically a fleshy calyx, a pseudoberry, dark blue black and covered in tiny hairs. The LEAVES are not covered by this entry: the same Forest Service review notes that many Gaultheria species contain oil of wintergreen, which is methyl salicylate, so do not read a cleared berry as a cleared leaf tea. Honest note on the evidence: no toxicity is documented for salal in any federal or Washington State source consulted, but the Forest Service review is a fire ecology document, so its silence on toxicity is not a toxicological clearance.

lookalikes.name: spurge laurel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Not a documented confusion, but it is an evergreen shrub sharing exactly this forest understory and bearing dark berries. The Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board states that all parts of spurge laurel are highly toxic to people and livestock, that its fruits are little black berries with one seed and are poisonous, and that it is a Class B noxious weed on the state quarantine list. Tell them apart by the LEAF and by where the fruit sits. Spurge laurel leaves are narrowly oval, smooth edged with NO teeth, and bunched at the shoot tips, with the berries tucked in the leaf axils below that bunch. Confirm salal by all three of these together: thick, leathery, alternate leaves 5 to 10 cm long with fine sharp teeth all round the edge; dark blue black fruit 6 to 10 mm covered in tiny hairs; fruit strung along an arching one sided stalk. If the leaves are untoothed and bunched at the branch tips, it is not salal. Do not eat it.

species.season: Flowers May to June. Berries ripen and are picked from midsummer into autumn, roughly July into September, and often hang on the plant afterward. Evergreen, so the leaves are there year round.
species.habitat: One of the most abundant understory shrubs around Silverdale. Coastal conifer forest, forest edges, bluffs and roadsides, tolerant of salt spray, forming dense knee high to head high thickets in maritime country from southeastern Alaska to southern California.
species.uses: Food (fruit). Leaves are a commercially valuable florist green, which is the local brush picking trade. Important winter browse for black tailed deer and Roosevelt elk.

species.scientific_name: Mahonia nervosa (Pursh) Nutt. (= Berberis nervosa Pursh)
species.protected: No species protection, but there is a harvest rule. Washington State law counts more than twenty pounds of cut or picked evergreen foliage as a specialized forest product and names Oregon grape explicitly in that category; a specialized forest products permit is required before harvesting or transporting that much (RCW 76.48.021, RCW 76.48.031). Picking berries to eat is not affected.
species.edible_detail: FRUIT ONLY, and it is tart. The Forest Service review records that Cascade barberry fruits are tart but edible and that Pacific Northwest peoples traditionally ate them; no cooking is required, though most people turn them into jelly. Fruit ripens July to August, so blue berries on a plant well outside that window are a reason to stop and re check the leaf before picking. The ROOTS and inner bark are not covered by this entry: the same source describes medicinal teas made from boiled roots, which is a medicine preparation, not a food. Honest note on the evidence: the Forest Service review is a fire ecology document, so its silence on toxicity is not a toxicological clearance.
species.toxic: None documented for the fruit. The ROOT and INNER BARK are the berberine bearing parts in this genus and are a medicinal preparation, not food. NIH sources name related species (Berberis aquifolium, Berberis vulgaris, Berberis aristata) as berberine plants, and NIH advice on berberine containing preparations is that they not be used by women who are pregnant or breastfeeding and not be given to infants or newborns, because berberine can displace bilirubin from the protein that carries it in blood and let bilirubin build up in an infant's brain. Whether this particular species has ever been measured for berberine content is not established from any public source consulted. Do not make root or bark preparations from it.

lookalikes.name: spurge laurel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The important one, because BERRY COLOUR DOES NOT SEPARATE THEM. Spurge laurel is an evergreen shrub 1.6 to 5 feet tall in the same forest understory, in sun or shade, with small BLACK poisonous berries; the Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board states that all parts of the plant are highly toxic, that it is a Class B noxious weed on the state quarantine list, and its sap causes severe skin and eye irritation, so do not handle it bare handed. The reliable Oregon grape test is the LEAF, not the berry: Oregon grape leaves are pinnately COMPOUND, made of 9 to 19 stiff, spiny, holly like leaflets ranged along a stalk, its flowers are bright yellow and its berries stand in erect clusters at the tip. Spurge laurel leaves are SIMPLE, smooth edged, spineless and narrowly oval, crowded at the shoot tips, its flowers are inconspicuous yellow green, and its berries sit in the leaf axils below the leaf bunch.

lookalikes.name: English holly
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A leaf level confusion: both are evergreen with spiny leaves in forest understory. Per the Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board, holly leaf spines tend to alternate between pointing up and pointing down, while Oregon grape leaf spines all point out or up; holly leaves are SIMPLE while Oregon grape leaves are pinnately compound; and holly grows far taller than any Oregon grape. Holly berries are bright red, Oregon grape berries are blue to black. The weed board lists English holly as a Class C noxious weed, listed in 2025, and flags it as toxic to humans without giving further detail. Do not eat the red berries.

species.season: Yellow flowers in spring. Fruit ripens July to August. Evergreen, so the leaves are there year round.
species.habitat: Submontane to montane forest west of the Cascades and the Sierra Nevada, from southern British Columbia to central California, in sun or shade. Indicates deeper soils, in contrast to tall Oregon grape, which indicates rocky, shallow ground. Common in the conifer understory around Silverdale, usually knee high or lower.
species.uses: Food (fruit, usually as jelly). Roots and inner bark were a traditional medicine and a yellow dye. Fruit feeds small birds and mammals.

species.scientific_name: Mahonia aquifolium (Pursh) Nutt. (= Berberis aquifolium Pursh)
species.protected: No species protection, but there is a harvest rule. Washington State law counts more than twenty pounds of cut or picked evergreen foliage as a specialized forest product and names Oregon grape explicitly in that category; a specialized forest products permit is required before harvesting or transporting that much (RCW 76.48.021, RCW 76.48.031). Picking berries to eat is not affected.
species.edible_detail: FRUIT ONLY, and it is marginal. Berries are edible raw, sour and seedy, ripening to a dusty blue black by early autumn; most people cook them down into jelly rather than eating them by the handful. No preparation is required to make them safe. Roots, stems and inner bark are not food: see the toxic field.
species.toxic: The berries are not toxic and are edible raw. The ROOT, STEM and INNER BARK contain berberine, an isoquinoline alkaloid. NIH LiverTox names Berberis aquifolium, Oregon grape, as a berberine containing plant. NIH LactMed states that berberine can displace bilirubin from serum albumin, the blood protein that carries it, which raises concern for newborns because bilirubin can then build up in an infant's brain and cause brain damage; NIH NCCIH advises that berberine containing preparations not be used by women who are pregnant or breastfeeding and not be given to infants. So do not prepare root, stem or bark teas, tinctures or decoctions for pregnant or breastfeeding women, infants or newborns. In healthy adults the reported berberine side effects are few, mild and transient, and gastrointestinal: nausea, bloating, diarrhea or constipation. How much berberine is in the BERRIES has not been measured in any public source consulted; all the federal sourcing refers to root, bark and stem.

lookalikes.name: English holly
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A LEAF level confusion only, not a berry one. Both are evergreen with spiny leaves in forest understory. The berries are not confusable: English holly berries are bright red, Oregon grape berries are blue to black. Per the Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board, holly leaf spines tend to alternate between pointing up and pointing down while Oregon grape leaf spines all point out or up; holly leaves are simple while Oregon grape leaves are pinnately compound with spiny leaflets on a stalk; and holly greatly exceeds the height of even tall Oregon grape. The weed board lists English holly as a Class C noxious weed, listed in 2025, and flags it as toxic to humans without giving further detail. Do not eat the red berries.

lookalikes.name: spurge laurel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Carried over from the dull Oregon grape entry because the same reasoning applies: this is an evergreen forest understory shrub with BLACK berries, so berry colour gives a forager no protection at all. The Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board states that all parts of spurge laurel are highly toxic and that its fruits are little black berries with one seed and are poisonous; it is a Class B noxious weed on the state quarantine list, and the sap causes severe skin and eye irritation. Separate them by leaf: spurge laurel leaves are SIMPLE, smooth edged, spineless and crowded at the shoot tips; Oregon grape leaves are pinnately COMPOUND with stiff spiny holly like leaflets and wavy spine tipped edges.

species.season: Bright yellow, lightly scented flowers in spring. Berries ripen to a dusty blue black by early autumn. Evergreen.
species.habitat: Shrublands, rocky woods and coniferous forest of western North America, tolerant of both shade and drought, typically 1 to 2 m tall and noticeably taller than dull Oregon grape. Around Silverdale expect it on drier, rockier and more open ground, along roadsides and forest edges, and widely planted in yards.
species.uses: Food (berries, usually as jelly). Roots and inner bark were a traditional medicine and yellow dye. Widely planted as an ornamental and it is Oregon's state flower. Compound leaves up to 25 cm long with wavy spine tipped edges that shift from bronze to bright green and take on red and burgundy in autumn.

species.protected: No species protection, but there is a harvest rule. Washington State law counts more than twenty pounds of cut or picked evergreen foliage as a specialized forest product and names fern explicitly in that category; a specialized forest products permit is required before harvesting or transporting that much (RCW 76.48.021, RCW 76.48.031). This matters here because sword fern fronds are a commercial florist green.
species.edible_detail: NOT ESTABLISHED AS A FOOD, so treat it as not food. The Forest Service review cited for this species contains nothing at all about human consumption of the rhizomes or fronds, raw or cooked, and no public domain authority consulted affirms that it is edible. That is an absence of information rather than a finding that it is poisonous, but the safe reading is the same: do not eat it, and do not upgrade this entry on the strength of a foraging blog.
species.toxic: NOT ASSESSED, which is not the same as none. The Forest Service review is a fire ecology and botany document with no toxicity section at all, and the silence of a fire ecology review is not a finding of non toxicity. No public domain authority consulted affirms that this plant is non toxic to humans.

lookalikes.name: western bracken fern
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The one that matters. Bracken grows in the same western Washington forests, is a documented human carcinogen in every part including the spores, and is the fern whose coiled spring croziers actually get picked and eaten. At the mature frond stage the two are not hard to separate: sword fern fronds are leathery, stay EVERGREEN for several years with the withered old fronds still attached to the rootstock, and arch outward from one point to form a crown, ranging from 20 to 250 cm long. Bracken dies back completely each winter and its spring croziers rise from bare ground. At the coiled crozier stage they are far harder to separate, which is exactly why no fern crozier in Kitsap County should be harvested on the strength of a sword fern identification made from mature fronds.

lookalikes.name: other sword ferns (Polystichum species)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The cited Forest Service review says outright that morphological similarity among Polystichum species may make identification difficult, so do not assume you have pinned the species. It carries no eating risk here, because none of them is established as a food and none should be eaten.

lookalikes.name: common lady fern
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Documented as sharing the same Pacific Northwest forest understory: the Forest Service records western swordfern, deer fern and lady fern dominating the understory together in both old growth and second growth. Lady fern is deciduous and dies back in autumn, while sword fern keeps its leathery fronds through the winter. Lady fern contains filicic acid and may be poisonous to some classes of livestock; neither fern is a food, so the practical rule is the same for both.

species.season: Evergreen: fronds are present all year and individual fronds last several years. New fronds uncoil in spring.
species.habitat: Moist coniferous and mixed evergreen forest at low to middle elevations, from southeastern Alaska to Baja California, sea level to about 7,200 ft. One of the three named Douglas fir and western hemlock forest associations in the Puget Trough is the swordfern type, so this is the default forest floor plant around Silverdale.
species.uses: Material and ornamental: fronds are a commercial florist green and a traditional layer for lining pits, drying racks and storage. No established food or medicine use in the sources consulted.

species.form: fern (deciduous, spreading from a creeping underground stem)
species.protected: No species protection, and it is generally treated as a weed of logged and disturbed ground. Note only that Washington State law counts more than twenty pounds of cut or picked evergreen foliage as a specialized forest product needing a permit, and the statute's list for that category includes fern (RCW 76.48.021, RCW 76.48.031). Nobody should be harvesting this one for food regardless.
species.edible_detail: DO NOT EAT IT. This entry exists precisely because bracken IS eaten in several food traditions and that history is real: the newly emerging croziers, the coiled spring fiddleheads, are picked in spring and consumed fresh or preserved by salting, pickling or sun drying, and the rhizome starch has been used as a substitute for arrowroot. None of that makes it safe. The US Forest Service states that all parts of the plant, including the spores, are carcinogenic, that the growing tips of the fronds are more carcinogenic than the stalks, and that bracken is implicated in some leukemias, bladder cancer, and cancer of the esophagus and stomach in humans. The same source says that boiling young fronds under alkaline conditions makes them SAFER to eat and less bitter. Safer is not safe: no consulted source describes any preparation that removes the cancer risk, and the harm here is a long term one that will not announce itself at dinner. This is not a spring green and it must not be filed alongside one.
species.toxic: CARCINOGENIC. All parts of the plant, including the spores, are carcinogenic, and face masks are recommended for people working in dense bracken; the growing tips of the fronds are more carcinogenic than the stalks. It is implicated in some leukemias, bladder cancer, and cancer of the esophagus and stomach in humans, and has been found mutagenic and carcinogenic in rats and mice. No human dose threshold is given by any consulted source, so no safe quantity can be stated. In livestock the poisoning splits by gut type: horses, pigs and other simple stomached animals develop a thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency within about a month, and vitamin B1 given early is an effective cure; in cattle and sheep the acute poisoning instead attacks the bone marrow, causing anemia and hemorrhaging that is often fatal, and sheep also develop bright blindness and tumours of the jaws, rumen, intestine and liver. The toxins pass into cow's milk. The chemical identity of the toxin is not named by the consulted sources and is deliberately not guessed at here.

lookalikes.name: ostrich fern
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This warning runs the opposite way to a normal lookalike. Ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris) is the fern sold and foraged as edible fiddleheads; bracken is the abundant spring crozier HERE, so a fiddlehead found in Kitsap County is far more likely to be the carcinogen than the food. University of Maine Cooperative Extension describes ostrich fern fiddleheads as about 1 inch in diameter, covered by a brown, papery, scale like coating, with a smooth (not fuzzy) fern stem and a deep U shaped groove down the inside of the stem, and states plainly that not all ferns are edible and that bracken ferns are carcinogenic and should not be consumed. Bracken lacks the deep U shaped groove. Whether ostrich fern even grows wild in Kitsap County is not established. Identify any fiddlehead to species before eating it. And note that even correctly identified ostrich fern must never be eaten raw or undercooked: the same bulletin says boil 15 minutes in lightly salted water or steam 10 to 12 minutes, and that improperly prepared fiddleheads cause diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and headaches within 30 minutes to 12 hours.

lookalikes.name: western sword fern
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Shares the same forests. Sword fern is EVERGREEN, its leathery fronds persist for several years with withered old fronds still attached, and the fronds arch outward from one point to form a crown; bracken dies back completely each winter and its croziers rise singly from bare ground over a creeping underground stem. At the coiled crozier stage in spring the two are much harder to separate, and confusing them in that direction means eating a carcinogen, so do not harvest croziers here at all.

lookalikes.name: common lady fern
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also deciduous, also uncoils in spring in the same damp Kitsap woods, and also not a food. There is no reliable crozier stage separator offered by any consulted federal source. The operative rule is the same one: do not eat fern fiddleheads gathered here.

species.season: Croziers uncoil in spring, roughly April into May. Fronds stand through summer, release spores in late summer, and die back brown after the first hard frosts.
species.habitat: Forests, pastures, open slopes, coastal prairie and riparian ground, on well drained soils that hold water, medium to very rich in nutrients, pH about 5.0 to 6.0. Occurs in every US state except Nebraska. Abundant on logged and disturbed ground all around Puget Sound, and often the dominant plant in clearcuts, road cuts and power line corridors near Silverdale. The western plant is var. pubescens Underw.
species.uses: Not food. Historically used for bedding, thatch and rough mulch, and it is a strong coloniser after fire and logging. It is listed in this dataset mainly so that it can be recognised and avoided.

species.protected: No species protection. Note only that Washington State law counts more than twenty pounds of cut or picked evergreen foliage as a specialized forest product needing a permit, and the statute's list for that category includes fern (RCW 76.48.021, RCW 76.48.031).
species.edible_detail: NOT ESTABLISHED AS A FOOD, and there is a caution attached. The Forest Service review contains nothing on fiddlehead or frond edibility, and the same review states that common ladyfern contains filicic acid and may therefore be poisonous to some classes of livestock. Do not treat it as a food. The only stage at which anyone would try to eat it, the spring crozier, is also the stage at which it is hardest to tell from bracken, which is a documented carcinogen growing in the same county in the same season.
species.toxic: The Forest Service review states that common ladyfern contains filicic acid and therefore may be poisonous to some classes of livestock. That source names no dose, no specific livestock species, and says nothing at all about humans. Human toxicity is UNKNOWN: not established as safe and not established as unsafe.

lookalikes.name: western bracken fern
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The dangerous one, and the reason this field exists. Bracken is abundant in the forests of western Washington, the US Forest Service states that all parts of it including the spores are carcinogenic and that it is implicated in some leukemias, bladder cancer and cancer of the esophagus and stomach in humans, and its newly emerging croziers are the ones people actually pick in spring. So this is an actively foraged carcinogen occupying the same county and the same season as lady fern, and no consulted federal source offers a reliable crozier stage separator between the two. The instruction that follows is blunt: do not eat fern fiddleheads of any kind gathered here.

lookalikes.name: western sword fern
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Documented co-occurrence: the Forest Service records western swordfern, deer fern and lady fern dominating the same forest understory in both old growth and second growth. Sword fern is EVERGREEN, its leathery fronds persisting several years with the withered old ones still attached, while lady fern is deciduous and dies back each autumn. No toxicity or edibility data exists for sword fern in the consulted federal sources, so treat it as unestablished rather than safe.

lookalikes.name: spreading wood fern
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Dryopteris expansa, which the Forest Service system indexes as D. austriaca, is listed as a direct associate of common lady fern and is closely similar in form. Its toxicity is NOT ESTABLISHED from any public domain source consulted; no Forest Service species review exists for it. Treat it as not food, the same as lady fern itself, and do not read the mild rating as a finding of mild harm: it means the mix up carries no eating risk only because neither plant should be eaten.

species.season: Fronds uncoil in spring and die back in autumn. Deciduous, so there is nothing above ground in winter.
species.habitat: Meadows, open thickets, moist woods and occasionally swamps; circumpolar, from Alaska to the Atlantic and south to California, Texas and Florida. Common in forest understory and tolerant of wet soils. Around Silverdale expect it in damp, shaded ground, along seeps and stream sides, growing with sword fern and deer fern. The Puget Sound plant is normally treated as var. cyclosorum, though that has not been verified for Kitsap County specifically.
species.uses: None documented as food or medicine in any source consulted. Ornamental in shade gardens; provides cover and moisture holding ground layer in moist forest understory.

species.edible_detail: Two parts, with different rules. BERRIES: edible raw, no preparation needed, an aggregate of soft drupelets ranging from yellowish through orange to deep red, ripe roughly June into August; too soft to dry. YOUNG SHOOTS: also a documented food, but not eaten as found. Snap the growing sprouts off with your fingers from April to early June, before they turn woody, then PEEL them, and eat raw or, more commonly, cooked by steaming or boiling. Both the large raspberry like fruit and the young shoots were widely eaten by coastal peoples of British Columbia and western Washington, and the fruit is still collected today. Sourcing note worth knowing: the Forest Service fire review often cited for this plant never says the fruit is human food, it records only the fruit description and fire ecology; the human food record comes from the USDA NRCS plant guide and the USDA Forest Service plant profile, and neither of those reports any toxic part.

lookalikes.name: red baneberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A habitat caution rather than a documented confusion: no federal source names baneberry as a salmonberry lookalike, but it is a red fruited poisonous plant of the same moist Kitsap forest, so a beginner reaching for a red berry should know it. The Forest Service describes red baneberry fruit as showy, poisonous, red or occasionally white berries, and names the poison as protoanemonin, found in all parts of the plant and most concentrated in the berries and root, with poisoning symptoms of gastroenteritis, stomach cramps, headache, dizziness, vomiting, diarrhea and circulatory failure. Tell them apart by fruit structure, never by colour. Salmonberry fruit is an aggregate of many small soft drupelets that lifts off its core, like a raspberry. Baneberry fruit is a single smooth glossy berry holding 9 to 16 seeds, and the berries are held apart from each other along an upright stalk. Baneberry leaves are two to three times compound, sharply toothed and lobed; salmonberry leaves are in threes with the terminal leaflet largest.

lookalikes.name: thimbleberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both are edible, so a mix up is harmless. Thimbleberry has thornless stems and big soft maple shaped leaves and its fruit is a shallow cap that pulls free like a thimble; salmonberry has prickly stems, leaves in threes, and a rounder, juicier fruit.

lookalikes.name: trailing blackberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also an edible native Rubus with aggregate drupelet fruit, so a mix up is harmless. It trails along the ground on thin prickly stems rather than standing up in a cane thicket.

species.season: Flowers very early, often February to April, among the first shrubs in these woods to bloom. Berries ripen June to July in the southern part of the range and July to August further north; around Puget Sound expect June into July. Young shoots April to early June.
species.habitat: Moist to wet, water receiving sites in forest and woodland along the Pacific coast from California to Alaska and east to Idaho. Riparian zones, forest openings and nutrient rich soils, typically below 3,000 ft. Forms dense thickets along Kitsap streams and in damp draws.
species.uses: Food (berries; peeled young shoots). Dense thickets stabilise stream banks and give cover to birds and small mammals, and the very early flowers feed hummingbirds. American Indians actively managed salmonberry with fire to improve berry yield.

species.edible_detail: BERRIES, raw, no preparation required. The fruit is a shallow cap of many small red drupelets that pulls free from its core like a thimble, which is where the name comes from. The USDA Forest Service records that the berries are tart and may be eaten raw, or cooked and made into jam or jelly and other foods such as pemmican or fruit leather. Sourcing note worth knowing: the Forest Service fire review often cited for this plant contains no edibility or toxicity information at all; the food record comes from the Forest Service plant profile. The fire review does say something useful, but at genus level only: historical accounts record that Indians in the Willamette Valley burned patches of Rubus spp. in forest openings to encourage fruit production in the first postfire growing season. That is Rubus generally, not thimbleberry specifically, and the sources give no motive beyond fruit production.

lookalikes.name: red baneberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A habitat caution rather than a morphological double, but a well documented one: the Forest Service review for red baneberry explicitly lists thimbleberry among its associated species, so the two genuinely grow together. Red baneberry fruits are showy, poisonous, red or occasionally white berries; the poison is protoanemonin, present in all parts of the plant and most concentrated in the berries and root, and poisoning symptoms are gastroenteritis, stomach cramps, headache, dizziness, vomiting, diarrhea and circulatory failure. Distinguish by fruit and leaf, never by colour. Baneberry berries are individual, smooth and glossy, each holding 9 to 16 seeds, and held apart from one another along an upright stalk; its leaves are alternate and two to three times compound, sharply toothed and lobed. Thimbleberry has a single soft five lobed maple shaped leaf and a matte cap of fused drupelets that lifts off hollow.

lookalikes.name: salmonberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both are edible, so a mix up is harmless. Salmonberry has prickly stems and leaves in threes; thimbleberry stems are thornless and its leaves are big, soft and maple shaped.

lookalikes.name: trailing blackberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Another edible native Rubus, so a mix up is harmless. It trails along the ground on thin prickly stems, while thimbleberry stands up on thornless canes.

lookalikes.name: vine maple
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Shares the leaf outline closely enough to fool people at a glance, but it is a small tree that bears paired winged seeds (samaras), not fruit. If there is no soft red cap of drupelets, it is not thimbleberry.

species.season: Large white flowers May to July. Berries ripen mid to late summer, roughly July into August, and go over quickly once ripe.
species.habitat: Mesic forest and riparian areas, on cool moist sites, particularly abundant in the understory of humid Pacific Northwest forest from sea level to subalpine, and widespread through western North America. Around Silverdale look along shaded roadsides, stream sides, forest edges and old logging tracks.
species.uses: Food (berries). The big soft leaves were used as a wrap and a liner. An erect, multibranched, leafy deciduous shrub to about 10 ft with THORNLESS stems and large maple shaped leaves, which is the quickest way to separate it from the prickly blackberries and salmonberry.

species.common_name: Trailing blackberry (also called Pacific blackberry, California dewberry, Douglasberry)
species.form: low trailing to climbing woody vine with slender, densely prickled stems
species.edible_detail: The fruit is the food. Eat it raw when fully ripe; no preparation is needed. It is sweet and flavorful at maturity. Native peoples ate it fresh in summer and also dried it and combined it with meat into cakes kept for winter. Only the fruit is documented as food. Leaves, canes and roots are not, and the canes are densely prickled.

lookalikes.name: Pacific poison oak
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The Forest Service puts poison oak west of the Cascade Range in Washington, so its range covers this side of the mountains, and it climbs as a woody vine with stems commonly 10 to 30 feet long. Its leaves have three (sometimes five) lobed, oak-shaped leaflets, which is the same low three-leaflet trailing silhouette as a blackberry vine, and the Forest Service lists California blackberry, an old name for this same Rubus ursinus, among the streamside plants poison oak grows beside. So the two can be tangled in one thicket. Use prickles as your test, not leaf shape and not size. Trailing blackberry stems are densely prickled and even the leaves feel prickly. If a three-leaflet trailing vine is completely smooth to the touch, do not touch it again. Poison oak fruit is a cluster of small white berries, never a black knot of tiny juice beads. The whole poison oak plant is coated in an oily resin that causes an itching rash on skin contact, including resin carried on clothing or firewood, and it must never be burned, because the resin vaporizes and the smoke is extremely hazardous to breathe.

lookalikes.name: Bittersweet nightshade (climbing nightshade)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A scrambling vine that twines up through other plants and is common on disturbed sites alongside Himalayan blackberry, so it threads through the very same thickets and fruits in the same season. It contains solanine, which is poisonous to people, and unripe berries hold the most. Tell them apart by the fruit. Nightshade berries are smooth single ovals a few millimeters long, red when ripe, hanging in loose drooping bunches, and the vine carries no prickles at all. A blackberry is a black knot of many small juice beads stuck together, on a prickly cane. Worth knowing around children, who pick at eye level.

lookalikes.name: Himalayan blackberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Introduced, a Washington Class C noxious weed, and also edible, so mixing the two up is not a safety problem. Do not try to separate them by length, because the ranges overlap: Himalayan canes reach 20 to 40 feet and trailing blackberry runs 15 to 20 feet, so this is not a low, slender vine. Use the cane instead. Himalayan canes are thick, woody and strongly angled, green through reddish to purplish red, armed with hooked sharp thorns on broad thick bases, and each leaf has 3 to 5 leaflets, usually 5. Trailing blackberry stems are slender and rounder and carry fine prickles.

species.season: Fruit ripens roughly June through August, earlier on warm open sites.
species.habitat: Prairies, clearings, waste ground, canyons and logged or burned sites, from sea level to middle elevations, so it is widespread in and around Silverdale and central Kitsap County. Tolerates a range of soils and periodic flooding. It increases after logging or fire and then fades again as the forest canopy closes back over it, unlike Himalayan blackberry, which holds on.
species.uses: Food: ripe fruit raw, dried, or made into jam, jelly and pies.

species.form: deciduous shrub, usually 6 to 12 feet tall, with slender bright green sharply angled twigs
species.edible_detail: The berries are the food and are eaten raw. Described as sour but good, or palatable with a pleasant flavor though somewhat dry. Native peoples gathered them fresh or preserved them, and they are still picked locally for pies, jelly, jam and preserves. No cooking or other preparation is required to eat them safely.

lookalikes.name: Yew (Pacific yew in the woods, English yew in yards)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The seeds are poisonous. A yew fruit is a red fleshy cup about 1 centimeter long, carried singly on a woody branch in the same deep Douglas-fir and western hemlock shade, at elevations down to Puget Sound level, and it tastes sweet, so flavor gives you no warning at all. The poison sits in the seed, which you crush the moment you chew. Identify by the plant, never by the fruit. Yew is evergreen, with flat dark green needles along the twig, and its fruit is an open-ended red cup with the seed visible down the hole. Red huckleberry drops its leaves in winter, has small oval leaves rounded at both ends, grows on slender bright green sharply angled twigs, and its berry is a closed translucent sphere with no hole. English yew is a common clipped hedge in Silverdale yards, so this is a suburban hazard as much as a forest one. A red berry on a needled evergreen branch is not a huckleberry.

lookalikes.name: Red baneberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Listed for Washington by the Forest Service and found on cool, moist, rich ground. Its berries are showy and red, occasionally white, and are poisonous; the toxin, protoanemonin, is in every part of the plant and is most concentrated in the berries and the root. Poisoning brings stomach cramps, headache, dizziness, vomiting, diarrhea and circulatory failure. Tell them apart by the whole plant. Baneberry is a soft-stemmed herb only 1 to 3 feet tall, not a woody shrub; its leaves are large, divided two or three times into separate toothed and lobed leaflets, and set alternately one at a time up the stem; and its berries sit in a spike of many berries on a stalk. Red huckleberry is a woody shrub with small simple oval leaves and berries carried singly, one at a time in the leaf joints.

lookalikes.name: Red elderberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A red-fruited shrub of the same moist Puget Sound forests. Its fruits and seeds may cause diarrhea and vomiting in people, especially when not fully ripe, and it is not eaten raw. Easy to separate: elderberry leaves are large and divided into several separate leaflets arranged in opposite pairs along the leaf stalk, and its berries come in dense branched sprays of many. Red huckleberry has small simple undivided leaves and single berries in the leaf joints.

lookalikes.name: Other huckleberries and blueberries
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Several other Vaccinium shrubs grow in the same woods with blue, black or red berries. None of them is toxic, so a mix-up inside this group is not a safety issue, only a flavor one.

species.season: Berries ripen roughly July through September, with the peak in July and August.
species.habitat: Moist to dry conifer and mixed forest, restricted to the coast side of the Cascades, so it is common in Silverdale and central Kitsap County second growth. Its signature habit is growing out of decaying wood: look on mossy rotting logs, snags and old stumps. Plants have been found perched on broken or sawn stumps up to 50 feet off the ground, where birds dropped the seeds. A red berry growing out of the top of a rotting stump in a Kitsap conifer stand is almost certainly this plant.
species.uses: Food: berries raw, or in pies, jelly, jam and preserves.

species.form: evergreen shrub, roughly 1.5 to 15 feet tall, with thick leathery glossy dark green leaves in flat sprays
species.protected: No protection on the plant, but Washington regulates picking its foliage. State law counts huckleberry foliage as cut or picked evergreen foliage, and more than twenty pounds of it is a specialized forest product (RCW 76.48.021). A specialized forest products permit is required before harvesting specialized forest products (RCW 76.48.031). Picking berries for the kitchen is not what this covers; cutting brush for the florist trade is.
species.edible_detail: The berries are the food and are eaten raw. They are sweet and good, though somewhat mealy and with a fairly strong musky flavor. Also cooked, canned, frozen and made into wine, and most of the commercial crop goes into pie filling. No preparation is required to eat them safely.

lookalikes.name: Spurge laurel
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A Washington Class B noxious weed that lives in the same shady forest understory, stands at about the same height (roughly 1.5 to 5 feet), and has the same dark green, glossy, leathery evergreen leaves and small black berries. All parts of it are poisonous to people and livestock, with irritating toxins in the sap, stem, leaves and fruit, and the berries are specifically described as poisonous. Check the edge of the leaf before you pick anything. Evergreen huckleberry leaves are small and clearly saw-toothed along the edge, held in flat sprays, with berries in clusters strung along the twig close to the branch. Spurge laurel leaves are larger, with a completely smooth edge and no teeth at all, and they crowd into a rosette at the tips of the shoots with berries tucked in among them at the leaf bases. If the leaf edge has no teeth, do not eat the berry.

lookalikes.name: Other huckleberries and blueberries
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Several other Vaccinium shrubs share these woods. None of them is toxic, so mixing them up is a flavor question, not a safety one. What all of them share, and what spurge laurel lacks, is a toothed leaf edge.

species.season: Berries ripen roughly July through September, later than most local berries, and often hang on into October.
species.habitat: Well drained ground in Douglas-fir and western hemlock forest, on open ridges and in the coastal fog belt, at low elevation on the Washington coast side. Needs acid soil, roughly pH 4.3 to 5.2. It is a signature shrub of the Kitsap Peninsula: the Kitsap Forest Natural Area Preserve protects a Douglas-fir, western hemlock and evergreen huckleberry forest community.
species.uses: Food: berries fresh, cooked, canned, frozen, in wine and pie filling. The foliage is cut commercially as florists' greens and Christmas decoration, and in the early 1970s roughly a million dollars' worth of this brush was cut each year in western Washington. See the permit note under protection before cutting brush.

species.form: perennial herb spreading by roots into dense patches, stout stems about 3 to 6.6 feet tall
species.edible_detail: Cooked only, and only the young growth. Three conditions, and all three are required. First, take only young shoots and young leaves, before the plant flowers. Second, take them in spring; do not harvest mature or flowering plants. Third, cook them, by boiling, blanching, steaming or sauteing. Never eat any part of this plant raw. Boiled nettle leaves are edible and can be used in place of spinach; cooking destroys the sting. Wear gloves to pick.
species.toxic: Not a systemic poison, but it has two documented hazards. First, contact: the leaves, stems and flowers carry stinging hairs, described by the Forest Service as sparse to moderate coverage, and they cause immediate burning and itching where they touch bare skin. Cooking destroys the sting. Second, pollen: the Forest Service states that nettle pollen is a major contributor to summer hay fever, so a flowering patch can set off allergies in someone who never touches it.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Not a close match leaf for leaf, and it is listed here for a different reason: it grows in the same rich, moist, disturbed ground where people cut nettle for spring greens, and every part of it is deadly poisonous to humans. Poison hemlock is a Washington Class B noxious weed that can reach 12 feet. Its leaves are fern-like, toothed, finely divided and strong smelling when crushed. Its stems are hollow, hairless, and marked with obvious purple blotches. Its flowers are small and white in flat umbrella-shaped clusters 4 to 8 inches across. Nettle leaves are simple and undivided, pointed and saw-toothed, set in opposite pairs, and the plant stings bare skin, which hemlock does not. Never grab and cut a mixed handful of spring greens from a patch. Look at every single stem you take.

lookalikes.name: Hedge nettle
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A harmless mint of the same damp ground, with much the same outline: opposite pairs of toothed, hairy, pointed leaves. Mistaking the two costs nothing worse than a sting. Hedge nettle has a square stem you can feel with your fingers, smells minty when you crush a leaf, carries showy pink to purple two-lipped flowers, and does not sting. Stinging nettle stings, has a rounder stem, and its flowers are drooping strings of tiny greenish beads with no color to them.

species.season: Young shoots come up in early spring, roughly March into May, and that is the harvest window. The plants flower and shed pollen through summer, after which they are no longer a food.
species.habitat: Moist ground: stream banks, ditches, gullies, damp woodland clearings and disturbed ground around Silverdale and central Kitsap County, from sea level well up into the mountains. It prefers deep, rich soil and forms dense clonal patches. Both native and introduced forms grow in North America. The Forest Service recognizes three subspecies: American stinging nettle and hoary nettle are both native, and European stinging nettle was introduced in the mid 1800s. Which of the three grows in Kitsap County has not been confirmed from a public source here.
species.uses: Food: young spring shoots and leaves, cooked.

species.form: deciduous shrub 3.3 to 10 feet tall, sparsely branched, spiny, growing in dense patches, with very large maple-shaped leaves
species.edible_detail: No source used here establishes any part of this plant as human food. The Forest Service fire ecology review has no section on human food or medicine at all; its only human use statement is that the plant is grown as an ornamental.
