The Forest Service wildflower profile records extensive traditional medicinal use, this being a close relative of ginseng, but names no food use and gives no part, season, preparation or dose. Bears eat the bright red berry clusters in quantity; whether people can is simply unknown and undocumented. Do not eat it.
species.toxic: The dominant hazard is mechanical, not chemical, and it is worse than a stem-only warning suggests. The Forest Service fire review describes sharp, dense prickles on the stems and on the raised leaf veins; the Forest Service wildflower profile puts the coverage more completely, saying the spines coat every exposed surface of the plant except the roots and the berries. Assume there is no safe place to grab it, not the leaf stalk, not the underside of a leaf. The injury that actually happens is grabbing a stem for balance on a wet slope, or falling into a patch: spines snap off under the skin, take days to work their way out, and the punctures infect easily. On chemistry the sources are silent rather than reassuring. The Forest Service reports pharmaceutical interest in devil's club for regulating blood sugar in diabetes, so extracts may lower blood sugar, which matters to anyone taking diabetes medication. Do not read silence about poisoning as permission to eat it.

lookalikes.name: none in this region
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No dangerous lookalike is documented for devil's club in the public sources used here, and because no part of it is food, mistaking something else for it will not poison anyone. The confusion that actually happens runs the other way: the huge maple-shaped leaves read as ordinary harmless understory right up until a hand closes on a stem. On steep, wet Kitsap ground, look before you reach, and remember the bare winter stems are just as spiny as the summer ones.

species.season: Deciduous: it leafs out in spring, carries flattened clusters of bright red berries later in the growing season, and drops its leaves in fall. The spines are a hazard in every season, including on bare winter stems hidden under snow or leaf litter.
species.habitat: Moist to wet ground, and a reliable wet-site indicator: along streams, springs and drainages, in shade, on acid soils, from sea level to about 5,000 feet across the Pacific Northwest. Around Silverdale expect it in the wet, shaded draws and stream bottoms of second growth forest, usually in dense patches. Browsing animals do not prefer it, probably because of the prickles, but they do not avoid it either: black-tailed deer, white-tailed deer and elk browse it lightly in spring and summer, and in one study it made up an average of 3.4 percent of the summer diet of Roosevelt elk. Grizzly and black bears eat the seeds, leaves and stems, and favor streamside patches.
species.uses: Documented traditional medicinal use, this being a close relative of ginseng. No documented food use. Also planted as an ornamental.

species.form: deciduous shrub, often low but reaching 7 to 20 feet, with large compound leaves in opposite pairs
species.edible_detail: Fully ripe fruit, cooked, and nothing else from the plant. This is the riskier of the two local elderberries and must not be treated like the blue one. The Forest Service records the fruit being made into pies, jelly and wine, but says it is sour and that people do not usually eat it raw, and it warns that the fruits and the seeds may cause diarrhea and vomiting in people, especially when the fruit is not fully ripe. So: pick only fully ripe fruit, cook it, and never eat it raw. Strip the berries off the stems, because the stems are not food. Whether straining the seeds out makes cooked fruit safe is not documented in any source used here, so do not rely on that.
species.toxic: Leaves, stems, bark, roots and seeds. The Forest Service says other parts of the plant may be poisonous to people year round, and that the browse contains cyanide, which is what makes it taste bitter. Unripe fruit and the seeds are named specifically as causing diarrhea and vomiting in people. No dose is documented anywhere used here, so treat any amount of raw fruit, and any amount of leaf, stem, bark or root, as unsafe.

lookalikes.name: Red baneberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is the dangerous red-berried plant to know here. Red baneberry is listed for Washington by the Forest Service and grows on cool, moist, rich ground in shaded forest and along water, which is exactly where red elderberry grows. Its berries are showy and red, occasionally white, and are poisonous; the toxin, protoanemonin, is in every part and is most concentrated in the berries and the root. Poisoning brings stomach cramps, headache, dizziness, vomiting, diarrhea and circulatory failure, far worse than an elderberry stomach upset. Identify by the plant, never by the color of the berry. Red elderberry is a woody shrub 7 to 20 feet tall whose large compound leaves sit in opposite pairs, two at each joint. Red baneberry is a soft-stemmed herb only 1 to 3 feet tall whose compound, sharply toothed leaves are alternate, one at a time up the stem, and whose berries sit in a single spike above the leaves. Opposite leaves on a tall woody shrub means elderberry. Alternate leaves on a knee-high soft plant means baneberry: leave it alone. And do not use fruit color as the test at all, because the Forest Service records a black-fruited variety of red elderberry in this range and notes the usual kind is rarely yellow or white.

lookalikes.name: Blue elderberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The other local elderberry, and the safer one, but the two must not be blurred together because they are handled differently. Blue elderberry's berries contain very little of the poisonous compounds and Native peoples ate them raw, cooked or dried; red elderberry fruit is not eaten raw and must be fully ripe and cooked. Separate them by the shape of the flower and fruit cluster, which cannot rub off the way a wax bloom on a berry can. Blue elderberry's cluster is flat topped and broader than it is high. Red elderberry's is a tall, showy, dome or pyramid shaped spray, higher than it is broad.

species.season: Flowers in spring. Fruit ripens roughly June through September in the Pacific Northwest, and in a mild winter ripening can run as late as December.
species.habitat: Thickets, woodland, forest and subalpine meadow from Alaska and Yukon south to California. It prefers moist, rich ground and is the common elderberry of western Washington forests: around Silverdale expect it in riparian strips, wet meadows, damp forest openings and canopy gaps. It does best where a gap lets light in.
species.uses: Food: fully ripe fruit, cooked, for pies, jelly and wine.

species.scientific_name: Sambucus nigra L. ssp. cerulea (Raf.) R. Bolli
species.form: deciduous shrub 6.5 to 13 feet tall and sometimes to 20 feet, occasionally a small single-stemmed tree, with compound leaves in opposite pairs
species.edible_detail: Ripe fruit only, and nothing else from the plant. The Forest Service says the berries contain very little of the poisonous compounds found elsewhere in this genus, and that Native peoples gathered the fruit to cook, dry, or eat raw; the NRCS says the same independently. It is widely gathered for wine, jelly, candy, pies and sauces. Raw ripe berries are therefore attested by two federal sources, but cooking is still the conservative choice. Green or unripe fruit is out. Strip the berries off the stems before use, because the stems carry intermediate amounts of the toxin and are not food.
species.toxic: Other species in this genus contain a cyanogenic glycoside and an alkaloid that cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and stomach pain. For blue elderberry the Forest Service places the amounts as follows: the berries contain very little, intermediate amounts are in the stems, and the roots contain enough to cause death in hogs. Avoid roots, stems, bark and leaves entirely, and do not eat unripe fruit.

lookalikes.name: Red elderberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The other local elderberry, and the one that must be cooked and fully ripe. Its fruits and seeds may cause diarrhea and vomiting in people, especially when not fully ripe, and other parts may be poisonous year round. Do NOT separate the two by berry color; that rule fails in both directions here. Blue elderberry's blue is a powdery white wax bloom sitting on a purple-black berry, and it rubs off on your hands, in the rain, and in the bottom of a picking bucket. Meanwhile red elderberry has a black-fruited variety, Rocky Mountain elderberry, whose range runs from British Columbia and Alberta south to California, so a purple-black elderberry cluster in Washington can be either species. Use the shape of the cluster, which cannot rub off. Blue elderberry's flower and fruit cluster is flat topped, 4 to 20 centimeters across, broader than it is high. Red elderberry's is a tall, showy, dome shaped spray, higher than it is broad. Check the cluster shape before you check the berry color.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This one matters if you pick elderflower rather than fruit. Both plants carry flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers on moist ground in early summer in western Washington, and poison hemlock kills people; it is a Washington Class B noxious weed and every part of it is dangerous. Look at what the flower cluster is growing on. Blue elderberry is a woody shrub 6 to 13 feet tall with thin grayish to dark brown bark that is furrowed and ridged, and leaves set in opposite pairs, each leaf divided into 5 to 9 saw-toothed leaflets. Poison hemlock is a soft plant up to 12 feet with a hollow, hairless stem marked with purple blotches, and fern-like, finely divided leaves that smell strongly when crushed. If the stem is hollow, hairless and purple spotted, walk away. Nothing on that plant is safe.

species.season: Flowers May through September; fruit ripens roughly July through October.
species.habitat: Moist but well drained sunny ground: riparian strips, valley bottoms, fence rows, stream valleys and forest openings, from sea level to high elevation. It is the most common elderberry in eastern Washington and eastern Oregon and is less common than red elderberry on this side of the mountains, so around Silverdale look for it on drier, sunnier ground rather than in deep wet forest. The two species do overlap in habitat, so expect to meet both.
species.uses: Food: ripe fruit for wine, jelly, candy, pies and sauces. The hard wood was used for combs, spindles and pegs, and the hollow stems were made into flutes. Also planted for streambank stabilization and erosion control.

species.scientific_name: Oemleria cerasiformis (Torr. & A. Gray ex Hook. & Arn.) Landon
species.form: deciduous shrub or small multi-stemmed tree, the first native shrub in these woods to leaf out and flower each year
species.edible_detail: Only the thin outer flesh, only in small quantities, and spit the pits out. The Forest Service seed manual records that Pacific Northwest Native peoples ate the fruit in SMALL QUANTITIES, fresh, cooked or dried, and the NRCS fact sheet says the fruit is edible for humans but is often bitter even when fully ripe. Flavor varies a lot by locality, from sweet to bitter. The fruit is about half an inch across, thin fleshed, and roughly half stone by weight, so there is very little actual food on it. Do not crush, chew, grind, mash or blend the pits, because the pit is the poisonous part.
species.toxic: The pit. The NRCS fact sheet states that the seed is a stone, or pit, that contains cyanoglucosides, the bitter, toxic compounds also found in almonds. Swallowing a whole stone is not the same as crushing one, so the rule is: do not chew, grind, mash or blend whole fruit, and spit the stones out. No dose is documented. The bark also tastes bitter and was used traditionally as a mild laxative, so do not chew bark or twigs casually. Indian plum belongs to the stone fruit group of the rose family, the group whose kernels typically carry cyanide-releasing compounds.

lookalikes.name: Black twinberry (twinberry honeysuckle)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A native shrub of the same moist forests, clearings, thickets and stream sides in Kitsap County, growing up to 12 feet, with shiny black berries that ripen in July or later. The USDA plant guide opens with the warning that twinberry honeysuckle is considered toxic and should be used with caution, and states that the berries have been noted as poisonous and are better avoided. The fact sheet is honest that severity is disputed: reports on the fruit range from poisonous, to mildly toxic, to bitter and unpalatable, to edible, depending on tribe, region and publication. Either way it is not something to eat on a guess. Telling them apart is easy once you look past the color. Twinberry leaves grow in opposite pairs and its berries come in PAIRS, sitting in a cup of showy purple-red bracts. Indian plum leaves are alternate, one at a time up the twig, lance shaped, 2 to 5 inches long with smooth edges rolled slightly under, and they smell distinctly of cucumber when crushed. Its fruit hangs in loose drooping strings, up to 5 plums per flower. Its twigs are smooth and purplish brown with obvious orange dots, and if you split a twig lengthwise the pith inside is divided into small chambers. Never identify Indian plum by fruit color alone: confirm the alternate leaves, the cucumber smell, and the hanging string of fruit.

species.season: Flowers very early, roughly February through April, often before anything else in the woods. Fruit ripens late spring into early summer, roughly May through July, starting tan to pale orange, turning through pink to reddish purple, and finally ripening bluish black under a thin waxy coat.
species.habitat: Moist open forests, woodland edges, clearings and thickets, mostly below 1,000 feet elevation, from extreme southwest British Columbia south through Oregon. Common at low elevation around Silverdale and central Kitsap County, and easy to pick out in late winter as the first shrub in the woods to leaf out and flower. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants, so only some bushes carry fruit at all.
species.uses: Food: the thin flesh of ripe fruit, in small quantities. Bark was used traditionally as a tuberculosis remedy and a mild laxative, and strips of bark were used to bind harpoon tips. An important early season nectar source for hummingbirds, moths, butterflies and native bees, and widely planted in Pacific Northwest restoration work.

species.form: small deciduous shrub with simple oval leaves in opposite pairs and waxy white berries in tight clusters at the branch tips
species.edible_detail: Do not eat it, raw or cooked. This is a white berry that looks exactly like something a child would pick, it hangs on bare branches all winter when nothing else is around, and it is not food. The Forest Service reports that eating the fruit has caused vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and, in severe cases, unconsciousness in people. Be honest about the evidence, because reports of severity genuinely vary: the Forest Service traces that symptom list to a single source, notes there are no reports of poisoning in animals, and says there is no definite information on the toxic ingredient. Native peoples in Washington and Oregon did eat the fruit fresh and also dried it for winter, but never favored it, and one record has a person eating one or two berries to settle the stomach after fatty food, which is a medicinal dose rather than a meal. None of that is permission. There is no documented safe preparation, and cooking is not a fix: the NRCS guide notes that the saponin in the fruit can be broken down by thorough cooking, but that is a general remark about one ingredient, not a statement that snowberry is safe cooked, and saponin does not explain unconsciousness.
species.toxic: The berries. Eating them has been reported to cause vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and, in severe cases, unconsciousness in people. No dose is documented anywhere used here. The NRCS identifies saponin, a bitter substance that foams in water, present in the fruit at low concentrations, but saponin alone does not account for the reported unconsciousness, so whatever causes the severe effects has not been identified. The Forest Service notes there are no reports of poisoning in animals, which is part of why accounts of how dangerous this is disagree with each other. Treat the severity as uncertain and the answer as no.

lookalikes.name: Red baneberry, white-fruited form
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Listed for Washington by the Forest Service. Usually red-fruited, but the Forest Service explicitly records red or occasionally WHITE berries. Its toxin, protoanemonin, is in every part and most concentrated in the berries and root, and poisoning brings stomach cramps, headache, dizziness, vomiting, diarrhea and circulatory failure, a far worse outcome than snowberry. Tell them apart by the plant. Baneberry is a soft-stemmed herb 1 to 3 feet tall with large leaves divided two or three times into separate sharply toothed and lobed leaflets, set alternately one at a time up the stem, and its berries sit in a spike on a stalk. Snowberry is a woody shrub with small, simple, undivided oval leaves in opposite pairs and berries in tight clusters at the branch tips.

lookalikes.name: Pacific poison oak
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Its fruits are white drupes and the Forest Service places it west of the Cascade Range in Washington. The hazard here is handling rather than eating: the whole plant is coated in an oily resin that causes an itching rash on skin contact, and burning it is extremely hazardous because the resin goes up in the smoke. Tell them apart by the leaf. Poison oak leaves are divided into three, sometimes five, lobed oak-shaped leaflets. Snowberry leaves are simple, undivided ovals in opposite pairs. A white berry on a three-leaflet plant is a reason to keep your hands off, not to pick.

lookalikes.name: Creeping snowberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Same genus, also white-fruited, also present in Washington, but low and trailing rather than upright. The Forest Service notes saponin in its leaves. Treat it as equally not food; there is no benefit in telling these two apart for eating purposes, because neither one is edible.

species.season: Flowers in early summer, roughly mid May through July. The white berries ripen in late summer and then hang on the bare branches through fall and winter, which is exactly when they are most conspicuous and most tempting.
species.habitat: Well drained ground, from warm dry slopes and open forest to moister slopes and riparian benches, sea level to middle elevations. Common around Silverdale on forest edges, roadsides, thickets and the margins of yards. Tolerates mildly acid to moderately alkaline soil and shows some salt tolerance. Prefers open ground but persists in partial shade.
species.uses: Not a food. Documented non-food uses: branches were made into brooms and hollowed twigs into pipe stems. Historical medicinal uses are on record, including an infusion of the fruit used as an eyewash and berries rubbed on the skin for burns, rashes and sores, but those are historical records and not instructions. It is an important browse, shelter and food plant for birds, small mammals and livestock.

species.form: deciduous shrub usually 3 to 10 feet tall, with arching branches and large drooping plumes of tiny cream flowers
species.edible_detail: Not a practical food, and this entry is not a foraging recommendation. Correcting an earlier error in this record: the Forest Service review DOES document human food use, saying Native Americans used oceanspray sometimes as food and that Native Americans in the Inland Northwest ate the seeds. But it gives no preparation, no season, no quantity and no raw-versus-cooked instruction, and the seeds are dry husks about 2 millimeters long carried in feathery plumes. With no usable instructions and almost nothing there to eat, treat it as not a food. Separately, the Forest Service records the Pima making a tea from the leaves, but the Pima are an Arizona people and the Forest Service warns in the same review that oceanspray is routinely conflated with two close relatives, one of which is the southwestern plant. Do not carry that leaf tea across to the shrub growing here. Note also that the source says nothing at all about toxicity, and silence is not a clearance.

lookalikes.name: Rockspirea and small-leaved rockspirea
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The Forest Service says these two relatives and oceanspray are taxonomically and morphologically very similar and are separated only on leaf shape and where they grow. Neither is documented as toxic, and both are largely out of range in western Washington, so a local mix-up is both unlikely and harmless. It matters for one thing only: do not transfer traditional-use records from a southwestern Holodiscus to the plant here.

lookalikes.name: Goatsbeard
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The plant most likely to be mistaken for oceanspray in western Washington: same family, same big creamy plume of tiny flowers, same early summer bloom, same woodland edges. No source used here documents it as toxic, and nothing is riding on the difference because oceanspray is not a practical food either. Tell them apart by the stem. Oceanspray is a woody shrub whose arching branches stand through winter and whose leaves are small and shallowly lobed. Goatsbeard is a soft plant that dies back to the ground each winter, with large leaves divided into many separate toothed leaflets.

species.season: Full flowering comes late, not until late June or July, and can run into August. The fruits mature in late summer and may persist into fall, and the dried tan flower plumes are what makes the shrub easy to spot out of season.
species.habitat: Dry ground, and it favors south-facing slopes: forest edges, open slopes, bluffs and roadsides from sea level to about 7,000 feet, from southern British Columbia south to southern California and east to western Montana. Around Silverdale expect it on the drier, sunnier margins of woodland rather than in wet bottoms. It tolerates shallow soils across a pH range of about 5.0 to 7.5. Browsing animals usually find it unpalatable, though new sprouts after a fire are more palatable.
species.uses: Material is the real use, not food. Native Americans valued the long, straight, very hard branchwood for arrow shafts, digging sticks and fishing hooks, which is where the name ironwood comes from. Bark and leaves were dried and pulverized to put on burns or sores. Today it is planted for erosion control, as an ornamental, and in windbreaks.

species.form: thornless multi-stemmed deciduous shrub to about 10 feet, with maple-shaped lobed leaves and hanging clusters of pink to deep red flowers
species.edible_detail: The berries are the food and no cooking is required. They are very tart. The NRCS describes them as considered suitable by some for jam, jelly, pie, juice or syrup, which is a hedge about the flavor and not about safety, and records that Native Americans ate the berries fresh or dried. Raw and dried are both attested, so there is no preparation requirement. The NRCS also states directly that the plant is non-toxic to humans and wildlife, which is stronger than mere silence. Do not oversell the taste: very tart, and not to everyone's liking.

lookalikes.name: Cascara buckthorn
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A native shrub or small tree of the same lowland western Washington forests, mostly distributed west of the Cascades, fruiting in the same season. Its fruit is a purplish-black drupe about 7.5 millimeters across, measured at close to 12 millimeters on average in Washington, which overlaps a currant berry in both size and color. Its bark and fruit are strongly purgative, the same chemistry that once sent millions of pounds of cascara bark a year into commercial laxatives, and eating the berries can cause severe cramping and diarrhea. Tell them apart by the leaf, which is not subtle. Red-flowering currant leaves are 1 to 3 inches long and shaped like a small maple leaf, with 3 to 5 shallow lobes and deep veins that make them look wrinkled. Cascara leaves are 3 to 5 inches long, plain unlobed ovals, with 10 to 12 pairs of strong parallel veins running off the midrib like ladder rungs. If the leaf has no lobes, it is not a currant.

lookalikes.name: Other wild currants and gooseberries
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Several other Ribes shrubs grow in western Washington with similar lobed leaves and similar blue-black berries under a waxy bloom. None of them is known to be toxic, so a mix-up inside this group is a flavor question rather than a safety one, though flavors vary widely. One handy mark: gooseberries in this genus carry spines on the stems, while red-flowering currant is completely thornless.

species.season: Flowers March through June, opening as the leaves emerge. Berries mature early to mid summer.
species.habitat: Open, sunny ground; this shrub will not tolerate shade. Look on forest edges, in early regrowth after logging, and in open-canopy Douglas-fir stands on well drained soil, from sea level to about 6,000 feet. Native from southwest British Columbia south through Washington, Idaho and Oregon into California, so it is thoroughly at home around Silverdale, and it is also planted in gardens everywhere here.
species.uses: Food: berries raw, dried, or made into jam, jelly, pie, juice and syrup. Widely planted as an ornamental and informal hedge, with more than a dozen named garden selections and hybrids. An important early nectar plant, and grouse, quail, robins, finches, towhees and woodpeckers all eat the berries.

species.common_name: Hardhack (also called Douglas spirea, rose spirea, steeplebush)
species.form: deciduous shrub with erect spreading stems 3 to 6 feet tall, spreading by underground runners into dense thickets, with narrow spire-shaped spikes of tiny pink flowers
species.edible_detail: Not documented as a human food by any source used here. The Forest Service review contains no mention of edibility, food or medicine at all, and USDA PLANTS holds no ethnobotanical record for this species. A separate NRCS fact sheet does record one human use, but it is medicine and not food: at least one tribe made a tea from the SEEDS to treat diarrhea. A seed decoction used as a remedy is not a forage food, no dose or preparation is given, and nothing here makes this plant something to eat.

lookalikes.name: none in this region
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No toxic lookalike is documented for hardhack in the public sources used here, and since it is not a food, mistaking something for it will not poison anyone. It is distinctive in its own right: dense, narrow, spire-shaped spikes of tiny pink flowers at the branch tips, leaves 1 to 4 inches long, and dense thickets in standing water. There is a naming trap that is not a safety trap: the names steeplebush and meadowsweet are also used for other spireas elsewhere in North America. Around Kitsap County hardhack means this plant, and none of the plants sharing those names is toxic.

species.season: Flowers in summer, roughly June through September, and the flower spikes dry to rusty brown on the shrub afterward.
species.habitat: Wet ground: wet meadows, floodplains, terraces, bogs, swamps, and the edges of streams, rivers, lakes, springs and ponds, from Alaska south to northern California and east to western Montana. It prefers moist to semiwet soils and tolerates permanently waterlogged peat and water tables that swing up and down. Around Silverdale it forms the dense pink-flowered thickets ringing wetlands and the margins of Dyes Inlet.
species.uses: No food use. Limited value as livestock forage: it is sometimes eaten by livestock in summer and fall and browsed by black-tailed deer in western Washington and Oregon, though palatability ratings are low, and grouse eat the dried seed spikes. A seed tea is recorded as a traditional remedy for diarrhea, which is medicine and not food. Branches were used to spread and cook salmon, to hang salmon for drying and smoking, and to make brooms. Widely used today in Pacific Northwest riparian restoration; provides nesting habitat for long-billed marsh wrens and cover for deer, elk and raptors.

species.scientific_name: Lysichiton americanus Hulten & H. St. John
species.form: perennial herb, arum family, from a thick rhizome
species.edible_detail: Not food. The National Park Service classifies skunk cabbage as a poisonous plant and says it is considered inedible. Historical accounts record use by Native peoples as a famine food only, and the Forest Service page that mentions this qualifies even that as purportedly. Do not eat any part, raw or cooked. Whatever processing traditional use involved is not reproduced here, and famine-food status is not an endorsement.
species.toxic: Whole plant. The National Park Service states that skunk cabbage contains poisonous acids that can irritate the gastrointestinal system. No public-domain source located names the specific compound, so this record does not name one; do not repeat the commonly-quoted calcium oxalate or oxalic acid attribution without a citation. No dose is documented.

lookalikes.name: Green false hellebore (Veratrum viride)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both push broad, strongly pleated, parallel-veined leaves out of the same wet ground in the same early spring weeks. The checks you can make standing over it: skunk cabbage smells strongly and unmistakably of skunk when you brush or break a leaf, and it sends up a bright yellow hood around its flower spike; false hellebore has no such smell and its pleated leaves wrap around an upright stem. The Forest Service states plainly that false hellebore can be fatal if eaten. False hellebore is documented in Washington at mountain elevations, and no public-domain source consulted confirms it at Puget Sound lowland elevation near Silverdale, so do not assume it is here and do not assume it is absent. Because neither of these plants is food, the working rule is simple: do not eat either one.

lookalikes.name: Claspleaf twistedstalk, also called watermelon berry (Streptopus amplexifolius)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Worth naming here because it is an edible plant of the same wet shady ground, and the Forest Service itself warns that twistedstalk can be mistaken for the poisonous Veratrum and suggests it is better left unsampled. So the skunk cabbage patch, the false hellebore and a plant people do eat all share the same seep. Twistedstalk is a slender arching herb with alternate leaves clasping the stem and single berries dangling underneath it; skunk cabbage is a huge-leaved plant with no stem to speak of. If you cannot separate all three with certainty, eat none of them.

species.season: Bright yellow flower hoods appear very early, generally before most other growth in late winter and early spring. The very large leaves follow and stand through spring and summer, dying back in fall.
species.habitat: A plant with enormous paddle-shaped leaves rising straight out of mud, with a yellow hood around the flower spike in early spring. Wet ground: swamps, seeps, boggy ground, ditches and stream margins. Common and conspicuous in the lowland swamps and wet woods around Silverdale and central Kitsap County.
species.uses: No food use. It has the largest leaves of any native plant in the region, up to 135 cm long and 80 cm wide, growing from a substantial rhizome, and its pungent smell attracts pollinators.

species.edible_detail: COOK IT, AND IDENTIFY THE WHOLE LIVING PLANT BEFORE YOU DIG. The Forest Service review states that broadleaf cattail is entirely edible, but it writes that as a historical account of Native American and settler use rather than as modern guidance, and every preparation it describes is cooked or processed: spring sprouts eaten as a green vegetable, flower stalks boiled and eaten like corn on the cob, pollen added to other flours, and rhizomes dug in fall and winter then cooked, or dried, pounded and used as flour. No source consulted clears any part as safe raw, so cook by default. Two further conditions. First and most important, the fall and winter rhizome harvest happens in the same marsh mud where western water hemlock grows, at the one season when the aboveground plants are gone and you are identifying by root alone; see the lookalikes. Identify and mark your cattail stand while it is standing and in flower, and dig only there. Second, do not harvest from water of unknown quality, from roadside ditches, or downstream of industrial or naval sites. That second caution is editorial, not sourced: no source consulted establishes whether cattail rhizomes concentrate heavy metals to unsafe levels, and the Forest Service says only that cattail tolerates industrially degraded habitats, which is tolerance, not tissue concentration.

lookalikes.name: Western water hemlock (Cicuta douglasii)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The one that can kill you, and the risk peaks exactly when you dig cattail rhizomes out of fall and winter mud, because both plants grow in the same wet ground and the aboveground cattail is gone by then. USDA calls water hemlock the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America and says the toxin is found principally in the tubers. The root check: a cattail rhizome is solid and starchy all the way through, the same material from end to end. Water hemlock's thick rootstalk is divided into small chambers, and USDA says those chambers hold a highly poisonous brown or straw-colored liquid that is released when the stem is broken or cut. If a root you have cut is chambered or hollow, or weeps colored liquid, you are holding water hemlock: stop, do not taste it, wash your hands, and be aware that cutting it is itself an exposure. The better practice is not to rely on the root check at all. Find your cattail stand in summer when the brown sausage-shaped flower spikes are unmistakable, mark it, and return to that marked spot to dig.

lookalikes.name: Yellow flag iris (Iris pseudacorus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Grows in the same shallow water and mud, and before it flowers its fan of leaves is genuinely easy to mistake for cattail. Washington's noxious weed board describes its basal leaves as broad, flat, sword-shaped and stalkless, and says it is most commonly found in very shallow water or mud. There is no shortcut here: the reliable check is to let the plant show you what it is. Iris opens obvious yellow flowers in late spring; cattail makes the brown sausage-shaped flower spike. Do not cut shoots from a stand you have never seen in flower. It is a Washington Class C noxious weed listed in 2002; the state says it will sicken livestock if eaten and that contact with its resins can cause skin irritation in people.

species.season: Sprouts in spring; flower stalks in early summer; pollen in early summer; rhizomes dug in fall and winter.
species.habitat: The familiar marsh plant with long flat strap-like leaves and a brown sausage-shaped flower spike on a tall stalk. Freshwater to slightly brackish marshes, pond and lake margins, ditches, swales and slow-moving water, from sea level to 7,500 ft. Common in wetlands, roadside ditches and the wet margins around Silverdale and Dyes Inlet.
species.uses: Food: cooked spring shoots, boiled flower stalks, pollen as a flour additive, and rhizomes cooked, or dried and pounded into flour. The Forest Service notes that shoots and rhizomes contain much more calcium, iron and potassium than potatoes or rice.

species.edible_detail: Not food. The Forest Service states that the berries are unpalatable and can cause illness to people eating them. There is no part, season or preparation that makes this plant safe. The documented Native American use was a weak decoction of the root as medicine, which uses the most poisonous part of the plant and is not an edibility claim.
species.toxic: Poisonous, whole plant, worst in the BERRIES and the ROOT. The Forest Service attributes it to a poisonous essential oil or glycoside, given there as protoanemonin, found in all parts but most concentrated in the berries and root. Symptoms of poisoning include gastroenteritis, stomach cramps, headache, dizziness, vomiting, diarrhea and circulatory failure. The National Park Service states that the berries are poisonous and will often send the heart into cardiac arrest, and the Forest Service lists baneberry among the plants that can be fatal if eaten. COLOR IS NOT A SAFETY TEST: the Forest Service describes the fruits as showy, poisonous, red or occasionally white berries, and white-fruited plants are equally poisonous. No human dose is documented, and no source consulted independently confirms protoanemonin as the toxin beyond the Forest Service attribution.

lookalikes.name: Claspleaf twistedstalk, also called watermelon berry (Streptopus amplexifolius)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The dangerous one, because like baneberry it is a knee-high woodland herb rather than a shrub, it grows in the same moist shady forest, and its red berries are eaten. The Forest Service describes twistedstalk as carrying only one flower on each flower stalk, hanging downward, each giving rise to a single elliptic yellow or red berry which is edible. That is the check you can make from where you stand: twistedstalk hangs ONE berry per stalk, dangling underneath the arching stem, roughly one below each leaf. Baneberry holds its berries bunched in a showy cluster on an upright stalk. Note that the Forest Service, writing about twistedstalk itself, warns it can be mistaken for the poisonous Veratrum and says it is perhaps better left unsampled. If you cannot say with certainty which of these you are holding, you are not certain enough to eat it.

lookalikes.name: Red elderberry (Sambucus racemosa)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also carries red berries in the same damp woods, and people do use them. The difference is obvious as soon as you look at the plant instead of the fruit: red elderberry is a woody shrub or small tree, commonly 7 to 20 feet tall, carrying many small berries in a large branched cluster. Baneberry is a soft-stemmed herb only 1 to 3 feet tall whose stem you could snap between your fingers. Elderberry is not a free pass either: the Forest Service says people do not usually eat the fruits raw, that the fruits and seeds may cause diarrhea and vomiting especially if the fruits are not fully ripe, and that other parts of the plant may be poisonous year round.

lookalikes.name: Red huckleberry (Vaccinium parvifolium)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Another red berry of the same forests and a common food here. Red huckleberry is a woody shrub with thin green twigs, and its berries hang singly along the branches. Baneberry is a non-woody herb with large leaves divided two to three times and sharply toothed, carrying its berries bunched on one upright stalk. Rule of thumb that covers this whole group: if the plant has a soft green stem you could break with your fingers and its berries are bunched on a single stalk held above the leaves, do not eat them.

lookalikes.name: Black cohosh and blue cohosh, sold as cohosh root
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Not a visual lookalike but a NAME trap, and it matters because baneberry's root is one of its two most poisonous parts. The Forest Service lists cohosh, red cohosh, necklaceweed and snakeberry among the other common names for red baneberry. Black cohosh (Actaea racemosa) is a different plant in the same genus and blue cohosh (Caulophyllum thalictroides) is a different plant entirely. Never dig or buy a root because somebody called it cohosh.

species.season: Small white flowers in late spring. Showy berries through summer and into early fall, which is the period when they are most likely to be picked.
species.habitat: A deciduous perennial herb usually 1 to 3 feet tall with branched stems and alternate leaves divided two to three times, sharply toothed and lobed, carrying a cluster of showy red, or occasionally white, berries on an upright stalk. Cool, moist, nutrient-rich forest understory in conifer and mixed forest, often near streams, in seepage areas and other damp microsites. Expect it in the shaded second-growth woods and ravines around Silverdale.
species.uses: No food use. A weak decoction of the root is recorded as a traditional medicine, but the root is among the most poisonous parts of the plant and no preparation is given here. Do not attempt it.

species.edible_detail: Never, in any amount, by anyone. USDA states that water hemlock is the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America, and that only a small amount of the toxic substance in the plant is needed to produce poisoning in livestock or in humans. There is no part, season or preparation that is safe, and there is no amount small enough to taste.
species.toxic: DEADLY. The toxin is cicutoxin, a highly poisonous unsaturated alcohol with a strong carrot-like odor, which acts directly on the central nervous system as a violent convulsant. USDA says it is found principally in the TUBERS, and is also present in the leaves and stems during early growth; leaves and stems lose most of their toxicity as they mature, but GREEN SEED HEADS stay poisonous. EXPOSURE IS NOT ONLY BY EATING: the thick rootstalk contains small chambers holding a highly poisonous brown or straw-colored liquid that is released when the stem is broken or cut, so cutting, mowing, pulling or clearing the plant is itself an exposure. Do not cut or handle it. Signs listed by USDA: nervousness, excessive salivation and frothing, muscle twitching, dilation of the pupils, rapid pulse, rapid breathing, tremors, violent convulsions and grand mal seizures, coma, death. The timings usually quoted, signs 15 minutes to 6 hours after eating and death within 15 minutes to 2 hours after signs appear, are USDA's LIVESTOCK figures; no human-specific onset window was found in a public-domain source and none should be invented. For a person, USDA's instruction is to contact a poison control center and obtain emergency medical assistance as quickly as possible, because the seizures and convulsions must be controlled.

lookalikes.name: Hemlock waterparsnip (Sium suave)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The most dangerous confusion in this county's wet ground. It is a carrot-family plant with white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters growing in exactly the same marshes and stream edges, it is native here, and it is treated as an edible root in foraging literature. USDA's own common name for it is hemlock waterparsnip, which tells you how close these two sit. One character IS sourced, and it is worth knowing: USDA ARS states that on water hemlock the "side veins of the leaves lead to notches, not to tips at the outer margin". Cut the rootstalk and it has small chambers holding a brown or straw-coloured liquid, which water parsnip does not. The other character people quote, that water parsnip leaves are divided once while water hemlock leaves are divided two or three times, is real but no public-domain source consulted here states it. Neither character makes this safe: they are fine distinctions on a plant where being wrong once is fatal. So here is the honest answer: a beginner cannot reliably tell these two apart in the field, and experienced foragers have died getting it wrong. Treat every white-flowered carrot-family plant growing in wet ground as water hemlock and leave it alone.

lookalikes.name: Water parsley (Oenanthe sarmentosa)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A native carrot-family plant of exactly the same Puget Sound wet ground, with divided leaves and white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters, and one that gets gathered. Same verdict as hemlock waterparsnip: this is not a distinction a beginner should attempt, and the sensible rule is to eat no carrot-family plant from wet ground at all. A useful habitat note that cuts the other way: water parsley often sprawls and roots along wet ditches and slow water, so a mat of divided leaves in a ditch is not automatically the harmless one.

lookalikes.name: Common cowparsnip (Heracleum maximum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A large native carrot-family plant with big white flower umbels in damp ground and along streams, whose peeled young stalks are a traditional food. It is much coarser and much larger-leaved than water hemlock, with broad lobed leaflets shaped a little like maple leaves rather than the narrow toothed segments of water hemlock, and it usually stands well over head height. That is a real difference an attentive person can see, but the two share habitat and the same white umbel silhouette, and a young cow parsnip is far less distinctive than a mature one. Cow parsnip carries its own separate hazard: the National Park Service notes that skin contact with juice from the plant followed by exposure to sunlight can cause dermatitis.

lookalikes.name: Wild parsnip and other wild carrot-family plants
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: USDA states that water hemlock has been confused with wild parsnips, other herbs, and medicinal plants. The whole white-umbel family is the hazard zone. This catch-all is deliberate and it is the part of this record that actually protects people: it never designates any white-umbel plant as safe. Do not eat any of them without certain identification, and certain means certain.

lookalikes.name: Broadleaf cattail (Typha latifolia)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Not a visual lookalike above ground, but the real-world path by which a forager actually meets water hemlock, because cattail rhizomes are dug from the same marsh mud in fall and winter when the standing plants are gone. A cattail rhizome is solid and starchy throughout. Water hemlock's rootstalk is chambered and weeps a brown or straw-colored liquid when cut. Do not dig roots in a marsh you have not already identified plant by plant during the growing season.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Two different deadly plants that genuinely resemble each other, not merely a similar-sounding name. USDA says poison hemlock is sometimes confused with western water hemlock, a more deadly species, and that water hemlock has itself been confused with poison hemlock. Both kill, but differently: water hemlock's cicutoxin causes violent seizures, poison hemlock's coniine causes progressive paralysis. Poison hemlock has a hollow stem marked with small purple spots and a white taproot and prefers fence lines, ditches and moist waste ground; water hemlock sits in standing water and wet meadows and has the chambered rootstalk. For eating purposes the distinction is academic: neither is survivable food.

species.season: Green shoots come up in spring, white flower umbels in summer, and the top dies back in fall. The tuberous root is the most poisonous part and it is in the ground year round, including winter, when nothing above ground shows where the plant is.
species.habitat: A slender carrot-family plant about 0.5 to 1.0 m tall, with small white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters and a thick chambered rootstalk. Wet meadows and pastures, seepage areas, marsh edges and the banks of streams; it prefers wet seepage ground. Native to the northwestern United States and western Canada. USDA PLANTS confirms native status for the lower 48, Alaska and Canada but does not itemize states, and no public-domain source consulted confirms Kitsap County occurrence specifically. Assume it can be present in any wet ground here: warning about a deadly plant that may be present is the safe direction, and assuming its absence is not.

species.edible_detail: Never. All parts are toxic, including the bulb that people dig and including the fruit and seed. USDA states that consumption of death camas has been linked to deaths of livestock and humans, and that eating one or two bulbs is enough to cause severe illness in children, while four or five can cause death depending on the species. There is no preparation, no cooking and no season that makes it safe.
species.toxic: DEADLY, all parts: bulbs, stems, leaves, flowers and seeds. The Forest Service names zygacine, a neurotoxic steroidal alkaloid, and USDA describes the genus as containing a wide range of toxic alkaloids, with meadow death camas having the most diverse group in the genus. HUMAN DOSE, which is the number that matters: one or two bulbs is enough to cause severe illness in a child, and four or five can cause death. For scale only, the livestock figure often quoted is that a 100-pound sheep may die from eating 0.5 to 2 pounds of green foliage, which is a large amount and reads misleadingly reassuring if you do not know the human number sitting beside it. Toxic year round, and the Forest Service states that dried meadow death camas remains toxic for at least 20 years, so old, dried or wilted material is not safe. Even the pollen is toxic: USDA records that pollen shaken into sugar water killed 89 percent of the bees that fed on it within 16 hours. Symptoms listed by the National Park Service include excessive salivation, burning and numbness of the lips and mouth, thirst, headache and dizziness; USDA adds frothy salivation, depression, vomiting, teeth grinding, and in severe cases loss of appetite, loss of coordination, weakness and death, with signs beginning several hours to a day after ingestion.

lookalikes.name: Common camas (Camassia quamash)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The classic fatal confusion, and the reason for the name. USDA states that the common name refers to the toxicity of the plant and its similarity in appearance to camas, and that death camas has been mistaken for other edible bulbous plants such as wild onion, sego lily and camas, ESPECIALLY WHEN FLOWERS ARE LACKING. The two grow in the same wet spring meadows, often side by side, both are grass-leaved, and both are dug for their bulbs. IN BLOOM there is a clear check anyone can make: camas flowers are blue to bluish-violet, while death camas petals are creamy white and about a quarter inch long with a large gland at the base. OUT OF BLOOM there is no reliable field character, and the bulbs cannot be told apart safely by a beginner. So the only safe practice is to find and mark individual plants WHILE THEY ARE IN FLOWER, and later dig only the ones you marked, one plant at a time, rather than working through a patch. One more thing worth knowing: camas is not a raw food either. The Forest Service describes the bulbs as steamed or pit cooked for one to three days to break down complex carbohydrates.

lookalikes.name: Wild onion, including nodding onion (Allium cernuum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Death camas has similar grass-like leaves and a similar bulb, and USDA lists wild onion among the edible bulbs it has been mistaken for. The check is SMELL: onions and their relatives smell strongly of onion or garlic when you crush a leaf or scratch the bulb, and death camas does not smell of onion at all. Use this test in the negative direction only. No onion smell means do not eat it, full stop. But smelling onion does not by itself prove that a particular bulb is an onion, because a bulb picks up the smell from your hands, from your knife, or from a crushed onion lying next to it in the basket. So smell every bulb separately, with clean hands, before it joins the others.

lookalikes.name: Sego lily (Calochortus species)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: USDA names sego lily among the edible bulbous plants death camas has been mistaken for, especially when flowers are lacking. Sego lily proper is an Intermountain species rather than a Puget Sound one, so around Silverdale this matters less than camas and wild onion, but the pattern is identical: a grass-leaved plant dug for its bulb, indistinguishable from death camas once the flowers are gone.

species.season: Green leaves appear early in spring, ahead of most other growth, which is part of why livestock and people encounter it. Creamy white flowers in late spring. The plant dies back by summer while the bulb stays in the ground, and the bulb is dangerous year round.
species.habitat: A grass-leaved plant 1 to 2 feet tall with linear leaves mostly rising from the base and a dense cluster of small creamy white flowers. Coastal prairies, wet and drying meadows, creek sides, open forest and forest edges, rocky bluffs and grassy hillsides. The Forest Service documents it as common on Puget Sound prairie at Fort Lewis in Pierce County, so regional presence at sea level is established; no public-domain source consulted confirms Kitsap County specifically, so treat its presence around Silverdale as likely but unconfirmed. Do NOT use the elevation band of 1,400 to 8,000 feet given in the USDA plant guide to rule it out here: that figure comes from Intermountain floras and does not describe the sea-level Puget prairies where the Forest Service documents the plant.
species.uses: No food use, ever. USDA records that several tribes applied mashed bulbs externally to bruises, sprains and boils. Handling is not risk free: USDA states that all portions of the plant, including the fruit and seed, are toxic and should be handled with care. Naming note: USDA PLANTS carries Zigadenus venenosus S. Watson as the accepted name, symbol ZIVE; modern floras often use the segregate name Toxicoscordion venenosum for the same plant. If you are looking this up in USDA PLANTS by symbol, the symbol is ZIVE. The symbol TOVE is Toxicodendron vernix, poison sumac, a completely different plant.

species.protected: Not protected; the legal status is the opposite. Washington State Class C noxious weed, listed 2009. Counties may require landowners to control it, or may instead provide education and encourage voluntary control.
species.edible_detail: The ripe black berries are eaten fresh, raw, no cooking required, and can also be canned or frozen. USDA NRCS states that Himalaya blackberry fruits are highly edible and commonly collected by berry pickers, and that the fruit can be canned, frozen, or eaten fresh. One real condition: this is a noxious weed under active control and USDA notes that several herbicides provide excellent control of blackberry, so do not pick from roadsides, utility corridors, ditch banks, or any managed control site, which may have been sprayed.

lookalikes.name: Trailing blackberry (Rubus ursinus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The native blackberry, also edible, so nothing is lost by confusing the two. It is a low slender vine trailing along the ground rather than a stout arching cane, and its berries are smaller.

lookalikes.name: Cutleaf or evergreen blackberry (Rubus laciniatus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The other introduced blackberry common in western Washington, also edible. Its leaflets are deeply cut and lacy rather than broadly oval.

lookalikes.name: Bittersweet or climbing nightshade (Solanum dulcamara)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Not a fruit lookalike, but it belongs on this list because it is a vine that climbs over shrubs and scrambles up through bramble thickets in the Pacific Northwest, so you reach past it while picking. The Forest Service says it contains solanine, a substance known to be poisonous to humans, with unripe berries the most concentrated. The berries are easy to separate once you look: nightshade berries are single smooth berries only 2 to 8 mm across that ripen from green to RED, never an aggregate of many small black segments. Point this out to children picking in a thicket, who are the people actually at risk here.

lookalikes.name: No toxic lookalike found for the ripe fruit
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No public-domain source consulted describes any toxic plant in western Washington producing a half-inch to seven-eighths-inch aggregate of shiny black drupelets on a prickly cane. Recorded as none found rather than none exists. The fruit architecture is itself the check: a blackberry is many small segments fused into one berry, on a thorny cane.

species.season: White to pink flowers in late spring and early summer; ripe black fruit in late summer into early fall.
species.habitat: An evergreen bramble with stout arching canes, leaves of three to five serrated leaflets, white to pink flowers in flat-topped clusters, and shiny black berries about half an inch to seven eighths of an inch. Mixed and deciduous forest and a wide range of disturbed sites: roadsides, railroad grades, logged land, field margins, fence lines and riparian areas; adapts to many soils. The single most abundant invasive shrub around Silverdale.
species.uses: Food: fresh fruit, jam, canning, freezing. Handle with care: the canes carry rigid hooked prickles up to 20 mm long and reach 20 to 40 feet in length, while the plant or thicket stands up to about 13 feet tall and the thickets are described as impenetrable. Wear long sleeves and eye protection when reaching in. It regenerates from rootstalks, rooting stem tips, and root and stem fragments, which is why cutting it back without follow-up spreads it.

species.protected: Not protected; the legal status is the opposite. Washington State Class B noxious weed, listed 1988. In regions where it is already widespread, counties can select it for control to meet local needs and priorities.
species.edible_detail: Not a food plant and not a tea. Treat the whole plant as poisonous, flowers included. Do not make any herbal preparation from any part of it.
species.toxic: Toxic to people as well as to livestock, and not only the seeds. NC State Extension rates the poison severity as HIGH, gives the toxic principle as quinolizidine alkaloids, lists the poisonous parts as leaves, seeds and stems, and gives the symptoms verbatim as: HIGHLY TOXIC, MAY BE FATAL IF EATEN! Vomiting, excitement, muscular weakness, convulsions. Washington's noxious weed board separately records the seeds as toxic to livestock and horses, which is where the older and much narrower wording on this plant comes from; that state page is a weed-control page, not a toxicology page, and reading it as the full hazard picture is how people conclude the abundant yellow flowers must be harmless. They are not established as safe by anything. Do not brew tea or make any other preparation from this plant. Its flattened brown to black pods look like small pea pods, which is worth knowing where children play. No dose is documented.

lookalikes.name: Spanish broom (Spartium junceum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Round, rush-like stems, against Scotch broom's young branches which carry five ridges you can feel by rolling a stem between your fingers. Neither plant is food, so confusing them costs nothing as long as you eat neither.

lookalikes.name: French broom (Genista monspessulana)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Another yellow-flowered broom of the same disturbed ground, and not a food plant either. If you are trying to tell brooms apart it is for control purposes, not for eating.

lookalikes.name: Gorse (Ulex europaeus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also yellow-flowered and in the same places, but gorse is armed with stiff sharp spines while Scotch broom's ridged stems are unarmed. The practical difference is that gorse draws blood. Not a food plant.

lookalikes.name: Portuguese or striated broom (Cytisus striatus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The Forest Service says striated broom is often misidentified as Scotch broom, but that it is neither as widely distributed nor as common. It is reported from California and Oregon rather than Washington, so it is unlikely around Silverdale. Not a food plant.

species.season: Bright yellow flowers in spring, roughly April into June. Brown to black pods through summer. The dark green ridged stems persist year round, so the shrub is recognizable in winter after the leaves have dropped.
species.habitat: A perennial shrub 3 to 10 ft tall with bright yellow pea-family flowers about three quarters of an inch long, woody dark green stems with FIVE RIDGES on the young branches, upper leaves simple and lower leaves three-parted and often shed early leaving bare green stems, and flattened brown to black seed pods with hairy margins. Roadsides, pastures, grasslands, open areas, clearcuts and any recently disturbed soil. Ubiquitous on Kitsap roadsides and logged ground.

species.protected: Not protected; the legal status is the opposite. Washington State Class C noxious weed, listed 2002, and on the Washington State quarantine list: it is prohibited to transport, buy, sell, offer for sale, or distribute plants or plant parts into or within Washington. The listing covers the invasive cultivars Baltica, Pittsburgh and Star of Hedera helix, plus Hedera hibernica cultivar Hibernica; the authority L. belongs to Hedera helix only, and USDA PLANTS does not carry Hedera hibernica as an accepted species or as a synonym of H. helix.
species.edible_detail: Not food. Every part is poisonous, and the leaves are more poisonous than the berries.
species.toxic: Toxic; do not eat any part, and handle it with gloves. All parts contain triterpenoid saponins and polyacetylene compounds. NC State Extension rates the poison severity as Medium, lists the poisonous parts as bark, flowers, fruits, leaves, roots, sap, seeds and stems, and states that FOLIAGE IS MORE TOXIC THAN BERRIES. Eating berries causes a burning sensation in the throat; eating leaves can cause vomiting, abdominal pain, hypersalivation, diarrhea, fever and rash, and in serious cases delirium, stupor, hallucinations and convulsions. Contact with the plant's sap causes severe skin irritation with redness, itching and blistering, and because that is a sensitizing reaction, repeated exposure builds the sensitivity rather than only affecting people who are already sensitive; describing it as a risk to sensitive individuals is circular reassurance. It is listed as poisonous to humans and as problematic for CATS, DOGS AND HORSES, which on a Kitsap homestead are the animals actually at risk, not cattle. Washington's noxious weed board instructs: wear gloves and protective clothing when pulling ivy, to protect against the irritating sap. That matters because landowners are actively encouraged to pull it, and pulling is the maximum sap-exposure activity. No dose is documented.

lookalikes.name: None confirmed in this region
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No public-domain source consulted names a plant that is confused with English ivy here. Washington's noxious weed board has a May Be Confused With field for this species, and it carries only a note about which ivy cultivars the listing covers, naming no other plant. Recorded as none found rather than none exists, so do not read this as a cleared field. The real-world risk with English ivy is not an adult misidentifying it anyway. It is the fruit: small dark blue to black berries, carried at a small child's eye level on walls, fences and tree trunks through the winter, on a plant everyone assumes is merely decorative.

species.season: Evergreen and present year round. Small greenish-white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters in fall; dark blue to black berry-like fruits mature in spring, each with 4 or 5 seeds.
species.habitat: An evergreen vine with two growth forms. The juvenile climbing form has deeply lobed leaves with 3 to 5 lobes; the adult shrubby form, which is the one that flowers and fruits, has mostly unlobed leaves, egg-shaped or diamond-shaped. Young stems are hairy, older stems hairless. Woodlands, forest edges, riparian areas, fields, hedgerows, coastal areas and disturbed ground; adapts to many soil types and light conditions. Common in and around Silverdale in older plantings, in greenbelts, on fences and climbing tree trunks.
species.uses: No food or medicinal use; it is toxic. Planted as an ornamental groundcover and wall cover, which is how it escaped into local woodland.

species.form: perennial herb with tall hollow cane-like stems
species.protected: Not protected; the legal status is the opposite. Washington State Class B noxious weed, listed 1995. Under RCW 17.10.010(13), Class B means control is REQUIRED in regions where the species is of limited distribution. Washington also quarantines invasive knotweed: on the state's Bohemian knotweed page the rule is stated as prohibited to transport, buy, sell, offer for sale, or distribute plants or plant parts of quarantined species into or within Washington. Treat all four invasive knotweeds the same way and do not carry cut stems anywhere.
species.edible_detail: CONDITION: only the YOUNG SHOOTS AND STEMS, and only in SPRING. Penn State Extension states that all species of knotweed found in the United States produce edible young shoots in spring, and NC State Extension says the young stems are edible with a sour rhubarb flavor. Mature canes are woody and are not the edible stage. Neither source imposes a cooking requirement. THREE HARD CONDITIONS BEFORE YOU EAT ANY OF IT. ONE, HERBICIDE, and this is the real hazard on this plant. Knotweed is a legally mandated control target in Washington and the standard treatment is herbicide sprayed onto exactly the streambank and roadside stands that are easiest to reach. Penn State names glyphosate in aquatic-labeled formulations such as Aquaneat and Glyphomate 41, and imazapyr such as Polaris and Habitat, noting that imazapyr persists in soil. In Kitsap County, county and salmon-recovery crews treat knotweed along streams, often without any sign a passer-by would see. Assume any stand has been sprayed unless you personally know that it has not. No source consulted gives a safe waiting interval after treatment, and that missing number is the single largest gap in this record. TWO, OXALATES. The sour rhubarb flavor is the usual signature of oxalic acid and no source consulted measures it, so anyone with kidney stones, gout, or on a low-oxalate diet should not rely on this entry. THREE, DO NOT TRANSPORT IT. Every node on a stem can root, so carrying cut stems home is how the plant spreads, and moving plant parts of quarantined knotweed within Washington is prohibited. Eat it where it grows or leave it.
species.toxic: No toxicity documented for the plant itself. Washington's noxious weed board records it as not known to be toxic, and USDA PLANTS holds no toxicity data for it either way. That is a weed-control agency's absence of evidence about contact and livestock hazard; it is NOT a food-safety clearance and must not be read as one. The hazard that actually applies to eating this plant is herbicide residue, not the plant; see edible_detail.

lookalikes.name: Bohemian knotweed (Polygonum x bohemicum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The hybrid of Japanese and giant knotweed, and genuinely hard to separate by eye. Bohemian's leaf bases are slightly indented to deeply heart-shaped and its leaf midveins have hairs; Japanese knotweed's leaf bases are flat or truncated with an abrupt tip. None of the invasive knotweeds is known to be toxic, so mixing them up is an identification error rather than a poisoning.

lookalikes.name: Giant knotweed (Polygonum sachalinense)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Larger, with heart-shaped leaf bases. HEIGHT IS NOT A RELIABLE TEST, despite being widely repeated: NC State gives Japanese knotweed 10 to 13 ft, which overlaps giant knotweed, and height means nothing at all for cut, mowed or immature stands. Washington's noxious weed board pairs its own shorter-than remark with a direction to contact your county noxious weed coordinator for help telling them apart.

lookalikes.name: Himalayan knotweed (Persicaria wallichii)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Washington Class B noxious weed, listed 2003, distinguished from the others by its long slender leaves. Also not known to be toxic.

lookalikes.name: No toxic lookalike confirmed
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No Washington state, federal or extension source consulted pairs Japanese knotweed with giant hogweed, poison hemlock, water hemlock or any other toxic plant as confusable, and their leaf shapes differ sharply. Recorded as none found rather than none exists. One editorial caution that follows from where you pick rather than from what the plant looks like: young knotweed shoots are gathered in spring on streambanks, which is also where poison hemlock and water hemlock grow. Identify the stand while it is in full summer growth, mark it, and come back to that marked stand in spring, rather than deciding what a young shoot is on the day you want to eat it.

species.season: Edible shoots in spring only, as the new reddish shoots push up. Whitish to greenish-white drooping flower clusters in late summer. Dead brown canes stand through winter.
species.habitat: A perennial 4 to 13 ft tall with reddish-brown, hollow, branched, bamboo-like stems, alternate leaves 4 to 6 in long, ovate with TRUNCATED, meaning flat, bases, whitish to greenish-white drooping flower clusters and small brown triangular fruits about an eighth of an inch. Waste ground, gardens, roadsides, and stream and river banks; it thrives on sites that are at least seasonally wet. Spreads by seed and by extensive rhizomes, forms dense stands that crowd out all other vegetation, and is very difficult to control once established.
species.uses: Food, conditionally; see edible_detail, because the conditions are the whole point. Naming note: USDA's National Invasive Species Information Center and ITIS give Fallopia japonica (Houtt.) Ronse Decr. as the accepted name and list Polygonum cuspidatum Siebold & Zucc. and Reynoutria japonica Houtt. as synonyms. Sources following Kew, including NC State Extension, treat Reynoutria japonica as accepted. Authorities genuinely disagree between Fallopia and Reynoutria, but none accept Polygonum cuspidatum, which is the name this record previously carried. Note also that the authority Siebold & Zucc. belongs to Polygonum cuspidatum only.

species.scientific_name: Polygonum x bohemicum (J. Chrtek & Chrtkova) Zika & Jacobson [cuspidatum x sachalinense]
species.form: perennial herb with tall hollow cane-like stems; hybrid of Japanese and giant knotweed
species.protected: Not protected; the legal status is the opposite. Washington State Class B noxious weed, listed 2004, and on the Washington quarantine list: it is prohibited to transport, buy, sell, offer for sale, or distribute plants or plant parts of quarantined species into or within the state of Washington (WAC 16-752). Every node on a stem can produce roots and new plants, and new plants sprout from small fragments, so cutting and carrying it is how it spreads. Report stands to the Kitsap County noxious weed coordinator.
species.edible_detail: Not documented as a food by any source consulted, and not cleared as one here. Its parent Japanese knotweed is eaten as a young spring shoot, and Penn State Extension's statement that all knotweed species found in the United States produce edible young shoots in spring would arguably extend to this hybrid, but no source consulted addresses this plant specifically, so this record does not clear it. Harvesting is the wrong action regardless of edibility: this is a quarantined plant, moving plant parts within Washington is prohibited, and every stem node can root, so cutting and carrying it spreads it.
species.toxic: No toxicity documented. Washington's noxious weed board records it as not known to be toxic, and USDA PLANTS holds no toxicity or palatability data for it either way. That is an absence of evidence, not a safety clearance, and it should not be rendered anywhere as non-toxic.

lookalikes.name: Japanese knotweed (Fallopia japonica)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: One of its two parents. Japanese knotweed's leaf bases are flat or truncated with an abrupt tip; Bohemian's leaf bases are slightly indented to deeply heart-shaped, its leaf midveins have hairs, and its leaf size is intermediate between the two parents. Washington's noxious weed board says the invasive knotweed species look very similar and directs people to their county noxious weed coordinator for identification help.

lookalikes.name: Giant knotweed (Polygonum sachalinense)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The other parent. Bohemian sits between the two in leaf size and in leaf base shape, which is exactly why it is hard to place. Do not use height as the test.

lookalikes.name: Himalayan knotweed (Persicaria wallichii)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The fourth invasive knotweed in Washington, Class B, listed 2003, told apart from the others by its long slender leaves. Also recorded as not known to be toxic.

lookalikes.name: No toxic lookalike confirmed
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: All four invasive knotweeds in Washington carry the same not-known-to-be-toxic record, so a mix-up inside this group is an identification error and not a poisoning. No toxic non-knotweed species was substantiated as a morphological lookalike in Kitsap County riparian ground by any source consulted. Recorded as none found rather than none exists.

species.season: Shoots in spring; white to pinkish-white flower clusters at the stem tips in late summer; dead brown canes standing through winter.
species.habitat: A tall perennial with large oval leaves and hollow reddish-brown stems, carrying white to pinkish-white flower clusters at the stem tips. Leaf characters fall between the two parent species, with leaf bases slightly indented to deeply heart-shaped and hairy leaf midveins. Waste places, neglected gardens, roadsides, streambanks and riverbanks, having escaped from ornamental cultivation. Particularly threatens riparian areas, and forms dense colonies that exclude native vegetation; established populations are extremely difficult to eradicate.
species.uses: None documented. Naming note: USDA PLANTS carries Polygonum x bohemicum (J. Chrtek & Chrtkova) Zika & Jacobson as the accepted name, symbol POBO10, with Fallopia x bohemica and Reynoutria x bohemica as synonyms; most non-USDA authorities now prefer Reynoutria x bohemica. Origin: both parent species are East Asian, but the hybrid's epithet and its Chrtek and Chrtkova authority point to a European origin for the hybrid itself, and no source consulted states where the hybrid arose, so the previously recorded origin of Asia is left unasserted here.

species.protected: Not protected; the legal status is the opposite. Washington State Class B noxious weed, listed 1988, and on the Washington State quarantine list (WAC 16-752): prohibited to transport, buy, sell, offer for sale, or distribute in Washington. Washington's noxious weed board advises contacting your county noxious weed coordinator if you are unsure of the identification.
species.edible_detail: Never, in any form. Washington's noxious weed board states that tansy ragwort can cause human liver damage and should never be used as an herbal remedy or tea. Drying does not make it safe: the state's toxic plant booklet says it is equally as toxic dried as green, and moreover more palatable when dried, and that wilted plants are more palatable than healthy plants. So a wilted or dried plant is both more tempting and just as poisonous.
species.toxic: Toxic to people and to livestock. The toxins are pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which damage the liver. ALL parts are toxic, with the highest concentration of alkaloids in the FLOWERHEADS, then leaves, roots and stems. It remains equally toxic when dried, which is why it is dangerous in hay, and drying and wilting make it MORE palatable rather than less. The direct human route is the one that matters most to a forager or homesteader: never use it as an herbal remedy or tea. Indirect food-chain routes exist but are smaller than they sound, and the state authority tempers them itself: milk from animals that graze it can be tainted, although it is unlikely to do so in toxic amounts, and honey containing its nectar tastes so unpleasant that it cannot be sold. Handling: wear gloves when working with it, and seal pulled flowering plants in a plastic bag and put them in the trash, not in compost or yard waste. No human dose is documented.

lookalikes.name: Common tansy (Tanacetum vulgare)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Look at the flower and the answer is immediate: common tansy has button-like yellow flowerheads with NO petal-like rays at all, while tansy ragwort's yellow flowerheads are daisy-like with a ring of rays, typically 13 of them. Common tansy is itself a Washington Class B noxious weed listed in 1988 and is not a food. Data note: the state's tansy ragwort page calls common tansy a Class C weed in its inline text; common tansy's own state page says Class B, and that is the correct value.

lookalikes.name: Common St. Johnswort (Hypericum perforatum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A Washington Class C noxious weed with yellow flowers, but the flowers have only 5 true petals, against tansy ragwort's ring of about 13 petal-like rays. Count the petals.

lookalikes.name: Common groundsel (Senecio vulgaris)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A western Washington lookalike named by the Jefferson County noxious weed board, which is the nearest neighbouring county authority to Kitsap, and therefore more relevant here than the eastern Washington lookalike the state page names. It is a much smaller plant, and its flowerheads generally do not open the spreading yellow rays that tansy ragwort shows. Getting this one wrong changes nothing about safety: common groundsel is also a pyrrolizidine alkaloid Senecio, so neither plant is food.

lookalikes.name: Woodland groundsel (Senecio sylvaticus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Also named by Jefferson County as a western Washington lookalike, and also a pyrrolizidine alkaloid Senecio. Same conclusion as common groundsel: neither plant is food, so the confusion degrades identification rather than creating a poisoning route.

lookalikes.name: Tall butterweed (Senecio serra)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The state page scopes this one explicitly to eastern Washington, so it is not a lookalike to expect around Silverdale and a Kitsap user should not be hunting for it. Where it does occur it has toothed rather than lobed leaves and only 5 to 8 petal-like rays. Its own toxicity was not verified from a public-domain source, so it is neither asserted nor ruled out.

species.season: First-year plants are low rosettes, present year round. Second-year plants bolt and flower through summer, roughly June into September, and the flowering stage carries the highest alkaloid concentration.
species.habitat: A biennial: in the first year a rosette of ruffled dark green basal leaves, in the second year a flowering stem up to about 4 ft carrying flat-topped clusters of yellow daisy-like flowerheads, each typically with 13 petal-like rays. Open, disturbed areas: roadsides, pastures, fields and cleared forest land, with no soil preference. Common on Kitsap roadsides and in cleared or logged ground.
species.uses: None. Do not use it as a herb or a tea. Naming note: ITIS gives Jacobaea vulgaris Gaertn. as the accepted name and Senecio jacobaea L. as not accepted. USDA PLANTS still carries Senecio jacobaea L. as accepted, symbol SEJA, with stinking willie as its primary common name; that is an authority lag rather than a disagreement about which plant this is.
