species.protected: Not protected; the legal status is the opposite. Washington State Class B noxious weed, listed 1988.
species.edible_detail: Never, in any amount. USDA states that all parts of poison hemlock, leaves, stem, fruit and root, are poisonous. There is no part, season or preparation that is safe.
species.toxic: DEADLY, whole plant. The toxic compounds are coniine, gamma-coniceine and related piperidine alkaloids, which cause progressive paralysis. USDA states that all parts, leaves, stem, fruit and root, are poisonous, and that the leaves are especially poisonous in spring, up to the time the plant flowers; the highest alkaloid concentrations are in the roots and the seeds. TWO ROUTES THAT ARE NOT EATING A MEAL: USDA records that whistles made from the hollow stems of poison hemlock have caused death in children, and Washington's noxious weed board states that the toxins remain potent in DRIED plant material, so pulled, cut, composted or hayed plants stay lethal. The sap is also a skin irritant, so wear protection when handling or removing it. If someone has eaten any part, treat it as a medical emergency and call poison control immediately. No human dose is documented here.

lookalikes.name: Wild parsnip (Pastinaca sativa)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The single most documented route to human poisoning. USDA states that poisoning commonly results from mistaking poison hemlock ROOT for wild parsnips, and that the roots of poison hemlock may easily be mistaken for wild parsnips; both are pale taproots in the ground, where none of the stem and leaf characters are available to you. The one sense you would reach for cannot help you either. Washington's noxious weed board records that the leaves have a strong odour when crushed, and no source consulted for this record says what that odour resembles or compares it to parsnip, so smell tells you a carrot-family plant is in your hand and nothing about which one. Do not use smell as your test, and never dig an unidentified white-flowered carrot-family root.

lookalikes.name: Parsley
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: USDA states that poisoning commonly results from mistaking poison hemlock LEAVES for parsley, and describes hemlock's leaves as delicate, like parsley. ITIS carries poison parsley as a common name for this plant, which is how close the resemblance is judged to be. This is the confusion that reaches a kitchen, so it applies to anyone gathering wild greens and to anyone with volunteer plants coming up in a herb bed. Do not harvest parsley-like leaves from a plant you did not plant and watch.

lookalikes.name: Anise
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: USDA states that poisoning commonly results from mistaking poison hemlock SEED for anise. Seeds carry one of the two highest alkaloid concentrations in the plant, so this is the most concentrated dose of the three classic confusions. Do not collect wild seed heads for spice.

lookalikes.name: Wild carrot, Queen Anne's lace (Daucus carota)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Confusable mainly at a distance, and this is where the one genuinely useful visual check lives: wild carrot is smaller and its stems are HAIRY, while poison hemlock's stem is hairless and marked with small purple spots or streaks. Poison hemlock is also far taller, reaching 2 to 3 metres. Do not run the test backwards: the absence of purple spots proves nothing on a young plant, because the spots develop as the plant bolts, and a first-year rosette has no marked stem to check at all.

lookalikes.name: Western water hemlock (Cicuta douglasii)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Two different deadly plants that genuinely resemble one another, not merely a similar-sounding name, which is how this pairing is often dismissed. USDA states that poison hemlock is sometimes confused with western water hemlock, a more deadly species. Both kill, but differently: water hemlock's cicutoxin is a violent convulsant that causes seizures, while poison hemlock's coniine causes progressive paralysis. Water hemlock sits in standing water and wet meadows and has a chambered rootstalk that weeps brown or straw-colored liquid when cut; poison hemlock prefers fence lines, irrigation ditches and moist waste ground, has a white taproot, and has the purple-spotted hollow stem. For eating purposes the distinction is academic: both are fatal.

lookalikes.name: Other carrot-family plants generally, especially when young
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Here is the honest answer, and it is the most important line in this record. Before it bolts, poison hemlock is a low rosette of finely divided fern-like leaves with no purple-blotched stem to check, because there is no stem yet. At that stage a beginner cannot reliably tell it from young parsley, chervil, carrot tops, cow parsley or the other divided-leaved carrot-family plants, and people better qualified than a beginner have died making exactly that call. There is no field character offered here that closes that gap, because there is not one that works. Do not eat any wild carrot-family plant.

species.season: The first-year rosette is present through fall, winter and early spring, which is when it is most likely to be mistaken for parsley in a garden or field edge. It bolts and flowers in late spring and early summer, then sets seed and dies, and the dead standing stems remain poisonous.
species.habitat: A tall biennial reaching 2 to 3 metres, roughly 6 to 10 ft, at maturity. KEY MARKS: stem HOLLOW, HAIRLESS, and marked with small PURPLE SPOTS or streaks; leaves delicate and fern-like, finely divided and toothed, with a strong unpleasant odor when crushed; small white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters 4 to 8 in across; a white taproot; hairless egg-shaped seeds about 2 mm with prominent ridges. The purple-blotched hairless stem is the single most reliable field mark, but only once the plant has bolted. It prefers moist, nutrient-rich soil and adapts readily; expect it along fence lines, irrigation ditches, roadsides, and other moist disturbed and waste ground.

species.edible_detail: No part of this plant is food. All parts are poisonous: flowers, leaves, stems and seeds. There is no season, no plant part and no method of cooking or drying that makes foxglove safe to eat or to brew as a tea.
species.toxic: Every part is poisonous, and the National Library of Medicine names four of them specifically: flowers, leaves, stems and seeds. The poisons are cardiac glycosides, which act directly on the heart muscle. Poisoning causes an irregular or slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, collapse and shock, blurred vision and halos around lights, confusion, disorientation or hallucinations, and nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. There is no safe amount to experiment with. The US Forest Service notes that the therapeutic dose of foxglove is very close to the toxic level at which side effects develop, which is exactly why the drugs taken from it are prescribed by milligram under medical supervision. A plant strong enough to be a heart medicine is strong enough to stop a heart.

lookalikes.name: common mullein
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The danger here runs backwards from the usual case. Nobody dies because a guide called foxglove edible; people die because they picked foxglove believing it was something else. Foxglove has NO flower spike for its entire first year and again in the early spring of its second year, and the flower spike is the only thing a non botanist recognises it by. In that stage it is a flat rosette of soft, hairy, grey green, wrinkled leaves on exactly the disturbed roadside and cleared ground where mullein grows, and mullein leaves are gathered for tea. DO NOT try to key the two apart from leaf descriptions. The rule that actually protects you: never harvest rosette leaves from any hairy grey green rosette on roadsides, clearcuts or forest edges unless you watched that individual plant flower and confirmed what it was. Mark the plant in summer, harvest from the marked plant later. Note on sourcing: that foxglove is poisonous in all parts is from the National Library of Medicine; the mullein pairing is a warning based on shared habitat and shared rosette form, and no federal authority naming the confusion was found, so treat it as a reason for caution and not as a key.

lookalikes.name: comfrey
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Comfrey is deliberately grown on Pacific Northwest homesteads and its hairy leaves are brewed and used as poultices, so a comfrey patch is a place where somebody is already in the habit of pulling large hairy leaves. A first year foxglove is a large hairy leaf. Same rule as above: harvest only from plants you identified in flower, and never take rosette leaves from volunteer plants on disturbed ground. No federal authority naming this specific confusion was found; it is listed so that a reader gathering comfrey knows what else is shaped like it.

lookalikes.name: broadleaf plantain
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Plantain is one of the most widely foraged wild plants there is, it forms a basal rosette, and it grows on the same trampled and disturbed ground as foxglove. Plantain leaves are smooth and strongly ribbed while foxglove leaves are softly hairy and wrinkled, but do not stake your heart on a texture. Identify the individual plant in flower first. No federal authority naming this confusion was found.

species.season: Biennial. It spends its whole first year, and the early spring of its second year, as a flat leaf rosette with no flower spike at all. The tall spike of tubular flowers comes up in late spring and summer of the second year, and then the plant dies. The rosette stage is the dangerous one because it is the anonymous one.
species.habitat: Naturalized on disturbed ground throughout western Washington: roadsides, clearcuts and logged land, powerline cuts, gravel banks, gardens and sunny forest margins. Expect it on road shoulders and cleared lots around Silverdale. This habitat description is general to western Washington and was not confirmed against a Kitsap County source. Kitsap occurrence is confirmed: the Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria holds 2 Kitsap County specimen records for Digitalis purpurea.
species.uses: Garden ornamental, and the origin of real medicine. The US Forest Service records that Dr William Withering documented 200 cases of foxglove used for dropsy and heart failure in the 1700s, and that the cardiac glycosides digoxin and digitoxin were eventually extracted from the plant. Those are prescription drugs, not home remedies. Do not make any preparation from this plant. One flag for a later sourcing pass: the Forest Service page is loose on this point, because commercial digoxin comes principally from a different foxglove, Digitalis lanata.

species.protected: No protection. The opposite. It is a Washington State Class B noxious weed, listed in 1998, and it is on the state quarantine list under WAC 16-752, which makes it illegal to transport, buy, sell, offer for sale or distribute the plant, plant parts, or seed and wildflower mixes containing it into or within Washington. One record level oddity worth knowing: the state noxious weed board gives its origin as Europe, Asia and northern Africa, while USDA PLANTS carries BOTH introduced and native occurrences for the species in the lower 48. In western Washington it is managed as an invasive.
species.edible_detail: Do not treat it as a food. No public authority describes any part as edible, and the state noxious weed page does not address edibility at all. The state's written findings do record a long history of folk medicinal use, including for toothache and nosebleed. A history of folk use is not an edibility finding, and it is not a recommendation.
species.toxic: No toxin is documented. Washington's noxious weed board answers the question 'Is this Weed Toxic?' with 'not known to be'. One caution from the same authority's written findings: there are unsubstantiated reports that its strong odor may trigger asthma attacks. That report is explicitly labelled unsubstantiated, so treat it as a ventilation and respiratory sensitivity caution rather than a confirmed poison. It is operationally live here, though, because the recommended control is hand pulling, the findings record densities up to 250 plants per square metre under closed canopy, and the plant's diagnostic feature is the pungent smell of crushed leaves. Pulling a dense stand means breathing it for an hour. If you have asthma, work upwind, take breaks, and consider a mask.

lookalikes.name: shining geranium
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Neither plant is poisonous, so this is a weeding and identification problem, not a poisoning one. Shining geranium (Geranium lucidum) is itself a Washington Class B noxious weed and the state notes it can successfully grow along with herb-Robert, so you will often find the two mixed. The Extension weed handbook even treats them in a single combined entry. Tell herb-Robert by the pungent smell of crushed leaves, the deeply cut light green leaves that turn red in late fall, and the hairy stems that redden in bright light.

lookalikes.name: dovefoot geranium
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Named in the state's own 'May Be Confused With' entry for shining geranium. Dovefoot geranium (Geranium molle) is hairy and soft to the touch, with hairy sepals that are not ridged. Again, use herb-Robert's own marks: the smell when crushed, the deeply dissected leaves, and the hairy red tinged stems.

lookalikes.name: native wild geraniums
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: USDA PLANTS lists several geraniums as native in the lower 48, including Bicknell's, sticky purple, Richardson's and Carolina geranium. None is poisonous. Identify a small pink flowered geranium to species before you pull it, so you do not weed out a native while going after the invader. No toxic lookalike for herb-Robert is documented by any public authority consulted, which is a finding of absence in the sources, not proof that none exists.

species.season: Germinates in autumn or early spring and flowers from spring through autumn. The foliage turns red in late fall, which is when a stand is easiest to spot from a distance.
species.habitat: Moist forest under a closed canopy, and also dry rocky outcrops, from sea level to mid mountain in the Cascades and Olympics. It is the unusual invader that thrives under FULL canopy cover, which is how it gets deep into intact Kitsap forest instead of staying on the edges. Increasingly a garden weed as well.
species.uses: No recommended use. The state's written findings note a history of folk medicinal use for toothache and nosebleed. That is recorded history, not a recommendation, and nothing here should be eaten or brewed.

species.protected: No protection. It is a Washington State Class B noxious weed, listed in 2007. Whether control is legally REQUIRED in Kitsap County was not established: Class B duties are set region by region, and neighbouring counties differ, with Island County listing it as control required and Jefferson County saying control is encouraged but not required.
species.edible_detail: No part is food, in any preparation. Six state and county documents were reviewed and every one of them says all parts are toxic; none names an edible part, a safe season, or a cooking method that changes that.
species.toxic: All parts are highly toxic: the sap, stems, leaves, bark and the black berries. There are two separate hazards and most people only hear about one. EATING it poisons humans, pets (dogs and cats are named repeatedly in the county sheets) and livestock. The toxins are daphnane and tigliane diterpenes plus coumarin glycosides. TOUCHING it is the more common injury: the caustic sap causes contact dermatitis and severe skin and eye irritation, which is why the state and county guidance is gloves, protective clothing AND eye protection, not just gloves. Cutting it releases volatile plant toxins, inhaled sap droplets cause respiratory irritation, and the guidance is explicit that you should never transport cut plant material inside an enclosed vehicle. On deaths: keep the strong warning, but do not claim documented fatalities. The state's own written findings temper that, noting that the bitter taste of the berries may stop a child eating enough to become fatally ill, and that there are few accounts of poisoning from eating the berries in North America.

lookalikes.name: salal
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Salal itself is harmless and its berries are eaten. The danger is the other way round: spurge laurel is a glossy dark leaved evergreen shrub carrying BLACK berries in the same Puget Sound forest understory where people pick salal, and Kitsap County has the heaviest spurge laurel infestation in the state. Be honest about the state of the sources: no federal, Washington State or Extension document reviewed names ANY lookalike for spurge laurel, so there is no authority backed key to give you. The safe rule instead: treat every glossy dark evergreen shrub bearing black berries as spurge laurel until you have positively identified it, and never eat a dark berry off an evergreen shrub you cannot name. Two differences worth carrying, flagged as general botanical description rather than sourced from an authority: spurge laurel leaves have smooth untoothed edges and crowd in a whorl near the tip of an upright stem, with the small berries clustered at the leaf bases below them, while salal has alternate oval leaves with finely toothed edges and carries its berries along a one sided drooping stalk with sticky hairs.

lookalikes.name: evergreen huckleberry
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Same geometry as salal. Evergreen huckleberry is a harmless native with small glossy evergreen leaves and dark blue black berries in the same understory. Again, no authority names this as a documented confusion; it is flagged because the hazard shape is real. Evergreen huckleberry leaves are small, about an inch, with sharply toothed edges on wiry reddish twigs. Spurge laurel leaves are larger, smooth edged and leathery. Do not eat a dark berry from an evergreen shrub on the strength of that alone.

species.season: Evergreen, so it is there all year and is easiest to spot in winter when little else is green in the understory. Flowers late winter into early spring; the black berries ripen in early summer.
species.habitat: Forest understory in sun or shade. Kitsap County is the worst infestation in Washington State: the state Department of Agriculture distribution map, updated February 2024, shades Kitsap in the highest category, more than 1000 acres, and Kitsap is the only county in the state in that top band. Expect it in wooded lots, greenbelts and the shady edges of yards around Silverdale. It is particularly damaging in Garry oak habitat, which is already rare around Puget Sound.
species.uses: None. It was planted as a garden shrub, which is how it escaped into the woods.

species.protected: No protection. It is a Washington State Class C noxious weed, listed in 2025.
species.edible_detail: No part is food, in any season, raw or cooked. The fruit is the poisonous part and there is no preparation that changes that.
species.toxic: The fruit is the poisonous part. The toxic principle is saponins, and eating the berries causes vomiting, diarrhea and drowsiness. The berries are described as particularly poisonous to children. Poison severity is rated low, meaning serious effects generally require a large dose, but there is no edible use at any stage. Washington's noxious weed board separately flags the plant as toxic to humans. One correction to a claim that circulates: the state page does NOT say the berries are attractive to children. It says they are popular with birds. Do not repeat the children version as though the state said it.

lookalikes.name: Oregon grape
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Oregon grape (Berberis aquifolium, previously Mahonia aquifolium) is the native evergreen the state itself names as the confusable species. It also has spiny glossy leaves in the forest understory, and ITS berries are genuinely edible, which is what makes the pair dangerous: someone gathering Oregon grape for jelly takes holly by mistake. IDENTIFY BY THE LEAF, NEVER BY THE BERRY. A holly leaf is SIMPLE, one blade on one stalk, 1 to 3 inches long. An Oregon grape leaf is ODD PINNATELY COMPOUND, 5 to 13 leaflets ranged along a central stalk like a fern frond, so what looks like a whole holly leaf is only one leaflet of a much longer Oregon grape leaf. That works on every plant, every month, on either sex. Second check, also year round: holly leaf spines alternate between pointing up and pointing down so the blade looks wavy, while Oregon grape spines all point out or up and the leaflet lies flat. DO NOT use flowers or berries as your test. English holly is dioecious, so male plants never bear fruit at all, at any age, in any year, and neither plant shows flowers or fruit for much of the year. Where fruit IS present: holly is red, and some planted forms are yellow or orange, while Oregon grape is dusty blue to blue black. Where flowers ARE present: holly white, Oregon grape bright yellow. Height only helps on a mature plant, because Oregon grape tops out around 3 to 6 ft while holly grows into a tree, but a holly sapling in the understory can be shorter than a full grown Oregon grape. One condition on the Oregon grape side: its berries are edible and are used for jelly and wine, but they are very tart and contain berberine, which can upset the stomach, especially in children. Eat them in moderation, not as a trail nibble.

species.season: Evergreen, so the leaves are there year round and the leaf test works in every month. It flowers in late spring; the berries ripen in autumn on female plants and can hang on into winter. Exact months come from an East Coast Extension source and probably run later in Puget Sound, so the seasons are given rather than dates.
species.habitat: Understory of healthy and disturbed forest, riparian areas and shady ground throughout western Washington. It adapts to many soil types and sets more seed with more light. Birds eat the berries and carry it deep into intact forest, so it turns up far from any garden. It was widely planted as an ornamental, which is where most escapes start. Common in Kitsap woodlots and greenbelts.
species.uses: Ornamental and Christmas greenery. Not food.

species.protected: No protection. It is a Washington State Class C noxious weed, listed in 2002.
species.edible_detail: No part is food, above ground or below. The US Forest Service does record a few marginal historical uses (rhizomes used medicinally in Turkey, dried seeds used as a coffee substitute, leaves smoked during the Second World War), but the same Forest Service page classes the plant as poisonous. Those are famine and folk uses, not edibility, and they must not be promoted into an edible flag.
species.toxic: POISONOUS IF EATEN. It contains large amounts of glycosides in BOTH the foliage and the rhizomes. Livestock have suffered gastroenteritis after eating hay containing it, and acute diarrhoea after eating the rhizomes, and the Forest Service classes the plant as poisonous without limiting that to animals. SEPARATELY, and in addition, resins in the leaves and rhizomes irritate human skin on contact, and the syrupy coating on the seeds has caused severe dermatitis. Keep the two apart in your head: resins are the contact irritant, glycosides are the ingestion poison. Eat no part of this plant, above ground or below, and wear gloves when digging it.

lookalikes.name: broadleaf cattail
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Cattail (Typha latifolia) is edible and grows in the same shallow water. Before either plant flowers the confusion is real, and the consequence is serious, because the cattail parts people harvest are the RHIZOME and the young shoot, which are exactly the iris parts loaded with glycosides. DO NOT use leaf cross section as your test. That test circulates widely and it is wrong: the Forest Service describes cattail leaves as thick, linear, FLAT and 6 to 29 mm wide. Both plants have flat leaves. The usable contrast is thickness and stance. Yellow flag iris leaves are thin, stiff and sword like, folded and overlapping at the base so the whole shoot stands in one rigid flat plane like a hand of cards. Cattail leaves are thick, spongy and limp rather than stiffly planar. If you cannot confirm the plant from its flower (iris yellow with brownish purple markings, cattail a brown sausage shaped seed spike) or from the iris's three angled seed capsule, do not harvest it.

lookalikes.name: sweet flag
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The other classic sword leaved wetland plant, and one that IS harvested for flavouring, which makes this potentially the more dangerous pairing of the two. USDA PLANTS confirms Acorus calamus is introduced in the lower 48, but its Washington distribution could not be confirmed from a public authority, so this is carried as a warning rather than a confirmed local pair. Do NOT use a smell test or a leaf shape test to decide that a sword leaved plant is the safe one. Work the other way: if you cannot see an iris flower or an iris seed capsule to rule the iris OUT, leave the whole patch alone.

species.season: Flowers in late spring and early summer, which is the only time it is unmistakable. The sword shaped leaves stand through the growing season and the three angled seed capsules persist after flowering.
species.habitat: Temperate wetlands: the margins of lakes, ponds and slow moving rivers, usually in very shallow water or wet mud. It also adapts to drier ground and acidic soils. Around Silverdale expect it at pond and wetland edges and in roadside ditches that hold water. It spreads by seed and by rhizomes that form dense interconnected clumps.
species.uses: None recommended. It was planted as a pond ornamental and for erosion control, which is how it escaped. Do not plant it: it is a listed noxious weed.

species.protected: No protection. It is a Washington State Class C noxious weed, listed in 1995. Its origin is genuinely disputed at the record level: the Washington noxious weed board gives the origin as Eurasia, while USDA PLANTS records the species as Native in the lower 48 and Canada and Introduced in Alaska. Whatever the origin, the aggressive form around Puget Sound behaves as an invasive and is managed as one. The US Forest Service adds nuance that is often misquoted: invasive North American populations are thought to be nonnative strains or hybrids between nonnative and native strains, and native populations that have never been exposed to gene flow from nonnative strains may no longer occur in North America. That is native strains possibly swamped, not native strains never existing.
species.edible_detail: Do not eat it. It is not a food plant. No federal source reviewed addresses human consumption at all, and wild stands carry variable alkaloid loads (see toxic). The Forest Service lists its non forage uses as erosion control, shoreline stabilization and pollutant filtration only.
species.toxic: Yes, alkaloids. Do not repeat the old 'no toxicity reported' line. The US Forest Service species review states that some strains of reed canarygrass contain high concentrations of alkaloid compounds, making them unpalatable and/or toxic. Alkaloid type and concentration vary genetically from strain to strain, which is precisely why low alkaloid forage cultivars (Palaton, Rival, Venture) were bred. The documented harm is in a livestock forage context, and whether wild Puget Sound stands reach a dose hazardous to PEOPLE specifically is not established. You cannot tell a high alkaloid stand from a low alkaloid one by looking at it, and wild stands are of uncontrolled strain, so treat every wild stand as high alkaloid. One important note about the state page: Washington's noxious weed board answers 'Is this Weed Toxic?' with 'not known to be'. That is a bare determination on a weed CONTROL page, not a toxicology finding, and the very same page links onward to the Forest Service review that does report the alkaloid toxicity. Never read a noxious weed board toxicity field as a foraging safety clearance for any species.

lookalikes.name: other tall wetland grasses
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Be honest about this field rather than leaving it blank. No specific toxic grass double for Kitsap County wetlands could be confirmed from a public authority, so no species is named here. That is an absence of sourcing, NOT a finding that confusion is unlikely. Grass identification is genuinely hard, grasses are the group where beginners misidentify most often, and there is no safe versus toxic shortcut available within the genus Phalaris. Reed canarygrass itself stands 3 to 6 ft, with flat hairless leaf blades a quarter to three quarters of an inch wide, sturdy often hollow stems up to half an inch thick that redden near the top, and a dense flower panicle that shifts from green purple to beige in May and June. Use those to recognise the weed for control work. Do not use them, or anything else in this entry, as permission to eat a wild grass.

species.season: Cool season perennial. Greens up early, blooms May through mid June, and the dead stems stand through winter.
species.habitat: Saturated or nearly saturated soil throughout the growing season: roadside ditches, river dikes, shallow marshes, wetlands and wet meadows. It is the dominant grass of degraded Kitsap wetlands, outcompeting most natives and forming large single species stands.
species.uses: Planted historically for forage, erosion control and shoreline stabilization, and it does filter pollutants from water. Not a human food. Low alkaloid forage cultivars exist (Palaton, Rival, Venture); a wild stand is not one of them.

species.form: mushroom (grows from soil, attached to living conifer roots; ridged underneath rather than gilled)
species.protected: Not protected, but collecting is regulated by the landowner. Olympic National Park allows up to one quart per person per day while warning that many fatally poisonous mushrooms live in the park. Washington's food rule WAC 246-215-03225 lists Pacific Golden Chanterelle (Cantharellus formosus, C. cascadensis, C. cibarius var roseocanus) among the wild mushrooms a licensed food establishment may sell or serve. Read that rule for what it is: a retail food code rule addressed to a permit holder, not a foraging clearance. It requires the mushrooms come from Washington, Oregon, Idaho, California, Montana or British Columbia, that EACH mushroom is individually identified in the fresh state by a named mushroom identifier whose name, signature, business and contact details the establishment keeps on file for 90 days, and that mushrooms prepared for immediate service are cooked to 135 degrees F. Do not cite it as state endorsement of foraging.
species.edible_detail: Edible and rated choice by the US Forest Service, but on TWO hard conditions. (1) COOK IT. Washington's food rule requires wild harvested mushrooms prepared for immediate service to be cooked to 135 degrees F and permits no raw service at all; Ohio State University Extension says plainly 'Do not eat mushrooms raw'; the Forest Service chanterelle report says to cook them thoroughly and start by eating small amounts, and warns that even safe edibles such as chanterelles cause allergic reactions in some people. Raw chanterelle tastes mildly peppery. (2) IDENTIFY THAT INDIVIDUAL MUSHROOM. Washington State does not trust unaided identification either: its rule requires a named identifier to examine every single mushroom in the fresh state. BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT A WRITTEN DESCRIPTION CAN DO. It cannot make you safe. The Forest Service's own chanterelle report says of its species descriptions: 'These descriptions are not meant as a definitive identification guide. If you are uncertain, seek additional information and advice.' Mount Rainier National Park says identifying wild mushrooms can be extremely difficult and consuming them can be deadly, that its own descriptions are intentionally brief and are not sufficient to positively identify edible mushrooms, and that you should not collect or eat any mushroom unless you are 100 percent confident of its identification. FDA puts it hardest: folklore notwithstanding, there is no reliable rule of thumb for distinguishing edible mushrooms from poisonous ones, and many poisonings happen to people who were using field guides, had a lot of experience, and were sure they had the right mushroom. A beginner should get their first chanterelles looked at in person by someone who knows them. Do not eat one on the strength of this entry.
species.toxic: The species itself is not poisonous when correctly identified and cooked. Two real caveats that belong on the label. Do not eat it raw. And even correctly identified chanterelles cause allergic reactions in some individuals, which is why the Forest Service instruction is cook thoroughly, then start with a small amount the first time.

lookalikes.name: poison pax (brown chanterelle)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is the deadly one the Forest Service names by name in its Pacific Northwest chanterelle report, and it is missing from most popular accounts. Paxillus involutus is sometimes CALLED the brown chanterelle. It is a dull yellow brown mushroom with crowded yellow to olive GILLS that run down the stem, stain brown when handled, and separate readily from the cap. Its spore print is yellowish to reddish brown and it tastes sour or bitter. A real chanterelle has a yellowish white spore print, a faint fruity apricot smell, and no gills at all. THE TEST THAT SEPARATES THEM: turn the mushroom over. A true chanterelle's underside is shallow arching RIDGES, blunt folds and wrinkles that run down the stem and are part of the cap flesh, so they will not scrape off with a thumbnail. Poison pax has thin crowded forked GILLS that scrape off easily because they are separate structures sitting on the cap. WHY IT IS SO DANGEROUS: it has been eaten in Europe for centuries and it still kills. It causes Paxillus syndrome, an immune hemolytic anemia, and the Forest Service says it has been implicated in a number of deaths. The mechanism is the worst part. The toxins accumulate in susceptible eaters over long periods with little effect, and then the next meal can cause sudden illness or death, so 'I have eaten these before and been fine' proves nothing about the next one. The Forest Service also calls it a common URBAN mushroom, which puts it in Silverdale yards and not only in the woods. FDA separately lists it, as the naked brimcap, among mushrooms producing severe gastroenteritis.

lookalikes.name: false chanterelle
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca. Not deadly, but not edible. The Park Service says that unlike chanterelles the false chanterelle is NOT edible, that it is a bright fluorescent orange yellow, that it typically comes up in pine needle beds, and, importantly, that amateurs often cannot tell the two apart. The Forest Service key separates them cleanly on the same test as above: the false chanterelle has crowded, forked, VERY THIN gills that are easily scraped off the underside of the cap, brilliant to pastel orange and not staining, with a WHITE spore print and a bland taste. A chanterelle has blunt ridges and folds that are part of the cap flesh and will not scrape off, and a yellowish white spore print.

lookalikes.name: jack-o'-lantern
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Omphalotus species. This is the classic chanterelle mistake nationally: FDA's table of poisonous mushrooms and their edible look-alikes lists Omphalotus olearius, the jack-o'-lantern, as mistaken for Cantharellus species, and FDA lists Omphalotus illudens among mushrooms that produce severe gastroenteritis, with vomiting and diarrhea that can last several days. TWO characters separate it. First, the underside: a jack-o'-lantern has true, sharp, bladelike gills, not blunt ridges. Second, and easier, WHERE IT GROWS: jack-o'-lanterns grow in dense clusters on wood, on stumps and on buried roots, while a Pacific golden chanterelle grows singly or scattered straight out of the soil, attached to living conifer roots. A chanterelle comes out of the ground, not out of wood. HONEST LIMIT ON THIS ENTRY: the Forest Service's Pacific Northwest chanterelle report does NOT list any Omphalotus among the look-alikes a Pacific Northwest picker will meet, and whether jack-o'-lanterns occur in Kitsap County could not be confirmed from any public source. Carry the character. Do not assume the species is absent.

lookalikes.name: woolly pine spike
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Chroogomphus tomentosus, named by the Forest Service as a Pacific Northwest chanterelle look-alike. It has TRUE bladelike gills, thick, distant and unforked, turning orange to smoky gray as its black spores mature, under a thick fleshed orange woolly cap. Harmless, but if you picked it, your ridge test failed and you should recheck everything else in the basket.

lookalikes.name: Clitocybe species
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The Forest Service names some Clitocybe species among the mushrooms cited as chanterelle look-alikes in field guides. They have true bladelike gills that are distinct from the flesh of the cap, not ridges. Worth knowing the genus because FDA records muscarine poisoning from Clitocybe species: profuse and prolonged sweating, tearing and salivation beginning 15 to 30 minutes after eating, usually with complete recovery in about 2 hours.

lookalikes.name: orange hedgehog
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Hydnum repandum and H. umbilicatum. Easily mistaken for a chanterelle from above or at a distance, and the Forest Service calls hedgehogs choice commercially harvested edibles in their own right, so this is a happy mistake rather than a dangerous one. Turn it over: the underside is covered with soft toothpick like SPINES rather than ridges, and the stem is white.

species.season: Fruits from midsummer through late fall, in young to old forest.
species.habitat: Grows from the soil in coniferous forest, attached to living tree roots. The Forest Service reports it from California, Oregon, Washington and British Columbia under hemlock, Douglas-fir and spruce. Around Silverdale that means second growth Douglas-fir and hemlock woods. It does not grow on wood, on stumps or in bark mulch, and that fact is part of how you rule out the jack-o'-lantern.
species.uses: Food, cooked. Commercially harvested across the Pacific Northwest, and the Oregon state mushroom, chosen by that legislature in 1999.

species.form: mushroom (grows from soil with living tree roots; a sponge of pores under the cap rather than gills)
species.protected: Not protected. Olympic National Park names king bolete among the park's fungi and allows collection of up to one quart per person per day, while warning that many fatally poisonous mushrooms live there. Washington's food rule WAC 246-215-03225 lists Porcini/King Bolete (Boletus edulis) among the wild mushrooms a licensed food establishment may sell or serve, on the same conditions as the chanterelle: approved source states only (Washington, Oregon, Idaho, California, Montana, British Columbia), each mushroom individually identified in the fresh state by a named identifier, records kept 90 days, cooked to 135 degrees F for immediate service. That is a commercial sourcing rule. It is not a statement that a bolete you picked yourself is safe to eat.
species.edible_detail: Edible only when thoroughly COOKED and only when that individual mushroom has been identified by someone who genuinely knows boletes. Be MORE careful here than with the chanterelle, because boletes are the group where written descriptions fail hardest. A 2021 DNA authentication study of wild mushroom products sold in the United States found that almost nothing labelled porcini actually was. Products sold as Boletus edulis or porcini contained Suillus species, Tylopilus microsporus, Retiboletus fuscus and Caloboletus yunnanensis, and one product labelled simply 'porcini' contained Amanita pseudoporphyria, which has caused renal failure in people. Buyers left reviews saying it made those who ate it violently ill and that they had never been so sick in their lives. If the commercial trade cannot reliably tell a porcini from what is not one, a beginner reading a paragraph cannot either. FDA states it flatly: folklore notwithstanding, there is no reliable rule of thumb for distinguishing edible mushrooms from poisonous ones, and many poisonings happen to experienced people using field guides who were sure they were right. Do not eat a wild bolete on the strength of any written description, including this one. Get your first ones checked in person.
species.toxic: Boletus edulis itself is not considered poisonous when correctly identified and cooked, and boletes are among the most sought after edible mushrooms. Two caveats belong on the label. Allergic reactions to B. edulis are reported in the clinical literature. And FDA lists Boletus among the genera containing species that produce gastrointestinal upset, naming the pepper bolete (Boletus piperatus) specifically. 'It is a bolete' is not a safety statement.

lookalikes.name: red-pored boletes (devil's bolete and relatives)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: LOOK AT THE PORE SURFACE UNDER THE CAP. A king bolete's pores are white when young, ageing to yellow and then olive. They are never red and never orange. Red or orange pores mark a group that contains toxic species, including Rubroboletus satanas, the devil's bolete. A clinical review of mushroom poisoning records that Boletus and Rubinoboletus species can contain enough muscarine to produce muscarinic poisoning, which FDA describes as profuse and prolonged sweating, tearing and salivation starting 15 to 30 minutes after eating. Whether a red pored toxic bolete occurs in Kitsap County specifically could not be confirmed from any public source, so carry the rule rather than assuming the group is absent from here.

lookalikes.name: bitter bolete
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Tylopilus species, the commonest disappointment rather than a poisoning. It is not toxic; it is simply so bitter that one in a pan ruins the whole dish. It resembles a king bolete closely enough that the DNA study above recovered Tylopilus microsporus from material being sold in the United States as porcini, so the confusion happens in commerce as well as in the woods. The customary field check is taste: a tiny nibble of raw flesh, chewed briefly and SPAT OUT, is strongly bitter in Tylopilus and mild and nutty in a king bolete. The Forest Service uses taste in exactly this way as a key character for separating chanterelle look-alikes. Two warnings. Taste testing is a technique for someone who already knows the group and knows which groups it is safe to use on; it is not a beginner's identification method. And it does nothing at all to protect you from the genuinely toxic species listed here.

lookalikes.name: lurid bolete
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Boletus luridus causes a disulfiram like reaction. The mushroom on its own may do nothing, but drinking alcohol within roughly 72 hours of eating it produces flushing, palpitations, rapid heartbeat and laboured breathing. FDA documents the same pattern for the inky cap, where alcohol within 72 hours brings on facial flushing, chest pain, nausea and projectile vomiting that can mimic a heart attack. Another reason 'it is a bolete' means nothing by itself.

lookalikes.name: slippery jacks
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Suillus species were the single most common substitution found in United States products labelled porcini. Ohio State University Extension lists slippery jack (Suillus) as an edible fleshy pore mushroom found under 2 needle and 3 needle pines, so this is not a poisoning risk, it is a quality and competence risk: if you believe you are picking porcini and you are actually picking Suillus, your identification is not working, and the same process that produced that error can produce a worse one.

lookalikes.name: Amanita species, including the deadly ones
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: In principle an Amanita cannot be confused with a bolete, because Amanitas have GILLS, thin blades under the cap, while a bolete has a sponge of PORES. In practice, DNA testing found Amanita pseudoporphyria in a product sold in the United States labelled porcini, and that species has caused renal failure in people, so the confusion evidently does happen once mushrooms are cut, dried and mixed. Two habits protect you. Look under EVERY cap, not one in the basket. And, per the Forest Service field guide, dig mushrooms rather than picking them, so that you can see the cup (volva) at the base of the stalk that marks an Amanita, along with the other Amanita signs: a ring on the stalk, white gills free from the stalk, and a white spore print. The Forest Service notes that Amanita virosa, A. verna and A. bisporigera can only be told apart from each other by their spore characteristics and that collectively they cause 95 percent of fatal mushroom poisonings.

species.season: Late summer and autumn. The season was not confirmed against a source specific to Kitsap County.
species.habitat: Grows from the soil in conifer forest, attached to living tree roots. Olympic National Park, directly west across Hood Canal, names king bolete among its fungi, so it is present on the Peninsula. Which king bolete taxon actually grows in Kitsap County is an open question: western North American king boletes are treated as a species complex in the mycological literature, and the binomial in the Washington food rule is a regulatory label rather than a local determination. The authority string for the binomial could not be confirmed from a public database, so none is given.
species.uses: Food, cooked and dried. One of the most sought after wild edible mushrooms, and ecologically important as a tree symbiont.

species.scientific_name: Pleurotus ostreatus, P. pulmonarius and P. populinus (three closely related species share this common name)
species.form: mushroom (wood rotting, growing in shelving clusters on logs and stumps)
species.protected: Not protected. Washington's food rule WAC 246-215-03225 lists Oyster (Pleurotus populinus, P. pulmonarius, P. ostreaus) among the wild mushrooms a licensed food establishment may sell or serve; note the rule itself misspells ostreatus, so a string match against the rule text will fail. The same conditions apply as for the other listed species: approved source states only, every mushroom individually identified in the fresh state by a named identifier whose details are kept on file for 90 days, and cooked to 135 degrees F for immediate service. A commercial rule, not a foraging clearance.
species.edible_detail: Edible, COOKED, and only when identified. Cook it: the state food rule requires 135 degrees F for immediate service and allows no raw service, and Ohio State University Extension says do not eat mushrooms raw. Identify it: that same state rule requires a named identifier to check each mushroom in the fresh state, which is the state of Washington declining to trust an unaided picker. THE DANGER IS NOT THE OYSTER MUSHROOM, IT IS WHAT ELSE GROWS ON WOOD. The Forest Service field guide prints the same warning at the foot of every page: do not eat any mushroom unless you are absolutely certain of its identity, many mushroom species look alike and some are highly poisonous, and many mushrooms can be identified only by examining the color of spore prints or by examining spores and tissues under a microscope. That is the honest answer here. A beginner should not eat a mushroom taken off wood on the strength of a written description, including this one. Take a spore print, and get the first batches checked in person by someone who knows them.
species.toxic: Not known to be toxic to humans when correctly identified and cooked. Two notes for completeness. A clinical review records encephalopathy in poisoning attributed to Pleurotus eringii, a different cultivated species in the same genus. And oyster fruiting bodies contain ostreolysin, a pore forming protein that is lethal to rodents by injection; no public source establishes that it is hazardous by mouth or that cooking destroys it, so the instruction to cook rests on the Washington food rule and not on that toxicology.

lookalikes.name: funeral bell (deadly Galerina)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: THIS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Galerina marginata grows on dead wood, in the same forests, in the same season, and Olympic National Park names both it and the oyster's habitat wood as present in the park. It carries amatoxins, the same toxin family as the death cap. FDA gives amatoxin mortality as a figure that depends on how fast you reach hospital: about 10 percent for people given aggressive support almost immediately, and 50 to 90 percent for those admitted 60 or more hours after eating. It records that the poison survives cooking, canning, freezing and blanching, and that symptoms are delayed, which its onset table gives as 6 hours to 3 days. That symptom free gap is the thing that kills people, because it runs out long after the meal looks fine. HOW THEY DIFFER. An oyster mushroom is PALE and SHELF SHAPED: cap white to pale tan, gills white and running down the stem, the stem usually lateral (off to one side) or absent altogether so the mushroom sits on the wood like a bracket, and no ring on the stem. Its spore print is white in P. ostreatus and P. populinus, and lilac in P. pulmonarius. The funeral bell is a SMALL BROWN MUSHROOM. FDA classes it under Little Brown Mushrooms. It has a brown cap and brown gills, an ordinary central stem usually carrying a ring, and a rusty brown spore print. Pale shelf with white gills and no proper stem, against a small brown toadstool with a ring, is a real and visible difference. SOURCING HONESTY: the oyster characters above are from the US Forest Service field guide and the Little Brown Mushroom classing is FDA's; the funeral bell's ring and rusty brown spore print are the standard mycological description and were not confirmed from a federal document in this pass, so treat them as description rather than as a verified key. WHY THE DIFFERENCE IS STILL NOT ENOUGH. The realistic accident is not mistaking one for the other. It is one funeral bell going into the basket alongside the oysters because it was on the same log and nobody looked at every single mushroom. So: check every mushroom individually, and take a spore print of the batch on white paper before cooking anything gathered from wood. White or lilac is consistent with oyster. Any rusty brown is a reason to throw the entire batch away. And if you may have eaten one, get emergency care during the symptom free window, not after symptoms appear; by the time you feel ill, liver damage is already under way.

lookalikes.name: angel wing
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Pleurocybella porrigens is pale, thin fleshed and shelf shaped on wood, which is the same shape, the same habitat and the same season as an oyster mushroom, making it the single most likely pale on wood confusion here. It is present in Olympic National Park. It was implicated in an outbreak of acute encephalopathy in Japan in autumn 2004, roughly 59 poisonings and 17 deaths, concentrated in people with chronic kidney disease. WARNING ABOUT THE SOURCE MOST PEOPLE WILL REACH FIRST: the Olympic National Park fungi page lists angel wing only as a benign nutrient recycling decomposer, in the same sentence as chicken of the woods, which is a popular edible, and it issues no warning about angel wing at all. Do NOT read that page as a safety clearance. Substrate helps a little: the Forest Service field guide places all three oyster species on hardwoods (P. populinus on aspen, P. pulmonarius and P. ostreatus on other hardwoods, P. ostreatus often in riparian settings), while angel wing is a conifer wood species. In Kitsap County, where Douglas-fir and hemlock dominate, that means substrate does NOT separate these two here, whatever an eastern field guide says. The Burke Herbarium gives Pleurotus pulmonarius, a Pacific Northwest oyster mushroom, as growing on conifer wood, and there is a Kitsap County specimen record for it. Use the structural characters instead: an angel wing has NO STEM AT ALL, its flesh is thin, tough and elastic rather than fleshy, and its cap is translucent striate at the margin. That is not reliable enough to eat on. If you have any kidney disease, do not eat pale mushrooms off wood at all.

lookalikes.name: honey mushroom
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Armillaria mellea and, locally, Armillaria nabsnona, both named as present in Olympic National Park. Honey mushrooms are edible when cooked and are the other thing people gather in bulk off stumps in autumn. They are not really an oyster lookalike; they are here because FDA names the honey mushroom as what the FUNERAL BELL gets mistaken for, so if you are working wood at all you need its marks. The Forest Service field guide gives the honey mushroom a tan to golden yellow cap, a prominent ring on the stem, a WHITE spore print, and black shoestring cords (rhizomorphs) running through the wood. The funeral bell's spore print is rusty brown. That contrast is the check that matters on any wood gathered mushroom.

lookalikes.name: little brown mushrooms, including Gymnopilus species
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA lists Gymnopilus spectabilis (the big laughing mushroom) and other Gymnopilus species among what the funeral bell is mistaken for, and notes that Gymnopilus ventricosus grows on the wood of conifers in western North America. These are not oyster lookalikes. They are listed here because any small brown mushroom growing on the same wood as your oysters is a reason to inspect every mushroom in the basket rather than the basket as a whole.

species.season: Summer through autumn.
species.habitat: On dead and dying HARDWOOD: logs, stumps, standing dead trunks and fallen limbs, in shelving clusters. The Forest Service field guide places P. populinus on aspen only, and P. pulmonarius and P. ostreatus on hardwoods other than aspen, with P. ostreatus often in riparian areas. Around Silverdale that points to alder and maple along creeks and in damp second growth rather than to Douglas-fir logs. One sourcing note: the Olympic National Park fungi page does not mention Pleurotus at all, so it cannot be cited for local occurrence of the oyster mushroom itself.
species.uses: Food, cooked. Also one of the easiest mushrooms to cultivate, which is by a wide margin the safe way to eat one.

species.form: mushroom (gilled, grows from soil with tree roots)
species.edible_detail: Never, under any preparation. This species is responsible for most deaths following ingestion of foraged mushrooms worldwide. The toxins are heat stable and are NOT inactivated by cooking, so preparation method is irrelevant to safety. FDA adds that most mushrooms causing human poisoning cannot be made nontoxic by cooking, canning, freezing or any other processing, and records amatoxin illnesses from fresh raw mushrooms, stir fried mushrooms, home canned mushrooms, mushrooms cooked in tomato sauce (which makes the sauce itself toxic even when no mushroom is eaten), and mushrooms blanched and frozen at home.
species.toxic: DEADLY. The poisons are amatoxins. Poisoning runs in three phases and the middle phase is the trap that kills people who think they have recovered. Phase one: delayed gastroenteritis with heavy body fluid loss, 6 to 24 hours after eating. Phase two: symptomatic recovery, about 24 to 36 hours after eating, when the patient feels better. Phase three: fulminant liver and multiorgan failure, typically 3 to 5 days after eating. CDC notes that patients seen early in the illness may be discharged home only to return later in liver failure, and its 2016 report documents exactly that happening to a patient sent home with a gastroenteritis diagnosis who came back the next day. Case fatality is 10 to 20 percent with modern hospital care; FDA does not give an unconditional figure: it reports mortality of only about 10 percent for those given aggressive support almost immediately and 50 to 90 percent for those admitted 60 or more hours after eating. In one cluster of 14 suspected ingestions over two weeks in December 2016 across five northern California counties, three patients needed liver transplants and one child survivor was left with permanent neurologic impairment after a postoperative course including cerebral edema. There is no antidote. If you may have eaten one, get emergency care DURING the symptom free window, not after symptoms appear. Getting to hospital early is the single biggest determinant of survival.

lookalikes.name: field mushrooms (Agaricus species)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA lists white Agaricus species among the mushrooms that the pure white form of the death cap and its white relatives get mistaken for, and this is the locally load bearing one, because Agaricus mushrooms come up in lawns and pasture around Puget Sound and get gathered by people who believe they know them. DIG, DO NOT PICK. The Forest Service field guide says mushrooms should always be dug rather than picked, in order to detect the cup (volva) at the base of the stalk, which is often below the soil surface and is the mark of a potentially poisonous Amanita. The full Amanita signature per the same guide: a ring (annulus) on the stalk, a cup at the base, white gills that are free from the stalk, and a white spore print. A mature Agaricus by contrast has pink and then chocolate brown gills and a brown spore print, and no cup at the base; that contrast is standard mycology rather than a quotation from a federal document, so use it alongside the dig-and-look-for-the-cup rule, not instead of it.

lookalikes.name: hooded grisette
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA lists Amanita calyptrodermia (usually written calyptroderma today) among what the green capped, normal coloured death cap is mistaken for. For a Pacific Northwest reader this is the most dangerous line on the whole list, because the hooded grisette is actually EATEN by Pacific Northwest foragers, which makes it a confusion somebody will act on rather than merely make. Both are Amanitas; both have a ring and a cup. There is no written description that safely separates them for a beginner. Do not attempt it.

lookalikes.name: grisette, false deathcap, smoothcap parasol and shiny cavalier
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA lists Amanita vaginata (grisette), Amanita citrina (false deathcap), Leucoagaricus naucina (smoothcap parasol) and Tricholoma resplendens (shiny cavalier) among what the PURE WHITE death cap variety, and the white destroying angels, are mistaken for. Note that some of FDA's binomials are dated (Leucoagaricus naucina is often now treated as L. leucothites); they are given as FDA prints them.

lookalikes.name: green brittlegill, tawny grisette, cavalier mushroom and sooty head
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA lists Russula virescens (green brittlegill), Amanita fulva (tawny grisette), Tricholoma flavovirens (cavalier mushroom, often now written T. equestre) and Tricholoma portentosum (sooty head) among what the GREEN capped, normal coloured death cap is mistaken for. Cap colour is the organising principle of this whole list, which should tell you how little cap colour is worth as a safety feature.

lookalikes.name: Caesar's mushroom
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA lists Amanita caesarea against the YELLOW death cap variety. Caesar's mushroom is a prized edible in Italy, so this is a confusion that travels with people who learned their mushrooms in another country. FDA names recent immigrants collecting American species that resemble edible species from home as one of the main ways Americans are poisoned.

lookalikes.name: puffballs
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA lists puffballs such as Lycoperdon perlatum among what the BUTTON stage of the white deadly Amanitas is mistaken for. A young Amanita still wrapped in its universal veil looks like a small white ball in the grass. The standard protection, which is technique rather than a federal quotation: cut every puffball in half from top to bottom before eating it. A real puffball is uniform solid white inside. An Amanita button shows the outline of a cap, gills and stalk in cross section.

species.season: Not established for western Washington from any public source. CDC records it as abundant in the early wet winter months in California, but that is a different climate and a different host tree, so no local season is claimed here.
species.habitat: Grows from the soil in a symbiotic relationship with tree roots. CDC reports research indicating that Amanita phalloides was introduced and is expanding its range on the west coast of North America, and a 1997 CDC report states that since 1979 it has been found in the region from northern California to Washington state, and that it has grown in places where it had not grown before, including backyards. The California association is with coast live oak, which does NOT grow in Kitsap County, so do not carry that host tree over: host trees and fruiting season for western Washington could not be established from any public source found, and there are no Kitsap County occurrence records to cite. What does carry over is the exposure pattern. Treat planted and landscaped hardwoods in yards, parks and street plantings as the risk setting, not deep forest.

species.form: mushroom (gilled, grows from soil with tree roots)
species.protected: Not protected. Olympic National Park allows collection of up to one quart per person per day, while warning that many fatally poisonous mushrooms live in the park and quoting the forager's adage that there are bold mushroom hunters and old mushroom hunters, but no old, bold mushroom hunters.
species.edible_detail: Do not eat it. Olympic National Park calls it poisonous. The US Forest Service field guide gives its edibility, in one word, as Poisonous. There IS folk literature about parboiling it, and people do eat some Amanita species, and that is exactly why this entry says no without qualification: parboiling is a way to make a poisonous mushroom less poisonous, not a way to make it food, and getting the species wrong inside the genus Amanita is a leading way people die. Nothing in this entry should be read as a method for preparing it.
species.toxic: Poisonous. It produces ibotenic acid and muscimol, and muscimol is roughly five times more potent than ibotenic acid. Symptoms generally begin 1 to 2 hours after eating. Abdominal discomfort may or may not be present; the chief symptoms are drowsiness and dizziness, sometimes with sleep, followed by hyperactivity, excitability, deranged senses, manic behaviour and delirium, with periods of drowsiness alternating with periods of excitement, and the whole thing generally fading within a few hours. Fatalities are rare in adults, but a child who accidentally eats a large quantity can suffer convulsions, coma or other neurologic problems for up to 12 hours. A clinical review hosted by the National Library of Medicine notes that although A. muscaria contains small amounts of muscarine, the levels are typically too low to cause cholinergic poisoning. On wording: Olympic National Park calls fly agaric poisonous and reserves fatally poisonous for the funeral bell. Do not upgrade or downgrade that without a federal or state source.

lookalikes.name: panther cap
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA pairs Amanita pantherina directly with the fly agaric: both produce ibotenic acid and muscimol, both are large, fleshy and colourful, and FDA treats them together throughout. The panther cap is the more dangerous of the two. There is no need to tell them apart for safety purposes, because the answer for both is the same: do not eat it.

lookalikes.name: Caesar's mushroom
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA states that the yellowish cap colours on some varieties of the fly agaric and the panther cap are similar to the edible Caesar's mushroom (Amanita caesarea), which is considered a delicacy in Italy. This is the confusion that travels with people who learned their mushrooms in another country. It is marked lethal rather than serious because FDA lists Caesar's mushroom against the YELLOW variety of the DEATH CAP as well, so a wrong guess in this colour range can land on a lethal species and not merely a poisonous one.

lookalikes.name: the blusher and the yellow blusher
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA names the yellow blusher (Amanita flavorubens) as an edible yellow capped mushroom occasionally confused with yellow varieties of A. muscaria and A. pantherina, and says orange to yellow orange forms of both may also be confused with the blusher (Amanita rubescens). The blusher is eaten in some places. This entry exists because it is the precise mechanism by which people who have read that some Amanitas are edible get hurt.

lookalikes.name: Amanita smithiana
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The Pacific Northwest's own deadly Amanita, and the one a Silverdale reader most needs to know exists. A clinical review hosted by the National Library of Medicine records that Amanita smithiana is prevalent in the Pacific Northwest of the United States and causes kidney injury through allenic norleucine, presenting as acute gastroenteritis and progressing to renal injury in 12 to 24 hours. The US Forest Service matsutake report records that poisonings from mistaking Amanita smithiana for matsutake have occurred, and that deadly Amanitas can fruit within metres of matsutake. The field character the Forest Service gives: Amanita flesh is BRITTLE, while matsutake flesh is FIBROUS and can be peeled like string cheese; matsutake also has a distinctive odour once you know it. The Forest Service then gives the rule that covers this entire genus: always make sure of your identification before eating any mushroom, and then start with small quantities.

lookalikes.name: death cap and the destroying angels
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The genus that contains the storybook red and white mushroom also contains the ones that kill. The Forest Service field guide gives the Amanita signature: a ring on the stalk, a cup (volva) at the base often hidden below the soil, white gills free from the stalk, and a white spore print. That is why mushrooms should be DUG rather than picked. Amanita virosa, A. verna and A. bisporigera can only be distinguished from one another by their spore characteristics, and together they cause 95 percent of fatal mushroom poisonings. The practical rule for a beginner: treat the whole genus as off limits.

lookalikes.name: poison champagne amanita
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Amanita crenulata. The Park Service at Gateway National Recreation Area describes it as looking similar to the fly agaric but smaller, with a cream coloured cap, lacking the concentric rings on the stem, and also toxic if eaten. That park is in New York and New Jersey, roughly 2,700 miles from Silverdale, and this species is NOT confirmed present in Washington State. It is carried here so the name is not a surprise if you meet it in a book, not as a local pair.

species.season: The fruiting season for western Washington was not established from any public source consulted. Expect it with the general autumn mushroom flush.
species.habitat: Forests of the Olympic Peninsula and the Puget Sound lowlands. It grows from the soil, attached to living tree roots (mycorrhizal). Olympic National Park, directly west across Hood Canal, names it as present and as mycorrhizal. Which infraspecific taxon occurs in western Washington was not established: the Park Service page for a New York and New Jersey park uses Amanita muscaria var. formosa for the yellow orange form, and that East Coast usage should not be copied onto a Pacific Northwest record.
species.uses: None. It is the storybook red mushroom with white spots, and it is worth learning by sight precisely so that you leave it alone.

species.form: mushroom (small, brown, wood rotting; a Little Brown Mushroom)
species.edible_detail: Never. There is no part, no season and no preparation that makes it safe. Cooking, canning, freezing and blanching do not destroy amatoxins. Beyond this one species, the honest general rule: a beginner should never eat a small brown mushroom on the strength of any written description. The US Forest Service field guide states that many mushrooms can be identified only by examining the color of spore prints or by examining spores and tissues under a microscope, and FDA states that most psychoactive and many poisonous mushrooms are small, brown and nondescript. Small and brown is the shape of most mushrooms in the woods, and it is the shape of this one.
species.toxic: FATALLY POISONOUS, in the explicit words of Olympic National Park. It contains amatoxins, the same toxin family as the death cap. FDA records amatoxin illnesses from fresh raw mushrooms, stir fried mushrooms, home canned mushrooms, mushrooms cooked in tomato sauce (which makes the sauce itself toxic even when no mushroom is eaten), and mushrooms blanched and frozen at home. THE COURSE: a latent period during which the patient has NO symptoms at all, which FDA gives as 6 to 72 hours after eating, its onset table reading 6 hours to 3 days; then sudden severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, watery diarrhea, extreme thirst and no urine production; then, if that phase is survived, an apparent recovery for a short time; then rapid and severe loss of strength, jaundice, and irreversible liver, kidney, cardiac and skeletal muscle damage. Mortality is about 10 percent for patients given aggressive support almost immediately, and 50 to 90 percent for those admitted 60 or more hours after eating. That difference is the entire reason for the following rule: if you may have eaten one, get emergency care DURING the symptom free window, not after symptoms appear.

lookalikes.name: honey mushroom
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is the pairing that kills. FDA's table of poisonous mushrooms and their edible look-alikes lists Armillaria mellea, the honey mushroom, among what the funeral bell is mistaken for, and Olympic National Park's own fungi page lists TWO honey mushrooms as present in the park, Armillaria mellea and Armillaria nabsnona. Honey mushrooms are gathered in bulk off stumps and dead wood in autumn, which is the same substrate and the same season as the funeral bell. The realistic fatal scenario is not a glamorous misidentification; it is one funeral bell going into the basket with a cluster of honey mushrooms because nobody checked every mushroom. SPORE PRINT IS THE CHECK. The Forest Service field guide gives the honey mushroom a WHITE spore print, along with a tan to golden yellow cap, a prominent ring on the stem, and black shoestring cords (rhizomorphs) running through the wood. The funeral bell's spore print is RUSTY BROWN. Print the whole batch on white paper before cooking, and throw the entire batch away if any brown appears. Do not gather clustered brown wood growing mushrooms for the table without expert identification of every individual specimen.

lookalikes.name: oyster mushroom
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both grow on dead wood in the same forests, and Olympic National Park names the funeral bell as present there. An oyster mushroom is pale and shelf shaped: white to pale tan cap, white gills running down the stem, a stem that is off to one side or absent altogether, no ring, and a white or lilac spore print. The funeral bell is a small brown mushroom with brown gills, a normal central stem usually carrying a ring, and a rusty brown spore print. The difference is real, but the failure mode is the same as above: check every single mushroom, and take a spore print of the batch.

lookalikes.name: little brown mushrooms, including Gymnopilus species
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA classes the funeral bell itself as a Little Brown Mushroom and lists Gymnopilus spectabilis (the big laughing mushroom) and other Gymnopilus species among what it is mistaken for, noting that Gymnopilus ventricosus grows on the wood of conifers in western North America. FDA also lists the deliberate pursuit of psychoactive mushrooms as one of the four main ways Americans are poisoned, and the psychoactive species people look for are little brown mushrooms growing on wood and wood chips. Same shape, same substrate, no antidote. There is no reliable way to separate little brown mushrooms in the field without spore and microscope work.

species.season: Fruits with the autumn mushroom flush, overlapping honey mushroom season. The exact season for Kitsap County was not confirmed from a public source.
species.habitat: A wood rotting fungus, so it appears on stumps, logs, buried wood and woody debris, and in landscape wood chips and bark mulch. Present in Olympic National Park, which names it by name, and NOT confined there: FDA states that poisonous species are ubiquitous and that geographical restrictions on the types of poisoning that may occur in one location do not exist. Treat it as present wherever dead conifer wood, stumps and wood debris occur in Kitsap County, INCLUDING residential yards and gardens, where FDA specifically flags pre school children eating mushrooms they find growing. Two sourcing notes. The bark mulch and wood chip habit is the standard description and was not confirmed from a public document for Puget Sound specifically. And the geography often quoted for this species is loose: the shoreline directly across Hood Canal from Silverdale is largely Olympic National Forest and the Toandos Peninsula, with the National Park boundary well west of the water. Federal safety literature files this hazard under the common name Autumn Skullcap (as Galerina autumnalis), so search under that name too; NCBI Taxonomy still carries Galerina autumnalis as a separate record (taxid 157599) from Galerina marginata (taxid 109633), and the widely used synonymising of the two could not be confirmed from a public source. KITSAP OCCURRENCE IS NOW DIRECT RATHER THAN INFERRED: the Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria holds 3 Kitsap County specimen records under Galerina autumnalis, plus further Washington records under Galerina marginata, so this fungus is collected and filed in this county and the argument from park boundaries is no longer needed.

species.scientific_name: Armillaria (Fr.) Staude. Several species carry this common name and they are not separable in the field. The Burke Herbarium's Washington macrofungi collection holds pages for Armillaria mellea (Vahl) P. Kumm., A. ostoyae (Romagn.) Herink, A. nabsnona T.J. Volk & Burds. and A. sinapina, and the US Forest Service field guide states that the genus contains 10 biological species which can be distinguished only by using laboratory techniques.
species.form: mushroom (gilled, clustered on stumps, tree bases and buried wood; ringed stem)
species.protected: Not protected, and NOT approved for sale. Washington's food rule WAC 246-215-03225 lists 16 wild mushroom taxa a licensed food establishment may offer for sale or service, and no Armillaria is among them. That is not a statement that honey mushrooms are unsafe; it is a statement that the state has not put this one on the list a permit holder may trade in, and it is worth knowing before you believe a roadside seller. If you are collecting in Olympic National Park, the park allows up to one quart per person per day and warns in the same breath that fatally poisonous mushrooms live there.
species.edible_detail: Edible, cooked, young, and only after every single mushroom in the basket has been checked. THE EDIBILITY IS DOCUMENTED. The Missouri Department of Conservation calls it a good edible when young and fresh, and says it causes stomach upset in some individuals, so the first time you eat it you should try just a small amount and make sure it is cooked thoroughly. The US Forest Service field guide rates Armillaria gallica as choice and Armillaria solidipes (A. ostoyae) as edible. The Burke Herbarium notes that A. ostoyae is edible when young but is considered worth collecting by relatively few mycophagists. Ohio State University Extension states flatly: do not eat mushrooms raw. THE CONDITION THAT MATTERS IS NOT COOKING, IT IS THE BASKET. Honey mushrooms are gathered in bulk off stumps and dead wood in autumn, and the funeral bell, which carries the same toxin family as the death cap and kills, grows on stumps and dead wood in autumn. FDA's own table of poisonous mushrooms and their edible look-alikes names Armillaria mellea, the honey mushroom, as one of the things the deadly Galerina gets mistaken for. The realistic accident is not a heroic misidentification; it is one funeral bell riding into the pan alongside forty honey mushrooms because nobody looked at all forty. Spore print the batch. See the funeral bell entry below for how. A beginner should not eat a clustered brown mushroom taken off wood on the strength of any written description, including this one.
species.toxic: The genus itself is not recorded as poisonous by the sources opened here, but two real qualifications belong on the label. First, the Missouri Department of Conservation states that it causes stomach upset in some individuals, which is why that source, and this record, tell you to eat a small amount the first time. Second, and far more seriously, FDA lists the honey mushroom among mushrooms that Galerina autumnalis, the funeral bell, is mistaken for; amatoxin poisoning turns on how fast you get treated, and FDA gives the two figures plainly: victims hospitalized and given aggressive support therapy almost immediately after ingestion have a mortality rate of only 10 percent, whereas those admitted 60 OR MORE HOURS after ingestion have a 50 to 90 percent mortality rate. FDA also states that most mushrooms that cause human poisoning cannot be made nontoxic by cooking, canning, freezing or any other means of processing, and that illnesses have followed fresh raw mushrooms, stir-fried mushrooms, home-canned mushrooms, mushrooms cooked in tomato sauce (which can render the sauce itself toxic even when no mushrooms are eaten), and mushrooms blanched and frozen at home. And FDA notes that some of the deadliest mushrooms produce no symptoms until 6 to 72 hours after ingestion, with its onset table giving 6 hours to 3 days. Those three facts together are why the treatment clock, not the cooking pot, is what decides the outcome. The hazard attached to this mushroom is a hazard of company, not of chemistry.

lookalikes.name: funeral bell (deadly Galerina)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: THIS IS THE PAIRING THAT KILLS, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS RECORD EXISTS. FDA's table of poisonous mushrooms and their edible look-alikes lists Armillaria mellea, the honey mushroom, among what Galerina autumnalis is mistaken for. Both fruit in autumn on stumps, logs and buried wood. THE SPORE PRINT IS THE CHECK, AND IT IS DECISIVE. A honey mushroom drops a WHITE spore print: the US Forest Service field guide gives a white print for Armillaria gallica, and the Missouri Department of Conservation gives a white print for A. mellea. The funeral bell drops a RUSTY BROWN print.
