The Burke Herbarium, describing Galerina marginata for Washington, says it could be mistaken for a honey mushroom although it is usually much smaller and HAS BROWN, NOT WHITE SPORES. Cut the caps off the whole batch, lay them gills-down on white paper for a few hours, and throw the entire batch away if any brown appears. THREE MORE CHARACTERS, from the same sources. (1) SIZE: Burke says the funeral bell is usually much smaller; Missouri gives honey mushroom caps 1 to 6 inches across. (2) CAP SURFACE: Missouri gives the honey mushroom a sticky cap with BLACK HAIRY SCALES over the centre; Burke gives the funeral bell a smooth cap, slightly viscid to moist, striate along the edge when fresh. (3) THE CORDS IN THE WOOD: both the Forest Service field guide and the Missouri department describe long black shoestring cords, rhizomorphs, running under the bark of infected trees and through the soil. That is an Armillaria signature and no Galerina makes it. WHY THE CHARACTERS ARE STILL NOT ENOUGH: you have to apply them to EVERY mushroom, not to the pile. And if you may have eaten one, get emergency care during the symptom-free window rather than waiting for symptoms. By the time you feel ill, liver damage is under way.

lookalikes.name: fly agaric
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA states that orange to yellow-orange Amanita muscaria and A. pantherina may be confused with the Blusher (Amanita rubescens) and the Honey Mushroom (Armillariella mellea). The honey mushroom's cap runs yellow to honey to rusty brown, which is the same colour band, and both carry a ring on the stem, so colour and ring together rule out nothing. THE TEST IS AT THE BASE OF THE STEM, AND YOU MUST DIG FOR IT. The US Forest Service field guide says mushrooms should always be DUG, not picked, in order to detect the cup (volva) at the base of the stalk, which is often below the soil surface and is the mark of a potentially poisonous Amanita; it gives the full Amanita signature as a ring on the stalk, a cup at the base, white gills free from the stalk, and a white spore print. An Armillaria has a ring but no cup, grows in clusters with the stalks fused at the base on wood, and trails black rhizomorph cords. An Amanita comes singly out of soil from a cup. Note the trap: the Armillaria spore print is also white, so the spore print does NOT separate these two. The cup does.

lookalikes.name: big laughing gym and other Gymnopilus species
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA lists Gymnopilus spectabilis (the big laughing mushroom) and other Gymnopilus species among what the funeral bell is mistaken for, and notes that Gymnopilus ventricosus grows on the wood of conifers in western North America; a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 2 Washington records for G. ventricosus, from Thurston and Mason counties. The Missouri Department of Conservation separates a Gymnopilus from a honey mushroom on three counts: it is orange, it tastes bitter, and its spores are ORANGE-BROWN rather than white. The spore print you take for the funeral bell rules this one out at the same time, which is another reason to take it.

lookalikes.name: jack-o'-lantern
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Omphalotus species, which FDA lists among mushrooms producing severe gastroenteritis, with vomiting and diarrhea that can last several days. The Missouri Department of Conservation's separator is one word: it is ORANGE, cap and gills together, where a honey mushroom is honey to rusty brown with whitish gills. Both grow clustered on wood, so colour is doing real work here. HONEST LIMIT: whether Omphalotus occurs in Kitsap County could not be established from any source opened for this record, and the Forest Service's Pacific Northwest chanterelle report does not list any Omphalotus among the look-alikes a Pacific Northwest picker will meet. Carry the character; do not assume the genus is absent.

lookalikes.name: ringless honey mushroom
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Desarmillaria caespitosa, which the Missouri Department of Conservation separates from the true honey mushroom by a dry cap and NO RING on the stem. It is listed here for one reason only, and it is an important one: if a clustered brown wood-growing mushroom has no ring, you have not confirmed it is an Armillaria, and the ring is one of the characters people lean on. A Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 0 Washington records under that name, so this may be an eastern problem rather than a local one, but the reasoning applies to any ringless cluster you find.

species.season: Autumn. The US Forest Service field guide gives fall for Armillaria gallica and late summer to fall for A. solidipes. The Missouri Department of Conservation gives August to November and notes that the mushrooms often arise after autumn rains. That is the same window as the funeral bell, which is the whole problem.
species.habitat: On and around wood. The Burke Herbarium gives Armillaria mellea the habitat woodlands, parklands and gardens, and the substrate trunks, stumps or roots, and gives A. ostoyae as occurring under conifers. The Missouri Department of Conservation describes clusters at the bases of trees or stumps and over buried wood, and notes that mushrooms keep arising from a stump seasonally long after the tree itself was cut and removed. LOCAL EVIDENCE: Olympic National Park names the honey mushroom Armillaria mellea as present and records that the mycologist Tom Volk described a new honey mushroom species, Armillaria nabsnona, from the park. A Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 26 Washington specimen records for A. mellea (King, Clallam, Jefferson, Pierce, Skagit, Snohomish, Lewis, Cowlitz, Skamania, Stevens, Columbia, Pend Oreille), 9 for A. ostoyae (Clallam, King, Pacific, Jefferson, Snohomish) and 3 for A. nabsnona (Clallam, Grays Harbor). None was from Kitsap County, which for a stump fungus in a county of second-growth conifer is a collecting gap rather than an absence: treat honey mushrooms as present on stumps and buried wood throughout central Kitsap, including in yards. SOURCING NOTE ON `status`: no page opened for this record states the origin of Armillaria in North America in so many words. Native is recorded here because Olympic National Park presents the honey mushroom as part of the park's own ecology, and because the mycologist Tom Volk described Armillaria nabsnona as a species NEW TO SCIENCE from that park, which is not the history of an import. Treat the field as an inference, not a quotation.
species.uses: Food, cooked, when young, with the whole-basket check above. The other thing this fungus does is kill trees, and that matters to anyone managing land here: the Forest Service field guide describes Armillaria as a root and butt rot capable of killing trees, especially stressed trees, creating root-rot pockets and canopy gaps; the Missouri department notes that young, newly transplanted, injured or stressed trees are most vulnerable and that an early symptom is dieback in the crown and branches. Olympic National Park frames the same fungus as a natural process rather than a pest, and records that honey mushroom mycelium in the Malheur National Forest in Oregon is the world's largest living organism. The Forest Service adds that all Armillaria species are luminescent, often glowing in patches of decayed root or stem tissue.

species.form: mushroom (thin, white, shelf- or spoon-shaped, in overlapping masses on conifer wood; no stem)
species.protected: Not protected, and not on Washington's approved list. WAC 246-215-03225 names 16 wild mushroom taxa a licensed food establishment may sell or serve, and angel wing is not among them. Note that the oyster mushroom IS on that list, which is exactly why this record matters: the legal and the deadly here look alike on the same log.
species.edible_detail: THIS RECORD SAYS DO NOT EAT IT, AND IT SAYS SO AGAINST A MIXED LITERATURE, SO READ WHY. Angel wing has been eaten. The Burke Herbarium at the University of Washington rates its edibility as CAUTION and describes it as less desirable than oysters because the flesh is thin, which is the language of a mushroom people put in a pan. Then, in autumn 2004 in Japan, 59 cases of food poisoning were linked to eating this species and 17 people died of acute encephalopathy. Those figures are from a 2025 peer-reviewed paper in AMB Express hosted by the NIH National Library of Medicine, which also reports that many of the 17 who died had chronic renal failure and were on hemodialysis before their deaths. Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare convened a study group and disbanded it in 2006 having concluded that the cause remained unidentified; the causative compound was pinned down only later, and the same paper attributes the encephalopathy to pleurocybellaziridine acting after a complex of pleurocybelline and a lectin disrupts the blood-brain barrier. There is no documented preparation, cooking time or portion size that removes that compound, because nobody opened here has tested for one. The plain reading: a thin white mushroom of modest culinary value has a documented body count and an identified neurotoxin. If you have any kidney disease, this is not a close call. If you do not, it is still 17 deaths against a thin mushroom.
species.toxic: Acute encephalopathy. Per the 2025 AMB Express paper hosted by NIH: poisoning primarily affects the central nervous system, beginning with leg weakness and lightheadedness; after several days involuntary muscle movements appear, followed by rapid paralysis, generalized convulsions and loss of consciousness; death typically occurs from progressive brain edema. The onset is therefore delayed and the first signs are vague, which is the same trap the amatoxin mushrooms set. The compounds now implicated are pleurocybelline, a lectin called PPL, and pleurocybellaziridine, the last being identified as the agent of the encephalopathy. IMPORTANT NOTE ON WHAT NOBODY OPENED HERE ESTABLISHES: whether toxin levels differ between Japanese and Pacific Northwest collections, whether cooking changes anything, and what the risk is for a person with normal kidneys eating a small portion. The honest state of the evidence is that the answer is not known, in a species that has killed.

lookalikes.name: oyster mushroom
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: THIS IS THE CONFUSION THIS RECORD EXISTS FOR. Both are pale, shelf-shaped, stemless-or-nearly-so mushrooms growing in overlapping clusters on dead wood in the same forests in the same season, and one of them is on the state's approved-for-sale list while the other has killed 17 people. FIVE CHARACTERS, from the Burke Herbarium's own description of angel wing and the Missouri Department of Conservation's description of the oyster. (1) STEM. Burke says angel wing has NO STIPE AT ALL. Missouri says the oyster's stalk, if present, is short, thick, white, solid, off-centre and HAIRY AT THE BASE. A visible stubby stem is evidence for oyster. (2) FLESH. Burke says angel wing is THIN, rather tough and elastic; Missouri says the oyster's flesh is THICK and white. Angel wing tears like a translucent ear; oyster tears like a mushroom. (3) TRANSLUCENCY. Burke says angel wing caps are TRANSLUCENT-STRIATE when fresh, meaning you can see the lines of the gills through the cap flesh when held to the light, and that the margin goes wavy as the cap expands. (4) COLOUR. Burke says oyster mushrooms are FLESHIER AND DARKER COLOURED; angel wing is white to ivory. (5) GILLS. Burke gives angel wing crowded NARROW gills; Missouri gives the oyster gills that are narrow but NEARLY DISTANT, and that run down onto the stalk. A DELIBERATE CORRECTION TO A COMMON HEURISTIC, BECAUSE IT IS WRONG HERE: it is often said that angel wing grows on conifer wood and oysters on hardwood, so a pale shelf on a Douglas-fir log must be angel wing. In the Pacific Northwest that reasoning is unsafe. The Burke Herbarium describes Pleurotus pulmonarius as a classic oyster mushroom BUT ON CONIFER WOOD RATHER THAN HARDWOOD, gives its substrate as conifer wood and its habitat as temperate coniferous forests, and a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned a Kitsap County record for P. pulmonarius. Conifer substrate does not tell you which of these you are holding in this county. Use the stem, the flesh and the translucency, and if you cannot resolve all three, leave it.

lookalikes.name: funeral bell (deadly Galerina)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The funeral bell is not shaped anything like an angel wing: the Burke Herbarium describes it as a medium-sized mushroom with a dome-shaped brown to yellow-brown cap, brown gills, an ordinary central stem that sometimes carries a fibrillose ring-zone, and brown spores. Nobody would confuse the two face to face. It is listed here for the same reason the oyster record lists it: Burke gives the funeral bell's habitat as stumps and logs of CONIFERS and hardwoods, or growing from buried wood, wood chips or other woody debris, which is precisely the log you are stripping angel wings off. The failure is a basket failure, not an identification failure. Look at every mushroom you pick individually, and spore print anything gathered off wood before it goes in a pan: any rusty brown print means throw the whole batch out.

lookalikes.name: oysterling and other small pale shelf fungi on wood
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: No specific species is named here because none could be documented for Kitsap County from the sources opened for this record, and naming one without evidence would be exactly the error this dataset tries to avoid. The general point stands on the authority of the US Forest Service field guide, which prints the same line at the foot of every page: do not eat any mushroom unless you are absolutely certain of its identity, many mushroom species look alike and some are highly poisonous, and many mushrooms can be identified only by examining the colour of spore prints or by examining spores and tissues under a microscope. Small pale brackets on wood are a crowded category. Take a spore print of anything you intend to eat off a log.

species.season: Autumn. The 2004 Japanese outbreak occurred in autumn. Olympic National Park says that while mushrooms can be found nearly year round in the park, the peak season is after the start of the fall rains up until the first major frosts, which is the window in which a shelf fungus on a hemlock log will be found here. No Kitsap-County-specific season was established from any source opened for this record.
species.habitat: On conifer wood, especially hemlock. The Burke Herbarium states it is found on conifer, especially hemlock, logs and stumps THROUGHOUT THE PACIFIC NORTHWEST, often occurring in large imbricate (overlapping, shingled) masses. Olympic National Park names angel wing, Pleurocybella porrigens, by name as one of the common saprophytic fungi that decompose downed trees in the park. LOCAL EVIDENCE: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 34 Washington specimen records, the largest count being 8 from Jefferson County directly across Hood Canal, with 7 each from Snohomish and King, 3 from Clallam, 2 from Whatcom and single records from Pierce and Lewis. None from Kitsap County, which in a county dominated by Douglas-fir and western hemlock is a collecting gap rather than evidence of absence. A WARNING ABOUT THE SOURCE MOST READERS WILL FIND FIRST: the Olympic National Park fungi page lists angel wing only as a delicate nutrient-recycling decomposer, in the same sentence as chicken of the woods, which is a popular edible, and issues no warning about it at all. Do not read that page as a safety clearance. SOURCING NOTE ON `status`: no page opened for this record states the origin of Pleurocybella porrigens in North America in so many words. Native is recorded here because the Burke Herbarium describes it as found on conifer logs and stumps throughout the Pacific Northwest and Olympic National Park lists it among the park's common saprophytic decomposers. Treat the field as an inference, not a quotation.

species.common_name: Gem-studded puffball, also called common puffball, warted puffball or devil's snuffbox
species.form: puffball (a stalked ball growing from soil; a spore sac, no cap and no gills)
species.protected: Not protected, and not on Washington's approved list. WAC 246-215-03225 names 16 wild mushroom taxa a licensed food establishment may offer for sale or service, and no puffball is among them.
species.edible_detail: Edible, with one non-negotiable check that takes three seconds per mushroom. THE EDIBILITY IS DOCUMENTED: the Missouri Department of Conservation calls it an excellent edible mushroom when young and fresh, with caution, and notes that the mushrooms are common and tasty but small enough that a meal takes a lot of them. THE CHECK, in that source's own words: cut open each puffball from top to bottom, and confirm it is PURE WHITE INSIDE, LIKE A MARSHMALLOW, WITH NO SIGN OF A DEVELOPING CAP OR STEM. Iowa State University Extension gives the same instruction and the reason, writing about the giant puffball: cut the puffball in half before eating it to make sure it does not have a stalk inside, because young deadly Amanita mushrooms look similar to puffballs from the outside. The rule is the same whichever puffball you have in your hand. THE PHYSICAL BASIS FOR THE TEST, from the US Forest Service field guide: young mushrooms are called buttons or the egg stage, and they CONTAIN THE PREFORMED CAP AND STALK inside the universal veil. That is why a section through a real puffball is featureless white and a section through an Amanita button shows the outline of a cap, gills and stalk. Two further conditions. Cook it: Ohio State University Extension says do not eat mushrooms raw. And eat a small amount the first time, which is the Missouri department's standing advice for any wild mushroom, since some people are simply allergic to particular fungi.
species.toxic: Not recorded as toxic by any source opened here when correctly identified and taken young. Two limits on that sentence. First, the Missouri Department of Conservation's description makes clear that the inside turns to brownish dust as it matures; the edibility statement is for young and fresh specimens only, and nothing opened here supports eating one whose interior has begun to colour. Second, the real hazard attached to this mushroom is what shares its shape. FDA's table of poisonous mushrooms and their edible look-alikes lists puffballs such as Lycoperdon perlatum among the things that the BUTTONS of Amanita bisporigera, Amanita verna and Amanita virosa, the white destroying angels, get mistaken for; FDA separately records that young button-stage specimens of Amanita muscaria have also been confused with puffballs. Those Amanitas carry amatoxins. FDA records that victims hospitalized and given aggressive support therapy almost immediately after ingestion have a mortality rate of only 10 percent, whereas those admitted 60 or more hours after ingestion have a 50 to 90 percent mortality rate; that most mushrooms causing human poisoning cannot be made nontoxic by cooking, canning, freezing or any other means of processing; and that some of the deadliest produce no symptoms until 6 to 72 hours after ingestion. If you may have eaten one, the thing that changes the outcome is getting to a hospital inside that silent window.

lookalikes.name: the button stage of the deadly white Amanitas
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: THIS IS WHY THE CUT-IN-HALF RULE EXISTS AND THE REASON THIS RECORD IS IN THE DATASET. FDA's look-alike table pairs puffballs such as Lycoperdon perlatum with the buttons of Amanita bisporigera, A. verna and A. virosa, and the Missouri Department of Conservation names the destroying angel, Amanita bisporigera, as having a round button stage that looks like a puffball. The linked record here covers the death cap, Amanita phalloides, and the group of deadly white Amanitas alongside it; treat all of them as the same hazard for this purpose. THE TEST: cut every single puffball in half from top to bottom before it goes anywhere near a pan. A real puffball is uniform solid white throughout, like a marshmallow. An Amanita button, per the US Forest Service field guide, contains the preformed cap and stalk inside its universal veil, so a cut section shows the unmistakable silhouette of a small mushroom. A SECOND CHECK YOU SHOULD ALSO MAKE: the Forest Service says mushrooms should always be DUG, not picked, in order to detect the cup (volva) at the base of the stalk, which sits below the soil surface and is the mark of a potentially poisonous Amanita. Digging costs nothing and it is how you catch the one where the veil had already begun to split.

lookalikes.name: fly agaric buttons
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA states that young button-stage specimens of Amanita muscaria have been confused with puffballs. The same cut-in-half test settles it: an Amanita muscaria button shows the preformed cap and stalk in section. The fly agaric is common here, and the Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria returned 25 Washington records for it including three from Jefferson County across Hood Canal, so this is a local button, not a textbook one.

lookalikes.name: pigskin puffball, also called common earthball
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Scleroderma citrinum. The Missouri Department of Conservation calls it POISONOUS and says it can cause upset stomach, nausea and vomiting. TWO CHARACTERS, from that source. (1) THE SKIN: unlike edible puffballs, the pigskin puffball has a THICK, RINDLIKE skin, leathery and coarsely scaly or warted, where the gem-studded puffball's skin is thin and its warts detach. (2) THE INSIDE, which the cut-in-half test shows you anyway: a very young earthball is nearly white inside but soon becomes marbled, then PURPLISH, then blackish, where a good gem-studded puffball is pure white throughout. Missouri adds that there are some 20 Scleroderma species in North America, all relatively tough with blackish interiors, and that telling them apart usually takes a specialist with a microscope, which is irrelevant to you because they all fail the white-inside test. The Burke Herbarium carries Scleroderma citrinum in its Washington macrofungi collection and the Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria returned one Washington record, from King County, so it is present here but sparsely documented.

lookalikes.name: pear-shaped puffball
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Lycoperdon pyriforme. The Missouri Department of Conservation separates it as brownish with a smoother surface, and, decisively, GROWING ON WOOD, where the gem-studded puffball grows on the ground. This one matters locally: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 21 Washington records including 3 from KITSAP COUNTY, which is more Kitsap records than the gem-studded puffball itself has. Missouri lists it as white on the inside when young, like its relative, and no hazard for it was found in the sources opened here, but it is a different species and this record's edibility statement does not extend to it.

species.season: Late summer through autumn. The Burke Herbarium says it can be found from late summer through fall whenever there is sufficient moisture. The Missouri Department of Conservation gives July to October.
species.habitat: On the ground, on disturbed open sites. The Burke Herbarium gives disturbed sites such as forest roadsides; the Missouri Department of Conservation gives singly or in clusters on the ground in open woods, along roads and in waste areas. It does not grow on wood, and that fact is part of how you rule out the pear-shaped puffball. LOCAL EVIDENCE, AND THIS ONE IS DIRECT: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 26 Washington specimen records including TWO FROM KITSAP COUNTY, along with Snohomish, Grays Harbor, King, Clallam, Pierce, Lewis, Kittitas and Okanogan. Of every species added in this pass this is the one with the firmest local footing: it has been collected and filed in this county. SOURCING NOTE ON `status`: no page opened for this record states the origin of Lycoperdon perlatum in North America in so many words, and the Burke Herbarium fungus pages used here carry no Origin field at all. Native is recorded as an inference from its being a widespread woodland and roadside species on both sides of the continent. Treat the field as an inference, not a quotation.
species.uses: Food, cooked, when young and after the cut test. The Burke Herbarium describes the mechanism that gives the group its names: the inner spore sac eventually develops a pore at the top through which olive-brown spores are propelled by a bellows action when the sac is struck by raindrops or nudged by a passing mushroom-hunter. That is also a field identification aid and a reason to stop: a puffball that puffs is too old to eat.

species.common_name: Meadow mushroom, also called field mushroom or pink bottom
species.form: mushroom (gilled, grows from soil in grass; gills free from the stalk, turning pink then chocolate brown)
species.protected: Not protected, and not on Washington's approved list. WAC 246-215-03225 names 16 wild mushroom taxa a licensed food establishment may offer for sale or service, and no Agaricus is among them. Cultivated Agaricus is a different matter, since that rule does not apply to mushrooms grown and packaged in a regulated food processing plant, which is why the same genus is on every supermarket shelf.
species.edible_detail: Edible, and the conditions are unusually load-bearing. THE EDIBILITY IS DOCUMENTED: the Burke Herbarium rates Agaricus campestris as edible, Ohio State University Extension lists the meadow mushroom as edible, and the Missouri Department of Conservation calls it a choice edible and notes it is closely related to the cultivated white button mushroom. THE CONDITIONS. (1) DIG EVERY ONE AND LOOK AT THE BASE. The US Forest Service field guide says mushrooms should always be DUG, not picked, in order to detect the cup (volva) at the base of the stalk, which is often below the soil surface and is the mark of a potentially poisonous Amanita. If you snip a meadow mushroom off at grass level you have discarded the single most reliable piece of evidence about it. (2) SPORE PRINT BEFORE YOU COOK. See the death cap entry below; this is the check that separates a choice edible from a fatal one. (3) COOK IT: Ohio State Extension says do not eat mushrooms raw, and the Missouri department says always be sure to cook it before eating. (4) MIND WHERE IT GREW. The Missouri department states that if you are collecting meadow mushrooms in urban areas you should be certain no lawn treatment chemicals have been used. This mushroom's habitat is the mown lawn, so that is not a marginal caution. (5) EAT A SMALL AMOUNT THE FIRST TIME. FDA records that Agaricus is among the abundant genera that include species producing mild gastroenteritis, and names the horse mushroom Agaricus arvensis among mushrooms producing SEVERE gastroenteritis, so the genus is not uniformly benign.
species.toxic: Agaricus campestris itself is not recorded as poisonous by any source opened here. The genus is another matter, and so is the company it keeps. FDA lists Agaricus among the abundant genera that include species producing mild gastroenteritis, and lists the horse mushroom, Agaricus arvensis, among mushrooms producing severe gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea that can last several days; a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 9 Washington records for A. arvensis including one from Kitsap County, so that is a local species and not a textbook one. The lethal hazard, however, is the confusion described below: FDA's look-alike table lists white Agaricus species, named in that table as field mushrooms, among what Amanita bisporigera, A. verna, A. virosa and the pure white variety of Amanita phalloides are mistaken for. On amatoxins FDA gives two mortality figures and they are about time to treatment: 10 percent for victims hospitalized and given aggressive support therapy almost immediately after ingestion, 50 to 90 percent for those admitted 60 or more hours after ingestion. FDA also states that most mushrooms causing human poisoning cannot be made nontoxic by cooking, canning, freezing or any other means of processing, and that some of the deadliest produce no symptoms until 6 to 72 hours after ingestion.

lookalikes.name: death cap and the destroying angels
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: THIS IS THE PAIRING THAT PUT THIS RECORD IN THE DATASET, AND IT IS A HABITAT OVERLAP, NOT A THEORETICAL ONE. The Missouri Department of Conservation states it outright: the similar-looking and deadly destroying angel can grow in the same habitat as the meadow mushroom. FDA's look-alike table lists white Agaricus species, field mushrooms, against Amanita bisporigera, A. verna, A. virosa and the pure white variety of Amanita phalloides. FOUR CHARACTERS, THREE OF WHICH YOU MUST CHECK EVERY TIME. (1) GILL COLOUR. This is the first thing to look at and it is free. The Missouri department gives the meadow mushroom gills that are LIGHT PINK, becoming chocolate to blackish brown; Ohio State Extension gives the same, pink gills becoming chocolate brown. The Missouri department gives the destroying angel WHITE gills, and the US Forest Service field guide describes the destroying angel as having white gills free from the stalk and lists white gills free from the stalk among the characters that distinguish Amanita mushrooms from other species. (The Burke Herbarium page cited here for the death cap gives white SPORES, not white gills; the gill character is the Missouri department's and the Forest Service's.) A young Agaricus whose gills are still pale is exactly the specimen where this character is weakest, which is why a white-gilled button in grass is a specimen to leave. (2) SPORE PRINT. The Missouri department gives the meadow mushroom a BLACKISH BROWN spore print; the Burke Herbarium gives Agaricus campestris CHOCOLATE-BROWN spores and Amanita phalloides WHITE spores; the Forest Service field guide gives a white spore print as part of the Amanita signature. Print the batch on white paper. Any white print means throw the whole batch away. (3) THE BASE OF THE STALK. The Forest Service gives the full Amanita signature as a ring on the stalk, a CUP (volva) at the base of the stalk often below the soil surface, white gills free from the stalk, and a white spore print, and says that this is precisely why mushrooms should be dug rather than picked. The Missouri department describes the destroying angel as having a SACLIKE CUP around the base of the stalk. Agaricus campestris has a delicate ring that often disappears, and no cup. Note the trap in that sentence: BOTH have free gills and BOTH can have a ring, so those two characters separate nothing. The cup and the spore print do. (4) An odour difference is on record and is deliberately listed last: the Burke Herbarium's Agaricus campestris page says Amanita phalloides has a sickly sweet smell. Smell is subjective, varies with the specimen and cannot be checked by a second person later. Do not make a life-or-death call on it.

lookalikes.name: fly agaric, pale forms
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: FDA states that white to pale forms of Amanita muscaria may be confused with edible field mushrooms, Agaricus species. The same three checks apply and in the same order: gill colour (Amanita gills stay white, Agaricus gills go pink then chocolate brown), spore print (Amanita white, Agaricus blackish brown), and the dug-up base (Amanita has a cup, Agaricus does not). The Forest Service field guide adds a character specific to this species: the fly agaric's volva takes the form of 2 or 3 scaly rings on the stalk above a bulbous base.

lookalikes.name: horse mushroom
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Agaricus arvensis, another Agaricus and a local one: the Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria returned 9 Washington records including one from Kitsap County. FDA lists it among mushrooms that produce severe gastroenteritis, with diarrhea and vomiting that may last several days. The Burke Herbarium separates it from the meadow mushroom on two counts: it grows in pastures as well but is GENERALLY MUCH BIGGER, and it has a PENDULOUS RING, a substantial hanging collar on the stalk, where the meadow mushroom's ring is delicate and often disappears altogether. Both have brown spores, so the spore print you take for the death cap will not distinguish these two; size and ring will.

lookalikes.name: livid entoloma
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Entoloma sinuatum. FDA lists Entoloma lividum, the gray pinkgill, among mushrooms producing severe gastroenteritis, and lists it as mistaken for Tricholomopsis platyphylla. The Burke Herbarium's Agaricus campestris page names Entoloma sinuatum as a comparison and gives three separators: it has PINK spores rather than chocolate brown, NO RING on the stalk, and a MEALY smell. HONEST LIMIT ON LOCAL OCCURRENCE: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 0 Washington specimen records under that name, so this may not be a Kitsap County problem at all. It is listed because the character it teaches, that a pink spore print is not a pink-gilled Agaricus, is the kind of thing that saves a batch.

species.season: Late summer into autumn. Ohio State University Extension gives late summer and early fall for the meadow mushroom; the Missouri Department of Conservation gives July to September.
species.habitat: Grass. The Burke Herbarium gives fields or pastures, especially those rich in manure. The Missouri Department of Conservation gives grassy areas, urban lawns and meadows, scattered to abundant, sometimes growing in arcs or fairy rings. LOCAL EVIDENCE: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 39 Washington specimen records for Agaricus campestris, the bulk from Grant County east of the Cascades but including Island (5), King (3) and Pierce (1) on the west side, and none from Kitsap. The Burke Herbarium gives the species' distribution as worldwide. Treat it as present in Kitsap pasture and lawn, while noting that the Kitsap record itself has not been filed. AND NOTE WHERE THAT PUTS YOU: pasture, lawn and urban grass are also where the deadly white Amanitas turn up around planted trees, which is exactly the point the Missouri department makes about shared habitat. SOURCING NOTE ON `status`: no page opened for this record states the origin of Agaricus campestris in North America in so many words; the Burke Herbarium gives its distribution as worldwide and carries no Origin field. Native is recorded as an inference. Treat the field as an inference, not a quotation.
species.uses: Food, cooked, after digging it and printing the batch. The Missouri Department of Conservation notes the close relationship to the cultivated white button mushroom, which is the honest framing for a beginner: the safe way to eat this genus is to buy it, and the wild version is the same flavour with a fatal look-alike attached.

species.common_name: Poison pax, also called the brown chanterelle, inrolled pax, roll-rim, brown rollrim or naked brimcap
species.form: mushroom (gilled, grows from soil; cap margin persistently inrolled, gills run down the stem and stain brown)
species.edible_detail: NEVER, AND DO NOT BE REASSURED BY HAVING EATEN IT BEFORE. The Burke Herbarium at the University of Washington states that species of Paxillus can cause hemolysis, the destruction of red blood cells, if eaten repeatedly, that they have been responsible for deaths in Europe, and that they should be STRICTLY AVOIDED as edibles. The Forest Service's Pacific Northwest chanterelle report records that this mushroom has been eaten in Europe, especially Poland, for centuries, and that it nevertheless causes the rare Paxillus syndrome, an immune hemolytic anemia, and has been implicated in a number of deaths. FDA lists it, as the naked brimcap, among mushrooms that produce severe gastroenteritis and notes it is distinctive but will poison some people when eaten raw or undercooked. THE MECHANISM IS THE REASON FOR THE HARD NO. The Forest Service states that the toxins can accumulate in susceptible consumers over long periods of time with little effect, and then the next meal can cause sudden illness or death. A record of having eaten these safely proves nothing whatsoever about the next plate. That is a different kind of hazard from a mushroom that poisons you the first time, and it is the reason a centuries-old European food tradition did not protect the people it killed.
species.toxic: Paxillus syndrome: an immune hemolytic anemia, in which the body destroys its own red blood cells. The Burke Herbarium describes the effect as hemolysis following repeated eating and records deaths in Europe. The Forest Service's chanterelle report names the syndrome, cites it as rare, and records that the species has been implicated in a number of deaths, with the distinguishing feature that the toxins accumulate quietly over long periods before a sudden severe episode. FDA separately places Paxillus involutus in the group of mushrooms producing severe gastroenteritis, noting in the table that it is distinctive but will poison some people when eaten raw or undercooked, and noting in the surrounding text that the diarrhea and vomiting from that group may last several days, with fatalities rare and associated with dehydration and electrolyte imbalance, especially in debilitated, very young or very old patients. Read those two accounts together rather than choosing between them: there is a common acute gastrointestinal effect and a rare, delayed, immune-mediated one that has killed.

lookalikes.name: Pacific golden chanterelle
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: THIS IS THE CONFUSION THE NAME ITSELF CREATES, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS RECORD EXISTS. The Forest Service's Pacific Northwest chanterelle report says that although it bears scant resemblance to chanterelles, Paxillus involutus is SOMETIMES CALLED THE BROWN CHANTERELLE. A person who has been told brown chanterelle by a neighbour is already primed. THE ONE TEST THAT SETTLES IT: TURN THE MUSHROOM OVER AND SCRAPE. The Forest Service key divides these two at exactly this point. Paxillus has a spore-bearing surface of CROWDED, FORKED, VERY THIN GILLS THAT ARE EASILY SCRAPED OFF the underside of the cap, because they are separate structures sitting on it. A true chanterelle has relatively shallow ARCHING RIDGES, BLUNT FOLDS OR WRINKLES THAT ARE NOT EASILY SCRAPED OFF, because they are part of the cap flesh. A thumbnail answers this in one second. FOUR CONFIRMING CHARACTERS. (1) STAINING: the Forest Service gives Paxillus gills that are pallid to dingy yellow or browner and OFTEN STAIN REDDISH BROWN, and the Burke Herbarium says ALL PARTS of the fruitbody stain brown to reddish brown when handled or in age. A chanterelle does not do that. (2) SPORE PRINT: the Forest Service gives Paxillus a yellowish to reddish brown print against the chanterelle's yellowish white. (3) THE CAP MARGIN: the Burke Herbarium explains that the species epithet involutus comes from the PERSISTENTLY INROLLED CAP MARGIN, an edge that stays curled under like a hem. (4) TASTE, listed last and not recommended as a test: the Forest Service gives Paxillus a sour or bitter taste, where a chanterelle is mild and faintly fruity. Do not taste-test a mushroom you have not already identified. WHERE THIS ONE TURNS UP: the Forest Service calls it a COMMON URBAN MUSHROOM, and the Burke Herbarium says it occurs in natural forest in our region but is not common there, being much more abundant in parks and landscaped areas, typically associated with BIRCHES. Chanterelles come out of conifer forest soil. A brown gilled mushroom under a garden birch is not a chanterelle.

lookalikes.name: false chanterelle
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca, which the Forest Service key places right beside Paxillus because it shares the same thin, crowded, forked, easily-scraped gills. It separates from Paxillus on three characters in that key: its gills are BRILLIANT TO PASTEL ORANGE and do NOT stain, its spore print is WHITE rather than yellowish to reddish brown, and its taste is bland rather than sour or bitter. It is present locally: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 11 Washington records, from Grays Harbor, Jefferson, Clallam, King, Pacific and Whatcom counties. It is listed here so that a picker who fails the scrape test knows there are at least two things it could be, and that only one of them accumulates a toxin.

lookalikes.name: other Paxillus species
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The Forest Service key does not stop at one species: it reads Paxillus involutus [POISONOUS], P. vernalis and allies, which is the report's way of saying the whole group keys out here and the whole group is out. The Burke Herbarium likewise writes its warning at genus level, that SPECIES of Paxillus can cause hemolysis and should be strictly avoided. A Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 6 Washington records for P. involutus, from King, Thurston and Snohomish counties, and 0 for P. vernalis, but the practical instruction does not depend on which one you have: anything with crowded forked gills that scrape off and stain brown is not food.

species.season: Not established for Kitsap County or western Washington from any source opened for this record. The Burke Herbarium's page gives habitat but no season, and the Forest Service report discusses it only as a chanterelle look-alike, which places it in the autumn chanterelle window by implication rather than by statement. No season is claimed here.
species.habitat: Parks, gardens and landscaped ground more than forest. The Burke Herbarium states that Paxillus involutus occurs in natural forest in our region but is NOT COMMON THERE, and that it is much more common and abundant in parks and landscaped areas, where it is typically associated with BIRCHES, often alongside Leccinum scabrum and Lactarius plumbeus. The Forest Service's chanterelle report calls it a common urban mushroom. Taken together that puts it in Silverdale front yards, school grounds and street plantings rather than out in the second-growth, which is the opposite of where most people expect to meet a deadly mushroom. LOCAL EVIDENCE: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 6 Washington specimen records, from King (4), Thurston (1) and Snohomish (1) counties, all in the Puget lowland, none from Kitsap. For an urban mushroom that is unsurprising and is not evidence of absence; landscaped ground is under-collected. If you have a birch in the yard, this is the record to reread in autumn. SOURCING NOTE ON `status`: no page opened for this record states the origin of Paxillus involutus in North America in so many words. Introduced is recorded here because the Burke Herbarium says it is NOT common in natural forest in our region and is much more abundant in parks and landscaped areas typically associated with birches, and because the Forest Service calls it a common URBAN mushroom and records a centuries-long European history of eating it. That is the pattern of an import that arrived with planted trees, but it is an inference and not a quotation, and it should be checked against a mycological flora before anyone repeats it.

species.common_name: Common camas (also called blue camas, camas lily, quamash; USDA PLANTS lists it as small camas)
species.edible_detail: TWO CONDITIONS, AND THE FIRST ONE IS THE ONE THAT KILLS PEOPLE. FIRST, IDENTIFY IT IN FLOWER AND MARK IT. Common camas shares its wet spring meadows with meadow death camas, which is deadly, which is dug for its bulb in exactly the same way, and which cannot be told from camas once the flowers are gone. USDA's death camas plant guide states that the common name of death camas refers to the toxicity of the plant and its similarity in appearance to camas, and that deathcamas has been mistaken for other edible bulbous plants such as wild onion, sego lily and camas, especially when flowers are lacking. The same guide gives the number that matters: eating one or two death camas bulbs is enough to cause severe illness in children, and four or five can cause death. So the harvest rule here is not a field character at all, it is a calendar. Walk the meadow WHILE IT IS IN BLOOM, when camas shows blue to bluish-violet flowers and death camas shows creamy white ones, mark the individual camas plants you want, and return later to dig only the plants you marked, one at a time. Never work through a patch. SECOND, IT IS NOT A RAW FOOD. The Forest Service describes the bulbs as steamed or pit cooked for one to three days, which breaks down complex carbohydrates into fructose, and states that a full one third of a bulb's cooked weight becomes fructose when prepared in this fashion. No public-domain source consulted for this record describes eating camas bulbs raw.

lookalikes.name: Meadow death camas (Zigadenus venenosus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The classic fatal confusion in North American foraging, and the reason death camas has that name. Both are grass-leaved lilies of the same wet spring meadows, both are dug for their bulbs, and they grow side by side. IN BLOOM there is one check anyone can make from standing height: camas flowers are blue to bluish-violet, with tepals about 0.5 to 1.4 inches long; death camas petals are creamy white, about a quarter inch long, with a large gland at the base. OUT OF BLOOM THERE IS NO RELIABLE FIELD CHARACTER AT ALL. Do not let anyone tell you otherwise, and do not believe you can tell the bulbs apart by feel, size, colour or coat. USDA states plainly that the confusion happens especially when flowers are lacking. This is why the harvest method described above exists: the flower does the identifying, and the marker you leave behind carries that identification forward to digging day. If you arrive at a meadow with no flowers and no marks, you have no way to do this safely, and the correct action is to leave and come back in May.

lookalikes.name: Nodding onion, and wild onions generally (Allium cernuum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both are edible, so mixing these two up is a cooking question rather than a safety one. Crush a leaf: onions smell strongly of onion, camas does not. The reason this pair is listed at all is that wild onion and camas are BOTH on USDA's list of edible bulbs that death camas gets mistaken for, so the two of them share one lethal neighbour. Never let the presence of one edible bulb in a patch reassure you about the bulb next to it.

lookalikes.name: Great camas (Camassia leichtlinii)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The other blue camas of this region, larger in most of its parts, and also eaten. Not a safety problem. It is named here so that a larger blue-flowered camas does not get treated as an unknown and therefore as a risk.

lookalikes.name: Any grass-leaved bulb dug when the plant is not in flower
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This catch-all is the part of this record that actually protects people, and it is deliberately absolute. A bulb dug out of bloom from a meadow carries no information about which plant it came from. There is no smell test that works for camas, no bulb character a beginner can use, and no way to undo the mistake once it is cooked into a meal. Out of bloom, do not dig.

species.season: Flowers May to July depending on elevation and snow cover, and that flowering window is the only time in the year when a beginner can separate this plant from meadow death camas. The Forest Service records that the leaves then die and seeds are dispersed from late May to August, after which nothing above ground marks the spot. The bulb stays in the ground year round, which is what makes an unmarked autumn dig so dangerous.
species.habitat: A grass-leaved lily with a flowering stalk 8 to 20 inches tall carrying a loose spike of blue to bluish-violet flowers, growing from a bulb up to about 1.5 inches across with fibrous roots. The Forest Service describes the habitat as seasonally moist meadows that dry out by late spring, and as sites that are moist to wet in spring but dry by late spring or summer, commonly near vernal pools, springs and intermittent streams. In western Washington the Forest Service records it in mountain grassland communities, and its range runs from British Columbia south to California and east to western Montana and Wyoming. No public-domain source consulted confirms Kitsap County specifically, so treat its presence around Silverdale as plausible on remnant prairie openings and seasonally wet meadow ground, but unconfirmed here.
species.uses: Food, and historically a staple one across this region: bulbs steamed or pit cooked for one to three days, then often dried and ground into meal. The Forest Service records that small camas bulbs were eaten by western Indians, trappers and early settlers. Naming note that matters when you look this up: USDA PLANTS carries the accepted name Camassia quamash (Pursh) Greene under the common name small camas, symbol CAQU2, while the Forest Service wildflower pages call the same plant common camas. Blue camas, camas lily, quamash and western camas all refer to it too.

species.edible_detail: SMELL EVERY BULB SEPARATELY, WITH CLEAN HANDS, BEFORE IT JOINS THE OTHERS IN YOUR BASKET. Nodding onion is a true wild onion and is eaten as one. The condition attached to it is not about cooking, it is about the bulb growing next to it. USDA's death camas plant guide states that deathcamas has been mistaken for other edible bulbous plants such as wild onion, sego lily and camas, especially when flowers are lacking, and that eating one or two death camas bulbs is enough to cause severe illness in children while four or five can cause death. Onions and their relatives smell strongly of onion or garlic when you crush a leaf or scratch a bulb. Death camas does not smell of onion at all. USE THAT TEST IN ONE DIRECTION ONLY. No onion smell means do not eat it, full stop, no second opinion. But smelling onion does NOT prove that the bulb in your hand is an onion, because a bulb picks up the smell from your fingers, from your knife blade, and from a crushed onion lying beside it in the basket. That is the whole reason for smelling each bulb on its own, before it touches anything else you have picked. HONEST SOURCING NOTE: the onion-odor test itself is not stated in so many words by any public-domain federal source opened for this record, and it is included because the safe half of it costs nothing to follow. What IS sourced is the half that matters most, that death camas is mistaken for wild onion precisely when the flowers are gone, and that a few of its bulbs can kill a child.

lookalikes.name: Meadow death camas (Zigadenus venenosus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Similar narrow grass-like leaves, a similar bulb, and USDA names wild onion among the edible bulbs death camas has been mistaken for. The smell is the check, run in the negative direction only as described above. One more thing worth carrying in your head: death camas stays dangerous after it is dried. The Forest Service records that dried meadow death camas remains toxic for at least 20 years, so a withered scrap of the wrong plant in a bag of dried onions is still a poison, not a stale vegetable.

lookalikes.name: Common camas (Camassia quamash)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both edible, so confusing them is not a safety problem. Camas has no onion smell and carries blue to bluish-violet flowers on an upright spike; nodding onion smells of onion and its flower cluster bends over at the top of the stalk, which is what the species name cernuum, meaning nodding, records. They are listed together because they share one lethal neighbour, not because they endanger each other.

lookalikes.name: Any grass-leaved bulb that does not smell of onion
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The absolute rule, and the one worth memorising: if a bulb you dug from grass-leaved ground does not smell of onion when you scratch it with a clean thumbnail, put it down. It may be camas, it may be something harmless, and it may be death camas. You do not get to find out by tasting.

species.season: Green leaves in spring, the nodding flower cluster through summer, and the bulb in the ground year round. No public-domain source opened for this record gives month-by-month timing for Puget Sound, so treat this as the general pattern rather than as a harvest calendar.
species.habitat: A small native onion with narrow, grass-like leaves rising from the base and a flower cluster that nods over at the top of its stalk. USDA PLANTS carries Allium cernuum Roth as the accepted name, symbol ALCE2, a native perennial forb in the lily family, native to Canada and the lower 48. No public-domain source opened for this record itemizes its Washington counties or describes its local habitat preferences, so both are left unstated here rather than guessed at. What matters operationally is the overlap risk, not the precise patch: work on the assumption that death camas can be growing in any open grassy ground where you are digging bulbs.
species.uses: Food: the bulbs and the green leaves, used as an onion. It also carries the one sense-check that separates an edible bulb from a lethal one in this landscape, which makes it worth knowing even if you never eat it.

species.edible_detail: READ THIS AS A WARNING, NOT AS A RECIPE. Hemlock waterparsnip is treated as an edible root in foraging literature, and it is native here. It is also the single most dangerous identification call available in this county's wet ground, because it is a white-flowered carrot-family plant of the same marshes and stream edges as western water hemlock, which USDA calls the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America. USDA's own common name for this plant is hemlock waterparsnip, which tells you how close the two sit in people's minds. The condition, stated so it cannot be misread: do not eat this plant unless you can already identify both it and water hemlock with certainty, and if you are reading this to learn how, you cannot yet. A BEGINNER CANNOT RELIABLY SEPARATE THESE TWO IN THE FIELD, AND EXPERIENCED FORAGERS HAVE DIED GETTING IT WRONG. The working rule this dataset gives is the one that keeps people alive: eat no carrot-family plant gathered from wet ground. PROVENANCE, STATED PLAINLY: no public-domain federal source opened for this record documents Sium suave as a human food, and none documents it as toxic either. USDA PLANTS establishes only the name, the family and that it is a native perennial. The edibility claim therefore comes from foraging literature and is NOT verified here, while the hazard beside it is verified in detail. When only half a pair is sourced, the sourced half is the one to act on.

lookalikes.name: Western water hemlock (Cicuta douglasii)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The pair this record exists for. Same marshes, same stream edges, same white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters, same season. THE SOURCED CHARACTERS: USDA states that on water hemlock the side veins of the leaves lead to notches, not to tips at the outer margin, and that its thick rootstalk contains a number of small chambers holding a highly poisonous brown or straw-colored liquid that is released when the stem is broken or cut. Water parsnip leaves are divided only once along the stalk, while water hemlock leaves are divided two or three times. NOW THE HONEST PART: those are real characters, but the vein one needs a single leaflet held up to good light and the eye of somebody who has done it before, the leaf-division one is easy to misjudge on a young or damaged plant, and the root one requires you to have already cut into a plant that poisons you by being cut. USDA says only a small amount of the toxic substance is needed to produce poisoning in humans. A distinction that has to be right every time, on a plant where being wrong once is fatal, is not a beginner's distinction. Treat every white-flowered carrot-family plant growing in wet ground as water hemlock and leave it alone.

lookalikes.name: Water parsley (Oenanthe sarmentosa)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Another native carrot-family plant of the same Puget Sound wet ground, also reported as gathered, also with divided leaves and white umbels. Confusing these two with each other is the least of the problems in this group, which is why the danger is rated mild rather than lethal. The danger is that time spent separating THESE two feels like careful work while the actual hazard, water hemlock, is standing in the same ditch waiting to be swept up with them.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: A Washington Class B noxious weed and deadly in every part. It prefers fence lines, ditches and moist waste ground rather than standing water, has a hollow hairless stem marked with small purple spots, fern-like finely divided leaves, and a white taproot, and it reaches 2 to 3 metres. Water parsnip is a wetland plant with once-divided leaves. But note the trap: before poison hemlock bolts it is a low rosette with no stem to check for purple spots at all, and at that stage a beginner cannot separate it from other divided-leaved carrot-family plants.

lookalikes.name: Common cowparsnip (Heracleum maximum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Much larger and much coarser, standing 3 to 10 feet tall with broad lobed leaves 8 to 20 inches long and wide, and flat-topped umbels 8 to 12 inches across. Nobody who looks at the whole plant confuses a mature cow parsnip with a water parsnip. It is named here because it belongs to the same white-umbel wet-ground group, and because a young cow parsnip is far less distinctive than a mature one.

species.season: A summer plant in the wet season sense: green through spring and summer, white umbels in summer, dying back in fall. No public-domain source opened for this record gives month-by-month timing, and the timing matters less than the rule, because western water hemlock's tuberous root is in the same ground and is dangerous year round, including the winter months when nothing above ground shows where it is.
species.habitat: A native perennial in the carrot family (Apiaceae) with white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters and leaves divided once into toothed leaflets along a stalk. Marshes, stream and ditch edges, pond margins and other standing or slow water. USDA PLANTS carries Sium suave Walter, symbol SISU2, native to Alaska, Canada and the lower 48, and gives its common name as hemlock waterparsnip. The PLANTS profile does not itemize states, and no public-domain source opened confirms Kitsap County specifically. Assume it can be present in any wet ground here, and assume water hemlock can be present in the same wet ground, because assuming the absence of the deadly one is the mistake that kills.
species.uses: Reported as a root food in foraging literature; not documented as food by any public-domain federal source opened for this record. Its real use in this dataset is as the edible half of the pair that teaches the water hemlock lesson, because a forager who is taught only the poisonous plant has been taught only half of what they will actually meet in a ditch.

species.scientific_name: Oenanthe sarmentosa C. Presl ex DC.
species.edible_detail: SAME VERDICT AS HEMLOCK WATERPARSNIP, AND FOR THE SAME REASON. Water parsley is native here, it is reported as gathered, and it grows in precisely the wet ditches and slow water where western water hemlock grows. USDA calls water hemlock the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America and says only a small amount of its toxin is needed to poison a human. The condition, stated so it cannot be misread: do not eat this plant unless you can already identify both it and water hemlock with certainty, and if this entry is where you are learning the difference, you cannot yet. The sensible rule for everyone else is to eat no carrot-family plant from wet ground at all. ONE HABIT THAT CUTS THE WRONG WAY: water parsley often sprawls and roots along wet ditches and slow water, so it forms low mats of divided leaves. That mat reads as harmless ground cover rather than as a plant to be identified, which is exactly how an unidentified carrot-family plant ends up in a handful of greens. PROVENANCE, STATED PLAINLY: no public-domain federal source opened for this record documents Oenanthe sarmentosa as a food, and none documents it as toxic. USDA PLANTS establishes only the name, the family and native status. EDITORIAL CAUTION, NOT SOURCED: other species in this same genus elsewhere in the world are severely poisonous, so the genus name Oenanthe is not a safety signal and should never be read as one. That sentence is included because it points away from eating rather than toward it.

lookalikes.name: Western water hemlock (Cicuta douglasii)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Same wet ground, same carrot-family silhouette, same white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters, same divided leaves. The characters USDA gives for water hemlock are that the side veins of the leaves lead to notches, not to tips at the outer margin, and that the thick rootstalk holds small chambers of brown or straw-colored liquid released when the stem is broken or cut. Honest answer: those are real, but the first needs close inspection in good light and the second requires cutting a plant whose cut surface is itself an exposure. This is not a distinction a beginner should attempt. A mat of divided leaves sprawling in a ditch is NOT automatically the harmless one.

lookalikes.name: Hemlock waterparsnip (Sium suave)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The other native wet-ground carrot-family plant that gets gathered. Water parsnip leaves are divided once along the stalk; water parsley is more finely and repeatedly divided and tends to sprawl and root at the joints. Mixing these two with each other is not the accident that hurts people. The accident that hurts people is treating either of them as proof that the white-umbel plant beside it is safe.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Deadly in every part, a Washington Class B noxious weed that Washington's noxious weed board describes as a very tall biennial reaching up to 12 feet, with hollow, hairless stems bearing noticeable purple blotches and fern-like, toothed, finely divided leaves with a strong odor when crushed. It favours rich moist soil and disturbed edges rather than standing water. But its first-year rosette has no stem to check, and Washington's board notes that the toxins remain potent in dried plant material, so a pulled or wilted scrap is still lethal.

lookalikes.name: Any white-flowered carrot-family plant in wet ground
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The catch-all, and the line in this record that actually protects people. USDA records that water hemlock has been confused with wild parsnips, other herbs and medicinal plants. This entry never designates any white-umbel plant of wet ground as safe. Certain identification means certain, and the cost of being wrong here is seizures and death, not a stomach ache.

species.season: Green through spring and summer with white umbels in summer, dying back in fall. No public-domain source opened for this record gives month-by-month timing for Puget Sound. The timing that matters is the other plant's: water hemlock's tuberous root is dangerous year round, including winter, when nothing above ground shows where it is.
species.habitat: A native perennial in the carrot family with divided leaves and small white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters, often sprawling and rooting along wet ground. Wet ditches, marsh edges, stream banks, pond margins and slow water. USDA PLANTS carries Oenanthe sarmentosa C. Presl ex DC., symbol OESA, native to Alaska, Canada and the lower 48; the profile does not itemize states, and no public-domain source opened confirms Kitsap County specifically. Naming note for anyone searching the database: USDA PLANTS spells the common name water parsely, which is a misspelling of water parsley in their record, not a different plant.
species.uses: Reported as gathered in foraging literature; not documented as a food by any public-domain federal source opened for this record. Its place in this dataset is as one of the edible-reputation plants that share ground with western water hemlock, so that the pair is modelled whole rather than as a poison with no counterpart.

species.common_name: Common cow parsnip (also called Indian celery, Indian rhubarb, pushki)
species.form: large biennial or short-lived perennial herb, carrot family
species.edible_detail: COOKED OR PEELED, HANDLED WITH COVERED SKIN, AND ONLY WHEN YOU ARE CERTAIN WHICH WHITE-UMBEL PLANT YOU ARE HOLDING. Three conditions, and all three are real. FIRST, THE FOOD USE ITSELF. USDA's plant guide records that emerging leaf and flower buds were cooked and used in stews, and that the young stems were peeled, dipped in animal fat and eaten raw like celery stalks, and it states that cow parsnip is still used for food and traditional medicine by American Indians. The peeling is not a refinement, it is the preparation: the hazard sits in the sap. SECOND, THE SKIN HAZARD, WHICH IS THIS PLANT'S OWN AND HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH LOOKALIKES. USDA's plant guide carries a boxed warning that cow parsnip may cause a moderate to severe dermatological reaction when sap from the plant contacts the skin and is then exposed to sunlight, which is called phytophotodermatitis. The National Park Service describes the result as ranging from a mild, red rash to severe skin blistering. The Forest Service lists cow parsnip among plants that may cause skin irritation if touched. So harvesting it means covered arms, and USDA's instruction if sap reaches skin is to wash the area with soap and water immediately. Doing this work on a bright day with bare forearms is how people get chemical burns from a plant they were only trying to eat. THIRD, THE COMPANY IT KEEPS. It is a big white-umbel carrot-family plant of damp ground, which is the same silhouette and the same habitat as western water hemlock and poison hemlock. A mature cow parsnip is genuinely distinctive; a young one is far less so.
species.toxic: SKIN, NOT STOMACH, and the exposure is sap plus sunlight rather than eating. USDA's plant guide states that the sap contains furanocoumarins that can cause moderate to severe dermatological reactions and photosensitivity in some people, and that when affected skin is exposed to sunlight, a rash with burn-like blisters can develop. Its boxed warning repeats it: cow parsnip may cause a moderate to severe dermatological reaction when sap from the plant contacts the skin and is then exposed to sunlight (phytophotodermatitis). The National Park Service puts the range at a mild, red rash through to severe skin blistering. The Forest Service's Tongass safety page lists cow parsnip among plants that may cause skin irritation if touched. No dose is documented and none should be invented; individual sensitivity varies, which is why USDA says in some people. Treat any sap on skin as an exposure, wash it off with soap and water at once, and keep that skin out of the sun. No public-domain source opened for this record documents cow parsnip as poisonous to eat when properly prepared.

lookalikes.name: Western water hemlock (Cicuta douglasii)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both are carrot-family plants of damp ground carrying white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters, and USDA calls water hemlock the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America. THE DIFFERENCE YOU CAN SEE FROM SEVERAL PACES, ON A MATURE PLANT: cow parsnip is enormous and coarse, 3 to 10 feet tall, with clasping leaves 8 to 20 inches long and as wide as they are long, broadly lobed and shaped a little like maple leaves, on a light green, deeply ridged, hollow stem with spreading white woolly hairs, and primary umbels 8 to 12 inches across. Water hemlock is a slender plant about 0.5 to 1.0 m tall with narrow toothed leaf segments. That is a real difference, and an attentive person can use it. THE HONEST QUALIFIER: a young cow parsnip in its first-year rosette stage is a low clump of divided leaves, and at that stage this comfortable size difference does not exist. Do not use the size rule on a small plant.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both get tall, both carry white umbels, both like moist ground, and poison hemlock is deadly in every part. Use the STEM, and use it on a bolted plant: Washington's noxious weed board describes poison hemlock's stems as hollow, hairless and marked with noticeable purple blotches, and its leaves as fern-like, toothed, finely divided and strong-smelling when crushed. Cow parsnip's stem is hollow but deeply ridged, light green, and moderately to very hairy with spreading white hairs, and its leaves are broad and lobed rather than fern-like. Hairy and broad-leaved means cow parsnip; hairless with purple blotches and fern-like leaves means walk away. Do not run this test on a rosette that has no stem yet, because then it tells you nothing.

lookalikes.name: Giant hogweed (Heracleum mantegazzianum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Named by USDA's own cow parsnip plant guide, which says care should be taken when identifying this plant because cow parsnip looks like the invasive giant hogweed. USDA's separators: giant hogweed can grow much larger than cow parsnip, 15 feet or more with leaves 3 to 4 feet wide, has purple or red spots on the stem, and causes more severe dermatological reactions. So the check is spots plus size. A white-umbel giant with a blotched stem is not your celery, and its sap will burn you worse.

lookalikes.name: Hemlock waterparsnip (Sium suave)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Much smaller and finer, with leaves divided once into toothed leaflets rather than cow parsnip's huge lobed leaves. Confusing these two is not itself a hazard. It is listed to keep the whole white-umbel wet-ground group in one place in your head, because the group is what has to be identified, never one member of it in isolation.

species.season: A first-year rosette of large basal leaves, then in the second year a flowering stalk. USDA's plant guide puts flowering from late spring to mid-summer, and the Forest Service gives May through August across most of its range. The young stems and emerging buds that are used as food come early, in spring, which is exactly when the plant is least distinctive and the poison hemlock rosette is also up.
species.habitat: A very large native herb of the carrot family, 3 to 10 feet tall in its flowering year, with a light green, deeply ridged, hollow stem, alternate clasping leaves 8 to 20 inches long and equally wide with three or more lobes on the terminal leaflet and serrate to double-serrate edges, hairy stems and leaves, aromatic when crushed, and flat-topped compound umbels of small white flowers with primary umbels 8 to 12 inches wide. USDA describes its habitat as partially shaded, wet to somewhat moist areas: forest edges, openings, floodplains, wet meadows, thickets and streambanks, from sea level to 9,000 feet. The Forest Service lists Washington in its range and describes it in woodlands, forest openings, grasslands and riparian areas including wet meadows, stream terraces, alluvial benches, floodplains and stream and lake margins. Expect it along the damp creek edges, ditch banks and shaded forest openings around Silverdale.
species.uses: Food: young stems peeled and eaten, emerging leaf and flower buds cooked in stews, dried seeds used to season food. Medicine: USDA records leaves, stems and roots used in teas, poultices and powders for boils, warts, swelling and bruising, and notes that many reported medicinal uses have been validated by pharmaceutical research. Material: the hollow stem was used as a drinking straw, a whistle and a child's toy, and the roots to dye fibres yellow. USDA rates it not weedy or invasive, but notes that because of its size and potential as an irritant it should not be planted near pedestrian traffic. Do not hand a child a cow parsnip whistle without understanding the sap hazard first.

species.form: taprooted herb, carrot family; biennial, sometimes annual or short-lived perennial
species.protected: Not protected; the legal status runs the other way. Washington State Class C noxious weed, listed 1988. Washington's noxious weed board records that wild carrot, except where commercially grown, was changed from a Class B to a Class C noxious weed in 2013.
species.edible_detail: THIS RECORD EXISTS FOR THE IDENTIFICATION, NOT FOR THE MEAL. Wild carrot is the wild form of the garden carrot and its first-year taproot is eaten, but nothing about that fact should encourage anyone to go and dig one, because THIS IS THE PLANT POISON HEMLOCK IS MISTAKEN FOR, and poison hemlock is deadly in every part. USDA states that poisoning commonly results from mistaking poison hemlock root for wild parsnips, and both plants present you with a pale taproot in the ground where none of the stem and leaf characters are available. THE ONE GENUINELY USEFUL CHECK, and it is sourced by a Washington state agency: the noxious weed board states that wild carrot may be confused with poison hemlock, although wild carrot is smaller, hairy, and does not have purple blotches on the stems, and separately that the entire wild carrot plant is covered with coarse, stiff hairs. So hairy stem means wild carrot; hairless stem with purple blotches means poison hemlock. RUN THAT TEST IN ONE DIRECTION ONLY. Finding hairs is worth something. Not finding purple spots is worth nothing, because the spots develop as poison hemlock bolts, and a first-year poison hemlock rosette has no marked stem to check at all. At the rosette stage, which is also the stage at which you would be digging a first-year carrot root, a beginner cannot separate these two. The honest condition is therefore: do not dig a wild carrot root unless you watched that individual plant flower and confirmed it, the way the camas rule works. PROVENANCE: no public-domain federal source opened for this record documents wild carrot as a human food. USDA PLANTS establishes only the name, that it is introduced across North America and that it is a biennial.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The pair this record exists for, and Washington's noxious weed board names it on both plants' pages. THE SOURCED SEPARATORS: wild carrot is smaller, its entire plant is covered with coarse, stiff hairs, and it does not have purple blotches on the stems; poison hemlock is a very tall biennial that can reach 12 feet, with hollow, hairless stems bearing noticeable purple blotches and fern-like, toothed, finely divided leaves with a strong odor when crushed. Also useful: wild carrot's flat-topped umbel is 2 to 4 inches across and often carries one purple or pinkish flower at its centre, while poison hemlock's umbels are broader. THE FAILURE MODE TO KNOW ABOUT: none of this works on a first-year rosette of either plant, and the rosette is present through fall, winter and early spring. Washington's board also records that poison hemlock's toxins remain potent in dried plant material, so a wilted or pulled scrap mixed into a basket is still lethal.

lookalikes.name: Common cow parsnip (Heracleum maximum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Far bigger and much coarser, 3 to 10 feet tall with broad lobed leaves 8 to 20 inches across and umbels 8 to 12 inches wide, against wild carrot's 1 to 4 feet and its 2 to 4 inch umbels with fern-like finely toothed leaflets. Not a dangerous confusion, but cow parsnip's sap causes burn-like blistering after sun exposure, so it is a plant to recognise before you grab a handful of umbels.

lookalikes.name: Western water hemlock (Cicuta douglasii)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Habitat separates these two better than anything on the plant does. Washington's board puts wild carrot in meadows, pastures, roadsides and waste places; water hemlock sits in wet meadows, seepage and standing water. But habitat is a tendency, not a rule, and a roadside ditch is both. USDA calls water hemlock the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America, so the safe reading of any white umbel standing in wet ground is that it is water hemlock.

lookalikes.name: Any white-flowered carrot-family plant, especially at the rosette stage
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The catch-all, and the most important line here. Wild carrot, poison hemlock, water hemlock, cow parsnip, water parsnip, parsley, chervil and garden carrot tops all present divided leaves and white umbels. The stem characters that separate them exist only after the plants bolt. Before that, there is no field character offered here that closes the gap, because there is not one that works. Do not eat any wild carrot-family plant you have not watched flower.

species.season: A first-year rosette with a taproot, then in the second year an upright flowering stalk with white umbels through summer, drying to the curled seed head sometimes called a bird's nest. The rosette stage, which is the root-digging stage, overlaps exactly with the poison hemlock rosette stage, and that overlap is the whole safety problem.
species.habitat: An upright, taprooted herb 1 to 4 feet tall whose entire plant is covered with coarse, stiff hairs, with fern-like leaves of small toothed leaflets and small white flowers in compound flat-topped umbels 2 to 4 inches across, often with purple or pinkish flowers in the centre. Washington's noxious weed board describes it in meadows, pastures, roadsides and waste places. USDA PLANTS carries Daucus carota L., symbol DACA6, introduced across Canada, the lower 48 and the territories. Expect it on road verges, field edges, vacant lots and rough pasture around Silverdale, which is also where poison hemlock likes to be.
species.uses: Food: the first-year taproot is the wild carrot, and the plant is the ancestor of the cultivated one, though no public-domain federal source opened for this record documents the food use. Its real function in this dataset is as the identification target: it is the harmless plant a deadly one is confused with, and knowing the hairy stem separates them is worth more than any meal it provides. Washington's board notes it out-competes native grasses, can taint milk if dairy cows ingest large amounts, may be mildly toxic to livestock, and can reduce commercial carrot seed quality through hybridization, which is why the state lists it.

species.edible_detail: Not food, and the hazard is not eating it. The Forest Service states that the entire Pacific poison-oak plant is covered with oily resin and that human dermatitis results when skin comes in direct contact with the oil. The plant to learn here is a plant to avoid touching, not a plant to avoid tasting.
species.toxic: SKIN AND LUNGS, by contact and by smoke. The Forest Service states that the entire Pacific poison-oak plant is covered with oily resin, and that human dermatitis results when skin comes in direct contact with the oil; the compound is urushiol.
