THE BURNING HAZARD IS THE ONE THAT PUTS PEOPLE IN HOSPITAL: the Forest Service states that urushiol volatilizes when burned, and that human exposure to Pacific poison-oak smoke is extremely hazardous. That matters directly here, because clearing brush and burning the pile is ordinary property work, and a vine tangled into a blackberry thicket goes on the fire unnoticed. The resin is also carried on clothing, tools, gloves and firewood and remains active on them, so a second exposure can arrive hours later from a jacket. No dose is documented; sensitivity varies between people and can change over a lifetime. The plant is leafless in winter and the bare stems still carry resin.

lookalikes.name: Trailing blackberry (Rubus ursinus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The confusion that matters most here, because both are low trailing three-leaflet vines that sprawl through the same streamside thickets, and the Forest Service lists California blackberry, an old name for Rubus ursinus, among the plants poison oak grows beside. USE PRICKLES, NOT LEAF SHAPE AND NOT SIZE. Trailing blackberry stems are densely prickled and even its leaves feel prickly. Poison oak has no prickles anywhere: if a three-leaflet trailing vine is completely smooth to the touch, do not touch it again. Backstop check on the fruit: poison oak fruit is a cluster of small white drupes, never a black knot of tiny juice beads.

lookalikes.name: Salmonberry (Rubus spectabilis)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Salmonberry also carries leaves divided into three leaflets, and it grows in the same damp streamside ground, so the three-leaflet silhouette alone tells you nothing. Salmonberry is an upright woody cane, commonly with scattered fine prickles, especially low on the cane, and it carries obvious pink to magenta flowers and orange to red raspberry-like fruit. Poison oak is prickle-free everywhere, has greenish-white flowers and white drupes, and its leaflets are lobed in an oak-like way with rounded lobes rather than evenly toothed. Prickle-free plus white fruit means hands off.

lookalikes.name: Common snowberry (Symphoricarpos albus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both carry white fruit in the same understory, which is where the confusion lives. Tell them by the LEAF, not the berry. Poison oak leaves are divided into three, sometimes five, round to ovate, lobed or toothed leaflets. Snowberry leaves are simple, undivided ovals set in opposite pairs. A white berry on a three-leaflet plant is a reason to keep your hands off, not to look closer.

lookalikes.name: Vine maple and other three-part or lobed shrubs of the same woods
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Several harmless shrubs here carry lobed leaves that read as oak-like at a glance. The working habit that covers all of them: count leaflets. Three separate leaflets on a single stalk, with the middle one on a longer stalklet than the two beside it, is the pattern to keep your hands out of, whatever the plant turns out to be. Nothing in this county is worth touching an unidentified three-leaflet vine to find out.

species.season: The Forest Service records flowering from March to June and fruit dispersal in summer and fall. It is deciduous, so it drops its leaves for the winter, which removes the only easy identification character for several months while leaving the resin on the bare stems. New spring leaves are often glossy and reddish. Do not treat a bare, leafless, prickle-free vine in winter as identified.
species.habitat: A many-stemmed native deciduous shrub or woody vine. The Forest Service gives erect shrubs 2 to 6 feet tall and vines 10 to 30 feet long, sometimes as long as 100 feet, with leaves of three, sometimes five, round to ovate, diversely lobed or toothed leaflets, and white drupes as fruit. It generally grows in acid soils on well-drained slopes and in riparian zones, in mixed evergreen forests, woodlands, chaparral, coastal sage scrub and riparian zones below 5,000 feet, and it associates with Douglas-fir, bigleaf maple and willows among others. RANGE, STATED CAREFULLY: the Forest Service states that it occurs west of the Cascade Range in Washington, Oregon and California, which puts its range on this side of the mountains. No public-domain source opened for this record confirms Kitsap County occurrence specifically, and it is generally far less common in the northern Puget Sound lowlands than it is further south. Do not use that as permission to grab an unidentified three-leaflet vine, and do not assume every three-leaflet vine you see here is poison oak either.
species.uses: No human use. Wildlife value is real: the Forest Service records that birds eat Pacific poison-oak fruits. If you are clearing it from a property, the two rules are cover your skin and never burn it, because the Forest Service calls exposure to the smoke extremely hazardous.

species.common_name: Green false hellebore (also called Indian hellebore, corn lily)
species.edible_detail: Never, in any amount, at any stage. The Forest Service states plainly that false hellebore can be fatal if eaten, listing it alongside water hemlock and baneberry as the plants on its safety page that are particularly dangerous if consumed. There is no part, no season and no preparation given here that makes it safe, and none should be sought. The reason this plant needs to be in a foraging dataset at all is that its early spring shoots come up in the same wet ground as plants people do gather, and it is one of the two things the Forest Service warns that an edible woodland plant gets mistaken for.
species.toxic: DEADLY IF EATEN. The Forest Service's Tongass safety page names Veratrum viride specifically and states that it can be fatal if eaten. ON THE MECHANISM, AND THE LIMITS OF WHAT IS SOURCED HERE: USDA's poisonous plant research describes the poisonous substances in false hellebore as steroidal alkaloids and states that the roots are 5 to 10 times as poisonous as leaves or stems, that it emerges as soon as snow melts in spring, and that in sheep slight or marked signs of poisoning follow eating 150 to 300 grams of green stems or leaves. THAT USDA PAGE IS ABOUT VERATRUM CALIFORNICUM, A DIFFERENT SPECIES IN THE SAME GENUS, and it is quoted here for the shape of the hazard, not as a measurement of this plant. No public-domain source opened for this record gives a human dose for Veratrum viride, and none should be invented. The livestock figure in particular must not be read as reassurance: a number given for a sheep tells you nothing usable about a person. USDA also records that in pregnant animals the plant causes severe birth defects, which is a second reason no amount is a safe experiment. Treat any suspected ingestion as a medical emergency and call poison control.

lookalikes.name: Western skunk cabbage (Lysichiton americanus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both push broad, strongly pleated, parallel-veined leaves out of the same wet seepy ground in the same early spring weeks, and this is the confusion that puts false hellebore within reach of a person. THE CHECKS YOU CAN MAKE STANDING OVER IT: skunk cabbage smells strongly and unmistakably of skunk when you brush or break a leaf, and it sends up a bright yellow hood around its flower spike; false hellebore has no such smell and its pleated leaves wrap around and clasp an upright leafy stem, so the plant has an obvious stem climbing up through its leaves while skunk cabbage has essentially none. Neither plant is food, so the working rule is the simple one: do not eat either.

lookalikes.name: Claspleaf twistedstalk (Streptopus amplexifolius)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: This is the confusion the Forest Service itself warns about, on its own page for twistedstalk: the species can be mistaken for the poisonous Veratrum, so perhaps twisted stalk is better left unsampled. Both carry alternate leaves that clasp an upright stem in moist shady ground. Twistedstalk is slender and arching, with a distinctive kink in each flower stalk and a single berry dangling underneath the stem below each leaf. False hellebore is a heavy, coarse plant with broad strongly pleated leaves and a branched spike of small green flowers at the top, and it carries no dangling berries at all. If you cannot separate these two with certainty, eat neither.

lookalikes.name: Common camas and other broad-leaved lilies of wet meadows in spring
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Not a close match leaf for leaf, since camas has narrow grass-like leaves and false hellebore has broad pleated ones, but they are both lily-family plants of wet spring ground and both come up early. The catch-all worth carrying: in a wet meadow in April, a big pleated-leaved plant with a stout upright stem is not a food crop, whatever else is growing around it. Identify the individual plant you intend to dig or cut, not the meadow.

species.season: Emerges very early, as soon as the ground thaws and while most other growth is still absent, which is exactly when skunk cabbage leaves are also coming up and when spring greens are being gathered. It stands through summer and dies back in fall. The roots are the most toxic part and stay in the ground year round.
species.habitat: A large native perennial herb in the lily family with broad, strongly pleated, parallel-veined leaves clasping a stout upright stem, and small green flowers in a branched spike at the top. USDA PLANTS carries Veratrum viride Aiton, symbol VEVI, a native perennial forb of Alaska, Canada and the lower 48. Wet ground: seeps, streamsides, wet meadows and moist forest openings. RANGE, STATED CAREFULLY: the Forest Service documents it in southeast Alaska on the Tongass, and it is recorded in Washington, but no public-domain source opened for this record confirms it at Puget Sound lowland elevation near Silverdale, where it is generally a mountain plant. Do not assume it is here, and do not assume it is absent. The safe reading of a big pleated-leaved plant in a local seep is that you do not know what it is.
species.uses: No food use, ever. It has documented traditional medicinal use in this region, which is not repeated here with any preparation, because the margin between a medicinal and a fatal quantity of a steroidal alkaloid is exactly the kind of thing a dataset like this must not encourage anyone to explore. Its place here is as a hazard to recognise while gathering something else.

species.common_name: Claspleaf twistedstalk (also called watermelon berry, wild cucumber)
species.edible_detail: THE FOREST SERVICE CLEARS THE BERRY AND THEN ADVISES AGAINST EATING THE PLANT, AND BOTH HALVES OF THAT ARE IMPORTANT. On the one hand it describes each flower stalk as giving rise to a single elliptic yellow or red berry, which is edible, and notes that the green shoots taste like cucumber when eaten raw. On the other hand, on the same page, it writes that populations tend to be small and the species can be mistaken for the poisonous Veratrum, so perhaps twisted stalk is better left unsampled. THE CONDITIONS THAT FOLLOW FROM THAT, in order of how badly they hurt if ignored. FIRST, this is a knee-high woodland herb with red berries, which is also an exact description of red baneberry, whose berries the Forest Service says are poisonous and which the National Park Service says will often send the heart into cardiac arrest. You must be able to tell those two apart before you pick anything, and the check is where the berries sit, not what colour they are. SECOND, the shoots you might gather in spring come up in the same wet shady seeps as green false hellebore, which the Forest Service says can be fatal if eaten. THIRD, the Forest Service's own note on small populations is a conservation point: this is not a plant to strip. Take the sourced advice at face value. A dataset that teaches foraging should pass along the Forest Service's own conclusion, which is that this one is better left unsampled, and treat any eating of it as a decision made by someone who already knows all three plants cold.

lookalikes.name: Red baneberry (Actaea rubra)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The confusion that matters, because unlike most red-berry mix-ups this one is between two plants of the same size and shape in the same woods. Both are soft-stemmed woodland herbs one to three feet tall growing in moist shady forest, and both carry red berries. THE CHECK IS THE ARRANGEMENT OF THE FRUIT, AND YOU CAN MAKE IT FROM WHERE YOU STAND. Twistedstalk hangs ONE berry per stalk, dangling underneath the arching stem, roughly one below each leaf, because the Forest Service describes only one flower on each flower stalk, hanging downward, each giving rise to a single berry. Red baneberry holds its berries BUNCHED in a showy cluster on a single upright stalk held above the leaves. One berry hanging under the stem means twistedstalk; a bunch of berries standing up above the leaves means baneberry, and baneberry is the one that stops hearts. Second check if you need it: baneberry's leaves are divided two or three times into separate sharply toothed leaflets, while twistedstalk's leaves are simple, undivided, parallel-veined and clasp the stem. Colour is NOT a check: the Forest Service records baneberry fruits as red or occasionally white, and twistedstalk berries as yellow or red.

lookalikes.name: Green false hellebore (Veratrum viride)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The Forest Service names this confusion itself and treats it as reason enough to leave twistedstalk alone. Both carry alternate leaves clasping an upright stem in the same wet shady ground, and the risk peaks in spring when the shoots are up and the berries that would identify twistedstalk do not exist yet. False hellebore is coarse and heavy with broad, strongly pleated, parallel-veined leaves and a branched spike of small green flowers; twistedstalk is slender and arching with a kink in each flower stalk and single berries dangling below. THE HONEST RULE: at the young-shoot stage, when both are just leafy stems coming out of a seep, a beginner should not attempt this call. Wait for the berries.

lookalikes.name: Western skunk cabbage (Lysichiton americanus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Shares the same wet shady seeps and comes up in the same weeks. Skunk cabbage is unmistakable once you touch it: huge leaves rising straight from the ground with no stem to speak of, and a strong skunk smell from a brushed or broken leaf, plus a bright yellow hood around its flower spike in early spring. Twistedstalk is a slender arching stem with leaves along it. Confusing them is not itself dangerous. It is named because these three plants, twistedstalk, false hellebore and skunk cabbage, share one seep, and only one of them is food.

lookalikes.name: Red huckleberry (Vaccinium parvifolium)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Another red berry of the same forest, and a safe one. Red huckleberry is a woody shrub with thin green twigs and berries hanging singly along the branches. Twistedstalk is a non-woody herb whose stem you could snap between your fingers. Both are edible, so this is a flavour question rather than a safety one, but it is worth knowing which red berries here are on wood and which are on soft stems, because the soft-stemmed one that is NOT twistedstalk is baneberry.

species.season: Greenish-white flowers of six tepals in late spring, hanging one per kinked stalk. Berries through summer into early fall, which is the only period when the plant identifies itself clearly. The spring shoot stage, when the plant is easiest to confuse with false hellebore, is the stage with no berries to check.
species.habitat: A native perennial herb with an arching, often branched stem, alternate simple leaves with parallel veins and smooth margins whose upper ones snugly embrace the stem, and a distinctive 90 degree twist in each flower stalk, which is what gives it its name. Each flower stalk carries only one downward-hanging flower and then a single elliptic yellow or red berry. The Forest Service describes it as typically found in moist, shady mountain forests and streamsides, distributed across Canada and south to California, the Rocky Mountains and much of the eastern United States. USDA PLANTS carries Streptopus amplexifolius (L.) DC., symbol STAM2. Expect it in shaded, damp second-growth woods, ravines and seep edges around Silverdale; no public-domain source opened for this record confirms Kitsap County specifically.
species.uses: Food, with the Forest Service's own caution attached: the berries are edible and the green shoots taste like cucumber raw, but the same page concludes that the species is perhaps better left unsampled because populations tend to be small and it can be mistaken for the poisonous Veratrum. If you take anything from this entry, take the berry-arrangement check against red baneberry, which is useful whether or not you ever eat a twistedstalk.

species.common_name: Bittersweet nightshade (also called climbing nightshade, bitter nightshade)
species.edible_detail: No part of it, at any stage of ripeness. The Forest Service states that climbing nightshade contains solanine, known to be poisonous to humans, livestock, mice, dogs and rabbits, and that unripe berries hold the highest concentration of toxins, followed by vegetative tissue, and then ripe berries. There is no preparation given here that makes it safe. The reason it matters more than its toxicity alone suggests is WHERE it grows: it threads up through blackberry thickets and hedgerows and fruits in the same season, at the height a child picks.
species.toxic: BERRIES WORST WHEN GREEN, AND THE LEAVES AND STEMS TOO. The Forest Service names solanine, a glycoalkaloid, and states that unripe berries have the highest concentration of toxins, followed by vegetative tissue, and then ripe berries. ON DOSE, WITH THE SOURCE'S OWN HEDGING KEPT INTACT: the Forest Service cites a handbook on poisonous plants indicating that climbing nightshade is only likely to cause symptoms in humans who have eaten 10 or more unripe berries, and that a fatal dose would require about 200 unripe berries. It adds that in large doses solanine will slow the heart, reduce body temperature, cause vertigo, delirium, convulsions and possibly death. DO NOT READ THE 200 FIGURE AS REASSURANCE. It is a figure for an adult-sized reference, it is drawn from a handbook rather than from clinical cases, and the Forest Service reports no actual human poisoning cases to calibrate it. A small child eating a handful off a fence line is the realistic scenario here, and 10 berries is the number that matters for them. Any ingestion by a child is a call to poison control, not a wait-and-see.

lookalikes.name: Trailing blackberry (Rubus ursinus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Nightshade twines up through blackberry thickets, so the two fruits hang in the same tangle at the same time of year. TELL THEM APART BY THE FRUIT, WHICH IS UNAMBIGUOUS: a blackberry is a black knot of many small juice beads stuck together on a prickly cane. A nightshade berry is a single smooth oval, 2 to 8 mm long, red when ripe, hanging in a loose drooping bunch, on a vine that carries no prickles at all. Prickles are the fastest check of the two: the nightshade vine is smooth.

lookalikes.name: Himalayan blackberry (Rubus armeniacus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The same story on the bigger thicket, and the more common one around Silverdale. The Forest Service records climbing nightshade in habitats associated with water and disturbed ground, which is where Himalayan blackberry dominates here. Same check: smooth single red ovals in drooping bunches on a prickle-free twining stem is nightshade; black aggregate fruit on a thick, angled, hook-thorned cane is blackberry. Worth teaching to anyone picking with children, who pick at eye level and take what is in reach.

lookalikes.name: Red huckleberry (Vaccinium parvifolium)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both produce small red berries, so colour alone will not do. Red huckleberry is a woody shrub with thin, distinctly green, angled twigs and small thin leaves, and its berries hang SINGLY along the branches. Nightshade is a scrambling vine whose base is woody and whose upper branches are herbaceous, with berries in loose DROOPING BUNCHES and, earlier in the season, unmistakable purple flowers with swept-back petals and a protruding yellow cone of anthers. If you ever saw purple-and-yellow flowers on that plant, it is not a huckleberry.

lookalikes.name: Red elderberry (Sambucus racemosa)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both carry clusters of small red berries in the same damp disturbed ground. Red elderberry is a woody shrub or small tree 7 to 20 feet tall with large compound leaves in opposite pairs and many small berries in a tall, showy, dome or pyramid shaped spray. Nightshade is a vine about 10 feet long that leans and scrambles on other plants, with simple leaves often lobed at the base and only a few berries in a small drooping bunch. If the plant cannot stand up by itself, it is not an elderberry.

species.season: The Forest Service gives flowers May to September and fruits July to October across North America. The long fruiting season is part of the hazard: green, half-ripe and ripe berries hang on the same plant at the same time, and the green ones are the most toxic.
species.habitat: A perennial rhizomatous vine or scrambling shrub with a woody base and herbaceous upper branches, with stems typically about 10 feet long, leaves about 2 to 5 inches long, purple flowers with a yellow centre borne in drooping clusters, and berries 2 to 8 mm in diameter ripening through green and orange to red. The Forest Service states it is a nonnative species in North America, native to Europe, north Africa and east and central Asia, and records it commonly in habitats associated with water such as riparian areas, marshes, wetlands, lake shores, pond edges and canal banks. It occurs in Washington. Expect it around Silverdale on wet ditch banks, hedgerows, fence lines, the edges of blackberry thickets and damp waste ground, including in yards.

species.common_name: Black twinberry (also called twinberry honeysuckle, bearberry honeysuckle)
species.edible_detail: Treat it as not food. USDA's plant guide opens with a boxed warning that twinberry honeysuckle is considered toxic and should be used with caution, and states in its management section that twinberry honeysuckle berries has been noted as poisonous, that the fruit is bitter and sour and is eaten by some, and that since European honeysuckle species are regarded as emetic and cathartic they are better avoided in favour of something less dubious. USDA's plant fact sheet is honest that the question is genuinely disputed: reports on the fruit vary from poisonous, to mildly toxic, to bitter and unpalatable, to edible and useful as food, depending on tribe, region or publication, and it states separately that the bitter ripe berries may be mildly toxic or poisonous to humans. WHEN A FEDERAL SOURCE SAYS ITS OWN LITERATURE DISAGREES, THE SAFE READING IS THE CAUTIOUS END OF THE RANGE, which is what this record takes. That is not a claim that anyone who has eaten one has been harmed; it is a refusal to guess on the reader's behalf. There is no shortage of good black fruit in these woods.
species.toxic: FRUIT, DISPUTED SEVERITY, NO DOSE DOCUMENTED. USDA's plant guide carries the warning that twinberry honeysuckle is considered toxic and should be used with caution and records that the berries have been noted as poisonous. USDA's fact sheet states that the bitter ripe berries may be mildly toxic or poisonous to humans and that there is some suggestion the foliage or other plant parts may have a mildly toxic effect on cattle. No compound is named and no dose is given in either document, so none is stated here. One further claim, attributed because it is unusual and no mechanism is offered for it: the National Park Service writes that the plant is notorious for absorbing toxins from the ground and nearby water. Take that as recorded rather than as established. The practical upshot is unchanged: this is a shrub to recognise and walk past.

lookalikes.name: Indian plum (Oemleria cerasiformis)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The pair this record exists for, because both are native shrubs of the same moist forests, clearings, thickets and streamsides here, and both end the season carrying dark, almost black fruit. TELL THEM APART BY THE LEAF ARRANGEMENT AND BY HOW THE FRUIT IS HELD, NOT BY COLOUR. Twinberry leaves grow in OPPOSITE PAIRS, two at each joint, and its berries come in PAIRS sitting in a cup of showy purple-red bracts, which is the character that names the plant. Indian plum leaves are ALTERNATE, one at a time up the twig, lance-shaped with smooth edges, and they smell distinctly of cucumber when crushed; its fruit hangs in a loose drooping string of up to five. A pair of black berries in a red-purple cup is twinberry. A dangling string of bluish-black plums on a plant that smells of cucumber is Indian plum. Timing overlaps too: USDA puts twinberry's shiny black berries ripening in July or later.

lookalikes.name: Evergreen huckleberry (Vaccinium ovatum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Another small black berry of the same understory, and a good food. Evergreen huckleberry has small, thick, glossy, clearly saw-toothed evergreen leaves held in flat sprays, arranged alternately, with berries in clusters strung along the twig. Twinberry is deciduous with larger, softer, untoothed leaves in opposite pairs and berries strictly in twos inside purple-red bracts. Count the berries at a fruiting point: two, in a cup, means put it down.

lookalikes.name: Salal (Gaultheria shallon)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Salal's dark blue-black fruit is one of the staple foods of these woods, so this is a confusion worth closing. Salal has thick, leathery, alternate evergreen leaves 5 to 10 cm long with fine sharp teeth all round the edge, and its hairy dark fruit is strung along an arching one-sided stalk. Twinberry's leaves are deciduous, untoothed and in opposite pairs, and its fruit sits in twos in a red-purple bract cup. Opposite leaves plus paired berries means twinberry.

lookalikes.name: Spurge laurel (Daphne laureola)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: The genuinely dangerous black berry of this group, and a Washington Class B noxious weed on the state quarantine list, whose fruits the state describes as little black berries with one seed and as poisonous, with all parts highly toxic to people and livestock. Spurge laurel is evergreen, with narrowly oval, completely smooth-edged leaves bunched in a rosette at the shoot tips and berries tucked into the leaf axils below that bunch. Twinberry is deciduous with leaves in opposite pairs spread along the branch. Neither is food, but they fail differently: twinberry is disputed and probably unpleasant, and spurge laurel is seriously poisonous.

species.season: Flowers in spring, in pairs, yellow and cupped by a large pair of green to purplish bracts that turn showy purple-red as the fruit sets. USDA's plant guide gives the paired blackish berries ripening in August or September, and USDA's fact sheet gives July or later; seed is collected from ripe berries July through September. Deciduous, so it is leafless and hard to identify in winter.
species.habitat: A native deciduous shrub. USDA's plant guide describes it as an erect clustered shrub one to three metres high with freely exfoliating bark, opposite short-stemmed leaves that are somewhat elliptical to broadly lance-shaped and pointed, often hairy beneath, with yellow flowers tinged with red cupped by a large pair of green to purplish bracts, and roundish or oval blackish berries paired on long axillary stalks. USDA's fact sheet gives the height as up to 12, sometimes 16, feet. It is typically found in moist forests, clearings, riparian habitats, swamps and thickets, from the sea coast to alpine elevations, and produces most fruit in open sunlight though it is most commonly found in shade. USDA PLANTS carries Lonicera involucrata (Richardson) Banks ex Spreng., symbol LOIN5, native to Alaska, Canada and the lower 48. Expect it along the damp forest edges, stream corridors and wetland margins around Silverdale.
species.uses: Not food in this dataset. Documented non-food uses: USDA records the Quileute and Kwakwaka'wakw using the berries as a black pigment, the Haida rubbing berries on the scalp, and varied medicinal uses of leaves, berries and bark among many tribes, sometimes as a ceremonial emetic, which is a use that turns on the plant making you vomit. Conservation value is high and undisputed: USDA describes it as a valuable shrub for streambank erosion control and riparian restoration, useful as live stakes and fascines, with berries eaten by bears, small mammals, grouse, quail and thrushes, and flowers feeding hummingbirds and butterflies. Plant it; do not eat it.

species.edible_detail: READ THE NO CAREFULLY: it means not established as food here, NOT poisonous. No public-domain federal source opened for this record documents any Stachys species as a human food, and none documents one as toxic either. Rather than guess in either direction, this record leaves it out of the food list. Its value is a different one, and it is real: hedge nettle is the plant stinging nettle gets confused with, and knowing that the confusion is harmless is itself worth having. If you reach into a damp thicket for spring nettle greens and come away with hedge nettle, you have made a disappointing mistake, not a dangerous one. The dangerous mistake in that same patch is poison hemlock, which is why that is listed below and why you look at every single stem you cut rather than grabbing a mixed handful.

lookalikes.name: Stinging nettle (Urtica dioica)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Much the same outline at arm's length: opposite pairs of toothed, hairy, pointed leaves on an upright stem in the same damp ground. FOUR CHECKS, ANY ONE OF WHICH SETTLES IT. Feel the stem: hedge nettle's is square, with edges you can roll between finger and thumb. Crush a leaf: hedge nettle smells minty, a mint-family smell, sometimes a rank one; nettle does not. Look at the flowers: hedge nettle carries showy pink to purple two-lipped flowers in whorls up the stem, while stinging nettle's flowers are drooping strings of tiny greenish beads with no colour to them. And the obvious one: stinging nettle stings bare skin and hedge nettle does not, though that check costs you the sting to perform. Getting this wrong costs nothing worse than a sting or a missed harvest.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum)
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Not a close match leaf for leaf, and listed for the same reason it is listed under stinging nettle: it grows in the same rich, moist, disturbed ground where people cut spring greens, and every part of it is deadly. Washington's noxious weed board describes it as a very tall biennial reaching up to 12 feet, with hollow, hairless stems marked with noticeable purple blotches and fern-like, toothed, finely divided leaves with a strong odor when crushed, and states that the toxins remain potent in dried plant material. Hedge nettle leaves are simple and undivided, toothed, hairy, pointed and in opposite pairs on a square stem. Simple opposite leaves on a square stem is a mint; fern-like divided leaves on a spotted round stem is a killer. Never cut a mixed handful from a patch.

lookalikes.name: Other mints of the same damp ground, including self-heal and the wild mints
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Several square-stemmed mint-family herbs share this habitat and none of them is a danger. The square stem and the minty smell mark the family, and within the family the identification stops mattering for safety purposes. What the square stem does NOT do is clear the plant next to it, so use it to identify one stem at a time.

species.season: Leafy growth through spring and summer with showy pink to purple flowers in summer, dying back in winter. No public-domain source opened for this record gives month-by-month timing for Puget Sound, so this is the general pattern rather than a harvest calendar. The period that matters is early spring, when stinging nettle shoots are being cut and the young growth of several damp-ground plants looks alike.
species.habitat: Damp, rich ground: stream edges, ditch banks, wet thickets, forest edges and the margins of clearings, often in the same patches as stinging nettle. Recognise the genus rather than the species: a square stem you can feel, simple toothed pointed leaves in opposite pairs, soft hairs, a minty smell when crushed, and two-lipped pink to purple flowers in whorls. USDA PLANTS carries the genus Stachys L., symbol STACH, common name hedgenettle, in the mint family (Lamiaceae), with native, introduced, annual, biennial and perennial members across North America. ITIS gives the genus as Stachys L. under the common names hedge nettle and hedgenettle. THE LOCAL SPECIES: the hedge nettles of western Washington are Cooley's hedgenettle, which ITIS now carries under the accepted name Stachys chamissonis var. cooleyae, with the older name Stachys cooleyae A. Heller treated as a synonym, and Stachys mexicana Benth. This record is kept at genus rank on purpose, because the safety point, that it is a harmless mint rather than a nettle, holds for all of them and does not depend on getting the species right.
species.uses: No food or material use documented by any public-domain federal source opened for this record. Its documented use in this dataset is as an identification aid: it is the harmless thing in the nettle patch, and a forager who knows it will stop treating every stinging-nettle-shaped plant as either a prize or a threat, and start looking at stems one at a time, which is the habit that protects them from the plant in that patch that actually kills.

species.common_name: Common mullein, also called great mullein, flannel mullein or woolly mullein
species.protected: No protection and no legal restriction found in Washington. It is not named in any of the three state noxious weed classes, WAC 16-750-005 (Class A), 16-750-011 (Class B) or 16-750-015 (Class C), all three of which were read for this record. USDA PLANTS records it as introduced in the lower 48, Alaska, Hawaii and Canada. Note for readers outside Washington: North Carolina State Extension's entry says the plant is listed as noxious in Colorado and Hawaii, so the answer is state by state.
species.edible_detail: READ THE NO CAREFULLY. It means not established as a food by any source opened for this record, NOT that the plant is known to poison people. Mullein is in this dataset for one reason: it is the plant a person is most likely to be holding when they have actually picked a first-year foxglove. The Forest Service's fire effects review records a long history of MEDICINAL rather than food use, in Europe, among Native American tribes, and today. Those are documented uses, not an edibility finding, and this record does not turn them into one. There is a specific documented hazard in one plant part, the seed: see the toxic field. If you gather mullein leaf for tea, the safety problem is not mullein, it is what else is growing in the same rosette-shaped, hairy, grey-green form on the same disturbed ground. See the foxglove entry below and act on it.
species.toxic: The SEED is documented as toxic. The Forest Service fire effects review records that early European settlers in the eastern United States crushed common mullein seed and put it into diked areas of slow-moving water to poison fish, that fish breathing was severely reduced or stopped by the toxic seeds, and that seed was brought from Europe and cultivated for this purpose before the Revolutionary War. No poisoning of humans by any part of the plant was found in the sources opened for this record, and North Carolina State Extension's entry for the species carries no poison section at all. Absence of a documented hazard is not permission to eat it; it means the question has not been answered by anything read here.

lookalikes.name: common foxglove
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: THIS IS THE ONLY REASON THIS RECORD EXISTS. Foxglove kills through the heart, its first-year rosette has no flower spike to identify it by, and mullein leaf is gathered for tea from exactly the same roadsides and cleared ground. Both plants are biennials that spend a whole year as a flat rosette of large, soft, hairy, greyish leaves. TWO CHARACTERS YOU CAN ACTUALLY CHECK, both taken from the University of Washington Burke Herbarium's own descriptions of the two species. (1) THE HAIRS. Burke describes mullein as having the ENTIRE PLANT covered with white-woolly, BRANCHED hairs, so a mullein leaf looks and feels like felt or flannel and a hand lens shows hairs that fork into several arms from one base; the Forest Service says the same, a thick coating of branched hairs on the stems and leaves, and North Carolina State Extension calls the leaves densely woolly and velvety and says the first-year rosette looks similar to lamb's ear. Burke describes foxglove as merely puberulent throughout and glandular upward, that is minutely short-hairy, not woolly, not felted. (2) THE LEAF EDGE. Burke gives mullein basal leaves as broadly oblanceolate and NEARLY ENTIRE, an unbroken margin, tapered to a long petiole. Burke gives foxglove leaves as oblong-ovate WITH SMALL, ROUNDED TEETH. A felted leaf with a smooth edge is mullein; a thinly hairy leaf with a scalloped edge is foxglove. NOW THE HONEST PART: those characters are real and checkable, and they are still not the rule that protects you. The rule that protects you is the one in the foxglove record, that you harvest rosette leaves only from a plant you personally watched flower: mark it in summer and come back. Use these two characters to raise an alarm, never to grant a clearance.

lookalikes.name: comfrey
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Comfrey is the other big hairy-leaved plant of tended ground in this part of the world, and it carries a documented liver hazard of its own, so picking it by mistake is not a harmless error. Burke's description gives comfrey the character that separates it from both mullein and foxglove at a glance: comfrey's erect stems are WINGED FROM THE LEAF BASES, that is, the leaf runs down the stem as a raised flange on each side instead of stopping at a stalk. Neither mullein nor foxglove is described that way. Comfrey is also plain green and stiff-hairy rather than grey-green and felted, and its flowers hang in small nodding clusters at the branch tips, dull blue or yellowish white and bell-shaped about 1.5 cm long, not a tall dense spike.

lookalikes.name: lamb's ear
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: North Carolina State Extension says outright that a first-year mullein rosette looks similar to lamb's ear, Stachys byzantina, the common silver-felted garden perennial. This is a harmless confusion, listed because it shows how little a silvery felted rosette narrows things down. Lamb's ear rarely escapes cultivation here: a search of the Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria returned only 6 Washington specimen records for Stachys byzantina, from King and Skamania counties, none from Kitsap. Mullein is the likely plant on an open roadside; lamb's ear is the likely plant inside a planted bed.

lookalikes.name: moth mullein
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Verbascum blattaria, the other Verbascum naturalized in Washington. A Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 96 Washington records for it, concentrated east of the Cascades in Walla Walla, Whitman, Klickitat, Stevens, Asotin and Spokane counties, with 6 from Pierce County and none from Kitsap, so it is much less likely here than common mullein. Burke describes common mullein as woolly over the entire plant; a Verbascum that is not woolly is not V. thapsus. No hazard is documented for either.

species.season: Biennial. Burke gives the life history plainly: a rosette of basal leaves in the first year, then a single erect stem 0.4 to 2 m tall in the second year, flowering June to September, after which the plant dies. The Forest Service adds that the second-year stem is stout, more than 1 cm thick, that the plant may pass 7 feet, and that rosettes often stay green through the winter. That evergreen winter rosette is the hazardous window, because it is the season when a forager sees a hairy rosette and no flower.
species.habitat: Disturbed open ground. Burke records it from both sides of the Cascades crest in Washington, in fields, roadsides, wastelots, disturbed forest edge, thickets and other disturbed open areas. The Forest Service review says it occurs in every US state including Alaska and Hawaii, that within the contiguous states it is often described as common, widespread, conspicuous or everywhere, that it is in most places limited to disturbed areas and rarely persists beyond the earliest stages of succession, and that it was observed in Mount Rainier National Park, Washington, in 1932. LOCAL EVIDENCE: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 144 Washington specimen records, including one from Kitsap County, so the plant is physically documented in this county and not merely inferred from a state map.
species.uses: Documented historical and medicinal use; no documented food use. The Forest Service review records yellow flowers used to dye hair as early as the 4th century BC; Romans dipping flowering stalks in tallow for torches; a folk-medicine literature covering respiratory disorders, urinary tract infections and skin disease; southwestern tribes including the Hopi smoking dried leaves and flowers, with giant-trumpets or other plants, to treat mental illness, and Potawatomi, Mohegan, Penobscot and Menominee smoking dried leaves to treat colds, bronchitis and asthma; a Catawba cough syrup from boiled roots and a poultice of mashed leaves for bruises and sprains; a Choctaw leaf poultice for headache; and, today, a place in herbal ear drops for children over 5, with leaves, flowers, capsules, alcohol extracts and flower oil sold for medicinal use in the United States. The same review notes a 2002 study reporting antibacterial and antitumor properties of extracts, and passes on a Northwest floral guide's suggestion that basal leaves make insoles for weary hikers. None of that is a recommendation from this record. One ecological note with practical value: the Forest Service reports that liquid smoke treatments increased emergence from soil seed banks, so expect mullein to appear in quantity after burns and clearing, which is also where foxglove appears.

species.common_name: Broadleaf plantain, also called common plantain or dooryard plantain
species.form: perennial herb; a flat basal rosette with leafless flowering stalks
species.protected: No protection and no legal restriction found in Washington. It is not named in any of the three state noxious weed classes, WAC 16-750-005, 16-750-011 or 16-750-015, all three of which were read for this record. USDA PLANTS records it as introduced across the lower 48, Alaska, Hawaii, Canada and the Caribbean territories.
species.edible_detail: Edible, on conditions. THE FOOD USE IS DOCUMENTED: the North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox states that the leaves of young plantain are used as a vegetable similar to spinach, that plantain is a highly nutritious wild edible high in calcium and vitamins A, C and K, that the young tender leaves can be eaten raw and the older stringier leaves boiled in stews, and that the seeds are also edible. THE CONDITIONS. (1) The same source states that ingesting large quantities can cause a drop in blood pressure. Treat it as a green, not a bulk staple, and treat that sentence as the reason. (2) IDENTIFY THE INDIVIDUAL PLANT, NOT THE PATCH. Plantain is one of the most widely gathered wild plants there is, and it grows as a flat rosette on exactly the trampled, disturbed ground where a first-year foxglove also grows as a flat rosette. See the foxglove entry below; it is the whole reason this record is in the dataset. (3) Plantain's habitat is the lawn, the vacant lot and the road verge, which are the places most likely to have been sprayed or to sit in vehicle runoff. Nothing opened for this record measures that, so it is a caution rather than a finding, but it is the obvious one for a plant whose preferred ground is the mown edge of a road.
species.toxic: No toxin is documented in any source opened for this record, and the North Carolina State Extension entry for the species carries no poison section. The one caution found is from that same entry: ingesting large quantities can cause a drop in blood pressure. One naming point that matters in a kitchen: this plantain is not related to the banana-like fruit called plantain, a distinction that source makes explicitly.

lookalikes.name: common foxglove
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: THIS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS RECORD EXISTS. A first-year foxglove has no flower spike, forms a flat rosette of large soft leaves, and grows on the same roadsides, disturbed ground and forest edges as plantain; Burke records foxglove chiefly west of the Cascades crest in Washington, which is here. Foxglove poisons the heart and there is no safe amount of it. THREE CHARACTERS YOU CAN CHECK, all from the Burke Herbarium's own descriptions of the two species. (1) VEINS. Burke gives plantain leaves as strongly 3- to several-nerved: several heavy ribs run the whole length of the blade side by side, and the University of Nevada Reno extension fact sheet independently gives three or more prominent veins. They stand proud enough to feel with a thumb and to see from the underside. Burke's foxglove description gives no such character; foxglove has a single midrib. (2) HAIR. Burke calls plantain MOSTLY GLABROUS, hairless, and specifically not woolly at the crown. Burke calls foxglove puberulent throughout, minutely hairy all over. Rub the leaf between finger and thumb: plantain is smooth and slightly rubbery, foxglove is fuzzy. (3) WHERE THE FLOWERS COME FROM. Burke says plantain's leaves are ALL BASAL and the flowers sit on a scape, a bare leafless stalk 5 to 25 cm long; the Nevada sheet says the same, a 5 to 15 inch LEAFLESS flowering stalk. Burke says foxglove has well-developed cauline leaves, that is, leaves growing all the way up a leafy stem. A leafy flowering stem is never plantain. THE RULE THAT ACTUALLY PROTECTS YOU is still the one in the foxglove record: harvest rosette leaves only from a plant you watched flower. Plantain flowers April to August on that bare spike, so mark your patch then.

lookalikes.name: narrowleaf plantain, also called buckhorn or ribwort plantain
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Plantago lanceolata, the other common plantain here, and the more abundant of the two in this state: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 296 Washington records for it, including 2 from Kitsap County, against 187 Washington records and 1 Kitsap record for broadleaf plantain. The University of Nevada Reno extension sheet separates the two by saying that broadleaf plantain can be told from buckhorn plantain by its WIDE, EGG-SHAPED LEAVES and LONG FLOWER SPIKE. That sheet gives no description of the narrowleaf plant's own leaves and none is invented here: the check is that the leaf you are holding is broad and egg-shaped, not that you have keyed out the other species. This is a harmless confusion and is listed as one, because no hazard is documented for either. It is here so that a reader following a recipe knows the word plantain covers more than one plant, and because the food use documented above was documented for Plantago major specifically and not for the genus.

lookalikes.name: comfrey
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Comfrey also produces large, broad, strongly veined basal leaves on tended and disturbed ground, and it carries a documented liver hazard, so this one is not harmless. Burke gives comfrey away twice over: it is COARSE AND STIFF-HAIRY where plantain is mostly glabrous, and its erect stems are WINGED FROM THE LEAF BASES, so the leaf continues down the stem as a raised flange instead of stopping. Plantain's flowering stalk is bare and carries a narrow dense spike of tiny flowers; comfrey's is leafy and carries nodding clusters of bell-shaped dull blue or yellowish white flowers about 1.5 cm long.

species.season: Perennial, present all year as a rosette. Burke gives flowering April to August in Washington. The University of Nevada Reno extension sheet says it blooms from late spring to summer and that plants regrow from the crown, which is why it survives mowing and trampling. Leaves are gathered young, so spring is the useful window, and spring is also when a first-year foxglove rosette is at its most anonymous.
species.habitat: Trampled and compacted ground. Burke records it from both sides of the Cascades crest in Washington, on roadsides, fields and other disturbed open areas. The Nevada extension sheet adds lawns, gardens, vacant lots and cultivated fields, and notes it tolerates compacted and wet sites. North Carolina State Extension notes it does particularly well in compacted or disturbed soils and survives repeated trampling, and records that it was called white man's footprint because it appeared and thrived in disturbed ground around European settlements. LOCAL EVIDENCE: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 187 Washington specimen records, including one from Kitsap County.
species.uses: Food, as a cooked or raw green when young, per North Carolina State Extension. That source also records that the seeds are eaten by birds and included in birdseed mixes, that the plant attracts pollinators and is wind-pollinated, and that its roots break up hardpan soil and help stop erosion. The University of Nevada Reno sheet treats the same plant as a lawn and garden weed and gives control methods, which is the other half of the picture: it is a salad green or a turf pest depending on who is looking at it.

species.common_name: Common comfrey, also called knitbone, boneset, bruisewort or Saracen's root
species.form: coarse, stiff-hairy perennial herb from a taproot
species.protected: No protection and no Washington restriction found. It is not named in any of the three state noxious weed classes, WAC 16-750-005, 16-750-011 or 16-750-015, all three of which were read for this record. USDA PLANTS records it as introduced in the lower 48 and Canada. A different kind of listing does apply: FDA carries Comfrey in its Information on Select Dietary Supplement Ingredients and Other Substances, with the plain statement that comfrey is a source of pyrrolizidine alkaloids, covering Symphytum officinale (common comfrey), S. asperum (prickly comfrey) and S. x uplandicum (Russian comfrey), and referencing an FDA safety communication of July 2001. That 2001 communication itself could NOT be opened for this record, because the only surviving copy is in a web archive that would not serve the page, so nothing is quoted from it here and nobody should assume what it says.
species.edible_detail: DO NOT EAT IT AND DO NOT DRINK IT. This is a hard no with a documented mechanism behind it, not a precaution. The NIH LiverTox database states that comfrey contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids which are toxic and capable of causing sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (previously called veno-occlusive disease) and severe liver injury, that several cases of acute liver injury due to ORAL comfrey have been published, and that oral comfrey has been banned or restricted in most countries. North Carolina State Extension puts it as bluntly: it is no longer deemed as safe for consumption. Comfrey tea, comfrey leaf in a salad, comfrey root powder and comfrey capsules are all the oral route. Topical use is a separate question that this record does not answer either way: LiverTox notes that topical ointments, creams and liniments are available and that human studies show comfrey creams have mild analgesic effects and decrease muscle and joint pain, and North Carolina State Extension calls the plant considered possibly safe to use externally. Neither statement is a clearance from this record, and broken skin is not external.
species.toxic: REAL, WELL DOCUMENTED AND SLOW. The toxins are pyrrolizidine alkaloids; NIH LiverTox names symphytine, echimidine, symglandine, lycopsamine and intermedine. Cytochrome P450 enzymes convert them into highly reactive pyrrole metabolites with alkylating properties that damage the endothelial cells lining the liver's small vessels, producing sinusoidal obstruction. THE COURSE, per LiverTox: injury usually arises within 1 to 2 months of starting a comfrey product, either an extract in tablet form or large amounts of comfrey tea. It begins with right upper quadrant pain, nausea and WEIGHT GAIN FROM FLUID RETENTION, followed by jaundice. Serum aminotransferase levels are usually only mildly elevated, which is part of why this is missed. It can be severe and lead rapidly to acute liver failure, but more commonly it presents insidiously as weight gain, ascites, weakness and minimal enzyme elevation. LiverTox gives comfrey a likelihood score of C, a probable cause of clinically apparent liver injury when taken orally; records that it has caused similar liver injury in laboratory animals and has been linked to liver cancer; records that the amount of pyrrolizidine alkaloid varies by the part of the plant used, its age and the time of harvesting; and records that INFANTS APPEAR PARTICULARLY SUSCEPTIBLE to pyrrolizidine alkaloid injury. North Carolina State Extension rates poison severity as medium, names the toxic principle as pyrrolizidine alkaloids, says ingestion can lead to liver damage, lung damage and cancer, and lists the poisonous parts as bark, flowers, fruits, leaves and roots, which is the whole plant. Two things follow from all of that. No source opened here states a safe oral dose. And because the damage accumulates while the early signs are weight gain and tiredness, a person can do real harm over a season of daily tea without ever feeling poisoned.

lookalikes.name: common foxglove
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: THIS IS THE PAIRING THAT PUT THIS RECORD IN THE DATASET. A comfrey patch is a place where somebody is already in the habit of pulling large hairy leaves by the armful, and a first-year foxglove is a large hairy leaf. Foxglove acts directly on the heart muscle and has no safe amount. Burke records both plants as occurring chiefly west of the Cascades crest in Washington, so both are here. THE CHARACTER THAT SEPARATES THEM, from Burke's own descriptions: comfrey's erect stems are WINGED FROM THE LEAF BASES. The leaf blade runs down the stem as a raised flange on each side rather than ending at a stalk, so a comfrey stem is ridged to the touch and shows two green fins below each leaf. Burke's foxglove description contains no such feature; foxglove's cauline leaves are ordinary alternate leaves that get smaller upward. Second character: Burke gives comfrey basal leaves as ovate or lance-ovate, 15 to 30 cm long and 7 to 12 cm wide, on a coarse stiff-hairy plant, against foxglove leaves that are oblong-ovate with small rounded teeth on a plant that is merely puberulent. THE LIMIT OF THAT CHARACTER, stated plainly: a first-year comfrey and a first-year foxglove are both just basal leaves with no stem to inspect, and that is exactly when the winged-stem test is unavailable. So the rule from the foxglove record stands unchanged here. Cut comfrey only from a clump you have watched flower and whose position you know. Never cut it from a volunteer that appeared on disturbed ground this year.

lookalikes.name: prickly comfrey and Russian comfrey
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Symphytum asperum and Symphytum x uplandicum. This entry exists to stop a reader concluding that a different comfrey is a safer comfrey. FDA's dietary supplement ingredient entry names all three, S. officinale, S. asperum and S. x uplandicum, on one line as sources of pyrrolizidine alkaloids, so the hazard described above is not confined to the species this record is named for. The Washington herbarium picture from the Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria: 45 records for S. officinale, 4 for S. asperum (Clallam and Stevens counties), and 0 for S. x uplandicum, though the hybrid is the comfrey most often deliberately planted and a zero in a herbarium search means only that nobody pressed and filed one, not that it is absent. Do not try to key these apart in order to make a safety decision; the decision is the same for all of them.

lookalikes.name: common mullein
lookalikes.how_to_tell_them_apart: Both are big, hairy, coarse-leaved plants of disturbed ground. No source opened for this record names the pairing as a documented confusion, so it is offered as a character contrast and not as a warning. Burke describes mullein as covered over the WHOLE PLANT in white-woolly BRANCHED hairs, felt-textured and grey-green, with basal leaves whose margin is nearly entire; comfrey is stiff-hairy and plain green with the winged stem described above. Mixing these two up is not documented to harm anyone. It is listed because if you cannot separate them, you are also not in a position to rule out foxglove, and that is the one that matters.

species.season: Perennial. Burke gives flowering May to August in Washington. North Carolina State Extension notes that it spreads easily and will sprout from any root pieces left behind after removal, so a comfrey patch, once established, is a fixture. That is worth knowing, because a known and permanent clump is the only kind you can safely cut from.
species.habitat: Escaped from cultivation. Burke records it chiefly west of the Cascades crest in Washington, escaped from cultivation and often found in disturbed areas, which in practice means homestead edges, old garden ground and back lanes rather than forest. LOCAL EVIDENCE: a Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria search returned 45 Washington specimen records, none from Kitsap County but 10 from Pierce, 7 from Skagit, 4 each from Whatcom and Clallam, 3 from King, and one from Jefferson County directly across Hood Canal. Treat it as present around Silverdale in gardens and on old cultivated ground. The Kitsap gap is a collecting gap rather than evidence of absence; a garden plant is under-collected by definition.
species.uses: Garden and soil use, not food. North Carolina State Extension records that the foliage is a good addition to a compost pile, that the plant can be pruned several times a year and is often used as compost for food crops, and that a liquid fertilizer is made by soaking the leaves in water for at least a week, the potassium being valued for growing tomatoes. That is the use this record supports. The same source records the long history of use as a medicinal herb for topical and internal injuries, which is where the names knitbone and bruisewort come from, and then states that it is no longer deemed as safe for consumption. The NIH LiverTox chapter records the same history and the same conclusion, adding that constituents including allantoin, rosmarinic acid, triterpene saponins, silicic acid and tannins are believed to be the basis of its anti-inflammatory and wound-healing activity. A history of use is not a recommendation.
